title: Embedding Inference Attack
summary: Embedding models are essential components of modern Information Retrieval (IR) systems, yet they are typically hidden behind APIs. Recent works have shown that dense IR system can lead to security vulnerabilities such as embedding inversion attacks. However, such attacks usually require that the attacker knows the embedding model for the attack to be applicable. In this paper, we study IR systems under a black-box setting in which the adversary observes only the unordered set of retrieved documents, without ranking or similarity scores. We demonstrate that in such contexts, tailored queries allow an adversary to identify which embedding model is in use from a set of known model candidate, which we coin as an embedding inference attack (EIA). We also show that certain queries remain discriminative even when the system includes a reranker as a potential defense mechanism. We further validate our method on a real Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system, in which the tailored queries bypass the LLM's tendency to reject inputs it does not recognize as well-formed questions. Finally, we propose and evaluate other mitigation strategies such as similarity thresholds.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Embedding Inference Attack (EIA), a black-box method that identifies which embedding model powers an IR system by observing only the unordered set of retrieved documents, without access to rankings or scores. The attack remains effective against rerankers and LLM-based input filters, and the authors evaluate mitigation strategies like similarity thresholds.
AI.motivation: Embedding models in IR systems are typically hidden behind APIs and treated as black boxes, yet prior inversion attacks assume model knowledge. The authors aim to expose a new vulnerability: an adversary can fingerprint the underlying embedding model from retrieval outputs alone, challenging the security-through-obscurity assumption.
AI.method: The authors design tailored queries that produce discriminative retrieval patterns across candidate embedding models. By observing only the unordered set of retrieved documents from a black-box IR system, the adversary matches the output pattern to a known model fingerprint. The attack is tested under defense mechanisms including rerankers, LLM-based input rejection (in a RAG system), and similarity thresholds.
AI.result: The EIA successfully identifies the embedding model in black-box settings using only unordered retrieved document sets. Tailored queries remain discriminative even with rerankers in place and can bypass an LLM's tendency to reject non-well-formed inputs in a real RAG system. Proposed mitigations like similarity thresholds are evaluated for their effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Black-box embedding model identification is feasible via inference attacks on retrieval outputs, exposing a new security vulnerability in IR systems. Current defenses such as rerankers and LLM-based filters are insufficient, and while similarity thresholds offer some mitigation, further research into robust countermeasures is needed.

title: Cognitive Firewall: A Proactive, Zero-Trust, Multi-Gate Framework for LLM Safety
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can be induced to produce harmful content through multi turn strategies in which no single user message appears clearly unsafe. Existing runtime safeguards commonly evaluate prompts or responses as isolated messages, which limits their ability to recover ac-cumulated intent, verify asserted authority, or detect harmful objectives decomposed across a dialogue. This paper presents the Cognitive Firewall, a proactive runtime oversight framework that interposes an independent oversight model between a user and a protected target mod l. The framework decomposes safety assessment into four categorical gates: an intent gate that identi-fies the operational objective of a request, a zero trust context gate that treats claimed roles and permissions as unverified evidence, a consistency gate that detects escalation and decomposition across turns, and an output risk gate that inspects candidate responses before release. Gate decisions are combined through escalation rather than score averaging, allowing any confident danger signal to block an interaction while preserving an auditable rationale. Experiments on four jailbreak benchmarks and a benign safety test set show that the Cognitive Firewall substantially reduces attack success across single turn, multi turn, authority based, and human crafted attacks. It lowers attack success to 2 percent or below on three attack sets and to 14 percent on the most difficult human crafted set, while maintaining an 8 percent over refusal rate. These results indicate that decomposed, conversation level oversight can improve proactive containment and auditability for LLM safety.

AI.tldr: The Cognitive Firewall is a runtime safety framework that inserts an independent oversight model between users and LLMs, decomposing safety assessment into four categorical gates (intent, zero-trust context, consistency, and output risk) that operate across multi-turn dialogues. Using escalation-based decision fusion rather than score averaging, it reduces attack success rates to ≤2% on three benchmarks and 14% on the hardest human-crafted set, with an 8% over-refusal rate.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM safeguards evaluate prompts or responses as isolated messages, making them vulnerable to multi-turn jailbreak strategies where harmful intent is decomposed across turns with no single message appearing clearly unsafe. They also fail to verify asserted authority or recover accumulated dialogue intent.
AI.method: The Cognitive Firewall interposes an independent oversight model between user and target LLM. It implements four categorical safety gates: (1) intent gate — identifies operational objectives of requests; (2) zero-trust context gate — treats claimed roles/permissions as unverified evidence; (3) consistency gate — detects escalation and harmful decomposition across turns; (4) output risk gate — inspects candidate responses before release. Gate decisions are combined via escalation (any confident danger signal blocks the interaction) rather than score averaging, preserving auditable rationales.
AI.result: On four jailbreak benchmarks and a benign safety test set, the Cognitive Firewall reduced attack success to ≤2% on three attack sets and 14% on the hardest human-crafted set, with an 8% over-refusal rate.
AI.conclusion: Decomposed, conversation-level oversight via the Cognitive Firewall significantly improves proactive containment and auditability for LLM safety compared to isolated-message evaluation approaches.

title: Generative AI and Federated Learning for Intrusion Detection Systems: A Survey
summary: Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) are essential for monitoring network traffic and identifying malicious activities in modern cyber-physical, Internet of Things (IoT), enterprise, and distributed network environments. However, developing reliable IDS models remains challenging because attack behaviors evolve over time, realistic datasets are difficult to obtain, traffic records may be incomplete, attack classes are often imbalanced, and privacy constraints limit centralized data collection. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) and Federated Learning (FL) provide new opportunities to address these limitations. Generative models can support anomaly detection, synthetic traffic generation, data augmentation, data imputation, adversarial traffic generation, and IDS alert explanation. FL enables distributed IDS training without directly sharing local network traffic, making it suitable for privacy-sensitive and geographically distributed environments. This survey provides a structured review of generative AI and FL techniques for IDS. We first summarize representative IDS research directions, including adversarial machine learning, anomaly-based detection, IoT-oriented IDS, explainable IDS, and benchmark datasets. We then categorize generative AI applications in IDS according to model families and task objectives, covering autoencoder-based models, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), diffusion models, and Large Language Models (LLMs). Finally, we review emerging studies that integrate generative AI with FL-based IDS and discuss open challenges, including synthetic data quality, realistic traffic generation, dual-use adversarial risks, non-IID client distributions, communication-efficient model sharing, federated IDS benchmarking, and domain-specific LLMs for network security.

AI.tldr: A structured survey reviewing the integration of generative AI (autoencoders, GANs, diffusion models, LLMs) and Federated Learning for Intrusion Detection Systems, addressing challenges like evolving attacks, data scarcity, class imbalance, and privacy constraints.
AI.motivation: Developing reliable IDS models is hindered by evolving attack behaviors, scarce realistic datasets, incomplete traffic records, imbalanced attack classes, and privacy constraints limiting centralized data collection. Generative AI and FL offer promising solutions to these longstanding limitations.
AI.method: The paper conducts a structured literature survey across three dimensions: (1) representative IDS research directions (adversarial ML, anomaly detection, IoT-IDS, XAI, benchmarks); (2) generative AI applications categorized by model families (autoencoders, GANs, diffusion models, LLMs) and task objectives (synthetic traffic generation, data augmentation, imputation, adversarial generation, alert explanation); and (3) FL-based IDS integrating generative techniques, with analysis of open challenges.
AI.result: The survey identifies that generative models serve six key IDS functions: anomaly detection, synthetic traffic generation, data augmentation, data imputation, adversarial traffic generation, and alert explanation. FL enables privacy-preserving distributed IDS training. Key open challenges include synthetic data quality assurance, realistic traffic generation, dual-use adversarial risks, non-IID client distributions, communication efficiency, federated benchmarking, and domain-specific LLMs for network security.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI and FL represent transformative technologies for next-generation IDS, but significant research gaps remain in ensuring synthetic data fidelity, mitigating dual-use risks, handling heterogeneous client data, and adapting LLMs to network security domains.

title: An alternative approach towards attacks against fully-split PLWE instances
summary: In the present work we address some key questions regarding the generalization of root-based attacks presented in a recent work by the authors. In particular, we analyze potential root-based attacks extensions via the construction of explicit isomorphisms from vulnerable instances, and provide a formal proof that this approach will not yield any new vulnerabilities under a fully-split setting. To do so, we first construct an explicit isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings and polynomial rings where previous attacks apply and show that the application of such an isomorphism will always distort the samples in a way that the resulting samples cannot be used to distinguish. Then, we prove that any isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings must be of the form of the constructed isomorphism.

AI.tldr: This paper formally analyzes whether root-based attacks on lattice problems can be generalized by mapping vulnerable instances to fully-split settings via isomorphisms. The authors prove that all isomorphisms between fully-split polynomial rings take a specific form, and demonstrate that applying such isomorphisms always distorts samples in a way that prevents distinguishing — thus no new vulnerabilities arise from this approach.
AI.motivation: The work is motivated by a prior paper by the same authors introducing root-based attacks on certain lattice-based cryptographic constructions. The key question is whether these attacks can be generalized or extended by constructing explicit isomorphisms from known vulnerable instances to other settings, particularly the fully-split case. Understanding the limits of such generalization is crucial for assessing the broader security implications of root-based attacks.
AI.method: The authors employ a two-part formal approach: (1) They explicitly construct an isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings and polynomial rings where prior root-based attacks are known to apply. They then analyze how this isomorphism affects the statistical properties of samples, showing that the transformed samples lose their distinguishing capability. (2) They prove a structural characterization theorem, demonstrating that any isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings must necessarily take the exact form of their constructed isomorphism.
AI.result: The principal results are twofold: first, the application of the constructed isomorphism always distorts samples such that the resulting samples cannot be used as a distinguisher, meaning no new vulnerable instances are generated. Second, the authors prove that all isomorphisms between fully-split polynomial rings are of the same form as their construction, implying there is no alternative isomorphism that could circumvent the distortion and yield a successful attack generalization.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that root-based attacks cannot be generalized to the fully-split setting via isomorphism-based extensions. The approach of mapping vulnerable instances through isomorphisms is formally shown to be incapable of producing new vulnerabilities, thereby establishing a fundamental limitation on the scope of root-based attacks. This provides a security boundary for constructions relying on fully-split polynomial rings.

title: ExPerT: Personalizing LLM Responses to Users' Domain Expertise via Query-Wise Semantic and Keystroke Behavioral Cues
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by end users, yet existing personalization methods relying on static profiles or text-only signals fail to capture query-specific expertise variation. We present ExPerT, a query-wise personalization framework that adapts LLM responses to users' query domain expertise by combining semantic and behavioral cues. ExPerT consists of two key components: (i) a semantic-behavioral expertise inference module that jointly interprets query text and keystroke dynamics via in-context LLM prompting, and (ii) an expertise-conditioned response generation that adapts the level of detail, terminology, and conceptual complexity. Our user study with 40 participants and 1270 queries demonstrated that ExPerT reduced expertise inference error by 65.7% compared to the strongest baseline (MAE = 0.398 vs. 1.162) and improved response satisfaction by 17.52% (from 3.71 to 4.36) on a 5-point Likert scale.

AI.tldr: ExPerT is a query-wise personalization framework that adapts LLM responses to a user's domain expertise by combining semantic (query text) and behavioral (keystroke dynamics) cues, achieving 65.7% lower expertise inference error and 17.52% higher response satisfaction compared to baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM personalization methods rely on static profiles or text-only signals, failing to capture how a user's expertise varies on a per-query basis. This motivates a dynamic, query-specific approach that leverages richer signals.
AI.method: The framework, ExPerT, has two components: (1) a semantic-behavioral expertise inference module that uses in-context LLM prompting to jointly interpret query text and keystroke dynamics, and (2) an expertise-conditioned response generation module that adapts detail level, terminology, and conceptual complexity accordingly. Evaluated via a user study with 40 participants and 1,270 queries.
AI.result: ExPerT reduced expertise inference error by 65.7% over the strongest baseline (MAE: 0.398 vs. 1.162) and improved response satisfaction by 17.52% on a 5-point Likert scale (from 3.71 to 4.36).
AI.conclusion: Integrating both semantic and behavioral signals enables substantially more accurate query-level expertise estimation and measurably better personalized LLM responses than profile-based or text-only approaches.

title: Cache Merging as a Convergent Replicated State for Multi-Agent Latent Reasoning
summary: Multi-agent latent reasoning composes agents' KV-caches into one context for a final agent. Prior work (Agent Primitives) does this by concatenating caches along the sequence axis with RoPE re-encoding, which we call BagMerge. BagMerge is non-commutative, and the best input ordering is unpredictable, shifting with the regime, the latent-step budget, and the model scale. We make this exchange a convergent replicated state. First, CanonicalMerge fixes the layout by content: ordering caches by mean K-norm at a middle layer renders the merged cache byte-identical under any input permutation, verified algorithmically (arity N<=5) and bit-for-bit on real Qwen3-1.7B and 4B state. Second, we separate the replicated state from decode-time layout: the state is a set of content-addressed latent fragments whose merge is set union, a state-based CvRDT (commutative, associative, idempotent, absorbing), and CanonicalMerge is its deterministic render. Because the render is byte-equivalent, every N=2 accuracy number carries over unchanged and re-delivered duplicates are absorbed rather than re-concatenated. On a partitioned-reasoning benchmark, CanonicalMerge matches the best BagMerge ordering in every regime-by-budget-by-ordering cell without knowing which order is best, trading a small, statistically insignificant accuracy margin for an unconditional structural guarantee. The behaviour transfers to real multi-document QA (HotpotQA), while the closest training-free output-fusion baseline (PackLLM) loses by 45 points at matched budget, placing cache-level merging in a regime distinct from output-level fusion. Finally, at k>2 the approach transports and colocates latent traces but does not by itself compose them, which we characterize to motivate future work.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CanonicalMerge, a method for merging KV-caches from multiple agents in multi-agent latent reasoning that is permutation-invariant. Unlike prior work (BagMerge) which concatenates caches sequence-wise using RoPE re-encoding — yielding non-commutative, ordering-dependent results — CanonicalMerge orders caches by mean K-norm at a middle layer, producing byte-identical merged caches regardless of input order. This transforms the merge into a convergent replicated data type (CvRDT) with set-union semantics (commutative, associative, idempotent, absorbing). The method matches BagMerge's best ordering accuracy across regimes without knowing the optimal order, transfers to real multi-document QA, and substantially outperforms output-level fusion baselines.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent latent reasoning systems merge agents' KV-caches for a final agent, but existing approaches (BagMerge) concatenate along the sequence axis with RoPE re-encoding, making the merge non-commutative. The best input ordering is unpredictable, varying with the regime, latent-step budget, and model scale. This motivated the need for a permutation-invariant merge that delivers consistent, predictable results.
AI.method: Two key contributions: (1) **CanonicalMerge**: orders caches by mean K-norm computed at a middle layer, rendering the merged cache byte-identical under any input permutation (verified for arity N≤5, bit-for-bit on Qwen3-1.7B and 4B). (2) **CvRDT formulation**: the replicated state is a set of content-addressed latent fragments whose merge is set union — satisfying commutativity, associativity, idempotence, and absorption properties. CanonicalMerge serves as the deterministic render of this state-based CvRDT.
AI.result: On a partitioned-reasoning benchmark, CanonicalMerge matches the best BagMerge ordering in every regime-by-budget-by-ordering cell with a small, statistically insignificant accuracy margin. On HotpotQA (multi-document QA), it transfers successfully, while the training-free output-fusion baseline PackLLM loses by 45 points at matched budget. The method absorbs re-delivered duplicates rather than re-concatenating them.
AI.conclusion: Cache-level merging occupies a distinct regime from output-level fusion, with substantial performance advantages. CanonicalMerge provides unconditional structural guarantees (permutation invariance) at negligible accuracy cost. For k>2 agents, the approach transports and colocates latent traces but does not independently compose them — this limitation is characterized to motivate future work on multi-agent latent composition.

title: Benchmarking Code Improvement with Progressive, Adaptive, and Interactive Feedback
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on code generation and program repair using binary functional correctness: a generated program or patch either passes or fails a test suite. This protocol is simple but coarse, as it ignores partial progress, feedback use, regressions, and the refinement trajectory through which models often improve code. We introduce PAIR-Bench, a progressive and adaptive benchmark for evaluating code improvement: transforming an incorrect or incomplete program into a more correct one through feedback-guided refinement. PAIR-Bench uses progressive hinting, a structured feedback protocol with two controls. Failure-region control determines what the feedback targets by grouping hidden failing tests into failure scenarios, while hint-depth control determines how much repair-relevant information is revealed, from coarse symptoms to implementation-level guidance. This design enables PAIR-Bench to measure whether a model repairs targeted failures, generalizes beyond the hint, preserves already-correct behavior, and how much assistance it requires. By evaluating repair trajectories progressive metrics rather than only final pass/fail outcomes, PAIR-Bench provides a finer-grained assessment of LLM code-improvement capability.

AI.tldr: PAIR-Bench is a new benchmark that evaluates how well LLMs iteratively improve incorrect code using structured, progressive feedback, offering finer-grained metrics beyond binary pass/fail.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM code evaluation relies on binary functional correctness (pass/fail), which is too coarse and ignores partial progress, feedback utilization, regression avoidance, and the iterative refinement process central to real-world code improvement.
AI.method: PAIR-Bench introduces progressive hinting with two control dimensions: failure-region control (grouping hidden failing tests into targeted scenarios) and hint-depth control (escalating from coarse symptoms to implementation-level guidance). It evaluates repair trajectories using progressive metrics that measure targeted failure repair, generalization beyond hints, preservation of correct behavior, and amount of assistance required.
AI.result: The benchmark enables measurement of whether models repair targeted failures, generalize beyond provided hints, avoid regressions on already-correct behavior, and quantifies the level of assistance needed.
AI.conclusion: PAIR-Bench provides a finer-grained, more informative assessment of LLM code-improvement capability by tracking the full refinement trajectory rather than relying solely on final pass/fail outcomes.

title: STRUCTSURVEY: Structured Agentic Retrieval for Automated Survey Paper Generation
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, appendices, SurgeLLM, RAG4Reports, ACL
summary: The rapid growth of scientific publications makes it increasingly difficult to track and synthesize research progress. While Large Language Models (LLMs) can support automated survey generation, existing methods retrieve unstructured data and require models to infer conceptual, methodological, and taxonomic relations from raw text at generation time. We introduce STRUCTSURVEY, a hierarchical multi-agent framework that shifts structural reasoning from generation to retrieval by dynamically constructing graph-based representations of entities, relations, and topical taxonomies. We evaluate STRUCTSURVEY on a new reference-grounded benchmark of ACL survey papers for reproducible long-form scientific summarization. Compared with embedding-only retrieval baselines, STRUCTSURVEY improves ROUGE-1 recall by +2.9 and ROUGE-2 recall by +1.0 on average, without reducing precision. It also improves LLM-as-a-Judge ratings for logical structure, depth, and synthesis, showing that explicit structural retrieval yields surveys closer to human-written organization and reasoning.

AI.tldr: STRUCTSURVEY is a hierarchical multi-agent framework that shifts structural reasoning from generation-time to retrieval-time by building graph-based representations of entities, relations, and taxonomies, improving automated survey generation quality over embedding-only baselines.
AI.motivation: The explosion of scientific publications makes manual literature surveys difficult. Existing LLM-based survey generation methods retrieve unstructured text and force models to infer conceptual and taxonomic relations during generation, which is suboptimal. The authors argue that structural reasoning should be handled at retrieval time rather than at generation time.
AI.method: STRUCTSURVEY is a hierarchical multi-agent framework that dynamically constructs graph-based representations capturing entities (papers, concepts), relations (citations, methodological links), and topical taxonomies during retrieval. This structured graph is then used to guide LLM-based survey generation, offloading structural reasoning from the generation stage.
AI.result: Evaluated on a new reference-grounded benchmark of ACL survey papers, STRUCTSURVEY improves ROUGE-1 recall by +2.9 and ROUGE-2 recall by +1.0 on average over embedding-only retrieval baselines, without reducing precision. LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations show superior logical structure, depth, and synthesis ratings.
AI.conclusion: Explicit structural retrieval, via graph-based entity-relation-taxonomy representations, produces surveys that more closely resemble human-written organization and reasoning compared to retrieval approaches that defer all structural reasoning to generation time.

title: Multilayer Q-Matrix-Embedded Neural Network for Cognitive Diagnosis (M-QCDNet): Structure-Aware Deep Learning Architecture for Psychometric Interpretability
summary: The research proposes a multilayer Q-matrix-embedded neural network for cognitive diagnosis (M-QCDNet), which integrates the structural interpretability of cognitive diagnostic models (CDMs) with the deep learning neural network (NN). M-QCDNet structures the item-skill relationship using the Q-matrix as a structural prior, ensuring latent mastery profiles remain interpretable and consistent with cognitive theory, followed by the proposed loss function with an L2 penalty to penalize skills not aligned with the Q-matrix and to balance predictive performance and structural alignment. Corresponding evaluation matrices, the interpretable alignment-based metrics that quantify the degree to which predicted skill activations correspond to item-level skills, were further developed. M-QCDNet offers practical benefits for classroom practice, enabling early detection of learning difficulties and supporting mastery-based interventions. By embedding diagnostic validity into model design, M-QCDNet bridges psychometric transparency and neural flexibility, advancing interpretable, fair, and actionable AI for cognitive diagnostics.

AI.tldr: M-QCDNet is a neural network for cognitive diagnosis that embeds the Q-matrix (mapping items to skills) as a structural prior, uses an L2-penalized loss to enforce alignment with cognitive theory, and introduces interpretable alignment-based evaluation metrics, bridging psychometric transparency with deep learning flexibility.
AI.motivation: Traditional cognitive diagnostic models (CDMs) offer strong structural interpretability via the Q-matrix but lack the representational power of deep neural networks. Conversely, neural networks for cognitive diagnosis often sacrifice psychometric transparency and theoretical alignment. M-QCDNet aims to unify both strengths—preserving the Q-matrix's interpretable item-skill structure while leveraging neural flexibility for improved predictive performance.
AI.method: M-QCDNet structures the item-skill relationship using the Q-matrix as a structural prior within a multilayer neural network, ensuring latent mastery profiles remain interpretable. A custom loss function incorporating an L2 penalty penalizes skills not aligned with the Q-matrix, balancing predictive accuracy with structural fidelity. Novel interpretable alignment-based metrics are developed to quantify how well predicted skill activations correspond to item-level skills defined in the Q-matrix.
AI.result: The paper proposes evaluation matrices (interpretable alignment-based metrics) that quantify the correspondence between predicted skill activations and Q-matrix-defined item-level skills. The framework demonstrates practical utility for classroom settings, including early detection of learning difficulties and support for mastery-based interventions.
AI.conclusion: M-QCDNet successfully bridges psychometric transparency and neural flexibility by embedding diagnostic validity directly into model design. This advances the development of interpretable, fair, and actionable AI systems for cognitive diagnostics, with direct practical benefits for educational interventions.

title: TokenScope: Token-Level Explainability and Interpretability for Code-Oriented Tasks in Large Language Models
summary: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) make token-level decisions during code generation remains a major challenge for both researchers and practitioners. While recent tools provide insights into model internals or generation outcomes, they often lack decoding-time signals, fine-grained uncertainty measures, and interactive mechanisms for exploring alternative generation paths. We present TokenScope, an interactive interpretability and analysis tool for decoder-based LLMs that exposes token-level metrics, attention patterns, and structural information during generation. TokenScope supports interactive token replacement, counterfactual branching, and code-aware aggregation via abstract syntax trees. By unifying decoding-time signals with structural program analysis, TokenScope enables systematic investigation of LLM behaviour during code generation.

AI.tldr: TokenScope is an interactive tool for analyzing LLM code generation at the token level, combining decoding-time signals (metrics, attention patterns), counterfactual branching, and AST-based structural analysis to enable systematic investigation of model behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM interpretability tools lack three critical capabilities during code generation: (1) decoding-time signals for real-time inspection, (2) fine-grained uncertainty measures at the token level, and (3) interactive mechanisms for exploring alternative generation paths. This gap hinders systematic understanding of how LLMs make token-level decisions during code synthesis.
AI.method: TokenScope operates on decoder-based LLMs and integrates multiple analysis dimensions: exposing token-level metrics and attention patterns during generation, enabling interactive token replacement and counterfactual branching for exploring alternative decoding paths, and performing code-aware aggregation via abstract syntax trees (ASTs) to connect token-level signals with structural program properties.
AI.result: TokenScope unifies decoding-time interpretability signals with structural program analysis, providing a comprehensive framework for investigating LLM code generation behavior. (The abstract does not report quantitative experimental results.)
AI.conclusion: By bridging real-time decoding signals with program structure analysis, TokenScope fills a critical gap in LLM interpretability tooling for code generation, enabling researchers and practitioners to systematically probe and understand model decision-making at the token level.

title: PACE: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Plausible and Actionable Counterfactual Explanations
summary: Counterfactual explanations explain machine learning predictions by identifying minimal input changes that would alter a model's decision. Although many existing methods successfully generate prediction-changing alternatives, they often produce unrealistic or infeasible recommendations due to a lack of explicit mechanisms for incorporating domain knowledge and intervention constraints. Neuro-symbolic AI offers a promising direction by combining data-driven predictive models with symbolic reasoning capable of representing human-understandable rules and feasible actions. This paper presents PACE, a modular neuro-symbolic framework for generating feasibility-aware counterfactual explanations. The framework separates prediction and reasoning into two components: a neural predictive model for classification and a symbolic reasoning layer that enforces domain-specific constraints during counterfactual generation. By explicitly modeling feasible interventions, the framework produces explanations consistent with domain knowledge while remaining interpretable and actionable. The approach is model-agnostic and adaptable to domains requiring realistic decision support. A case study is conducted on the Adult Income dataset, combining a multilayer perceptron classifier with Answer Set Programming (ASP) rules encoding feasible modifications to education, occupation, and working hours while preserving immutable attributes. Results highlight the trade-off between counterfactual validity and plausibility and show that symbolic constraints yield explanations that better satisfy domain-specific feasibility requirements, illustrating the potential of neuro-symbolic methods for transparent, feasibility-aware counterfactual explanation in explainable AI.

AI.tldr: PACE is a modular neuro-symbolic framework that generates counterfactual explanations constrained by domain knowledge encoded as symbolic rules (ASP), ensuring feasibility and actionability. Evaluated on the Adult Income dataset, it demonstrates a trade-off between validity and plausibility.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual explanation methods produce prediction-changing alternatives but often lack mechanisms to incorporate domain knowledge and intervention constraints, yielding unrealistic or infeasible recommendations. There is a need for explanations that are both actionable and consistent with real-world feasibility.
AI.method: PACE separates prediction and reasoning into two modular components: (1) a neural predictive model (MLP classifier) for classification, and (2) a symbolic reasoning layer using Answer Set Programming (ASP) to encode domain-specific constraints (e.g., feasible modifications to education, occupation, working hours) and preserve immutable attributes during counterfactual generation. The approach is model-agnostic.
AI.result: On the Adult Income dataset, PACE demonstrates a clear trade-off between counterfactual validity and plausibility. Symbolic constraints consistently yield explanations that better satisfy domain-specific feasibility requirements compared to unconstrained methods.
AI.conclusion: Neuro-symbolic integration is a promising direction for generating transparent, feasibility-aware counterfactual explanations. PACE illustrates that explicitly encoding domain knowledge as symbolic rules produces more realistic and actionable explanations for explainable AI applications.

title: Chameleon: Recovering Cyber-Physical Systems from Memory Corruption Attacks via ML Surrogates
summary:
Cyber-physical systems (CPSs) are increasingly deployed in every aspect of our lives and can be compromised through memory corruption vulnerabilities, allowing attackers to hijack the control flow and take over the system. Existing techniques mostly focus on detecting such attacks but respond by terminating or halting execution upon attack detection, which is not acceptable in CPSs used in safety-critical tasks, as interrupted tasks can have catastrophic consequences. Other techniques replace compromised CPS components with simplified defaults that degrade system behavior, or reboot the system upon attack detection.
  We propose Chameleon, a novel framework for automatically recovering CPSs from memory corruption attacks using machine learning (ML)-based surrogates trained at compartment granularity that nearly replicate their original compartments' behavior but do not have the same memory corruption vulnerabilities. Upon attack detection, Chameleon replaces the compromised compartment with its trained surrogate. We implemented Chameleon using the LLVM compiler and evaluated its efficiency and effectiveness on seven different robotic vehicles (RVs), including simulated and real ones. We found that Chameleon can generate surrogates that closely approximate the original compartments (with an average R$^2$=0.96), successfully recover the system despite real-world memory corruption attacks unlike prior approaches, and complete their tasks while incurring low performance and memory overhead.

AI.tldr: Chameleon is a framework that uses ML-based surrogate models to automatically recover cyber-physical systems from memory corruption attacks by replacing compromised software compartments at runtime, enabling continued safe operation without termination or degradation.
AI.motivation: Existing memory corruption defenses either terminate/halt CPS execution upon attack detection (unacceptable for safety-critical systems) or degrade to simplified defaults/reboot. Neither approach preserves full system functionality during and after an attack.
AI.method: Chameleon trains machine learning surrogate models at the granularity of individual software compartments. These surrogates replicate the compartment's behavior but lack the original's memory corruption vulnerabilities. Upon attack detection, the compromised compartment is seamlessly replaced with its pre-trained surrogate. Implementation uses the LLVM compiler infrastructure and is evaluated on seven robotic vehicles (simulated and real).
AI.result: Surrogates closely approximate original compartments with an average R² of 0.96. Chameleon successfully recovers systems from real-world memory corruption attacks where prior approaches fail, and completes tasks with low performance and memory overhead.
AI.conclusion: ML-based compartment surrogates offer a viable, low-overhead approach for graceful recovery of safety-critical CPSs under memory corruption attacks, avoiding the catastrophic consequences of system termination or degraded fallback modes.

title: Mitigating Confirmation Bias through Hand-Drawing Videos
comment: Accepted to IEEE VIS 2026 Short Papers. 4 pages plus references
summary: Understanding data visualizations is essential for informed decision-making, yet interpretation is often shaped and even distorted by prior beliefs. We investigate whether an embodied pedagogical approach, in which viewers observe the dynamic hand-drawing of a visualization, can mitigate confirmation bias and improve interpretation accuracy. We conducted a study comparing static bar charts to videos in which charts are constructed through hand-drawing, across contexts that either align with or challenge participants' prior beliefs. The results indicate that hand-drawn videos helped participants accurately interpret data, even when the data conflicted with their prior beliefs. This approach also reduced belief-consistent errors and increased belief-overriding responses. These findings suggest that exposing the construction process of a visualization supports more accurate reasoning and mitigates the influence of confirmation bias. Consequently, this work introduces a promising design space for bias-mitigating data interfaces.

AI.tldr: Hand-drawn animated visualizations reduce confirmation bias and improve data interpretation accuracy compared to static charts, even when data conflicts with viewers' prior beliefs.
AI.motivation: Data visualization interpretation is frequently distorted by viewers' pre-existing beliefs (confirmation bias). The authors seek to explore whether an embodied pedagogical approach—watching visualizations being constructed by hand—can counteract this bias and improve reasoning accuracy.
AI.method: A controlled study comparing two conditions: static bar charts versus videos depicting bar charts being hand-drawn in real time. Both conditions were tested across contexts that either aligned with or contradicted participants' prior beliefs. Interpretation accuracy, belief-consistent errors, and belief-overriding responses were measured.
AI.result: Hand-drawn videos significantly improved participants' ability to interpret data accurately, even in belief-incongruent contexts. The approach reduced belief-consistent errors and increased the frequency of belief-overriding correct responses compared to static charts.
AI.conclusion: Exposing the construction process of a visualization fosters more accurate, less biased reasoning. This opens a promising design space for bias-mitigating data interfaces grounded in embodied and pedagogical visualization techniques.

title: Simulation Based Reward Function Validation for Multi-Agent On Orbit Inspection
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures. This submission integrates a published correction made to the original manuscript. The DOIs for both the original manuscript as well as the correction are provided
summary: A proposed method for the control of groups of inspection spacecraft is Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). While MARL has already been employed for this purpose in previous work, the reward functions used focus on reaching a finite set of predetermined inspection points around the target. In this work, we study and develop a generalized reward function for the MARL inspection task informed by the analysis of 3D reconstructions of inspected objects in orbit. Because the reward function is generalized such that any number of images at arbitrary locations may evaluated, we also allow trained agents to have complete control over when images are collected. With this approach, we gather insights into best practices for not only the specific MARL inspection task, but also gain key takeaways informative to the broader inspection task outside of a MARL context.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a generalized MARL reward function for spacecraft inspection that uses 3D reconstruction quality as feedback, enabling agents to autonomously decide when and where to capture images rather than visiting predetermined waypoints.
AI.motivation: Previous MARL approaches for spacecraft inspection used reward functions based on reaching fixed, predetermined inspection points, which limits agent autonomy and may not optimize for the actual goal of building a complete 3D reconstruction of the target object. The authors aim to create a more flexible framework where inspection quality is directly tied to reconstruction fidelity.
AI.method: The authors design a generalized reward function that evaluates the quality of 3D reconstructions generated from images collected at arbitrary locations by the agents. This reward function is agnostic to the number and positions of images, giving agents full control over image acquisition timing and viewpoints. The approach is validated through MARL training and analysis of resulting inspection behaviors.
AI.result: The generalized reward function enables trained agents to autonomously determine optimal image collection strategies. The study yields insights into best practices for the MARL inspection task and broader lessons applicable to spacecraft inspection outside of a MARL context.
AI.conclusion: Tying the reward signal directly to 3D reconstruction quality, rather than waypoint visitation, produces more autonomous and potentially more effective inspection policies. The findings offer transferable takeaways for both MARL-based and traditional spacecraft inspection mission design.

title: A global predicted-fMRI drive signal from TRIBE does not predict YouTube replay heatmaps
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure. Code, video-ID manifest, and per-video results: https://github.com/mercurialsolo/tribe-replay-heatmaps
summary: Deep multimodal brain-encoding models now predict fMRI responses to naturalistic video with high accuracy. Whether their predicted neural signals also forecast behavioral engagement is unknown. We run TRIBE, the winning model of the 2025 Algonauts brain-encoding challenge (Llama-3.2 + V-JEPA2 + Wav2Vec-BERT), on 48 YouTube videos and reduce its predicted cortical response to a per-second engagement curve, the global field power. Correlated against each video's "most replayed" heatmap, a passively-collected proxy for which moments viewers return to, the curve shows no evidence of predicting re-watch behavior. The pooled position-controlled partial correlation is +0.058 (95% CI [-0.04, 0.15]; one-sample t(47)=1.21, p=0.23), indistinguishable from zero and not significantly above simple loudness and motion baselines (loudness +0.04, paired p=0.74). The raw correlation is also near zero; the moderate values reported for music videos reflect a genre-specific intro/onset-replay artifact rather than content prediction, and do not generalize. The null holds across six cortical-network readouts and under an autocorrelation-preserving permutation test. We release the code, the video-ID manifest, and an acquisition method that works despite YouTube's SABR-only streaming.

AI.tldr: A state-of-the-art multimodal brain-encoding model (TRIBE) fails to predict real-world behavioral engagement (YouTube "most replayed" data) from its predicted cortical responses, with near-zero correlations that do not exceed simple acoustic/motion baselines.
AI.motivation: While deep multimodal models can accurately predict fMRI responses to naturalistic video, it is unknown whether these predicted neural signals translate to forecasting behavioral engagement — a critical gap between neural encoding and real-world relevance.
AI.method: The authors applied TRIBE (Llama-3.2 + V-JEPA2 + Wav2Vec-BERT), the 2025 Algonauts challenge winner, to 48 YouTube videos. They reduced predicted cortical responses to a per-second global field power engagement curve and correlated it against YouTube's passively-collected "most replayed" heatmaps. Analyses included position-controlled partial correlations, comparisons to loudness and motion baselines, six cortical-network readouts, and autocorrelation-preserving permutation tests.
AI.result: The pooled position-controlled partial correlation was +0.058 (95% CI [-0.04, 0.15]; p=0.23), indistinguishable from zero. It did not significantly exceed simple loudness (+0.04, paired p=0.74) or motion baselines. Previously reported moderate correlations for music videos were shown to reflect a genre-specific intro/onset-replay artifact. The null result held across all six cortical-network readouts and under permutation testing.
AI.conclusion: State-of-the-art brain encoding models do not yet capture the neural correlates of naturalistic behavioral engagement. The dissociation between encoding accuracy and behavioral prediction highlights a fundamental limitation and an important direction for future model development.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation to Support Railways Engineering Tasks: A Case Study
summary: The growing number and complexity of technical regulations represent an important challenge for all professionals in regulated industries. This paper describes a case study, from design to deployment, of building a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system for the consultation of complex technical regulations in the railway domain. Although developed for the railway sector, this testimony of an industrial experience is of particular value for technical domains where regulatory compliance and accurate information retrieval from complex documentation are essential requirements. It also constitutes a human-centered approach for implementing LLM-powered technical documentation consultation across various regulated industries, balancing technological capabilities with domain expertise.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an industrial case study on designing and deploying a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system for consulting complex technical regulations in the railway domain, offering a human-centered approach applicable to other regulated industries.
AI.motivation: The growing volume and complexity of technical regulations pose significant challenges for professionals in regulated industries, who need accurate and efficient access to compliance-critical documentation.
AI.method: The authors conducted a case study covering the full lifecycle from design to deployment of a RAG system tailored for railway technical regulation consultation, employing a human-centered approach that integrates LLM capabilities with domain expertise.
AI.result: The paper shares practical industrial experience on implementing an LLM-powered documentation consultation system, demonstrating how to balance technological capabilities with domain-specific requirements in a regulated environment.
AI.conclusion: The human-centered RAG approach described is transferable across regulated industries where accurate information retrieval from complex technical documentation is critical, providing a model for balancing AI capabilities with expert domain knowledge.

title: I\textsuperscript{2}RiMA: Spectral Riemannian Representation with Temporal Attention for Mental Stress Detection based on EEG Signals
summary: Cross-subject EEG stress detection remains challenging because discriminative stress-related patterns are both subject-dependent and frequency-specific. Conventional Riemannian methods model spatial covariance mainly in the time domain, overlooking neural oscillations that are critical for high-level cognitive state decoding, while standard temporal tokenization often fragments inter-slice temporal coherence. To address these limitations, we propose \method{}, an Intra-Inter Riemannian Manifold Attention Network for EEG-based stress detection. \method{} constructs spatial covariance matrices independently at each frequency point and maps them to the SPD tangent space, preserving channel-wise geometry together with frequency-specific discriminative cues. It further introduces frequency cluster aggregation to select informative spectral components and reduce redundancy by forming compact, data-driven frequency clusters aligned with EEG rhythms. Finally, an intra-inter slice attention module adaptively integrates local slice-level spectral dynamics and global temporal context across EEG sequences. Experiments on three datasets show that \method{} consistently outperforms five state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 82.78\% balanced accuracy while remaining efficient with only 1.60M parameters and 31.95M FLOPs.

AI.tldr: The paper presents I2RMAN, a Riemannian manifold attention network that models EEG spatial covariance per frequency, aggregates spectral clusters, and fuses local/global temporal context, achieving state-of-the-art cross-subject stress detection with 82.78% accuracy at low computational cost.
AI.motivation: Existing Riemannian methods for EEG stress detection operate in the time domain and ignore frequency-specific neural oscillations critical for cognitive state decoding. Additionally, standard temporal tokenization disrupts inter-slice coherence. Cross-subject stress detection suffers from patterns that are both subject-dependent and frequency-specific, motivating a method that jointly addresses spectral and temporal modeling on the manifold.
AI.method: I2RMAN has three core components: (1) frequency-wise spatial covariance matrix construction mapped to the SPD tangent space to preserve channel geometry and spectral cues; (2) frequency cluster aggregation that learns compact, data-driven spectral clusters aligned with EEG rhythms to select informative components and reduce redundancy; (3) an intra-inter slice attention module that adaptively integrates local slice-level spectral dynamics with global temporal context across EEG sequences.
AI.result: On three datasets, I2RMAN consistently outperforms five state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 82.78% balanced accuracy with only 1.60M parameters and 31.95M FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: I2RMAN effectively addresses the dual challenges of frequency-specific and temporal modeling in EEG stress detection by combining SPD manifold geometry, data-driven spectral clustering, and intra-inter attention, delivering strong performance with high parameter efficiency.

title: Safeguarding LLM Agents from Misalignment through Provenance Analysis
summary: As LLM agents gain increasing access to powerful tools, ensuring that their actions are aligned with the user's intent becomes critical. When an agent's proposed tool invocation deviates from the user's intent -- a phenomenon called misalignment -- it may lead to harmful consequences that are difficult to undo. Existing runtime guardrails rely on an LLM-as-a-judge paradigm that lacks a systematic framework for reasoning about alignment, often producing judgments that are inconsistent or difficult to audit. Motivated by provenance analysis, we propose a provenance-based conceptual framework that formalizes misalignment detection as determining whether a proposed tool call is supported by traceable evidence in the agent's context. Building on this framework, we propose ProvenanceGuard, a multi-stage pipeline that analyzes the agent's action for three types of misalignment before the selected tool is executed and only allows the action to take place when it is considered aligned with the user's input query. We evaluated our proposed approach on two different benchmarks, Agent-SafetyBench and WorkBench, across 10 backbone LLMs. Compared to the LLM-as-a-judge baseline, ProvenanceGuard reduces error rate on misaligned traces from 42.9% to 1.8% on Agent-SafetyBench and from 32.1% to 17.3% on WorkBench, while reducing intervention burden on task-successful traces from 30.5% to 12.8% and introducing no statistically significant increase in unnecessary interventions on aligned traces. These results demonstrate that structured, provenance-based reasoning provides an effective and practical foundation for safeguarding LLM agents from misalignment.

AI.tldr: ProvenanceGuard is a multi-stage, provenance-based pipeline that detects misalignment in LLM agent tool calls by verifying whether proposed actions are supported by traceable evidence in the agent's context. It dramatically reduces error rates on misaligned traces (42.9% → 1.8% on Agent-SafetyBench; 32.1% → 17.3% on WorkBench) compared to LLM-as-a-judge baselines, while also lowering unnecessary interventions on successful traces.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly wield powerful tools, but existing runtime guardrails use an LLM-as-a-judge paradigm that lacks systematic reasoning frameworks, producing inconsistent and hard-to-audit judgments. There is a need for a principled, auditable approach to detect misalignment—when a tool invocation deviates from user intent—before harmful actions are executed.
AI.method: The authors propose a provenance-based conceptual framework formalizing misalignment detection as determining whether a proposed tool call is supported by traceable evidence in the agent's context. Building on this, ProvenanceGuard is a multi-stage pipeline that analyzes agent actions for three types of misalignment before tool execution, permitting only actions deemed aligned with the user's input query.
AI.result: Evaluated on Agent-SafetyBench and WorkBench across 10 backbone LLMs, ProvenanceGuard reduced the error rate on misaligned traces from 42.9% to 1.8% (Agent-SafetyBench) and from 32.1% to 17.3% (WorkBench). It also reduced intervention burden on task-successful traces from 30.5% to 12.8%, with no statistically significant increase in unnecessary interventions on aligned traces.
AI.conclusion: Structured, provenance-based reasoning provides an effective and practical foundation for safeguarding LLM agents from misalignment, offering substantial improvements in both detection accuracy and reduced false positives over the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm.

title: Auto-FL-Research: Agentic Search for Federated Learning Algorithms
summary: Federated learning (FL) research often depends on many small but consequential algorithmic choices: optimizer variants, server aggregation rules, local training schedules, normalization, regularization, and model architecture. These choices are expensive to explore manually and difficult to compare fairly when candidate changes can also alter the FL training or evaluation path. In this work, we present Auto-FL-Research (AFR), a constrained coding-agent workflow for FL algorithmic recipe search. Agents may propose and implement candidate training algorithms, including server aggregation rules, client update schedules, local objectives, and registered model variants, while task profiles fix the mutation surface, compute budget, communication contract, and final model evaluation. Each campaign records candidate scores, runtime, edited files, artifacts, and failure status. We evaluate AFR on five healthcare cross-silo FLamby tasks and on grouped-client profiles for the five fixed LEAF datasets plus the LEAF synthetic task. Five-seed repeat evaluations support gains on four FLamby tasks and five of six LEAF profiles, while also exposing seed-sensitive and search-selected failure cases. Same-budget controls show that several gains correspond to FL-recipe changes, whereas other improvements are recovered by fixed-surface scalar controls or fail under repeat or held-out evaluation. These mixed outcomes are part of the contribution: they show how agent-generated candidates can be separated into repeated FL mechanisms, fixed-surface tuning effects, and selected single-run artifacts.

AI.tldr: Auto-FL-Research (AFR) is a constrained coding-agent system that automates the search for effective federated learning (FL) algorithmic recipes. It enables agents to propose and implement candidate training algorithms under fixed compute budgets and task profiles. Evaluated on five healthcare FLamby tasks and six LEAF benchmarks, AFR yields mixed but informative results — some gains are genuine FL recipe improvements, while others stem from fixed-surface tuning or single-run artifacts. The paper's core contribution is a methodology for disentangling these outcomes.
AI.motivation: FL research involves many interdependent algorithmic choices (optimizers, aggregation rules, local schedules, normalization, architecture) that are costly to explore manually and difficult to compare fairly, since changing one component can alter the entire training/evaluation path. A systematic, automated search under controlled constraints is needed.
AI.method: AFR employs a constrained coding-agent workflow: agents propose and implement candidate FL algorithms (server aggregation, client update schedules, local objectives, model variants) while task profiles lock down the mutation surface, compute budget, communication contract, and evaluation protocol. Each campaign records candidate scores, runtime, file diffs, artifacts, and failure status.
AI.result: Across five FLamby healthcare tasks and six LEAF profiles (five fixed plus synthetic), five-seed evaluations showed gains on four FLamby tasks and five of six LEAF profiles. However, same-budget controls revealed that some gains are attributable to FL-recipe changes, others to fixed-surface scalar tuning, and some fail under repeat or held-out evaluation — exposing seed-sensitive and search-selected failure cases.
AI.conclusion: The primary contribution is not simply performance gains but a framework for separating agent-generated candidates into three categories: repeated FL mechanisms, fixed-surface tuning effects, and selected single-run artifacts. This taxonomy helps clarify whether observed improvements reflect genuine algorithmic advances or experimental noise.

title: From Forgeries to Foundation Models: A Systematic Survey of Identity Document Attack and Detection
summary: Identity document forgery has undergone a fundamental capability shift: generative AI tools now enable high-fidelity document synthesis and field-level manipulation with minimal technical expertise, while detection methods remain constrained by benchmarks that do not reflect this threat. The resulting attack surface spans physical presentation, digital injection, and fully generative synthesis, introducing distinct forensic failure modes that require a unified threat model and evaluation framework. This survey provides, to our knowledge, the first unified treatment of Presentation Attacks, Digital Injection Attacks, and GenAI-driven synthesis within a single identity verification threat model. We trace detection methodologies from rule-based heuristics through forensic localisation, injection-aware pipelines, foundation models, and few-shot frameworks. A systematic audit of public datasets from 2019--2025 exposes a persistent Reality Gap between benchmark conditions and operational deployment. We further analyse large multimodal models for identity document manipulation, identifying Script-Dependent Generative Instability (SDGI) as a recurring typographic failure mode in non-Latin script inpainting. Finally, zero-shot benchmarking on unseen synthesised ID cards shows that even the strongest publicly available models achieve APCER values above 25% under security-oriented operating conditions, highlighting substantial limits in cross-domain generalisation. We conclude by outlining future directions toward forensically grounded, privacy-preserving, and legally accountable identity verification systems.

AI.tldr: Survey unifying three ID document forgery attack vectors—Presentation, Digital Injection, and GenAI synthesis—into one threat model. Audits 2019–2025 benchmarks revealing a Reality Gap, identifies Script-Dependent Generative Instability (SDGI) in multilingual inpainting, and demonstrates that top models still fail (>25% APCER) under operational zero-shot conditions.
AI.motivation: Generative AI has democratized high-fidelity ID document forgery, yet existing detection benchmarks fail to capture real-world attack diversity. No prior work unifies physical presentation, digital injection, and fully synthetic generation into a single threat model, leaving a critical gap between academic evaluation and operational identity verification.
AI.method: A systematic survey and audit: (1) unified threat model encompassing Presentation Attacks, Digital Injection Attacks, and GenAI synthesis; (2) taxonomy tracing detection evolution from rule-based heuristics to foundation models and few-shot frameworks; (3) systematic audit of public datasets (2019–2025); (4) analysis of large multimodal models for document manipulation, characterizing SDGI; (5) zero-shot benchmarking on unseen synthetic ID cards under security-oriented operating conditions.
AI.result: Persistent Reality Gap identified between benchmark conditions and operational deployment. Script-Dependent Generative Instability (SDGI) emerged as a recurring typographic failure mode in non-Latin script inpainting. Zero-shot evaluation showed even the strongest public models exceed 25% APCER under security-oriented conditions, revealing severe cross-domain generalization limits.
AI.conclusion: Current detection systems are insufficient for GenAI-era threats. Future directions require forensically grounded, privacy-preserving, and legally accountable identity verification architectures that bridge the Reality Gap and address cross-domain generalization failures.

title: Mind the Trust Gap: Identifying (Mis)alignments in Teacher-Student Views Toward Control and Agency in K-12 Classroom AI
comment: To be published in Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, Volume 10, Issue 6, Article CSCW124 (October 2026)
summary: As Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based technologies have been integrated into school classrooms where multiple stakeholders (with different roles) interact with each other, it is critical to deeply understand stakeholder views in the classroom. In particular, prior work has not fully uncovered how teachers' and school students' views might or might not align well with each other, especially in K-12 classrooms. We conducted a speed-dating study using storyboards with 16 school students and 15 school teachers in Germany to investigate alignments and misalignments between their views on student-AI decision-making control in K-12 classroom. Through an explicit pair-matching analysis, we found that students and teachers had misaligned views on several key topics, including how much they trust AI and social and emotional aspects of student learning with AI. Findings also revealed the importance of teacher-student relationships outside of AI use that shape stakeholders' views and interactions. We discuss potential reasons for the observed misaligned views and strategies to fill the perspective gaps. This study illustrates the complexities of preferences in teacher-student-AI interactions that depend on the dynamic relations among the stakeholders.

AI.tldr: A speed-dating study using storyboards with 16 students and 15 teachers in Germany revealed misaligned views between teachers and students on AI decision-making control in K-12 classrooms, particularly regarding trust in AI and the social-emotional dimensions of learning with AI. Teacher-student relationships outside AI use also emerged as influential.
AI.motivation: As AI technologies enter K-12 classrooms with multiple stakeholders, prior work has not adequately examined how teachers' and students' views align or diverge, especially regarding student-AI decision-making control. Understanding these alignments and misalignments is critical for responsible integration of AI in educational settings.
AI.method: A speed-dating study using storyboards was conducted with 16 school students and 15 school teachers in Germany. An explicit pair-matching analysis was employed to systematically compare and contrast stakeholder views on student-AI decision-making control in K-12 classrooms.
AI.result: Students and teachers held misaligned views on several key topics: (1) the degree of trust they place in AI, and (2) the social and emotional aspects of student learning with AI. Additionally, teacher-student relationships formed outside of AI use significantly shaped both stakeholders' views and their interactions around AI in the classroom.
AI.conclusion: The study illustrates the complexities of preferences in teacher-student-AI interactions, demonstrating that these preferences depend on the dynamic, relational context among stakeholders. The authors discuss potential reasons for misalignments and propose strategies to bridge perspective gaps between teachers and students.

title: Congestion-Based Slot Pricing in a Railway Auction Game
summary:
We present a multi-agent system for studying the allocation of discrete, congested resources among heterogeneous strategic agents, motivated by the problem of railway slot allocation under deregulation. Multiple operator-agents, differing in size and capacity, interact through a shared auction mechanism over repeated rounds under time-constrained decision-making. The mechanism combines a congestion-based base price that increases with aggregate demand with an asymmetric corrective adjustment that penalises the agent requesting the most slots and rewards the agent requesting the fewest, and is designed to mitigate strategic dominance by large agents while preserving transparency and congestion sensitivity. We formulate the interaction as a repeated game with incomplete information and implement the system as a real-time, web-based multi-agent environment in which human participants control individual agents and observe live marginal-cost and competitor feedback.
  We report exploratory observations from two structured sessions with domain experts acting as operator-agents. The congestion mechanism responds to aggregate demand as designed and the corrective incentives are actively triggered, but agents representing large operators persist with high-request strategies despite the penalty, suggesting that corrective pricing is necessary but not sufficient to neutralise strategic dominance in this multi-agent setting. A post-session debrief indicates that participants' decisions were driven by the assumed agent role rather than personal disposition, and provides qualitative support for strategic motives, such as preserving market presence and raising rivals' costs, operating alongside short-term profit maximisation. We discuss implications for multi-agent mechanism design under asymmetric budgets and outline directions for analytical validation and larger-scale multi-agent experiments.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent auction system for congested resource allocation (railway slots) is tested with human participants. A congestion-based pricing mechanism with corrective penalties fails to fully neutralize the strategic dominance of large agents, who persist with high-request strategies despite penalties, revealing that corrective pricing alone is insufficient to curb strategic behavior by dominant players.
AI.motivation: Railway slot allocation under deregulation involves heterogeneous strategic agents competing for discrete, congested resources. Large operators can strategically dominate auctions, undermining fairness and efficiency. The authors aim to design and empirically test a transparent auction mechanism that mitigates such strategic dominance through congestion-sensitive pricing with asymmetric corrective incentives.
AI.method: A repeated game with incomplete information is formulated and implemented as a real-time, web-based multi-agent environment. The mechanism features a congestion-based base price (increasing with aggregate demand) and an asymmetric corrective adjustment penalizing the highest-requesting agent while rewarding the lowest. Human domain experts participate in structured sessions controlling individual operator-agents with live marginal-cost and competitor feedback.
AI.result: The congestion mechanism responds to aggregate demand as designed, and corrective incentives are actively triggered. However, large-operator agents persist with high-request strategies despite penalties. Post-session debriefs reveal participants were driven by assigned agent roles rather than personal disposition, with strategic motives (preserving market presence, raising rivals' costs) operating alongside short-term profit maximization.
AI.conclusion: Corrective pricing is necessary but insufficient to neutralize strategic dominance in asymmetric multi-agent settings. Large agents' persistence with high-request strategies suggests deeper strategic motives beyond price sensitivity. The authors call for analytical validation and larger-scale experiments to advance mechanism design under asymmetric budgets.

title: GPUAlert: A Zero-Instrumentation Process-Boundary Monitor for Diagnosing GPU Training-Job Failures
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables,3 Listings. Submitted as an arXiv preprint. Source, corpus and evaluation harness available at https://github.com/Parv-01/gpualert and https://github.com/Parv-01/gpualert-eval
summary: GPU training jobs fail often, roughly two in five on large production clusters, yet the operator typically learns of a failure only by reconnecting hours later. Experiment trackers require editing the training script and maintaining a cloud connection; the scheduler's mail hook delivers a single status line with no cause and no logs. GPUAlert is a command-line wrapper that monitors any training command at the process boundary, and with no change to that command, emails a structured notification on completion carrying a classified failure cause, durable logs, and output artifacts. The tool is organized around three reliability primitives: a pre-launch log guarantee that establishes the durable destination before the child process can crash, notifier isolation that makes the wrapper's exit code a pure function of the child's status regardless of whether the email succeeds, and a non-silent artifact budget that bounds attachment size without ever dropping output silently. We release a labelled corpus of 474 GPU training logs across 15 failure classes and a reproducible evaluation harness. On the twelve hardware-reproduced classes, the ordered-rule classifier reaches 0.997 macro-F1, against 0.830 for unordered keyword matching and 0.133 for exit-code inspection. Wrapper overhead is a constant approximately 3ms per job; the pre-launch guarantee preserves a log where a shell redirect yields nothing; and across all 15 failure modes the wrapper returns the child's exit code unchanged even when the SMTP relay is unreachable.

AI.tldr: GPUAlert is a lightweight command-line wrapper that monitors GPU training jobs, sending structured email notifications upon completion with classified failure causes, durable logs, and output artifacts — requiring zero changes to training scripts. It achieves 0.997 macro-F1 on failure classification across 12 hardware-reproduced classes, with approximately 3ms overhead per job.
AI.motivation: GPU training jobs fail frequently (~40% on large production clusters), but operators often learn of failures only hours later upon reconnection. Existing solutions are inadequate: experiment trackers require script modification and cloud connectivity; scheduler mail hooks provide minimal information (a single status line) without failure causes or logs. There is a clear need for a non-invasive, reliable monitoring tool that delivers actionable failure diagnostics without modifying training code.
AI.method: GPUAlert operates as a process-boundary wrapper with three reliability primitives: (1) a pre-launch log guarantee that establishes durable log destinations before the child process starts, preventing log loss from early crashes; (2) notifier isolation ensuring the wrapper's exit code reflects only the child's status, independent of email delivery success; (3) a non-silent artifact budget that bounds attachment sizes without silently dropping output. Failure classification uses an ordered-rule classifier trained on a corpus of 474 labeled GPU training logs across 15 failure classes.
AI.result: The ordered-rule classifier achieves 0.997 macro-F1 on 12 hardware-reproduced failure classes, substantially outperforming unordered keyword matching (0.830) and exit-code inspection (0.133). Wrapper overhead is constant at ~3ms per job. The pre-launch log guarantee successfully preserves logs where a naive shell redirect produces nothing. Across all 15 failure modes, the wrapper faithfully returns the child's exit code even when the SMTP relay is unreachable.
AI.conclusion: GPUAlert provides a practical, non-invasive solution to GPU training job monitoring that delivers high-accuracy failure classification, durable logging, and reliable artifact delivery with negligible performance overhead — addressing a significant operational gap in production ML infrastructure.

title: Bi-NAS: Towards Effective and Personalized Explanation for Recommender Systems via Bi-Level Neural Architecture Search
summary: Recommender systems are vital in helping users navigate vast amounts of information, offering personalized suggestions and effective explanations for these recommendations. While previous efforts have attempted to provide such explanations, evaluating their effectiveness across various scenarios remains a challenge. Enhancing these explanations is essential for improving user engagement, trust, and decision-making. To facilitate effective explanations within the recommender system, we propose a Bi-level Neural Architecture Search (Bi-NAS) framework to optimize explanations. This approach simultaneously refines cross-attention mechanisms and feature interaction functions by exploring both intra-layer and inter-layer design spaces. Furthermore, we integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance explanation generation, leveraging zero-shot prompting to produce more effective and personalized justifications. By aligning user feature preferences with item quality scores, our approach ensures that explanations reflect both user intent and item attributes, improving transparency and reasoning depth. Extensive evaluations on four real-world datasets demonstrate that Bi-NAS not only boosts recommendation accuracy but also significantly improves the effectiveness of explanations for recommender systems, providing users with clear and reliable insights into the suggestions they receive.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Bi-level Neural Architecture Search (Bi-NAS) framework that jointly optimizes cross-attention mechanisms and feature interaction functions across intra- and inter-layer design spaces, augmented with LLM-based zero-shot prompting, to generate personalized, transparent explanations in recommender systems. Experiments on four datasets show improvements in both recommendation accuracy and explanation quality.
AI.motivation: Existing recommender systems struggle to provide explanations whose effectiveness can be consistently evaluated across diverse scenarios. Improving explanation quality is critical for boosting user engagement, trust, and decision-making, yet prior efforts lack a principled, automated way to co-optimize the underlying model architecture and the explanation generation process.
AI.method: Bi-NAS, a bi-level neural architecture search framework that simultaneously optimizes: (1) cross-attention mechanisms at the intra-layer level, and (2) feature interaction functions at the inter-layer level. LLMs are integrated via zero-shot prompting to produce personalized justifications. User feature preferences are aligned with item quality scores to ensure explanations reflect both user intent and item attributes.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on four real-world datasets demonstrate that Bi-NAS improves both recommendation accuracy and explanation effectiveness, delivering clear and reliable insights to users.
AI.conclusion: The Bi-NAS framework, combined with LLM-enhanced explanation generation, successfully addresses the dual challenge of accurate recommendation and high-quality explanation, offering a scalable and automated solution for building transparent, trustworthy recommender systems.

title: Fixed-Set Robustness in Programming by Example: Example Corruption and Semantic Partition Recovery
summary: Programming-by-example systems infer programs from a small set of input-output examples. Robust PBE work usually models wrong examples as samples from a stochastic noise process and then minimizes an expected or empirical loss. This paper studies a different failure mode: an adversary who sees the synthesizer and chooses the examples whose corruption most damages the returned program.
