We formalize fixed-set worst-case corruption for finite PBE version spaces, implement exact-within-bounded-pool and heuristic corruption searches for a string-transformation DSL, and introduce version-space partition aggregation (VPA), a defense that synthesizes on disjoint example groups and votes by semantic signatures. The central claim is deliberately bounded and partly negative: low-margin PBE tasks have an adversarial robustness dimension that random-typo and noisy-PBE evaluations miss, while semantic partition aggregation helps only when the clean semantics keep a partition vote margin, which often fails on realistic tasks. Evidence from curated/generated DSL tasks, accepted public SyGuS PBE_SLIA slices, SYNTRA Playgol v2, and noisy-PBE objective baselines supports that boundary. One curated edit flips all 8 spike tasks while 200-trial typo, DSL-pool, and distance-matched random controls succeed on 10.3%, 11.0%, and 16.7%; generated margin-1 rows flip under budget 1 yet VPA recovers them; on public SyGuS the vote margin is near one, so an adaptive attacker drives VPA accuracy to zero; accepted public SyGuS slices move across exact-within-pool budget boundaries; and Playgol shows positive paired-bootstrap gaps against typo and same-pool random controls on the 141 accepted rows. A small exact-output prompt harness over 20 controlled margin-1 tasks shows the same qualitative clean-to-attacked pattern across local and API models, while it is treated as a scope check, not a broad LLM benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates adversarial robustness in Programming-by-Example (PBE) systems, where an attacker who understands the synthesizer can craft worst-case corrupted examples to maximally damage the synthesized program. It introduces exact and heuristic corruption search methods for a string-transformation DSL and proposes Version-space Partition Aggregation (VPA) as a defense. The findings are sobering: low-margin PBE tasks are inherently vulnerable to adversarial perturbation, and VPA helps only when clean semantics retain sufficient vote margin — a condition that often fails on realistic tasks.
AI.motivation: Traditional robust PBE research models errors as stochastic noise (e.g., typos) and minimizes expected loss. This overlooks a more dangerous threat model: an adaptive adversary who observes the synthesizer and strategically selects examples whose corruption inflicts maximal damage. The paper argues that this adversarial dimension is fundamentally missed by random-noise evaluations, exposing a blind spot in PBE robustness research.
AI.method: The authors formalize fixed-set worst-case corruption over finite PBE version spaces. They implement exact-within-bounded-pool and heuristic corruption search algorithms targeting a string-transformation DSL. The proposed defense, Version-space Partition Aggregation (VPA), splits examples into disjoint groups, synthesizes independently on each, and votes using semantic signatures. Evaluation spans curated/generated DSL tasks, SyGuS PBE_SLIA benchmarks, SYNTRA Playgol v2, and a small LLM prompt harness on 20 controlled margin-1 tasks — the latter treated as a scope check, not a broad benchmark.
AI.result: One curated edit flips all 8 spike tasks, while typo (10.3%), DSL-pool (11.0%), and distance-matched random (16.7%) controls mostly succeed. Generated margin-1 rows are flipped under budget 1 yet recovered by VPA. On public SyGuS instances, vote margins hover near one, allowing an adaptive attacker to drive VPA accuracy to zero. SyGuS slices demonstrate movement across exact-within-pool budget boundaries. Playgol shows positive paired-bootstrap gaps against typo and same-pool random controls on 141 accepted rows. The LLM scope check reproduces the same clean-to-attacked qualitative pattern across both local and API models.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers a deliberately bounded, partly negative conclusion: low-margin PBE tasks possess an adversarial robustness dimension that stochastic noise evaluations cannot capture. VPA provides meaningful defense only when clean semantic partitions maintain a sufficient vote margin — a condition that frequently collapses on realistic benchmarks. This delineates a fundamental robustness boundary rather than offering a universal solution.

title: Kara: Efficient Reasoning LLM Serving via Sliding-Window KV Cache Compression
summary: Reasoning language models often generate long chain-of-thought (CoT), which accumulates a massive KV cache during the decoding phase and incurs high decoding latency and limited throughput. To address these issues, KV cache compression has emerged as a promising technique for reducing memory overhead by selectively removing unimportant KV pairs while preserving useful ones for subsequent decoding. Nevertheless, we identify two key limitations in existing KV cache compression methods: 1) their threshold-triggered compression policy may provide limited throughput improvement or even reduce throughput, and may fully eliminate KV pairs from certain blocks of the sequence, potentially worsening information loss. 2) they typically retain either isolated KV pairs or fixed-size chunks with rigid boundaries, failing to preserve important flexible-sized chunks at arbitrary token positions. To overcome these limitations, we propose Kara, a sliding-window KV cache compression method that performs decoding-time compression by operating only on the recently generated context. Kara leverages bidirectional attention to score and select informative KV pairs in the window. To enable flexible preservation of important semantic information, we design a Token2Chunk module to expand a subset of selected KV pairs into chunks. Furthermore, we adapt Kara to PagedAttention and develop KvLLM, an inference framework built upon vLLM, which reduces KV cache memory usage and effectively improves output throughput. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements of proposed Kara and KvLLM.

AI.tldr: Kara is a sliding-window KV cache compression method that addresses limitations of existing approaches by operating on recently generated context, using bidirectional attention for token scoring, and introducing a Token2Chunk module for flexible chunk preservation, all integrated into KvLLM—a vLLM-based inference framework that reduces memory and improves throughput.
AI.motivation: Reasoning language models produce long chain-of-thought sequences, causing massive KV cache accumulation that leads to high decoding latency and limited throughput. Existing KV cache compression methods suffer from two key problems: (1) threshold-triggered policies can hurt throughput and may entirely drop KV pairs from certain blocks, causing information loss; (2) they retain either isolated KV pairs or rigid fixed-size chunks, failing to preserve semantically important flexible-sized chunks at arbitrary positions.
AI.method: Kara employs a sliding-window approach that compresses only the recently generated context during decoding. Within the window, bidirectional attention scores KV pairs to select the most informative ones. A Token2Chunk module then expands a subset of selected KV pairs into variable-sized chunks, enabling flexible preservation of semantically meaningful spans at arbitrary token positions. The method is adapted to PagedAttention and implemented as KvLLM, an inference framework built on top of vLLM.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show consistent performance improvements from both Kara and the KvLLM inference framework, demonstrating effective KV cache memory reduction and improved output throughput compared to existing compression methods.
AI.conclusion: Kara successfully overcomes the two key limitations of prior KV cache compression methods: threshold-triggered policies and rigid retention granularity. By combining sliding-window compression with bidirectional attention scoring and flexible Token2Chunk expansion, Kara achieves better memory efficiency and throughput when integrated into the vLLM-based KvLLM framework.

title: The Wiola Architecture for Efficient Small Language Models
summary: We present Wiola, a fully original Small Language Model (SLM) architecture built from first principles, sharing no structural lineage with any existing model family including GPT, LLaMA, Mistral, or Falcon. Wiola introduces five independently novel components: (i) Spiral Rotary Positional Encoding (SRPE), which embeds token positions on a three-dimensional helical manifold combining absolute, relative, and hierarchical positional signals; (ii) Gated Cross-Layer Attention (GCLA), providing each decoder layer with soft cross-attention access to compressed summaries of two preceding layers for inter-layer coherence; (iii) Adaptive Token Merging (ATM), which dynamically merges se mantically redundant adjacent tokens in middle network layers to reduce attention complexity without information loss; (iv) Dual Stream Feed-Forward (DSFF), replacing the conventional MLP with two parallel streams fused by a learned per-dimension gate; and (v) WiolaRMSNorm, a modified normalisation introducing a per-dimension learned offset vector that prevents representation collapse. We provide complete mathematical derivations, architectural block diagrams, complexity analyses, and systematic comparisons against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral. Wiola is released in four sizes (120M, 360M, 700M, and 1.5B parameters) and is fully compatible with the HuggingFace Transformers ecosystem, with all 22 architectural unit tests passing.

AI.tldr: Wiola is a novel Small Language Model (SLM) built from scratch with five independent architectural innovations: Spiral Rotary Positional Encoding (3D helical position encoding), Gated Cross-Layer Attention (soft cross-attention to prior layers), Adaptive Token Merging (dynamic redundancy reduction), Dual Stream Feed-Forward (parallel gated MLP streams), and WiolaRMSNorm (normalization with learned offset). Released in sizes from 120M to 1.5B parameters, it is HuggingFace-compatible and compared against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to design a fully original SLM architecture from first principles, deliberately avoiding any structural lineage with established families (GPT, LLaMA, Mistral, Falcon). The motivation is to explore whether independently conceived architectural components can yield competitive performance while introducing novel mechanisms for position encoding, inter-layer communication, token efficiency, feed-forward processing, and normalization stability.
AI.method: Wiola integrates five novel components: (i) Spiral Rotary Positional Encoding (SRPE) — token positions embedded on a 3D helical manifold capturing absolute, relative, and hierarchical signals; (ii) Gated Cross-Layer Attention (GCLA) — each decoder layer accesses compressed summaries of two preceding layers via soft cross-attention; (iii) Adaptive Token Merging (ATM) — dynamically merges semantically redundant adjacent tokens in middle layers to reduce attention complexity; (iv) Dual Stream Feed-Forward (DSFF) — replaces the standard MLP with two parallel streams fused by a learned per-dimension gate; (v) WiolaRMSNorm — extends RMSNorm with a learned per-dimension offset vector to prevent representation collapse. The paper provides mathematical derivations, block diagrams, complexity analyses, and systematic comparisons against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral.
AI.result: Wiola is released in four model sizes (120M, 360M, 700M, and 1.5B parameters) and demonstrates full compatibility with the HuggingFace Transformers ecosystem, with all 22 architectural unit tests passing. The abstract indicates systematic comparisons were conducted against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral, though specific quantitative benchmark results are not disclosed in the abstract itself.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that a fully original SLM architecture can be successfully constructed from first principles, with five independently novel components that are individually motivated and complementary. The release of multiple model sizes and HuggingFace integration suggests practical utility and reproducibility. The passing of all 22 architectural unit tests validates the implementation correctness of the proposed design.

title: Hamm-Grams: An Algorithm for Mining Regular Expressions of Bytes
comment: To appear in Machine Learning for Malware Detection
summary: Malware poses a critical and ever-evolving threat, and robust and effective systems for detecting and classifying malware are of essential importance. $n$-grams features are among the common static features used in effective machine learning systems for malware, but these features are inherently brittle. We propose an algorithm for constructing more robust features, hamm-grams, which are a special class of regular expressions having a fixed length and single-character wildcards. We devise an efficient algorithm for finding common hamm-grams using a new locality-sensitive hash designed to produce collisions among pairs of small Hamming distance and a clustering within hash buckets to place wildcards. We then demonstrate the advantages of these features in malware classification and detection tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "hamm-grams," a robust alternative to n-gram features for malware detection. These are fixed-length regular expressions with single-character wildcards, constructed via a novel locality-sensitive hashing scheme that clusters similar patterns by small Hamming distance. The authors demonstrate improved classification and detection performance over standard n-grams.
AI.motivation: Traditional n-gram features used in machine learning-based malware detection are inherently brittle—small changes to the malware (e.g., single-byte modifications) can completely break n-gram matches, degrading detection robustness.
AI.method: The authors introduce hamm-grams: fixed-length patterns with single-character wildcards (a restricted class of regular expressions). They develop an efficient discovery algorithm using a custom locality-sensitive hash (LSH) designed to maximize collisions among strings with small Hamming distance, followed by clustering within hash buckets to optimally place wildcards.
AI.result: Hamm-gram features outperform traditional n-gram features in both malware classification and malware detection tasks, demonstrating greater robustness to byte-level perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Hamm-grams provide a more robust static feature representation for malware analysis, effectively handling minor byte variations that defeat standard n-grams, while remaining computationally feasible to extract via the proposed LSH-based algorithm.

title: OrchestrXR: A Multi-Agent System for Idea-to-Prototype XR Study Authoring
summary: Extended Reality (XR) has become an important interaction paradigm in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI). XR studies are used to investigate interaction, perception, and user behavior in immersive environments, and typically involve experimental tasks, 3D scenes, and interactive logic. However, turning an initial XR study idea into a runnable prototype remains fragmented across study design, scene construction, and interaction implementation. We present OrchestrXR, a multi-agent human-AI workflow for early-stage idea-to-prototype XR study authoring. Rather than treating XR study creation as one-shot generation, OrchestrXR supports a controllable workflow across study design, scene generation, and interaction generation through structured schemas, multi-agent orchestration, and interactive human-agent interfaces, producing a Unity-based prototype from a researcher's idea. A user study with 12 XR researchers suggests that OrchestrXR provides effective support for early-stage XR study authoring with strong intent preservation across stages.

AI.tldr: OrchestrXR is a multi-agent human-AI workflow that helps XR researchers go from an initial study idea to a runnable Unity prototype by structuring the process into design, scene generation, and interaction generation stages with human oversight.
AI.motivation: The process of turning an XR study idea into a working prototype is fragmented across study design, 3D scene construction, and interaction implementation. Existing approaches lack a cohesive, controllable pipeline that preserves researcher intent from concept through to functional prototype.
AI.method: OrchestrXR employs a multi-agent human-AI workflow with three staged components: (1) structured schemas for study design specification, (2) multi-agent orchestration for coordinating scene and interaction generation, and (3) interactive human-agent interfaces allowing researcher intervention. The system outputs a Unity-based prototype and was evaluated through a user study with 12 XR researchers.
AI.result: The user study with 12 XR researchers demonstrated that OrchestrXR provides effective support for early-stage XR study authoring, with strong intent preservation across the design, scene generation, and interaction generation stages.
AI.conclusion: OrchestrXR demonstrates that a controllable, multi-agent workflow with structured schemas and human-in-the-loop interfaces can effectively bridge the gap between XR study ideation and functional prototyping, offering a promising direction for HCI research tooling.

title: CausalSteward: An Agentic Divide-Conquer-Combine Copilot for Causal Discovery
summary: Learning causal models from high-dimensional data is a significant challenge, particularly in real-world settings where violations of core assumptions lead to causal identifiability issues. Although massive amounts of prior knowledge are available, and contain valuable causal information, effectively integrating this knowledge into the causal discovery process remains an open problem. We introduce CausalSTeward (CAST), a novel human-in-the-loop framework for interactively assembling large causal models. CausalSteward is a multi-agent collaborative system that tackles high-dimensional causality through a divide-and-conquer approach where large clusters of variables are iteratively partitioned and then separately analyzed. Our framework fuses prior knowledge with a data-driven approach by using tailored tools such as retrieval augmented generation and conditional independence tests. Finally, we use this work to examine the capabilities and limitations of causal reasoning in multi-agent frameworks, and how the human-in-the-loop can contribute to accurate and trustworthy results.

AI.tldr: CausalSteward (CAST) is a human-in-the-loop, multi-agent framework that uses a divide-and-conquer strategy — combining prior knowledge, retrieval-augmented generation, and conditional independence tests — to assemble large causal models from high-dimensional data, while also examining the capabilities and limitations of causal reasoning in multi-agent systems.
AI.motivation: Learning causal models from high-dimensional data is challenging due to causal identifiability issues arising from violated assumptions in real-world settings. Although abundant prior knowledge exists, effectively integrating it into causal discovery remains an open problem.
AI.method: CAST employs a multi-agent collaborative system using a divide-and-conquer approach: large variable clusters are iteratively partitioned and analyzed separately. The framework fuses prior knowledge with data-driven methods through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and conditional independence tests, all within a human-in-the-loop paradigm.
AI.result: The paper evaluates CAST's performance in assembling large causal models and examines both the capabilities and limitations of causal reasoning within multi-agent frameworks, highlighting how human-in-the-loop interaction contributes to accuracy and trustworthiness.
AI.conclusion: Human-in-the-loop multi-agent systems like CAST offer a promising direction for scaling causal discovery to high-dimensional settings by synergistically combining prior knowledge, automated statistical testing, and human oversight to produce accurate and trustworthy causal models.

title: Adoption and Impact of Command-Line AI Coding Agents: A Study of Microsoft's Early 2026 Rollout of Claude Code and GitHub Copilot CLI
summary: Organizations rolling out agentic command line tools like Anthropic's Claude Code and GitHub's Copilot CLI need to know who will try them, who will keep using them, and whether the tools produce enough output to justify their cost. At organizational scale, token spend can run into millions of dollars annually, so misreading adoption, retention, or impact can make a rollout expensive without changing engineering velocity. Studying tens of thousands of engineers at Microsoft over its early-2026 rollout, we find that first use spread primarily through social networks, retention was associated more with engineers' coding activity than with demographics, and adopters merged roughly 24% more pull requests than they would have otherwise. We use merged pull requests as our proxy for output -- acknowledging that a merged PR is not the same as the value it delivers -- and the lift persists across our four-month window. These results suggest that CLI coding agents are neither uniformly adopted nor mere novelty effects and that organizations should treat visible peer use as central to rollout strategy.

AI.tldr: A large-scale study at Microsoft (early 2026) of CLI coding agent adoption among tens of thousands of engineers found that initial use spread via social networks, retention correlated with coding activity rather than demographics, and adopters merged ~24% more pull requests over four months — suggesting peer visibility is key to rollout strategy.
AI.motivation: Organizations deploying agentic CLI tools (e.g., Claude Code, Copilot CLI) need evidence on who adopts them, who persists, and whether they yield measurable productivity gains — especially given that token spend can reach millions annually. Without this, rollouts risk high cost without improved engineering velocity.
AI.method: Observational study of tens of thousands of Microsoft engineers during an early-2026 rollout of CLI coding agents. Adoption patterns were analyzed through social network analysis, retention was modeled against coding activity metrics and demographic variables, and causal impact on output was estimated using merged pull requests as a proxy, tracked over a four-month window.
AI.result: First use diffused primarily through social networks; retention was more strongly associated with engineers' coding activity than with demographics; adopters merged approximately 24% more pull requests than they would have otherwise, with the effect persisting across the full four-month observation period.
AI.conclusion: CLI coding agents show neither uniform adoption nor mere novelty effects. Organizations should treat visible peer use as a central element of rollout strategy, and the sustained ~24% PR lift suggests meaningful productivity impact that can justify the token cost at scale.

title: CoPersona: Collaborative Persona Graphs for Robust LLM Personalization
comment: Accepted at KDD '26. 12 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables
summary: Real-world LLM personalization is often constrained by sparse and skewed user histories: most users provide only a handful of interactions, while even frequent users' logs capture an incomplete and biased view of their preferences. As a result, weakly observed user attributes are difficult to infer, leading to brittle personalization when test-time requests shift toward under-supported facets. Motivated by this limitation, we present CoPersona, a graph-based collaborative personalization framework that completes sparse user profiles by borrowing signals from behaviorally similar peers. However, directly transferring signals is difficult because uneven facet coverage introduces bias into interaction histories, obscuring user similarity in the unstructured global space. To address this issue, CoPersona decomposes interaction histories into multiple facet-level representations and explicitly models peer-to-peer, facet-level alignment through a multiplex persona graph. To effectively leverage peer information at inference time, we employ a dual-branch architecture that combines non-parametric peer retrieval with parametric graph reasoning. Experiments across multiple domains and model scales demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, validating CoPersona as an effective approach for robust LLM personalization.

AI.tldr: CoPersona addresses sparse LLM personalization by decomposing user histories into facet-level representations and constructing a multiplex persona graph that aligns behaviorally similar peers. A dual-branch architecture combining non-parametric retrieval with parametric graph reasoning enables robust inference even when test queries target under-supported facets.
AI.motivation: Real-world LLM personalization suffers from sparse, skewed user histories — most users contribute few interactions, and even active users' logs are incomplete and biased. This makes it difficult to infer weakly observed user attributes, causing personalization to fail when test-time requests shift toward under-supported facets. Existing methods lack a mechanism to borrow complementary signals from similar users in a structured, facet-aware manner.
AI.method: CoPersona introduces a graph-based collaborative personalization framework with three key components: (1) Decomposition of interaction histories into multiple facet-level representations to address uneven coverage; (2) A multiplex persona graph that explicitly models peer-to-peer, facet-level alignment among behaviorally similar users; (3) A dual-branch inference architecture combining non-parametric peer retrieval (for direct signal borrowing) with parametric graph reasoning (for propagating information across the persona graph).
AI.result: Experiments across multiple domains and model scales demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, validating CoPersona's effectiveness for robust LLM personalization under sparse and skewed data conditions.
AI.conclusion: CoPersona provides an effective solution for robust LLM personalization by leveraging collaborative signals through facet-level decomposition and graph-based peer alignment. The approach consistently outperforms baselines, demonstrating that structured peer borrowing mitigates the brittleness caused by sparse, biased user histories.

title: Domain Knowledge Based Temporal-Spatial Graph Convolution Network for ECG Recognition
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Presented at ICONIP 2024, Auckland, New Zealand. Published in LNCS 15290, Springer, 2025
summary: In light of strides in Arti cial Intelligence (AI) and its wide spread application, challenges persist in the interpretability of AI models, particularly within specialized domains like healthcare, such as electro cardiograph (ECG) recognition. Rather than relying solely on end-to-end convolutional neural networks, this paper introduces a novel approach using a domain knowledge-based graph convolution network for ECG recognition. Key landmarks points of PRQST, vital to ECG interpreta tion, are incorporated as domain knowledge. The double-stream directed graph is employed to model both intra and inter ECG cycles. Speci cally, spatial directed graphs capture the positional relationships among key points, while temporal directed graphs delineate temporal dependencies between adjacent cycles in extended ECG sequences. Experimental re sults on the First Chinese ECG Intelligent Competition dataset, which speci cally classify ECG into nine categories, prove the e cacy of the proposed model. The overall average F1 score is 88.1%, the average F1 score of rare categories is 76.3%, both outperform the state-of-the-art models. The introduction of domain knowledge did enhance the detec tion performance, especially for rare categories.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a domain knowledge-based graph convolution network for ECG recognition that explicitly models PRQST landmark points using a double-stream directed graph (spatial + temporal), achieving superior performance on a 9-class ECG dataset, especially for rare categories.
AI.motivation: Despite advances in AI, interpretability remains a key challenge in specialized domains like ECG recognition. The authors argue that relying solely on end-to-end CNNs overlooks clinically meaningful domain knowledge (PRQST landmarks), which are essential for ECG interpretation and can improve detection, particularly for rare categories.
AI.method: A double-stream directed graph convolution network is proposed: (1) spatial directed graphs capture positional relationships among PRQST key landmark points within a single ECG cycle; (2) temporal directed graphs model inter-cycle temporal dependencies across adjacent cycles in extended ECG sequences. PRQST landmarks are incorporated as explicit domain knowledge.
AI.result: Evaluated on the First Chinese ECG Intelligent Competition dataset (9-class classification), the model achieves an overall average F1 score of 88.1% and a rare-category average F1 of 76.3%, both outperforming state-of-the-art models. Domain knowledge integration notably boosted detection performance for rare categories.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating domain-specific knowledge (PRQST landmarks) via graph convolutional networks significantly enhances ECG recognition performance and interpretability, particularly benefiting the detection of rare categories compared to purely data-driven CNN approaches.

title: SPARCLE: SPeaker-aware Aligned Representations via Contrastive Language Embeddings
summary:
Recent advances in speech synthesis have shifted from phoneme representations to direct grapheme modeling. While phonemes address the one-to-many mapping between text and acoustics, they rely on grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) systems that fail to capture speaker-specific acoustic variation. Prior work demonstrates that grapheme-based models outperform phoneme-based systems at scale, but not in low-resource settings.
  In this paper, we propose SPARCLE, a speaker-aware grapheme representation model that enriches characters with their precise acoustic realizations. SPARCLE is trained with a contrastive objective to align graphemes with corresponding Wav2Vec2 acoustic representations while conditioned on speaker identity. The resulting model serves as a replacement to G2P systems for downstream text-to-speech (TTS) tasks. We demonstrate that SPARCLE improves generation quality, reducing word error rates by half in extreme low-resource settings compared to standard grapheme-based models.

AI.tldr: SPARCLE introduces a speaker-aware grapheme representation that aligns characters with Wav2Vec2 acoustic features via contrastive learning, conditioned on speaker identity. It replaces G2P systems in TTS and reduces word error rates by half in low-resource settings compared to standard grapheme models.
AI.motivation: Existing phoneme-based TTS relies on G2P systems that discard speaker-specific acoustic variation. Grapheme-based models perform well at scale but struggle in low-resource settings. The gap is a grapheme representation that captures speaker-conditioned acoustic realizations without requiring large datasets.
AI.method: SPARCLE trains a speaker-aware grapheme encoder using a contrastive objective that aligns grapheme representations with Wav2Vec2 acoustic embeddings, conditioned on speaker identity. The learned representations then serve as a direct replacement for G2P modules in downstream TTS pipelines.
AI.result: SPARCLE improves TTS generation quality, achieving a 50% reduction in word error rate in extreme low-resource settings compared to standard grapheme-based models.
AI.conclusion: Speaker-aware grapheme representations trained via contrastive alignment with acoustic features offer a viable alternative to G2P, particularly beneficial in low-resource TTS scenarios where traditional grapheme models underperform.

title: Agent4cs: A Multi-agent System for Code Summarization in Large Hierarchical Codebases
comment: Accepted to the main track of the 23rd European Conference on Multi-Agent Systems (EUMAS 2026)
summary: Understanding large, complex codebases, especially those with obfuscated structures and incomplete documentation, remains a significant challenge. Existing code summarization solutions often rely on a single language model or coding assistant like Claude Code, and treat source code as flat text, underutilizing the rich interdependencies and hierarchical information within a repository. To address these shortcomings, we propose Agent4cs - a multi-agent framework that summarizes large codebases in a bottom-up fashion, where a summarization agent focuses on producing robust summaries; a keyword-extraction agent proactively identifies critical information from subfolders; and a quality-assurance agent iteratively refines the outputs for readability, coherence, and completeness. Evaluated on 7 frontier models, Agent4cs improves semantic consistency across all folder levels by average 8% compared to two structured prompting baselines with code segments. Furthermore, extensive evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates up to 38% gains in normalized keyword coverage rate over the same baselines.

AI.tldr: Agent4cs is a multi-agent framework for summarizing large codebases using a bottom-up approach with specialized agents for summarization, keyword extraction, and quality assurance, achieving up to 38% improvement in keyword coverage and 8% gains in semantic consistency over structured prompting baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing code summarization tools treat source code as flat text and rely on single models, failing to exploit the hierarchical structure and interdependencies within code repositories, especially those with obfuscated or poorly documented code.
AI.method: A multi-agent framework operating bottom-up across folder hierarchies: (1) a summarization agent generates robust code summaries, (2) a keyword-extraction agent identifies critical information from subfolders, and (3) a quality-assurance agent iteratively refines outputs for readability, coherence, and completeness.
AI.result: Evaluated on 7 frontier models, Agent4cs improved semantic consistency by an average of 8% over two structured prompting baselines at all folder levels, and achieved up to 38% gains in normalized keyword coverage rate on real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent, bottom-up approach effectively leverages repository structure and interdependencies, significantly outperforming flat-text baselines in both semantic consistency and keyword coverage for large-scale code summarization.

title: Overthink-Triggered Slowdown Attacks on LVLM-Based Robotic Systems
summary:
Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have been increasingly integrated into robotic systems. However, these models may exhibit overthinking behaviors, where they generate excessively long reasoning traces, incurring an excessive inference time. This overthinking behavior poses a serious risk to robotic systems, as the adversary can deliberately trigger overthinking to slow down the decision making of a victim robotic system, causing a variety of safety issues (i.e., an overthinking-induced slowdown attack). To initiate this attack, an adversary can embed carefully crafted, human-readable scene text into the visual scene observed by a victim robotic agent, causing significant inference delays even under a strict black-box setting. Therefore, the embedded scene text serves as a significant "trigger" for the attack.
  This work systematically identifies and validates transferable triggers of overthinking in robotic systems by introducing a three-stage framework. First, we construct a diverse corpus of reasoning-intensive scene text and extract overthinking-correlated lexical features from short response prefixes. Second, we perform an efficient black-box search guided by a prefix-based proxy score while selectively confirming a small set of top candidates with full latency measurements. Third, we evaluate black-box transfer using a fixed pool of triggers on unseen images and multiple LVLMs, reporting latency amplification and attack success rates under standard thresholds. Across three representative LVLMs, all triggers yield slowdown ratios greater than 1.0x, with the strongest single-trigger case reaching 6.96x. The physical printing of the text trigger still causes up to 4.74x latency amplification. These results demonstrate that our discovered triggers are transferred between multiple LVLM models and consistently cause significant slowdowns in robotic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies that LVLMs in robotic systems can be attacked by embedding adversarial scene text that triggers "overthinking" — excessively long reasoning traces leading to dangerous inference delays. The authors propose a three-stage framework to discover transferable text triggers, achieving up to 6.96x slowdown in digital settings and 4.74x when physically printed, across multiple LVLM models.
AI.motivation: LVLMs integrated into robotic systems may exhibit overthinking behaviors (excessively long reasoning traces), which adversaries can exploit to deliberately slow down decision-making. This creates a safety risk — an "overthinking-induced slowdown attack" — where even human-readable scene text embedded in the environment can trigger significant inference delays under black-box conditions.
AI.method: A three-stage framework: (1) Construct a corpus of reasoning-intensive scene text and extract overthinking-correlated lexical features from short response prefixes. (2) Perform efficient black-box search using a prefix-based proxy score, validating only top candidates with full latency measurements. (3) Evaluate black-box transferability by testing a fixed trigger pool on unseen images and multiple LVLMs, measuring latency amplification and attack success rates.
AI.result: Across three representative LVLMs, all discovered triggers yielded slowdown ratios above 1.0x, with the strongest single trigger achieving 6.96x latency amplification. Physical printing of text triggers still caused up to 4.74x slowdown. Triggers transferred effectively between different LVLM models and consistently caused significant delays in robotic systems.
AI.conclusion: The discovered overthinking triggers are transferable across multiple LVLMs and consistently cause significant slowdowns in robotic systems, revealing a practical and dangerous attack vector where adversarial scene text can compromise real-time robotic decision-making.

title: Made to Feel: How Designers Bring Emotions into Affective Visualization
summary: Affective visualization is increasingly studied in visualization research, yet how designers bring emotions into their visualization work remains unexplored. This paper addresses this gap through semi-structured interviews with 15 visualization practitioners. Using hybrid thematic analysis, we identify: (1) three functions that emotions can serve for viewers (entry, engagement, outcome); (2) three facets of how designers work with emotion (data, design, audience), along with design strategies; and (3) ethical considerations in the design process. We also observe that affective intent often emerges during the design process rather than being planned from the outset, and that emotional impact arises from accumulated design choices rather than isolated visual elements. Finally, we highlight evaluation as a key challenge identified by our participants.

AI.tldr: Through interviews with 15 visualization practitioners, this study reveals how designers incorporate emotions into visualization: emotions serve three functions (entry, engagement, outcome), designers work across three facets (data, design, audience) with specific strategies, and ethical considerations emerge throughout. Key findings show affective intent often develops during design rather than being pre-planned, emotional impact stems from cumulative design choices, and evaluation remains a major challenge.
AI.motivation: Affective visualization is a growing area of research, but existing literature focuses on viewer experience while neglecting the designer's perspective — specifically, how practitioners intentionally or intuitively bring emotions into their visualization work. This gap motivates the study.
AI.method: Semi-structured interviews with 15 visualization practitioners, analyzed using hybrid thematic analysis (combining deductive and inductive coding approaches).
AI.result: Three main findings: (1) Three functions of emotion for viewers — entry (capturing attention), engagement (sustaining interaction), and outcome (lasting impression or behavioral change); (2) Three facets of designers' emotional work — data (emotional qualities of the dataset), design (visual strategies), and audience (tailoring emotional impact to viewers), each with associated design strategies; (3) Ethical considerations in emotionally-driven design. Two emergent observations: affective intent often arises iteratively during the design process rather than being predetermined, and emotional impact results from cumulative, holistic design choices rather than isolated visual elements. Evaluation of affective visualization was identified as a key unresolved challenge.
AI.conclusion: Designing for emotion in visualization is a complex, emergent, and ethically nuanced practice. The paper contributes a descriptive framework of how practitioners work with emotion and highlights evaluation as a critical area for future research.

title: AgentsCAD: Automated Design for Manufacturing of FDM Parts via Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning and Geometric Feature Recognition
summary: Parts manufactured with Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) often require Design for Additive Manufacturing (DFAM) modifications to ensure printability, structural integrity, and reduced post-processing. Current slicers identify defects such as steep overhangs but are unable to modify the underlying geometry. This work presents AgentsCAD, a multi-agent system that bridges raw boundary-representation (B-Rep) geometry and Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning to automate targeted DFM. The workflow begins by parsing a STEP file. The agentic system detects overhangs above a 45°threshold, constructs a face-adjacency topology graph, and optionally injects semantic feature labels from a GraphSAGE model trained on MFCAD++ (59,665 parts), before dispatching a Claude Sonnet design-reasoning agent that recommends reorientations, fillets, chamfers, and similar modifications. A GPT-4o vision-language verifier inspects rendered views to confirm geometric integrity. Outputs include a modified STEP file and a human-readable report. A test case on a birdhouse model demonstrates that the system correctly diagnoses overhangs, selects appropriate defect mitigation strategies, and proposes physically valid corrections, partially solving the geometry-to-language translation problem central to LLM-driven CAD modification.

AI.tldr: AgentsCAD is a multi-agent system that combines B-Rep geometry parsing with LLM reasoning to automate Design for Additive Manufacturing modifications for FDM parts, detecting overhangs, recommending corrections, and verifying geometric integrity.
AI.motivation: Current FDM slicers can detect printability defects like steep overhangs but lack the capability to modify the underlying geometry. This gap necessitates manual DFAM interventions, motivating an automated solution that bridges CAD geometry with LLM-driven design reasoning.
AI.method: The system parses STEP files, detects overhangs exceeding a 45° threshold, builds a face-adjacency topology graph, and optionally enriches it with semantic feature labels via a GraphSAGE model trained on MFCAD++ (59,665 parts). A Claude Sonnet agent then recommends modifications (reorientations, fillets, chamfers). A GPT-4o vision-language verifier inspects rendered views to confirm geometric correctness. Outputs include a modified STEP file and a human-readable report.
AI.result: A test case on a birdhouse model demonstrated that AgentsCAD correctly diagnoses overhangs, selects appropriate defect mitigation strategies, and proposes physically valid corrections, partially addressing the geometry-to-language translation problem in LLM-driven CAD modification.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent architecture shows promise in automating DFAM by combining symbolic geometry processing with LLM reasoning, though the geometry-to-language translation problem remains only partially solved, indicating room for further refinement.

title: Risk Architecture for AI-Native Engineering Teams: An Organizational Framework for Agentic System Governance
summary: Engineering management research has produced mature frameworks for software risk: ownership by feature, escalation by severity, and assurance by test coverage. These frameworks implicitly assume deterministic behavior, discrete and auditable change events, and clear component-to-owner mappings. Teams that build and operate agentic AI systems violate all three assumptions at once: outputs are probabilistic, systems take autonomous multi-step actions, and the risk surface mutates silently between deployments. Existing AI risk literature addresses this from above (policy frameworks such as the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001) or below (threat taxonomies such as OWASP's agentic AI guidance), but not at the layer where an engineering manager (EM) operates: roles, decision rights, and escalation structures. This paper contributes (i) a seven-dimension profile distinguishing pure software-engineering, hybrid, and AI-native teams; (ii) a six-cluster failure-mode taxonomy including a previously unarticulated cluster, dependency-boundary determinism mismatch; and (iii) a synthetic framework-adequacy methodology scoring how well each profile's risk architecture detects, contains, and escalates a defined scenario set. Because the object of study is framework adequacy rather than human behavior, the evaluation yields derived rather than observed coverage claims. Coverage degrades as teams move from pure software engineering to AI-native operation, monotonically in the median and abruptly in the count of uncovered, high-consequence failures appearing only at the AI-native step. The degradation concentrates in specific failure-mode categories, and the most severe, least-covered failures arise not inside AI-native teams but at the organizational boundary where their probabilistic outputs are consumed by determinism-assuming dependencies.

AI.tldr: Traditional software risk management frameworks assume deterministic behavior, discrete changes, and clear ownership — all violated by agentic AI systems. This paper identifies how engineering team structures degrade in risk coverage when moving from pure software to AI-native operations, introduces a novel failure-mode taxonomy, and reveals that the most severe failures occur at organizational boundaries where probabilistic AI outputs meet deterministic dependencies.
AI.motivation: Existing software risk management frameworks (ownership by feature, escalation by severity, assurance by test coverage) are built on assumptions of determinism, auditable changes, and component-owner mappings — all broken by agentic AI systems. Current AI risk literature operates either at the policy level (NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001) or at the threat-taxonomy level (OWASP), but neither addresses the operational layer where engineering managers make decisions about roles, decision rights, and escalation structures. This gap motivates the paper.
AI.method: The paper proposes three contributions: (i) a seven-dimension profile that distinguishes pure software-engineering, hybrid, and AI-native teams; (ii) a six-cluster failure-mode taxonomy, including a newly identified cluster called "dependency-boundary determinism mismatch"; and (iii) a synthetic framework-adequacy methodology that scores how well each team profile's risk architecture detects, contains, and escalates failures across a defined scenario set. The evaluation produces derived (not observed) coverage claims, since the object of study is framework adequacy rather than human behavior.
AI.result: Risk coverage degrades as teams move from pure software engineering toward AI-native operation. This degradation is monotonic in the median and abrupt in the count of uncovered high-consequence failures, which appear only at the AI-native step. Degradation concentrates in specific failure-mode categories. Critically, the most severe and least-covered failures do not originate within AI-native teams but at the organizational boundary where probabilistic outputs are consumed by dependencies that assume deterministic behavior.
AI.conclusion: Engineering management frameworks must evolve to address the unique risk profile of agentic AI systems. The most dangerous failures emerge at seams between probabilistic and deterministic subsystems, not within AI components themselves, suggesting that organizational boundary design — not just internal team practices — is the critical locus for AI risk governance.

title: IntentTune: Using user demand and personalization to resolve "unknown" query intents for e-commerce search
summary: Understanding user intent is fundamental to delivering relevant search results in e-commerce. However, substantial fraction of real-world queries are under-specified (e.g., "watch" or "shirt"), lacking explicit attributes such as gender or age group. This ambiguity poses a significant challenge for query intent detection models in e-commerce search systems, which must accurately infer latent user intent (e.g., age, gender) to support effective downstream retrieval. We introduce IntentTune, a framework for resolving ambiguous or under-specified query intents by leveraging either (1) user-specific behavioral signals including search history, browsing activity, and profile attributes or (2) population-level demand patterns aggregated across all users. Through experiments on real-world e-commerce data, we first demonstrate that population-level demand patterns alone are insufficient to reliably infer intent in under-specified queries. We then demonstrate that user-specific behavioral signals -- particularly prior search queries -- outperform both population-level statistics and static profile information for inferring gender, age group, product category, and size intent from underspecified queries.

AI.tldr: IntentTune is a framework for resolving under-specified e-commerce queries by leveraging user-specific behavioral signals (search history, browsing, profile attributes) and population-level demand patterns, demonstrating that personal behavioral signals—particularly prior search queries—significantly outperform population-level statistics for inferring latent intent attributes like gender, age group, category, and size.
AI.motivation: Many real-world e-commerce queries are under-specified (e.g., "watch", "shirt"), lacking explicit attributes like gender or age group, which creates ambiguity for search systems and degrades downstream retrieval relevance. Reliably inferring latent user intent from these ambiguous queries is a critical and unsolved challenge.
AI.method: IntentTune leverages two complementary signal sources: (1) user-specific behavioral signals (search history, browsing activity, profile attributes) and (2) population-level demand patterns aggregated across all users. The framework is evaluated on real-world e-commerce data, comparing the efficacy of these signal types for inferring gender, age group, product category, and size intent from under-specified queries.
AI.result: Population-level demand patterns alone are insufficient for reliable intent inference on under-specified queries. User-specific behavioral signals—particularly prior search queries—consistently outperform both population-level statistics and static profile attributes across all inferred dimensions (gender, age group, product category, size).
AI.conclusion: Personal behavioral history, especially past search queries, is the most effective signal for disambiguating under-specified e-commerce queries, and static profile attributes or aggregate population patterns are comparatively weak proxies for true user intent.

title: Scaling Laws for Grid-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in High Dimensions
summary: Grid-based approaches to approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search have been absent from modern scaling analyses. We present a systematic characterization of a multiprobe grid algorithm with respect to dataset size $N$ and dimensionality $d$. Our experiments reveal a previously unreported $d$-scaling crossover on the GloVe embedding family, in which multiprobe grid search maintains an approximately constant dimensional scaling exponent while other graph-, tree-, and partitioning-based methods exhibit degrading throughput. The advantage comes with near-linear query scaling in $N$, but also with lower indexing cost than competing ANN methods. Our results suggest that grid-based methods such as multiprobe grid may be competitive in rebuild-heavy or high-dimensional settings where indexing cost and dimensional robustness dictate performance. More broadly, recent work has formalized self-attention as an ANN operation. Thus, the $N$- and $d$-scaling properties of ANN algorithms may guide cost analysis of efficient transformer architectures. Code is available at: https://github.com/weiz345/MultiProbeANN.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically characterizes multiprobe grid search for ANN, revealing a previously unreported crossover in dimensional scaling where grid-based methods maintain constant scaling exponents while competing methods degrade. The approach offers near-linear query scaling, lower indexing cost, and may inform efficient transformer design.
AI.motivation: Grid-based ANN methods have been overlooked in modern scaling analyses. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically evaluating multiprobe grid search across dataset size (N) and dimensionality (d), and to understand where these methods may be competitive against contemporary graph-, tree-, and partitioning-based approaches.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic empirical characterization of a multiprobe grid algorithm, measuring query throughput scaling as a function of dataset size N and dimensionality d on the GloVe embedding family. They compare scaling behavior against other ANN paradigms (graph-based, tree-based, partitioning-based methods).
AI.result: A key finding is a d-scaling crossover on GloVe embeddings: multiprobe grid maintains an approximately constant dimensional scaling exponent, while competing methods show degrading throughput with increasing dimensionality. The method also exhibits near-linear query scaling in N and lower indexing cost than alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Grid-based methods like multiprobe grid may be competitive in rebuild-heavy or high-dimensional settings where indexing cost and dimensional robustness are critical. The authors also suggest that ANN scaling properties can inform cost analysis of efficient transformer architectures, given that self-attention has been formalized as an ANN operation.

title: Breaking Safety at the Token Boundary: How BPE Tokenization Creates Exploitable Gaps in LLM Alignment
summary: Character-level perturbations bypass safety alignment in modern LLMs despite leaving prompts human-readable. We identify and test a central structural mechanism: BPE tokenization fragments safety-critical words into sub-word pieces, and the three public alignment datasets we surveyed contain no intentionally fragmented inputs. The mechanism is a chain, tested end-to-end on five model families (Qwen-3-4B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B). An optimization targeting safety-token fragmentation flips the first-token refusal trigger on 80-100% of refused HarmBench prompts, with 48% of those flips producing genuinely harmful outputs (per-model 29-65%; gap-vs-behavior ROC-AUC 0.66-0.98, pooled 0.84). Activation patching localizes the disrupted signal to the last ${\sim}30\%$ of layers; an alignment-data scan finds zero fragmented prompts among 30,000 examples (positive-control recall $\geq 99\%$ at attack-relevant intensities); and targeted-mutation experiments isolate safety words as the disruption locus. On the defense side, a 68-cell grid (55 trained checkpoints) shows that no DPO configuration achieves seed- and pool-stable ASR closure on the three families with closed pool-size confounds. SFT trained on fragmented prompts closes ASR on 3/5 families but only via global collapse that raises refusal on benign prompts as well, indicating the missing distribution is necessary but not sufficient under the LoRA-16 recipe we tested. To distinguish selective repair from global collapse, we introduce Conv-Benign, a candidate paired diagnostic. All ASR claims are 3-judge-calibrated (cell rankings stable across judges; absolute levels $\pm$18pp; see App.~B.13).

AI.tldr: BPE tokenization fragments safety-critical words, and alignment datasets lack such fragmented inputs. This structural gap enables character-level perturbations to bypass refusal in LLMs. Activation patching localizes disruption to final layers; defense experiments show fragmented-prompt SFT closes the gap but causes global refusal collapse.
AI.motivation: Modern LLMs exhibit safety alignment that can be bypassed by character-level perturbations (e.g., altering spacing, capitalization, or inserting symbols) that remain human-readable. The authors hypothesize this vulnerability stems from a structural mechanism: BPE tokenization fragments safety-critical words into sub-word tokens, and alignment training datasets contain no such fragmented inputs, creating a distributional blind spot that attackers can exploit.
AI.method: The paper tests a causal chain: (1) An optimization procedure targets safety-token fragmentation to flip first-token refusal on HarmBench prompts across five model families (Qwen-3-4B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B). (2) Activation patching localizes the disrupted signal to the last ~30% of transformer layers. (3) An alignment-data scan of 30,000 examples confirms zero fragmented prompts (with positive-control recall ≥99%). (4) Targeted-mutation experiments isolate safety words as the disruption locus. (5) Defense evaluation uses a 68-cell grid of 55 trained DPO checkpoints, plus SFT on fragmented prompts. A new diagnostic metric, Conv-Benign, is introduced to distinguish selective repair from global refusal collapse. All ASR claims use 3-judge calibration.
AI.result: The optimization flips the first-token refusal trigger on 80–100% of refused HarmBench prompts, with 48% producing genuinely harmful outputs (per-model range 29–65%). Gap-vs-behavior ROC-AUC ranges 0.66–0.98 per model (pooled 0.84). Alignment-data scan finds zero fragmented prompts among 30,000. No DPO configuration achieves seed- and pool-stable ASR closure. Fragmented-prompt SFT closes ASR on 3/5 families but induces global collapse, raising refusal on benign prompts. Conv-Benign diagnostic confirms the trade-off.
AI.conclusion: The missing distribution of fragmented safety tokens in alignment data is a necessary but not sufficient condition for robust safety under the tested LoRA-16 recipe. Character-level attacks exploit a fundamental tokenization-level blind spot, and naive SFT-based defenses collapse into indiscriminate refusal. True robustness requires training data that covers fragmented token distributions without sacrificing benign-prompt responsiveness.

title: When Should Service Agents Reconsider? Difficulty-Routed Control in Customer-Service Operations
summary: Autonomous customer-service agents are shifting from conversational interfaces toward operational execution roles: they retrieve firm records, apply service policies, and execute backend writes such as refunds, cancellations, exchanges, order modifications, and reservation changes. This shift creates a service-control problem: firms must keep routine service fast and low-friction while preventing operational errors on requests where customer instructions, policy constraints, firm records, and backend writes interact. We propose a difficulty-routed service-control architecture that asks when service agents should reconsider before acting. A lightweight router keeps routine sessions on a low-cost baseline path and routes operationally coupled sessions to an escalated workflow. The escalated path uses conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration to concentrate deliberation and safeguards before consequential backend writes, rather than applying additional control uniformly across all service sessions. We evaluate the architecture on human-verified retail and airline tasks from $τ^{2}$-bench. In retail, the method improves reliability consistently on service requests with operational conflict. Routing evidence shows that stronger control is directed toward conflicted requests rather than broadly applied to routine ones. Dialogue and tool-use profiles suggest that gains do not come from indiscriminate interaction expansion or broader tool chains; instead, added turns and tool calls support evidence gathering, write separation, and pre-write reconsideration. Case-level evidence shows that the escalated workflow preserves fallback plans, binds retrieved records to the correct action, sequences writes, and decomposes multi-entity requests. Airline results extend the same service-control logic to reservation operations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a difficulty-routed service-control architecture for autonomous customer-service agents that distinguishes routine requests from operationally coupled ones. A lightweight router sends complex sessions (where customer instructions, policy, records, and backend writes interact) to an escalated workflow featuring conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration, improving reliability on consequential operations without burdening simple sessions.
AI.motivation: As autonomous agents move from conversation to backend execution (refunds, cancellations, order modifications), firms face a tension between keeping routine service fast and preventing costly operational errors. Uniformly applying heavy safeguards is inefficient; the paper addresses the need for selective, targeted control that only escalates deliberation when backend writes could interact dangerously with policy, records, and instructions.
AI.method: A difficulty-routed architecture: a lightweight router classifies sessions, sending routine ones to a low-cost baseline and operationally coupled ones to an escalated path. The escalated workflow uses conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration — concentrating deliberation and safeguards specifically before consequential backend writes rather than across all sessions.
AI.result: Evaluated on human-verified retail and airline tasks from τ²-bench. In retail, the method consistently improved reliability on requests with operational conflict. Routing evidence showed stronger control is directed at conflicted requests, not routine ones. Dialogue and tool-use profiles revealed gains come from evidence gathering, write separation, and pre-write reconsideration — not indiscriminate interaction expansion. Airline results extended the logic to reservation operations.
AI.conclusion: Selective escalation via difficulty routing effectively balances service speed and operational safety. Targeting deliberation before consequential writes — rather than applying uniform control — yields reliability gains without burdening routine interactions. The approach generalizes across retail and airline domains.

title: LIB-TRAP: Standard Cell Library Hardware Trojan Risk Assessment and Prevention
summary: Vulnerabilities inherent to the fabless semiconductor manufacturing model have significantly increased the risk of malicious Hardware Trojan (HT) insertion, posing severe threats to hardware security. Several HT mitigation and detection strategies have been developed, and existing works explore the insertion of HTs in the space between standard cells in an integrated circuit. However, there is a lack of research into the vulnerabilities posed by the building blocks of most digital designs on the market today, the standard cells. This work investigates a novel threat model in which standard cells are considered untrusted. Our proposed threat model provides the design house with a tampered standard cell library. The intended netlist is synthesized and implemented using the tampered library. During fabrication, a nefarious foundry replaces the library's deactivated HT cells with activated counterparts. Using open-source and industry-standard Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools, existing standard cell libraries, Saed32nm and Sky130nm, are converted into malicious libraries capable of masking the presence of arbitrary HTs from IC designers. The malicious library is then applied and characterized in multiple standard benchmark designs. To demonstrate the efficacy and stealthiness of this standard cell-based attack vector, three benchmark circuits, an AES-128 encryption core, an Ethernet controller, and a WISHBONE DMA engine, were synthesized using both clean and Trojan-infected libraries across Synopsys 32nm and SkyWater 130nm technologies. Design-level features, including total cell count, total area, dynamic power consumption, and static power, were extracted from these synthesized circuits to serve as inputs for binary classification

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel hardware Trojan attack vector where standard cell libraries themselves are weaponized. By providing a tampered library containing deactivated malicious cells, attackers can have designs unknowingly synthesized with hidden Trojans that are activated during fabrication by a colluding foundry. Experiments on AES-128, Ethernet, and DMA benchmarks across 32nm and 130nm nodes demonstrate the attack's stealth, with design-level features (cell count, area, power) used to assess detectability.
AI.motivation: Existing HT research focuses on inserting Trojans in inter-cell spaces or during design stages, but overlooks the foundational building blocks of digital designs—standard cells. With the fabless model, standard cell libraries sourced from third parties present an untrusted vector. The authors aim to expose this overlooked vulnerability and quantify the threat.
AI.method: The authors propose a threat model where a tampered standard cell library containing deactivated HT cells is supplied to the design house. Normal synthesis flows using open-source and industry EDA tools map designs onto this library. At fabrication, a malicious foundry swaps deactivated cells for activated HT counterparts. The method was validated by converting Saed32nm and Sky130nm libraries into malicious versions, then synthesizing three benchmarks (AES-128, Ethernet controller, WISHBONE DMA) on both technologies. Design metrics (cell count, total area, dynamic and static power) were extracted for binary classification analysis.
AI.result: The attack was successfully demonstrated across multiple benchmark circuits and two process technologies. Design-level features extracted from Trojan-infected vs. clean synthesized circuits were collected to serve as classification inputs, implying that distinguishing infected designs purely from these metrics is challenging, thereby confirming the attack's stealth.
AI.conclusion: Standard cell libraries represent a critical and under-explored attack surface for hardware Trojans. The demonstrated attack vector is practical, stealthy, and effective across different process nodes and benchmark designs, raising urgent concerns for hardware security in the fabless semiconductor ecosystem.

title: Evaluating Glanceable Multi-Device Family Health Tracking with Smartwatches and Home Displays
comment: Accepted with minor revisions for IMWUT 2026
summary: While ubiquitous computing research has explored diverse devices for personal health tracking, we know less about multi-device designs for family informatics, where health management is inherently collaborative. To understand how families adopt and perceive ubiquitous access to shared health data across contexts, we evaluated smartwatch-only, home display-only, and combined designs for tracking moods and goals, domains central to family health behavior regulation. 44 people across 12 families alternated between these designs over nine weeks. Log analysis revealed that mood tracking and goal reporting were significantly more frequent with the home display present compared to smartwatch-only use, despite an overall decline in mood tracking over time. Tracking peaked in afternoons, dropped on weekends, and occurred 2.6X more at home, with children tracking more consistently than adults across all designs. From interview analysis, we learned how family data glanceability on smartwatches supported opportunistic tracking and awareness while apart, whereas displays reminded families to self-track and collaborate during home routines including members that avoided wearables (e.g., non-participants). Multi-device redundancy accommodated diversity in routines, mobility patterns, and device preferences among members in the same family. We discuss opportunities for multi-device family informatics that accommodates different preferences through inclusive, glanceable, and adaptable ubiquitous data sharing.

AI.tldr: A nine-week study with 12 families (44 participants) compared smartwatch-only, home display-only, and combined designs for family mood and goal tracking. The home display significantly increased tracking frequency, children tracked more consistently than adults, and multi-device designs accommodated diverse family routines and preferences through glanceable, redundant data sharing.
AI.motivation: Ubiquitous computing research has focused extensively on personal health tracking devices, but there is limited understanding of how multi-device designs can support family informatics—where health management is inherently collaborative and involves shared data across household members with diverse device preferences, mobility patterns, and routines.
AI.method: A within-subjects, nine-week field study with 44 participants across 12 families. Families alternated between three conditions: (1) smartwatch-only tracking, (2) home display-only tracking, and (3) a combined smartwatch + home display configuration. Data collection combined quantitative log analysis (tracking frequency, timing, location) with qualitative semi-structured interviews to capture adoption patterns and perceptions.
AI.result: Mood and goal tracking were significantly more frequent when the home display was present versus smartwatch-only, despite an overall decline in mood tracking over time. Tracking peaked in afternoons, dropped on weekends, and occurred 2.6× more at home. Children tracked more consistently than adults across all conditions. Smartwatch glanceability supported opportunistic tracking and ambient awareness while apart; home displays served as reminders and collaborative anchors during home routines, including non-participant family members who avoided wearables. Multi-device redundancy accommodated diversity in routines, mobility, and device preferences within the same family.
AI.conclusion: Multi-device family informatics should embrace inclusive, glanceable, and adaptable ubiquitous data sharing to accommodate heterogeneous family member preferences. Redundancy across device form factors is not wasteful but functional, enabling families with diverse routines and attitudes toward wearables to sustain collaborative health tracking.

title: Adoption and Ecosystem Health: A Longitudinal Analysis of Open-Source Multi-Agent Frameworks
summary: Since ChatGPT's launch in November 2022, open-source agentic frameworks have proliferated, making framework selection important for engineering teams while obscured by popularity signals such as GitHub stars. This paper analyzes 15 major open-source AI agent framework repositories from late 2022 to early 2026, using 808,042 stars, 73,997 pull requests, 86,241 commits, and 987,330 user profiles to assess ecosystem health across awareness, adoption, and retention. Three findings emerge. First, headline popularity is unreliable. Star counts reflect hype cycles and inorganic activity. AutoGPT gained 111,967 stars in one month but converted fewer than 9 contributors per 1,000 stars, defined as contributor density in this research, compared with LangChain's 41. Lower-profile frameworks such as Pydantic-AI show higher contributor density, indicating deeper adoption. Second, mapping awareness against adoption shows that visibility and engagement diverge. MetaGPT and LangFlow have contributor density ratios below 5 even with their high visibility. Openai-agents-python's limited contributor base suggests institutional backing alone does not ensure community depth. By analyzing cross-framework contribution, we discover that LangChain functions as a shared infrastructure, attracting 82.5% of cross-ecosystem contributors. Third, retention drops most steeply in the first 30 days of initial contribution and stabilizes near 90 days. Overall, ecosystem health is better measured by contributor density, cross-ecosystem engagement, and retention than by stars alone. These metrics offer teams a more robust basis for framework evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates 15 open-source AI agent frameworks using 808K+ stars, 74K PRs, 86K commits, and nearly 1M user profiles, finding that GitHub stars are unreliable for assessing ecosystem health. Instead, contributor density, cross-ecosystem engagement, and retention provide more meaningful signals. LangChain serves as shared infrastructure with 82.5% of cross-ecosystem contributors, and retention drops sharply within the first 30 days.
AI.motivation: Open-source agentic frameworks have proliferated since ChatGPT's launch, and engineering teams face a difficult framework selection problem. GitHub stars — a widely used popularity signal — may be misleading due to hype cycles and inorganic activity, obscuring genuine community health and long-term viability.
AI.method: The authors collected and analyzed data from 15 major open-source AI agent framework repositories spanning late 2022 to early 2026. Metrics include 808,042 stars, 73,997 pull requests, 86,241 commits, and 987,330 user profiles. They assessed ecosystem health through three lenses: awareness (stars/visibility), adoption (contributor density, defined as contributors per 1,000 stars), and retention (contributor longevity over time). Cross-framework contribution analysis was also conducted.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Star counts are unreliable — AutoGPT gained ~112K stars in one month but had fewer than 9 contributors per 1,000 stars, versus LangChain's 41; lower-profile frameworks like Pydantic-AI showed higher contributor density. (2) Visibility and engagement diverge — MetaGPT and LangFlow had contributor density ratios below 5 despite high visibility; OpenAI's agents-python showed institutional backing alone does not ensure community depth. (3) Retention drops steeply in the first 30 days and stabilizes near 90 days. LangChain attracts 82.5% of cross-ecosystem contributors, functioning as shared infrastructure.
AI.conclusion: Ecosystem health is better measured by contributor density, cross-ecosystem engagement, and retention than by star counts alone. These metrics provide engineering teams with a more robust basis for open-source AI agent framework evaluation and selection.

title: From Anatomy to Smells: An Empirical Study of SKILL.md in Agent Skills
summary: Agent Skills provide on-demand domain knowledge to LLM agents without requiring model retraining. Each Agent Skill is defined by a mandatory SKILL.md file containing metadata and an unstructured Markdown body whose contents are left entirely to the skill author. Despite the rapid adoption of Agent Skills, little is known about how these files are authored or whether existing authoring guidelines are followed in practice. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of SKILL.md files as a software artifact. We qualitatively analyze 238 real-world skills and derive a taxonomy of 13 higher-level and 44 lower-level semantic components. We then conduct a multivocal literature review of 29 sources to identify best practices for authoring SKILL.md files and introduce skill smells as violations of these practices. Finally, we develop an automated detector and apply it to real-world skills, finding that over 99% of SKILL.md files contain at least one skill smell, and once introduced, skill smells rarely disappear as skills evolve. These findings reveal a substantial gap between recommended and actual authoring practices, motivating the development of automated techniques to remediate skill smells while increasing developer awareness of this emerging quality issue.

AI.tldr: First systematic study of SKILL.md files as software artifacts. Analyzes 238 real-world Agent Skills, deriving a taxonomy of 13 higher-level and 44 lower-level semantic components. Identifies best practices from 29 sources, introduces "skill smells" as violations, and builds an automated detector revealing >99% of skills contain at least one smell, with smells rarely removed once introduced.
AI.motivation: Despite rapid adoption of Agent Skills (which provide on-demand domain knowledge to LLM agents via SKILL.md files), there is no empirical understanding of how these files are authored or whether community guidelines are followed. This gap motivates a systematic investigation into SKILL.md authoring practices and quality.
AI.method: (1) Qualitative analysis of 238 real-world SKILL.md files to derive a taxonomy of semantic components (13 higher-level, 44 lower-level). (2) Multivocal literature review of 29 sources to identify best practices. (3) Introduction of "skill smells" as violations of those best practices. (4) Development of an automated detector applied to real-world skills, including longitudinal analysis of smell persistence.
AI.result: The taxonomy captures the structural and semantic building blocks of SKILL.md files. The multivocal review yields a catalog of best practices and corresponding skill smells. The automated detector reveals that over 99% of real-world SKILL.md files contain at least one skill smell, and once introduced, skill smells rarely disappear over the evolution of a skill.
AI.conclusion: There exists a substantial gap between recommended and actual authoring practices for Agent Skills. This motivates the development of automated remediation techniques and calls for increased developer awareness of skill smells as an emerging quality concern in the LLM-agent ecosystem.

title: Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Academic Texts
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems use the question-answering capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to access information outside their parameters. We evaluate if cluster-based semantic chunking improves retrieval and answer quality compared to fixed-size and recursive chunking evaluating on long, structured academic theses using the Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment (RAGAs) framework. RAGAs based faithfulness shows limited reliability in this setup.
