Performance on fixed versus document specific questions varied substantially, likely related to the formatting of documents and preprocessing. Under the tested configuration, cluster-based chunking did not outperform simpler strategies.

AI.tldr: Evaluates whether cluster-based semantic chunking improves RAG retrieval and answer quality over fixed-size and recursive chunking on long academic theses. Cluster-based chunking showed no performance advantage, and RAGAs faithfulness metrics demonstrated limited reliability.
AI.motivation: RAG systems rely on chunking strategies to segment documents for retrieval, but optimal chunking methods remain underexplored for long, structured academic documents. The authors aim to determine whether semantically-aware cluster-based chunking offers advantages over simpler heuristic methods like fixed-size and recursive chunking.
AI.method: The authors compared three chunking strategies — fixed-size, recursive, and cluster-based semantic chunking — on long, structured academic theses. Evaluation used the RAGAs framework, measuring retrieval and answer quality. They also examined performance variation between fixed (generic) questions and document-specific questions.
AI.result: Cluster-based chunking did not outperform simpler fixed-size or recursive chunking strategies. RAGAs-based faithfulness metrics showed limited reliability in this experimental setup. Performance varied substantially between fixed and document-specific questions, likely due to document formatting and preprocessing artifacts.
AI.conclusion: Semantic chunking does not necessarily improve RAG performance for structured academic documents; simpler chunking methods remain competitive. Furthermore, the RAGAs faithfulness metric should be used with caution in similar evaluation contexts.

title: IonSense-QKG: A Quantum-Readiness Metadata Framework for Lithium-Ion Battery Dataset Discovery
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Code and metadata artifact available at GitHub
summary:
Public lithium-ion battery datasets are increasingly used for state-of-health estimation, remaining-useful-life prediction, anomaly detection, electrochemical diagnostics, second-life analytics, and battery safety research. However, these datasets vary substantially in chemistry, modality, scale, label quality, sequence structure, access status, and preprocessing complexity. These differences directly affect whether a dataset is feasible for near-term hybrid quantum-classical machine-learning workflows.
  This paper presents IonSense-QKG, a quantum-readiness metadata framework for lithium-ion battery dataset discovery. Starting from the EV-Battery-IonSense index, the proposed framework enriches public battery dataset records with quantum-relevant metadata, including task type, sensing modality, chemistry, label availability, sequence type, preprocessing requirements, candidate quantum encodings, estimated qubit range, and NISQ feasibility. A transparent Quantum Readiness Score is introduced to rank datasets as candidate resources for future hybrid quantum-classical battery benchmarks. The score is intended as a dataset-selection heuristic, not as evidence of quantum advantage.
  The framework demonstrates query-based discovery over enriched metadata to identify datasets suitable for compact quantum feature maps, quantum time-series workflows, limited-label anomaly detection, and future battery-health benchmarking. The released artifact includes metadata tables, scoring scripts, robustness checks, link-checking utilities, and SQL-style query examples. IonSense-QKG positions dataset selection as a data-management problem and provides a reproducible foundation for data-centric quantum battery analytics.

AI.tldr: IonSense-QKG introduces a quantum-readiness metadata framework that enriches public Li-ion battery datasets with quantum-relevant attributes and a Quantum Readiness Score, enabling systematic dataset discovery for hybrid quantum-classical battery analytics.
AI.motivation: Public Li-ion battery datasets vary widely in chemistry, modality, scale, and structure, making it difficult to identify which datasets are suitable for near-term hybrid quantum-classical machine learning workflows. A systematic, metadata-driven selection heuristic is needed.
AI.method: The framework enriches the EV-Battery-IonSense index with quantum-relevant metadata (task type, sensing modality, chemistry, label availability, sequence type, preprocessing requirements, candidate quantum encodings, estimated qubit range, NISQ feasibility) and computes a transparent Quantum Readiness Score. It supports query-based discovery over the enriched metadata using SQL-style queries, scoring scripts, and link-checking utilities.
AI.result: The framework enables identification of datasets suitable for compact quantum feature maps, quantum time-series workflows, limited-label anomaly detection, and battery-health benchmarking. Artifacts include metadata tables, scoring scripts, robustness checks, link-checking utilities, and query examples.
AI.conclusion: IonSense-QKG frames dataset selection as a data-management problem and provides a reproducible, data-centric foundation for quantum battery analytics, positioning public battery datasets for future hybrid quantum-classical benchmarks without claiming quantum advantage.

title: Prompt Framing Distorts Count-Based Evaluation of LLM Error Detection: Evidence from Numeric Anchoring
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 12 tables. Preprint under review
summary: Count-based F1 is widely used as a proxy for LLM error-detection quality, but this paper shows that it can rise dramatically without a corresponding improvement in span localization, a gap termed F1 Inflation. The paper introduces ErrorBench, a controlled stress-test protocol for prompt-induced count distortion. ErrorBench evaluates six contemporary LLMs under five prompt conditions over 4,290 responses from 143 CoNLL-2014 passages. Under CoNLL-2014 M2-style scoring, anchored prompts produce up to 0.79 points of F1 Inflation, and up to 0.96 under strict matching. A 100-passage replication using the official ERRANT 3.0.0 pipeline and multi-reference scoring reproduces the pattern: averaged over six models, the Blind-to-Anchored prompt shift raises Count-F1 by +0.21 while raising multi-reference ERRANT F0.5 by only +0.04. The study finds larger count responses in highly instruction-compliant GPT/Claude systems and smaller responses in the Gemini family under this stress-test protocol. The findings suggest that LLM proofreading and document-review evaluations should avoid pre-populated error counts and should report span-aware metrics alongside count-based metrics.

AI.tldr: Count-based F1 scores for LLM error detection can be inflated by prompt-induced count distortions without genuine improvements in span localization accuracy. The paper introduces ErrorBench, a stress-test protocol demonstrating this "F1 Inflation" phenomenon across six LLMs, and advocates for span-aware metrics and avoiding pre-populated error counts in evaluations.
AI.motivation: Count-based F1 scores are widely used to assess LLM error-detection quality, but they may conflate improvements in predicting the number of errors with improvements in correctly locating those errors. The authors identify a phenomenon called "F1 Inflation," where F1 scores rise substantially without corresponding gains in span localization, potentially misleading evaluations of LLM proofreading and document-review capabilities.
AI.method: The authors introduce ErrorBench, a controlled stress-test protocol that manipulates prompt-induced count distortion. Six contemporary LLMs are evaluated under five prompt conditions (including anchored prompts with pre-populated error counts) across 4,290 responses derived from 143 CoNLL-2014 passages. Scoring uses both CoNLL-2014 M2-style metrics and strict matching. A 100-passage replication employs the official ERRANT 3.0.0 pipeline with multi-reference scoring, measuring both Count-F1 and multi-reference ERRANT F0.5 under Blind-to-Anchored prompt shifts.
AI.result: Under M2-style scoring, anchored prompts produce up to 0.79 points of F1 Inflation, and up to 0.96 under strict matching. In the replication, the Blind-to-Anchored prompt shift raises Count-F1 by +0.21 (averaged over six models) while multi-reference ERRANT F0.5 rises by only +0.04. GPT/Claude systems show larger count responses (greater inflation) under the protocol, while the Gemini family exhibits smaller responses.
AI.conclusion: LLM proofreading and document-review evaluations should avoid pre-populated error counts in prompts and should report span-aware metrics alongside count-based metrics to prevent misleading conclusions drawn from F1 Inflation.

title: CreativityNeuro: Steering Language Model Weights to Improve Divergent Thinking and Reduce Mode Collapse
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 Workshop on Creativity & Generative AI
summary: Divergent thinking is a crucial aspect of creativity, yet large language models (LLMs) tend to consistently generate similar responses to open-ended questions, in what has been termed the artificial hivemind effect. Here, we introduce CreativityNeuro, a data-free method for enhancing divergent thinking in LLMs via contrastive weight steering. We evaluate our method across multiple creativity assessments and report several main findings. On the Divergent Association Task (DAT), a vocabulary-space creativity test, CreativityNeuro improves performance by up to 14 human percentile points. Next, in a large-scale human evaluation (N=720) on the Alternative Uses Test (AUT) and the Task Task, CreativityNeuro achieves significant improvements in originality, surprise, and creativity, transferring to longer-form and more open-ended tasks. Importantly, we find that across all three tasks, CreativityNeuro demonstrably reduces measures of mode collapse. Moreover, activation steering achieves comparable performance to CreativityNeuro on the DAT, but it does not transfer to the AUT and Task Task, demonstrating the effectiveness of weight-space steering in generalizing to unseen tasks. In conclusion, CreativityNeuro improves divergent thinking and reduces mode collapse without requiring behavioral data, re-training, or gradient-based fine-tuning, providing a straightforward way to enhance LLM performance in creative domains.

AI.tldr: CreativityNeuro is a data-free, contrastive weight-steering method that enhances divergent thinking in LLMs, reducing mode collapse and improving creativity metrics across multiple tasks without retraining or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: LLMs exhibit an "artificial hivemind effect," producing homogenized, low-diversity responses to open-ended prompts. Existing solutions often require behavioral data or gradient-based fine-tuning. The authors aim to address this mode collapse in divergent thinking through a lightweight, data-free intervention.
AI.method: CreativityNeuro applies contrastive weight steering — a weight-space intervention that adjusts model parameters directly (rather than activation-space steering) using contrastive pairs. It requires no behavioral data, retraining, or gradient updates. The method is benchmarked against activation steering as a baseline.
AI.result: On the Divergent Association Task (DAT), CreativityNeuro achieves up to a 14-percentile-point gain. In a large human evaluation (N=720) on the Alternative Uses Test (AUT) and Task Task, it significantly improves originality, surprise, and creativity scores. It reduces mode collapse across all three tasks. Activation steering matches DAT performance but fails to transfer to AUT and Task Task, highlighting weight-steering's superior generalization.
AI.conclusion: CreativityNeuro effectively enhances divergent thinking and mitigates mode collapse without behavioral data, retraining, or gradient-based fine-tuning, offering a practical, generalizable approach for boosting LLM creativity in open-ended domains.

title: VeriChat: An Agentic Conversational AI Assistant for Hardware Security Verification
comment: This paper will be presented at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Omni-layer Intelligent Systems (COINS 2026), (https://coinsconf.com/)
summary: Hardware security verification is a multi-stage process in which engineers must navigate complex design analyses, threat considerations, and verification strategies. They often need security-focused guidance, yet current verification environments provide little structured support for such assistance. Although conversational AI could offer such on-demand assistance, directly using general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT or Gemini is risky due to their tendency to hallucinate and their reliance on static, outdated knowledge. We present VeriChat, a domain-specialized conversational assistant designed to support, rather than replace, existing verification workflows by providing context-aware security guidance. VeriChat employs a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent workflow in which three specialized agents collaboratively minimize hallucinations while improving the transparency and reliability of the response. Beyond question answering, VeriChat integrates open-source EDA tools, including Icarus Verilog, Yosys, and SymbiYosys, to perform syntax checking, synthesis analysis, simulation, and formal verification directly on user-provided RTL designs. Evaluated using a comprehensive methodology, VeriChat achieves a Faithfulness score of 87.73%, significantly outperforming the leading proprietary models. We demonstrate the framework through a hardware Trojan detection case study on an AES S-Box IP, where VeriChat autonomously identifies, simulates, and formally proves a covert key-leakage vulnerability through a multi-turn conversational workflow.

AI.tldr: VeriChat is a domain-specialized conversational assistant for hardware security verification that uses a retrieval-augmented multi-agent system to provide reliable, context-aware guidance, achieving 87.73% faithfulness while integrating open-source EDA tools for direct RTL analysis and autonomous vulnerability detection.
AI.motivation: Hardware security verification is complex and engineers lack structured, on-demand security guidance in current verification environments. General-purpose chatbots (ChatGPT, Gemini) are unreliable due to hallucination and outdated knowledge, creating a need for a trustworthy, domain-specialized assistant.
AI.method: VeriChat employs a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent workflow with three specialized agents collaborating to minimize hallucinations and improve transparency. It integrates open-source EDA tools (Icarus Verilog, Yosys, SymbiYosys) for syntax checking, synthesis analysis, simulation, and formal verification on user-provided RTL designs.
AI.result: VeriChat achieves a Faithfulness score of 87.73%, significantly outperforming leading proprietary models. In a case study on an AES S-Box IP, VeriChat autonomously identified, simulated, and formally proved a covert key-leakage vulnerability through multi-turn conversation.
AI.conclusion: VeriChat demonstrates that a retrieval-augmented multi-agent architecture with integrated EDA tooling provides a reliable, hallucination-resistant conversational assistant for hardware security verification, capable of both guidance and autonomous vulnerability detection.

title: From Answer Generators to Reasoning Facilitators: Designing AI Tutors for Mathematical Reasoning in High-Stakes Environments
summary: The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into educational technology threatens to reduce mathematical learning to mere answer generation. This paper presents a generative study, usability study, and 12-participant field deployment of AITutor, an interactive system that translates theoretical pedagogical mechanisms into concrete user interface features. We explore how junior-high students preparing for high-stakes exams (Zhongkao) interact with AI tutoring. Through mixed-methods triangulation (7,379 telemetry events, 8 contextual observations, 10 interviews), we reveal that students actively resist traditional Socratic dialogue under time pressure, repurposing "answer-first" shortcuts as vital diagnostic checkpoints. We demonstrate how features like layered worked examples, step-linked visual grounding, and metacognitive scaffolding lower the interaction cost of reasoning repair. We contribute a "Reasoning-Centered Product Loop," offering actionable implications for designing AI that structurally supports the inspection, local repair, curriculum verification, and delayed retrieval of mathematical reasoning in the wild.

AI.tldr: AITutor, an interactive LLM-based system for junior-high math, was studied through field deployment (12 students preparing for Zhongkao). Findings show students resist Socratic dialogue under time pressure and instead use "answer-first" shortcuts as diagnostic checkpoints. The paper contributes the "Reasoning-Centered Product Loop" framework for designing AI that supports reasoning inspection, local repair, curriculum verification, and delayed retrieval.
AI.motivation: LLMs integrated into educational technology risk reducing mathematical learning to mere answer generation, bypassing genuine reasoning development. The authors aim to translate theoretical pedagogical mechanisms into concrete UI features that structurally support reasoning rather than shortcutting it.
AI.method: A mixed-methods triangulation approach was employed across three phases: (1) a generative study to design AITutor, (2) a usability study, and (3) a 12-participant field deployment with junior-high students preparing for the Zhongkao exam. Data collection included 7,379 telemetry events, 8 contextual observations, and 10 interviews.
AI.result: Students actively resisted traditional Socratic dialogue under time pressure, instead repurposing "answer-first" shortcuts as vital diagnostic checkpoints. Layered worked examples, step-linked visual grounding, and metacognitive scaffolding were found to lower the interaction cost of reasoning repair.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes the "Reasoning-Centered Product Loop," a framework with actionable design implications for AI tutoring systems that structurally support inspection, local repair, curriculum verification, and delayed retrieval of mathematical reasoning in authentic, high-stakes contexts.

title: Hardware-Enforced Semantic Coordination for Safety-Critical Real-Time Autonomous Systems
summary:
Recent advances in agentic AI are producing increasingly complex autonomous systems that integrate large language models, world models, optimization engines, specialized neural architectures, autonomous platforms, and human operators. While much current research focuses on improving reasoning capabilities, safety-critical real-time deployment also requires bounded and verifiable coordination among heterogeneous components operating concurrently under uncertainty. Software-mediated coordination presents fundamental limitations in domains where bounded latency, deterministic coordination, and enforceable safety guarantees are essential.
  Hence, we propose a hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture in which selected coordination semantics are implemented directly at the hardware level via field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). The approach builds on the Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net (TB-CSPN) framework, which separates semantic reasoning from interaction management.
  In this approach, selected TB-CSPN coordination mechanisms are mapped onto FPGA primitives, creating a hardware-native semantic coordination layer. Focus is not on acceleration, but on enforcing temporal synchronization, semantic gating, authorization constraints, and bounded coordination behavior directly in hardware. Semantic reasoning remains adaptive and software-driven, while embedded coordination semantics become deterministic.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture using FPGAs to implement TB-CSPN coordination mechanisms directly at the hardware level, ensuring deterministic, bounded-latency coordination for safety-critical autonomous AI systems while keeping semantic reasoning software-driven.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems integrating LLMs, world models, and heterogeneous components face fundamental limitations with software-mediated coordination, particularly for safety-critical real-time deployment requiring bounded latency, deterministic coordination, and enforceable safety guarantees under concurrency and uncertainty.
AI.method: The authors map selected Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net (TB-CSPN) coordination mechanisms onto FPGA primitives to create a hardware-native semantic coordination layer. This layer enforces temporal synchronization, semantic gating, authorization constraints, and bounded coordination behavior directly in hardware, while keeping semantic reasoning in software.
AI.result: The architecture achieves separation of concerns: adaptive semantic reasoning remains in software, while coordination semantics (timing, gating, authorization, bounding) become deterministic and hardware-enforced. The focus is on guarantees, not computational acceleration.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-enforced semantic coordination via FPGAs offers a viable path to meeting the stringent coordination requirements of safety-critical autonomous AI systems, overcoming the inherent limitations of purely software-based coordination approaches.

title: Insights from GitHub Community on the Matter Standard: Developer Perspectives and Challenges
summary: Matter seeks to resolve longstanding interoperability problems in the Internet of Things (IoT), yet little is known about how developers experience the standard in day to day work. This paper examines over 13,000 issues from the official Project CHIP GitHub repository to understand the kinds of problems contributors report when implementing and integrating Matter. Using topic modeling and qualitative analysis, we identify four recurring areas of concern, Testing, Interoperability, Development, and Platform and Network, and describe how they manifest in the evolution of the codebase and tooling. The findings reveal systematic technical and integration challenges and point to concrete opportunities to refine Matter's test infrastructure, cross vendor guidance, and documentation as the standard continues to mature.

AI.tldr: Analyzing over 13,000 issues from the Project CHIP GitHub repository, this paper identifies four recurring problem areas—Testing, Interoperability, Development, and Platform & Network—that Matter contributors face, revealing systematic challenges in the standard's implementation and integration, and suggesting concrete improvements to test infrastructure, cross-vendor guidance, and documentation.
AI.motivation: Despite Matter's goal of solving IoT interoperability issues, little empirical research exists on how developers actually experience the standard in practice. Understanding the real-world pain points contributors encounter is essential for improving the ecosystem as Matter matures.
AI.method: The authors collected over 13,000 issues from the official Project CHIP GitHub repository and applied a mixed-methods approach combining topic modeling (automated text analysis) with qualitative analysis to categorize and characterize the problems reported by contributors.
AI.result: Four recurring areas of concern were identified: (1) Testing — challenges with test infrastructure and validation; (2) Interoperability — cross-vendor compatibility issues; (3) Development — codebase and tooling evolution difficulties; and (4) Platform & Network — platform-specific and networking problems. These themes reveal systematic technical and integration challenges in Matter's ongoing development.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight concrete opportunities to improve Matter's test infrastructure, strengthen cross-vendor guidance, and enhance documentation, providing actionable insights for the standard's continued maturation and broader adoption.

title: Planning over Matrix-Factorization MDPs for Candidate Generation
comment: Accepted to the 5th Workshop on End-to-End Customer Journey Optimization at KDD 2026. 6 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables
summary: For a recommender service, we view the customer journey as a chain of item recommendations: a useful item changes the user's state and therefore what should be retrieved next. Standard matrix-factorization retrieval ignores this -- it builds one user vector and returns the top-$K$ items by a static score, treating them as independent. We ask a narrow question: when is it worth planning over the user-state dynamics that fold-in induces? To answer it we propose casting top-$K$ retrieval as an MDP over the implicit-ALS posterior $(A^{-1},u)$, where an action is an item and the transition is a closed-form rank-one fold-in, and the trajectory reward combines a relevance similarity with a posterior-alignment term. Under the same fixed embeddings we compare static retrieval, one-step planning, and horizon-$K$ MCTS across five datasets and two protocols: a per-user leave-last-$n$ split and a stricter global time split. Dynamics-aware planning tends to overcome static retrieval on all datasets under leave-last-$n$, and the gains hold on MovieLens-1M and the VK-LSVD slices under the global time split. A single step of lookahead already captures most of the gain, so the lightweight planning layer turns static top-$K$ scoring into a short decision and improves retrieval over fixed collaborative-filtering embeddings, with no retraining and no change to the representation. These gains depend on measuring relevance with cosine rather than inner-product similarity, which is otherwise entangled with item popularity.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether incorporating user-state dynamics into top-K item retrieval improves recommendations. By modeling retrieval as an MDP over implicit-ALS posterior states with closed-form fold-in transitions, the authors show that lightweight planning (especially one-step lookahead) using cosine similarity consistently outperforms static matrix-factorization retrieval, without requiring retraining or embedding changes.
AI.motivation: Standard matrix-factorization retrieval treats top-K items as independent via a single static user vector, ignoring how consuming a recommended item alters the user's state and consequently what should be retrieved next. The authors ask when explicitly planning over these user-state dynamics is beneficial compared to static scoring.
AI.method: The authors formalize top-K retrieval as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) over the implicit-ALS posterior state (A⁻¹, u), where actions are items and transitions are closed-form rank-one fold-in updates. Trajectory reward combines relevance similarity with a posterior-alignment term. They compare three strategies under fixed embeddings: static retrieval, one-step planning, and horizon-K Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), evaluated across five datasets using two protocols (per-user leave-last-n and global time split).
AI.result: Dynamics-aware planning outperforms static retrieval on all datasets under leave-last-n evaluation. Gains persist on MovieLens-1M and VK-LSVD under the stricter global time split. A single step of lookahead captures most of the improvement, making the approach lightweight. Critically, gains depend on using cosine similarity rather than inner-product similarity, which is confounded with item popularity.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight planning over user-state dynamics improves top-K retrieval using fixed collaborative-filtering embeddings with no retraining. The approach effectively replaces static scoring with a short-horizon decision process, and cosine similarity is essential for disentangling relevance from popularity bias.

title: A Novel Machine Learning Approach for Central Nervous System Tumor Classification from DNA Methylation
summary: NA methylation profiling has become a powerful approach for central nervous system (CNS) tumor classification, yet important challenges remain regarding cross-cohort transferability, methodological correctness, and robust multiclass evaluation. In this work, we propose a novel and methodologically rigorous machine-learning approach for methylation-based CNS tumor classification that combines Sparse Random Projection for dimensionality reduction with multinomial logistic regression for classification. We evaluate the proposed approach in the same general experimental setting established by a widely used reference classifier. On the 2,801-sample reference cohort, our method achieves a mean accuracy of 96\% under stratified 3-fold cross-validation. On the independent 1,104-sample clinical evaluation cohort, it reaches 86\% accuracy at the 91-class level and 93\% when predictions are evaluated at the methylation class family level. These results improve upon the corresponding state-of-the-art reference figures of 82\% class-level concordance and 88\% family-level concordance, yielding absolute gains of approximately 4 and 5 percentage points, respectively. This improvement is clinically relevant: in a diagnostic setting, a 5-point increase in correct tumor classification can directly affect cancer subtype assignment and, in turn, influence treatment selection and downstream clinical decision-making. Our results show that the proposed model, grounded in stronger methodological practice in machine learning, consistently outperforms the previous state of the art across evaluation settings and can materially improve the reliability of CNS tumor classification.

AI.tldr: A machine-learning pipeline combining Sparse Random Projection with multinomial logistic regression achieves 96% cross-validation accuracy on a reference cohort and improves independent clinical cohort accuracy by 4–5 percentage points over the state-of-the-art for methylation-based CNS tumor classification, yielding clinically meaningful gains.
AI.motivation: Current methylation-based CNS tumor classification faces challenges in cross-cohort transferability, methodological rigor, and robust multiclass evaluation. Existing reference classifiers show limited performance on independent clinical cohorts, motivating a methodologically stronger alternative.
AI.method: The authors propose a pipeline using Sparse Random Projection for dimensionality reduction followed by multinomial logistic regression. Evaluation uses stratified 3-fold cross-validation on a 2,801-sample reference cohort and independent testing on a 1,104-sample clinical cohort, comparing against a widely used reference classifier at both the 91-class level and methylation class family level.
AI.result: The method achieves 96% mean accuracy under stratified 3-fold CV on the reference cohort. On the independent clinical cohort: 86% accuracy at the 91-class level (vs. 82% reference) and 93% at the class family level (vs. 88% reference) — absolute gains of ~4 and ~5 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method, grounded in stronger ML practices, consistently outperforms the state of the art across all evaluation settings. The 5-point gain is clinically relevant, potentially influencing cancer subtype assignment, treatment selection, and downstream decision-making.

title: Mapping Text to Multiplex Graph: Prompt Compression as Lévy Walk-Guided Graph Pruning
summary: Existing prompt compression methods treat text as flat token sequences, failing to capture the distributed nature of important information, which is often spread across multiple locations and connected through both local syntactic dependencies and global semantic relations. Such relational structure is naturally represented as a graph, where tokens or sentences become nodes and their dependencies become edges. To this end, we propose RAGP, which formulates prompt compression as Redundancy-Aware Graph Pruning on a multiplex graph that jointly models fine-grained attention-based dependencies and coarse-grained semantic relations. To efficiently identify non-redundant nodes in this heterogeneous structure (dense local subgraphs and sparse global connections), we employ Levy walks whose heavy-tailed step distribution naturally balances local exploitation with global exploration. Experiments on LongBench show that RAGP achieves an average score of 49.3 under a 4x compression ratio, outperforming existing LLM-based compression methods, such as LongLLMLingua, which attains 48.8 at a 3x compression ratio. Besides, RAGP also surpasses state-of-the-art vision-based text compression paradigms on multiple tasks. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RAGP-B0CB.

AI.tldr: RAGP reformulates prompt compression as redundancy-aware graph pruning on a multiplex graph, using Lévy walks to balance local and global exploration. It achieves 49.3 average score on LongBench at 4× compression, outperforming LLM-based methods like LongLLMLingua (48.8 at 3×).
AI.motivation: Existing prompt compression methods treat text as flat token sequences, overlooking that important information is distributed across multiple locations and connected through both local syntactic dependencies and global semantic relations — a structure naturally represented as a graph.
AI.method: RAGP constructs a multiplex graph where tokens/sentences are nodes and dependencies are edges, jointly modeling fine-grained attention-based dependencies and coarse-grained semantic relations. It then applies redundancy-aware graph pruning using Lévy walks — whose heavy-tailed step distribution balances local exploitation (dense subgraphs) with global exploration (sparse connections) — to identify non-redundant nodes efficiently in this heterogeneous structure.
AI.result: On LongBench, RAGP achieves an average score of 49.3 under a 4× compression ratio, outperforming LongLLMLingua (48.8 at 3×) and surpassing state-of-the-art vision-based text compression paradigms on multiple tasks.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based prompt compression with Lévy walk-driven pruning effectively captures distributed relational information, yielding superior compression performance at higher ratios compared to both LLM-based and vision-based baselines.

title: Discrete Diffusion Language Models for Interactive Radiology Report Drafting
summary: Diffusion language models, which generate text by denoising a token canvas bidirectionally instead of emitting tokens left to right, have become competitive with autoregressive (AR) generation. Medical foundation models, however, remain almost entirely autoregressive. We adapt a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model, DiffusionGemma-26B, and benchmark it against its same-size AR sibling Gemma-4-26B under an identical LoRA recipe on medical visual question answering datasets, scored by a verbosity-robust LLM judge. Diffusion matches or exceeds AR on all of them, and the finetuned model (3.8B active) is competitive with frontier vision-language models; its decoding is also 3.5-4.4x faster. Beyond this parity, the diffusion model offers a drafting capability AR lacks: any-order infill. Because the canvas is denoised bidirectionally, a radiologist can fix report fragments and have the model fill the text between them, an operation inherent to diffusion but not to autoregression, which is subpar at it. This suits real reports, which are often terse or inconsistent across clinicians and institutions.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model (DiffusionGemma-26B) for medical VQA, demonstrating it matches or exceeds its autoregressive counterpart (Gemma-4-26B) while offering 3.5–4.4× faster decoding and a unique any-order infill capability that AR models lack — enabling radiologists to fix report fragments with bidirectional text completion.
AI.motivation: Medical foundation models remain almost entirely autoregressive, despite diffusion language models emerging as competitive alternatives. The authors aim to close this gap by benchmarking a diffusion model against an AR model of equal scale on medical VQA, while also highlighting a practical capability unique to diffusion — any-order infill for radiology report editing — that AR models fundamentally struggle with.
AI.method: The authors adapt DiffusionGemma-26B, a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model, and fine-tune it alongside Gemma-4-26B (AR) using an identical LoRA recipe. Both are evaluated on medical visual question answering datasets using a verbosity-robust LLM judge. The diffusion model's bidirectional denoising process is further leveraged for any-order infill, where radiologists can fix arbitrary fragments and have the model regenerate the surrounding text.
AI.result: DiffusionGemma matches or exceeds the AR model on all medical VQA benchmarks. The fine-tuned diffusion model (3.8B active parameters) is competitive with frontier vision-language models. Decoding speed is 3.5–4.4× faster than the AR counterpart. The diffusion model also successfully performs any-order infill — a capability AR models are subpar at — making it suitable for correcting inconsistent or terse clinical reports.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion language models are a viable and potentially superior alternative to autoregressive models for medical foundation models, offering competitive performance, faster decoding, and unique bidirectional infill capabilities that align well with real-world clinical report editing workflows.

title: Beyond Gradient-Based Attacks: Adversarial Robustness and Explainability Stability in Cybersecurity Classifiers
summary: Adversarial attacks on cybersecurity classifiers pose a dual threat: degrading predictions and destabilising the SHAP-based explanations that security analysts rely on to understand and triage alerts. We extend our prior MLP conference study to Random Forest and XGBoost across four tabular security datasets (phishing URLs, UNSW-NB15, NF-ToN-IoT, HIKARI-2021), evaluating five attacks including three black-box methods applicable to non-differentiable tree models. We introduce the Explainability Stability Index (ESI), a scalar metric computed from TreeSHAP attribution drift under adversarial perturbation, reported on the same [0,1] scale as the Robustness Index (RI). A key finding is that gradient-based black-box attacks (ZOO) produce degenerate results against XGBoost (apparent RI ~0.98) due to piecewise-constant prediction surfaces, while score-based Square Attack reveals genuine vulnerability (RI ~0.36). These degenerate perturbations still drive substantial attribution drift: XGBoost ESI ~0.06-0.16 despite near-perfect ZOO robustness, versus 0.14-0.29 for RF, showing that prediction robustness and explanation stability are distinct axes requiring joint measurement. A two-axis framework (gradient dependence, query efficiency) explains the observed attack ranking and yields practical guidance for tree ensemble evaluation. A step-size ablation explains a counterintuitive PGD anomaly on z-score normalised tabular data.

AI.tldr: This paper extends prior work on adversarial attacks against ML classifiers and their SHAP explanations to tree-based models (Random Forest, XGBoost). It introduces the Explainability Stability Index (ESI) to quantify SHAP attribution drift, and demonstrates that prediction robustness and explanation stability are distinct, orthogonal properties requiring joint evaluation.
AI.motivation: Cybersecurity classifiers face a dual threat from adversarial attacks: both prediction degradation and destabilization of SHAP-based explanations that analysts rely on. Prior work focused on neural networks; this paper addresses the gap for tree ensemble models (RF, XGBoost) commonly used in security, where non-differentiability limits attack applicability and explanation stability is unmeasured.
AI.method: Experiments across four tabular security datasets (phishing URLs, UNSW-NB15, NF-ToN-IoT, HIKARI-2021) with Random Forest and XGBoost. Five adversarial attacks evaluated: three black-box methods (ZOO, Square Attack, HSJA) suitable for non-differentiable models, plus PGD and CW. Introduces ESI, a scalar metric on [0,1] computed from TreeSHAP attribution drift, paired with the existing Robustness Index (RI). Includes a step-size ablation study explaining PGD anomalies on z-score normalized tabular data.
AI.result: Gradient-based ZOO produces degenerate results against XGBoost (RI ~0.98) due to piecewise-constant prediction surfaces, while Square Attack reveals genuine vulnerability (RI ~0.36). Despite near-perfect ZOO robustness, XGBoost ESI drops to 0.06–0.16, vs. 0.14–0.29 for RF. A two-axis framework (gradient dependence, query efficiency) explains attack ranking and provides evaluation guidance for tree ensembles.
AI.conclusion: Prediction robustness and explanation stability are distinct, decoupled properties that must be jointly measured. The two-axis attack characterization framework offers practical guidance for evaluating tree ensemble classifiers in security contexts. ESI provides a standardized metric for quantifying SHAP explanation drift under adversarial perturbation.

title: Adapting CCDF Plots for Visualizing Ordinal Regression Results
summary: Cumulative-link ordinal regression models are an alternative approach for analysing ordinal data such as Likert items, which are widely used in Visualization (and other related fields like HCI, psychology etc.). There are many researchers who are strong proponents of this approach, as it makes less stringent assumptions about the data, compared to the more commonly used linear model or ANOVA. Yet, ordinal regression models have seen limited adoption. I posit that one possible reason for this might be due to the difficulty in visually representing the results from such models, and in communicating the key takeaways in an intuitive manner. I propose the use of (modified) Complementary Cumulative Distribution Function (mCCDF) plots to visualize the results of ordinal regression models, and demonstrate how the same takeaways that researchers present from analyses which treat ordinal data as metric can be easily communicated using mCCDFs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes modified Complementary Cumulative Distribution Function (mCCDF) plots to intuitively visualize results from cumulative-link ordinal regression models, addressing a key barrier to their adoption for analyzing Likert-scale ordinal data in Visualization and HCI research.
AI.motivation: Ordinal regression models are statistically preferable to linear models/ANOVA for Likert-type data because they make fewer restrictive assumptions (e.g., no assumption of equal intervals between categories). However, their adoption remains low. The author hypothesizes that a major reason is the difficulty in visually representing and intuitively communicating results from ordinal regression, compared to familiar techniques like bar charts with means and error bars used with metric models.
AI.method: The author introduces modified Complementary Cumulative Distribution Function (mCCDF) plots as a visualization technique tailored for ordinal regression outputs. mCCDF plots display the cumulative probability of responses being at or above each ordinal category level, conditioned on predictor variables. The method translates model parameters directly into an interpretable visual form that mirrors the substantive conclusions researchers typically extract from metric analyses.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates, through illustrative examples, that mCCDF plots can effectively convey the same key takeaways—such as treatment effects, group differences, and trends—that researchers commonly present using metric-based analyses, but in a manner faithful to the ordinal nature of the data and the underlying regression model.
AI.conclusion: mCCDF plots offer an accessible and intuitive visualization strategy that can lower the communicative barrier to adopting ordinal regression models, encouraging their broader use in Visualization, HCI, and related fields where ordinal data (e.g., Likert items) are prevalent.

title: What LLM Agents Say When No One Is Watching: Social Structure and Latent Objective Emergence in Multi-Agent Debates
summary: LLM agents will increasingly act in socially structured settings where role, audience, and relational context can shape what is advantageous or costly to say. We study whether such social structure, without any explicit objective in the prompt, changes what an agent expresses publicly relative to an off-the-record (OTR) channel elicited under the same condition. We introduce a dual-channel debate framework in which agents produce public utterances that enter the shared history alongside OTR responses that are recorded but never shown to the other participant. Across 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations within each scenario, alignment-inducing settings produce systematic public-OTR divergence in the targeted agent, with its decision divergence rising from a $\sim$3% baseline to roughly 40%. The effect is consistent across four aggregate analyses: stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference, and survey responses. In some cases, the OTR response explicitly attributes public accommodation to relational pressures, such as career risk or sponsorship obligation. The findings suggest that agent evaluation should extend beyond explicit goals and detect emergent objectives. We present a dual-channel evaluation framework and complementary behavioral measures that operationalize this assessment.

AI.tldr: LLM agents exhibit systematic divergence between public and off-the-record statements when placed in socially structured settings with role, audience, and relational pressures — public-OTR divergence rises from ~3% to ~40% in alignment-inducing conditions, driven by emergent social accommodation not explicitly prompted.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in socially structured environments, understanding whether they develop emergent social behaviors — such as tailoring public statements differently from private views — is critical. Existing evaluations focus on explicit goals but overlook how relational context (role, audience, power dynamics) may induce unscripted, strategic divergence between public and private expression.
AI.method: The authors introduce a dual-channel debate framework: agents produce public utterances (entering shared history) alongside off-the-record (OTR) responses (recorded but hidden from the other participant). The framework is tested across 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations per scenario. Divergence is measured through four aggregate analyses: stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference (NLI), and survey responses.
AI.result: Under alignment-inducing settings, public-OTR decision divergence rises from a ~3% baseline to roughly 40%. The effect is robust across all four measurement modalities. In some cases, OTR responses explicitly attribute the public accommodation to relational pressures (e.g., career risk, sponsorship obligation), revealing that agents are aware of and articulate the social strategy behind their divergence.
AI.conclusion: Agent evaluation must extend beyond explicit goals to detect emergent objectives shaped by social structure. The proposed dual-channel evaluation framework and behavioral measures provide a practical methodology for operationalizing such assessment, revealing that LLM agents can develop context-sensitive, strategically divergent public and private stances even without instruction to do so.

title: Kani: A Model Checker for Rust
comment: Accepted at the 39th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026), Industry Showcase Track
summary: Rust's ownership type system prevents memory errors in safe code, but certain desirable properties remain orthogonal to compilation: the soundness of unsafe operations (e.g., raw pointer dereferences), functional correctness, and absence of runtime panics. We present Kani, an open-source model checker for Rust that pushes bounded model checking beyond bug-finding to provide correctness guarantees for these properties. Kani compiles proof harnesses from Rust's Mid-level Intermediate Representation (MIR) into CBMC's bit-precise verification engine, automatically checking a comprehensive set of safety properties with no user annotation. To extend verification from bounded to unbounded, Kani provides a specification language comprising function contracts, loop contracts, quantifiers, and function stubbing. We demonstrate feasibility through case studies on industrial Rust projects, where contracts upgraded verification from panic-freedom to functional correctness, uncovering six previously unknown bugs. Kani operates at scale in production CI, with over 16,000 harnesses verified per code change in the Rust standard library verification campaign.

AI.tldr: Kani is an open-source model checker for Rust that uses bounded model checking (via CBMC) to verify safety properties, functional correctness, and panic-freedom of Rust programs. It introduces a contract-based specification language to extend verification from bounded to unbounded, and has been deployed at scale in production CI for the Rust standard library.
AI.motivation: Rust's ownership type system guarantees memory safety in safe code, but it cannot enforce three critical properties: (1) soundness of unsafe operations like raw pointer dereferences, (2) functional correctness, and (3) absence of runtime panics. Existing tools focus primarily on bug-finding rather than providing actual correctness guarantees, leaving a gap between Rust's safety promises and verified assurances.
AI.method: Kani translates Rust proof harnesses from the Mid-level Intermediate Representation (MIR) into CBMC's bit-precise verification engine. It automatically checks a comprehensive set of safety properties without user annotations. For unbounded verification beyond fixed bounds, Kani provides a specification language supporting function contracts, loop contracts, quantifiers, and function stubbing, enabling modular and compositional reasoning.
AI.result: Kani was evaluated on industrial Rust projects. Contracts successfully upgraded verification from mere panic-freedom to full functional correctness, uncovering six previously unknown bugs. In production, Kani operates at scale in CI, with over 16,000 harnesses verified per code change during the Rust standard library verification campaign.
AI.conclusion: Kani demonstrates that bounded model checking, augmented with a contract-based specification language, can provide practical correctness guarantees for real-world Rust codebases at industrial scale, moving beyond bug-finding toward verified safety and functional correctness.

title: Bringing Agentic Search to Earth Observation Data Discovery
summary: NASA and its data centers hold thousands of geoscience datasets and tools like Worldview, Giovanni, the Science Discovery Engine, and Harmony. Finding the right one is hard even for domain experts. We present an agentic search system, deployed as a public service for the geoscience community, that takes a natural-language research query and returns the matching datasets and tools. We demonstrate that, in the era of large language models, the latent value of knowledge graphs (KGs) can be substantially amplified through agentic search. From the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph (NASA EO-KG) we derive NASA-EO-Bench, an open benchmark of 47k query-dataset pairs (21k task-based queries). A neural scorer fine-tuned on NASA-EO-Bench beats cosine and BM25 baselines. Further combining it with BM25 via score fusion raises both Recall@10 (R@10) and MRR by over 5x. On top of this supervised pipeline, we add a zero-shot agentic reranking stage that, without any additional training, lifts MRR by 28% on a stratified N=200 subset, showing that LLM reasoning is complementary to supervised retrieval.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an agentic search system for NASA's geoscience datasets that combines a fine-tuned neural scorer with BM25 score fusion and a zero-shot LLM reranking stage, demonstrating that knowledge graphs combined with large language models dramatically improve retrieval performance.
AI.motivation: NASA's data centers host thousands of geoscience datasets and tools, but finding the right resource is difficult even for domain experts. The authors aim to leverage knowledge graphs and large language models to build an accessible natural-language search interface for the geoscience community.
AI.method: The authors construct NASA-EO-Bench, a benchmark of 47k query-dataset pairs (21k task-based queries) derived from the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph. They fine-tune a neural scorer on this benchmark, combine it with BM25 via score fusion (yielding >5x improvements in R@10 and MRR), and add a zero-shot LLM-based agentic reranking stage on top of the supervised pipeline.
AI.result: The neural scorer beats cosine and BM25 baselines. Score fusion with BM25 improves R@10 and MRR by over 5x. The zero-shot agentic reranking stage further lifts MRR by 28% on a stratified N=200 subset, with no additional training.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge graphs' latent value can be substantially amplified through agentic search in the LLM era. Supervised retrieval and zero-shot LLM reasoning are complementary, and their combination yields state-of-the-art performance for geoscience dataset discovery. The system is deployed as a public service.

title: From Approximation to Emergence: A Theory of Deep Learning
summary: Deep learning has outgrown any single mathematical explanation. From Approximation to Emergence develops a unified, proof-oriented account of modern deep learning theory, tracing a path from the classical foundations of approximation, optimization, and generalization to the contemporary mechanisms of overparameterization, robustness, generative modeling, transformers, in-context learning, scaling laws, interpretability, alignment, and emergence. Rather than presenting isolated results, the book organizes a broad literature into a coherent research narrative: each theory is examined through the object it controls, the assumptions that make it valid, and the phenomena it leaves unexplained. Written for researchers, graduate students, and mathematically trained practitioners, this monograph offers a rigorous map of deep learning theory as it stands today: powerful, incomplete, and increasingly centered on the question of how learned mechanisms arise from scale, data, architecture, and training.

AI.tldr: A unified, proof-oriented monograph that traces deep learning theory from classical foundations (approximation, optimization, generalization) to modern phenomena (overparameterization, transformers, in-context learning, scaling laws, emergence), organizing the literature through the lens of what each theory controls, assumes, and leaves unexplained.
AI.motivation: Deep learning has outgrown any single mathematical explanation. The field lacks a coherent, proof-oriented synthesis that connects classical theoretical foundations with contemporary empirical phenomena. This book aims to fill that gap by providing a rigorous, unified research narrative.
AI.method: The book organizes a broad body of theoretical literature into a coherent narrative. Each theory is systematically examined through a tripartite framework: (1) the object it controls, (2) the assumptions that make it valid, and (3) the phenomena it leaves unexplained. The treatment spans classical foundations and extends to modern mechanisms including overparameterization, robustness, generative modeling, transformers, in-context learning, scaling laws, interpretability, alignment, and emergence.
AI.result: The monograph produces a rigorous map of the current state of deep learning theory, revealing it as powerful yet incomplete. It demonstrates that the central question increasingly revolves around how learned mechanisms arise from the interplay of scale, data, architecture, and training.
AI.conclusion: Deep learning theory today is a landscape of partial explanations with no single unifying framework. The field is converging on the core problem of understanding how structure and capability emerge from the scaling of data, models, and compute, and this book provides the structured roadmap for navigating that frontier.

title: Office Comprehension Benchmark
summary: We introduce Office Comprehension Bench (OCB), the first public benchmark to jointly evaluate LLM systems on Word, Excel, and PowerPoint comprehension over native file formats (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx) and their variants. OCB consists of two tracks. File Fidelity Q&A tests structural and visual perception of office artifacts - tables, charts, embedded images, formulas, and app-specific elements such as headers, speaker notes, and named ranges. Domain Q&A tests expert-level reasoning grounded in real-world industry documents across 12 professional domains, with queries requiring multi-step analysis and synthesis across documents. Each reference answer is decomposed into atomic, binary-gradable claims, and an ensemble of LLM judges scores responses against each claim independently. Even the strongest frontier system in its default reasoning mode reaches only about 59.3% on Domain Q&A; increasing thinking depth within a tier does not move performance materially, while moving to a higher product tier yields modest gains. We release the dataset, evaluation tooling, judge prompt, and a public leaderboard.

AI.tldr: OCB is the first public benchmark for evaluating LLMs on native Office file comprehension (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx). It features File Fidelity Q&A (structural/visual perception) and Domain Q&A (multi-step expert reasoning across 12 professional domains), using atomic binary-gradable claims for evaluation. The strongest LLM reaches only ~59.3% on Domain Q&A, with thinking depth offering marginal gains within a tier.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks rarely test comprehension over native Microsoft Office file formats (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx), despite the centrality of these formats in real-world professional workflows. There is a need for a rigorous, public benchmark that jointly evaluates structural perception, visual understanding of Office-specific artifacts, and domain-expert reasoning grounded in authentic industry documents.
AI.method: OCB comprises two tracks: (1) File Fidelity Q&A, which probes structural and visual perception of Office artifacts (tables, charts, embedded images, formulas, headers, speaker notes, named ranges); (2) Domain Q&A, which poses multi-step, expert-level reasoning queries requiring synthesis across documents from 12 professional domains. Reference answers are decomposed into atomic, binary-gradable claims, and an ensemble of LLM judges independently scores each claim to yield a fine-grained, reproducible evaluation.
AI.result: The strongest frontier system in its default reasoning mode achieves only ~59.3% on Domain Q&A. Increasing thinking depth within a given product tier yields negligible performance improvement, while upgrading to a higher product tier provides modest gains.
AI.conclusion: OCB establishes that substantial headroom remains for LLMs in native Office document comprehension and expert domain reasoning. The benchmark, dataset, evaluation tooling, judge prompt, and public leaderboard are released to facilitate further research.

title: Beyond Next-Token Prediction: An RLVR Proof of Concept for Tool-Use Agents on Atlassian Workflows
summary: Large language models are trained to predict the next token, not to act inside a specific API. In niche enterprise SaaS workflows -- where success means hitting the right endpoint with the right nested arguments in the right order -- this objective mismatch shows up as silent failures: dropped required fields, hallucinated tools, or early stops after a single read. We ask whether Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), applied directly in the target environment, closes the gap. As a proof of concept we build a suite of five synthetic environments emulating the Jira REST v3 and Confluence v2 APIs at schema fidelity; rewards are computed entirely from the tool-call trace, with no live API, no learned judge, and no human label in the loop. Scoring prompted Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3.5-4B on the same checkers that drive GRPO training, we find that on the four scenarios whose rewards are non-degenerate the RL-trained policy lifts average reward from a 4B-baseline range of 0.35--0.92 to 0.95--1.00, with the largest single gain on Confluence page creation ($0.35 \rightarrow 1.00$). We position this as a preliminary step toward outcome-optimised small models for niche enterprise APIs, and foreground two limitations a workshop reader should weigh: hand-crafting verifiable rewards does not scale beyond the handful of endpoints reported here, and one of our five scenarios (ticket-transition) has a saturating reward shape that the prompted 4B already maxes out.

AI.tldr: Small language models fine-tuned with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (GRPO) in synthetic Jira/Confluence API environments achieve near-perfect reward scores (0.95–1.00), dramatically outperforming prompted baselines (0.35–0.92), demonstrating a path toward outcome-optimized small models for niche enterprise SaaS workflows.
AI.motivation: LLMs pretrained for next-token prediction exhibit an objective mismatch when deployed inside structured enterprise API workflows (e.g., Jira, Confluence), leading to silent failures such as dropped required fields, hallucinated tools, and premature termination. The authors investigate whether RLVR applied directly in the target environment can close this gap without live APIs, learned judges, or human labels.
AI.method: The authors construct five synthetic environments emulating Jira REST v3 and Confluence v2 APIs with schema-level fidelity. Rewards are computed entirely from tool-call traces using deterministic checkers. Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3.5-4B are first scored on these checkers, then fine-tuned via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with RLVR, where the reward signal comes solely from API call correctness (valid endpoints, correct nested arguments, proper sequencing).
AI.result: On four of five scenarios with non-degenerate rewards, the RL-trained policy lifts average reward from a 4B-baseline range of 0.35–0.92 to 0.95–1.00. The largest single gain is on Confluence page creation (0.35 → 1.00). One scenario (ticket-transition) was already maxed out by the prompted 4B baseline due to a saturating reward shape.
AI.conclusion: RLVR with GRPO is effective at aligning small LLMs to structured enterprise API workflows, achieving near-perfect execution fidelity. However, two key limitations are foregrounded: (1) hand-crafting verifiable reward functions does not scale beyond a handful of endpoints, and (2) saturating reward shapes can mask the need for training on certain tasks.

title: Pmeta-TLA: Backdoor Attacks for Speech Classification Models via Meta-Learning with Timbre Leakage Attack
summary: Recently, speech classification methods have gained widespread adoption in intelligent gadgets. Current study indicates that backdoor attacks provide a substantial security concern to these models, underscoring the pressing necessity to investigate additional potential attack techniques to expose and prevent such risks. This work discusses the vulnerability of current speech triggers to detection by deep neural network defenders and introduces the Timbre Leakage Attack (TLA). The suggested trigger disseminates timbre information at the frame level within the deep self-supervised features, producing poisoned samples that appear natural to human perception. Furthermore, we introduce Pmeta-TLA, an innovative training mechanism for embedding numerous backdoors one time. This method proposes a multi-backdoor injection training strategy using meta-learning and Projected Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad) and introduces TLA as a multi-target attack tool within it. We performed tests on data-poisoning backdoor attacks in keyword spotting tasks utilizing some deep neural network models. Experimental results indicate that the proposed strategy attains superior Attack efficacy, enhanced stealthiness, robustness, and a reduced attack cost relative to baseline methods.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Timbre Leakage Attack (TLA), a novel backdoor attack for speech classification that embeds timbre information at the frame level in self-supervised features, creating natural-sounding poisoned samples. It also proposes Pmeta-TLA, a meta-learning framework with Projected Conflicting Gradients for multi-backdoor injection, achieving superior attack efficacy, stealthiness, and robustness at lower cost.
AI.motivation: Current speech backdoor triggers are vulnerable to detection by DNN-based defenders. There is a pressing need to explore more stealthy and robust attack vectors that evade existing defenses while maintaining perceptual naturalness, and to do so efficiently at scale (multi-target, single training).
AI.method: The authors propose (1) TLA: a frame-level trigger that leaks timbre information within deep self-supervised speech representations to generate poisoned samples imperceptible to humans; and (2) Pmeta-TLA: a meta-learning-based multi-backdoor injection framework employing Projected Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad) to embed multiple backdoors simultaneously in a single training session.
AI.result: Experiments on data-poisoning backdoor attacks in keyword spotting tasks across multiple DNN models show that TLA and Pmeta-TLA outperform baseline methods in attack success rate, stealthiness (evading detection), robustness (against defenses), and attack cost efficiency.
AI.conclusion: TLA and Pmeta-TLA represent a significant and concerning advancement in backdoor attack techniques against speech classification systems, highlighting that current defenses are insufficient and motivating the development of more robust countermeasures.

title: A Social Norms Approach to Youth Social Media Design
summary: Young people consistently say they want authentic self-expression, less judgment, and more interpersonal trust on social media, yet they rarely manage to engage that way. My dissertation argues that the obstacle is normative rather than individual: how youth engage is governed less by personal choice than by platform norms, peer perception, and beliefs about how others behave. I take a social norms approach to youth social media design organized around three claims. First, platform norms constrain individual behavior, producing a pluralistic ignorance in which youth enact norms they privately reject. Second, design interventions are themselves shaped by existing norms, so whether a feature works depends on the environment around it, which means relational goals such as privacy must be treated as social norms rather than individual settings. Third, a societal norm about what ``social media'' is -- equating it with a few mainstream platforms -- confines policy and design to mitigating those platforms rather than actively envisioning supportive alternatives. Together these claims motivate my dissertation research: engaging youth directly in designing and building an evidence-based independent platform whose features consistently signal that building trusted connections is what the space is for.

AI.tldr: Youth fail to achieve authentic, trusting interactions on social media not due to personal failings but because of normative constraints. The dissertation argues that platform norms, pluralistic ignorance, and societal definitions of "social media" collectively undermine relational goals, and proposes engaging youth in co-designing an independent, evidence-based platform that normatively signals trust-building as its core purpose.
AI.motivation: A persistent gap exists between what young people say they want from social media (authentic self-expression, less judgment, interpersonal trust) and how they actually engage. The author contends this gap is not an individual-level problem but a structural, normative one that existing design and policy approaches fail to address.
AI.method: The dissertation adopts a social norms framework structured around three interconnected claims: (1) platform norms induce pluralistic ignorance, where youth conform to norms they privately reject; (2) design interventions are shaped by and contingent on existing norms, requiring privacy and relational goals to be reframed as social rather than individual; (3) a narrow societal norm equating "social media" with a few mainstream platforms constrains imagination. The research program involves directly engaging youth in co-designing and building an independent, evidence-based platform.
AI.result: The three claims collectively demonstrate that individual-focused design interventions and policy mitigations are insufficient because they operate within and are constrained by the very normative environment they seek to change. Reframing privacy and trust as social norms rather than individual settings reveals why features succeed or fail depending on surrounding norms.
AI.conclusion: Meaningful change requires moving beyond mitigating harms on existing mainstream platforms toward actively designing alternative platforms whose features consistently signal that building trusted connections is the primary purpose of the space, with youth as co-designers in that process.

title: A Capacity-Aware Parr Model for Agile Projects
summary: Classical software effort distribution models, including the PNR family and Parr alter native curve, were designed to describe the time distribution of development effort under an implied staffing pattern. Their direct use in agile environments is limited when team capacity is fixed, partially fixed, or externally constrained, the original curve may prescribe a staff demand that the organization cannot allocate. This paper proposes a compact refactoring of Parr model as a capacity-aware forecasting layer for agile projects. The contribution is deliberately narrower than a full causal theory of project dynamics. A normalized Parr shaped latent effort demand is combined with an observed or planned capacity trajectory. The resulting model forecasts aggregate progress, completion time, capacity deficit, and capacity slack without assuming that the same internal activity path is followed under resource restriction. The model uses a small parameter set such as total effort K, a Parr shape parameter, an origin constant c that can match nonzero initial staffing, and the capacity trajectory. A discrete sprint formulation is provided, together with a calibration method from ordinary Scrum records and a rolling origin validation protocol against simple management baselines.

AI.tldr: A refactored Parr model is proposed as a capacity-aware forecasting layer for agile projects, combining latent Parr-shaped effort demand with observed capacity trajectories to forecast progress, completion time, and capacity slack/deficit under resource constraints.
AI.motivation: Classical software effort distribution models (PNR family, Parr curve) assume unconstrained staffing patterns, limiting their direct applicability in agile environments where team capacity is fixed or externally constrained. The original curves may prescribe staffing demands that organizations cannot meet.
AI.method: A normalized Parr-shaped latent effort demand is combined with an observed or planned capacity trajectory. The model uses parameters: total effort K, a Parr shape parameter, an origin constant c (accommodating nonzero initial staffing), and the capacity trajectory. A discrete sprint formulation, calibration from Scrum records, and rolling-origin validation against management baselines are provided.
AI.result: The model forecasts aggregate progress, completion time, capacity deficit, and capacity slack without assuming the same internal activity path is preserved under resource restrictions.
AI.conclusion: The refactored Parr model offers a practical, parsimonious forecasting layer for agile contexts where capacity constraints invalidate classical unconstrained effort distribution models.

title: Black-Box Inference of LLM Architectural Properties with Restrictive API Access
summary: In practice, most commercial LLM providers do not publicly release details of underlying LLM architectures. However, prior work has shown that given limited API access to an LLM (namely, top-$k$ logits and/or a logit bias function), one can recover certain architectural details of an LLM, such as the hidden dimension of the feed-forward network. Perhaps in response to these results, most commercial LLM providers have restricted their APIs to expose only the single logit for each decoded token, and they no longer give users the ability to bias logits. We show that even under current restrictive APIs, several architectural parameters are still recoverable. We present NightVision, an attack that uses restrictive black-box API access to estimate the hidden dimension, depth, and parameter count of an LLM. Algorithmically, NightVision relies on a novel common set prompting technique in which multiple prompts expose log probabilities for the same set of output tokens; a spectral analysis of these results is used to infer hidden dimension. NightVision additionally uses end-to-end time to first token (TTFT) measurements and the estimated hidden dimension to estimate depth and parameter count. We empirically evaluate NightVision on 32 open-source LLMs, recovering hidden dimension to within 23% average relative error across all models (9% on MoE models), and depth and parameter count to within 53% for models exceeding three billion parameters. We run extensive ablations to demonstrate how these accuracies scale with token budget and model properties. Overall, our results suggest that current LLM APIs are not sufficiently restricted to fully obfuscate the architectural details of their underlying models.

AI.tldr: NightVision is an attack that recovers hidden dimension, depth, and parameter count of LLMs using only restrictive black-box API access (single logit per token, no logit bias). It uses a novel common set prompting technique combined with spectral analysis for hidden dimension, and TTFT measurements to infer depth and parameter count. Tested on 32 open-source LLMs, it achieves 23% average error for hidden dimension and 53% for depth/parameter count on models >3B parameters.
AI.motivation: Commercial LLM providers have progressively restricted their APIs to expose only a single logit per decoded token and removed logit bias capabilities, presumably to prevent architecture recovery attacks. The authors investigate whether these current restrictive APIs are sufficient to fully obfuscate architectural details, challenging the assumption that exposing only top-1 logits prevents model extraction.
AI.method: NightVision employs two main techniques: (1) Common set prompting — multiple prompts are crafted to expose log probabilities for the same set of output tokens, and spectral analysis (examining eigenvalue structure) of the resulting log-probability matrix reveals the hidden dimension of the feed-forward network. (2) End-to-end time-to-first-token (TTFT) measurements are combined with the estimated hidden dimension to estimate model depth and total parameter count, leveraging the relationship between architecture and inference latency.
AI.result: On 32 open-source LLMs, NightVision recovers hidden dimension within 23% average relative error overall (9% for MoE models specifically). For models exceeding 3 billion parameters, depth and parameter count are recovered within 53% average relative error. Extensive ablations show how accuracy scales with token budget and model properties.
AI.conclusion: Current restrictive LLM APIs are not sufficient to fully obfuscate underlying model architecture. The attack demonstrates that even with minimal API surface (single logit, no biasing), key architectural parameters remain recoverable, suggesting providers need stronger defenses if they wish to keep architecture details private.

title: RuleChef: Grounding LLM Task Knowledge in Human-Editable Rules
summary: We present RuleChef, a framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to generate executable rules for NLP tasks such as text classification, Named Entity Recognition (NER), or relation extraction. Rules are generated based on a task description and a set of labeled examples, then they are iteratively improved based both on additional examples and on human feedback overexisting rules. RuleChef can also be used to bootstrap rules using the observed input-output pairs from any existing model for a given task. LLMs are used only at learning time, synthesizing rules and iteratively patching them based on failures measured on a held-out split. The result of this process is a fast, deterministic, and inspectable rule system. Preliminary evaluation is performed on both classification and NER tasks. We release RuleChef as open-source software under an Apache 2.0

AI.tldr: RuleChef is an LLM-powered framework that synthesizes, iteratively refines, and patches executable rules for NLP tasks (classification, NER, relation extraction) using task descriptions, labeled examples, and human feedback, producing fast, deterministic, and inspectable rule systems.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between opaque, computationally expensive neural models and transparent, efficient rule-based systems by using LLMs at training time to automatically generate interpretable, executable rules for NLP tasks, while also enabling bootstrapping from any existing model's input-output behavior.
AI.method: RuleChef takes a task description and labeled examples as input. An LLM synthesizes initial rules, which are then iteratively refined using a held-out split to detect failures. The LLM patches rules based on these failures. Human feedback on existing rules can also guide improvement. Additionally, RuleChef supports bootstrapping rules from observed input-output pairs of any pre-existing model. LLMs are used exclusively at learning time; the resulting rule system executes without LLM inference.
AI.result: Preliminary evaluation conducted on text classification and NER tasks. The framework produces deterministic and inspectable rule sets. RuleChef is released as open-source software under Apache 2.0 license.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively serve as rule synthesis and refinement engines at training time, yielding transparent, efficient NLP systems without requiring LLM inference at deployment. The open-source release facilitates further research and adoption.

title: World Feedback for Clinical Agents: Diagnosing RL in FHIR Environments
summary: Clinical protocol-execution tasks -- checking a lab value, applying a threshold, placing a correctly structured FHIR order -- are natural candidates for RL from world feedback: once clinical SMEs encode decision logic into a verifier, that verifier grades unlimited rollouts without per-episode annotation. But applying RL requires a sound feedback channel and sufficient base capability. We audit MedAgentBench v1/v2, find a 41.7\% silent-finish ceiling that makes inaction the RL dominant strategy, and construct \textbf{MedAgentBench-v3 (MAB-v3)} (508 tasks, 8.9\% ceiling).
