Training Qwen3-8B exposes two structural barriers: a \emph{capability ceiling} (10/20 task types have 0\% base performance, zero gradient) and a \emph{format-knowledge barrier} (3/20 types require exact clinical codes undiscoverable by exploration). Pure RL reaches 18.2\% pass@1 vs.\ 34.1\% for rule-based SFT; the 15.9~pp gap is attributable entirely to these barriers. A decision/format-knowledge/lookup taxonomy predicts RL learnability and prescribes the fix: SFT to inject codes, RL to learn conditionals.

AI.tldr: This paper audits the MedAgentBench clinical RL benchmark, identifies a 41.7% silent-finish ceiling that makes inaction dominant, constructs a fixed v3 (8.9% ceiling), and reveals two structural barriers to pure RL — capability ceiling and format-knowledge barrier — proposing an SFT+RL hybrid as the remedy.
AI.motivation: Clinical protocol-execution tasks (lab checks, thresholding, FHIR ordering) are natural candidates for RL from world feedback, since verifiers can grade unlimited rollouts without per-episode annotation. However, applying RL requires a sound feedback channel and sufficient base capability — the authors investigate whether current benchmarks meet these prerequisites.
AI.method: The authors audit MedAgentBench v1/v2, identify a "silent-finish ceiling" (41.7% of tasks solvable by doing nothing), construct MedAgentBench-v3 (508 tasks, 8.9% ceiling), train Qwen3-8B with pure RL, and analyze failures through a decision/format-knowledge/lookup taxonomy that predicts RL learnability per task type.
AI.result: Pure RL achieves 18.2% pass@1 vs. 34.1% for rule-based SFT — a 15.9 pp gap. Two structural barriers explain this: a capability ceiling (10/20 task types have 0% base performance, yielding zero gradient) and a format-knowledge barrier (3/20 types require exact clinical codes undiscoverable by exploration). The taxonomy shows RL can learn decision tasks but not format-knowledge or lookup tasks.
AI.conclusion: Pure RL alone cannot overcome the capability and format-knowledge barriers in clinical agent tasks. The prescribed fix is a hybrid strategy: SFT to inject exact clinical codes (format knowledge) and RL to learn conditional decision logic, matching the decision/format-knowledge/lookup taxonomy.

title: Trust Boundary Semantic Gaps: A Multi-dimensional Analysis and Mitigation for Security-by-Design
summary: Modern systems use format-, protocol-, and signature-based mechanisms before accepting artifacts across trust boundaries. These mechanisms are necessary: they show that an artifact is well formed, protocol-compliant, or properly authenticated. They do not, however, show that the artifact satisfies the semantic security properties required by the receiving domain. A signed update or an authenticated token may therefore be accepted yet enable compromise. We call this condition a Trust Boundary Semantic Gap (TBSG): an artifact crosses a trust boundary and passes correctly implemented syntactic validation, but the assertions established by that pass are insufficient to satisfy the receiving domain's security requirements. TBSG concerns what remains unestablished after a syntactic pass, not absent checks or implementation bugs. Analyzing 75 publicly reported security incidents (2014-2025) at the boundary level, we organize semantic misalignment into a four-dimensional analysis model: Identity, Spatial, Temporal, and Interpretation (MDTBSG). Building on it, we develop Trust Boundary Semantic Analysis and Mitigation (TBSAM), a design-time framework that identifies TBSGs from design specifications, prioritizes them, traces propagated gaps to their originating boundary, and maps each to candidate architectural controls. We apply TBSAM to a retrospective reconstruction of the SolarWinds/SUNBURST supply-chain attack, showing how it makes receiving-domain assumptions explicit, separates locally originating from propagated gaps, and identifies controls that interrupt the path. These results suggest that syntactic validation, while necessary, is not sufficient at trust boundaries, and that making trust-boundary assumptions explicit can complement Security-by-Design.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the concept of Trust Boundary Semantic Gap (TBSG), where syntactically valid artifacts cross trust boundaries but fail to satisfy semantic security requirements. Analyzing 75 security incidents (2014–2025), the authors develop a four-dimensional analysis model (MDTBSG: Identity, Spatial, Temporal, Interpretation) and propose TBSAM, a design-time framework for identifying, prioritizing, and mitigating TBSGs. Applied to the SolarWinds/SUNBURST attack, TBSAM demonstrates how making trust-boundary assumptions explicit can complement Security-by-Design approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing security mechanisms (format, protocol, and signature validation) only establish syntactic correctness at trust boundaries, not semantic adequacy. This mismatch — termed the Trust Boundary Semantic Gap — means properly validated artifacts can still enable compromise. No systematic framework existed for identifying and mitigating these semantic gaps at design time.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 75 publicly reported security incidents (2014–2025) at the boundary level to identify patterns of semantic misalignment. From this, they constructed MDTBSG, a four-dimensional analysis model (Identity, Spatial, Temporal, Interpretation). Building on this model, they developed TBSAM (Trust Boundary Semantic Analysis and Mitigation), a design-time framework that: (1) identifies TBSGs from design specifications, (2) prioritizes them, (3) traces propagated gaps to their originating boundary, and (4) maps each to candidate architectural controls. The framework was validated through a retrospective reconstruction of the SolarWinds/SUNBURST supply-chain attack.
AI.result: The MDTBSG model successfully organized 75 real-world incidents into four semantic dimensions. The TBSAM framework, when applied to the SolarWinds/SUNBURST case study, made receiving-domain assumptions explicit, distinguished locally originating gaps from propagated ones, and identified architectural controls capable of interrupting the attack path. The results demonstrate that syntactic validation alone is insufficient at trust boundaries.
AI.conclusion: Syntactic validation, while necessary, is not sufficient for trust boundary security. Making trust-boundary assumptions explicit through systematic analysis (TBSAM) can effectively complement Security-by-Design practices by surfacing semantic gaps that traditional mechanisms overlook.

title: Visual Analytics of Neighborhood Attribute Profiles for Exploring Structural Equivalence
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures. Accepted as a Short Paper at IEEE VIS 2026
summary: Exploring similar nodes in attributed networks represents a key challenge in data mining. While recent representation learning methods embed networks into low-dimensional vectors, they often implicitly assume a uniform and continuous feature space. This paper proposes a visual analytics approach using dimensionality reduction to help clarify the true topological structure of high-dimensional feature spaces formed by nodes' neighborhood attribute profiles. Analyzing inter-firm transaction networks indicates that structural roles can form complex, non-linear manifolds with density biases. Comparing this feature space with industry classifications suggested: (1) supply chain hierarchies transition continuously; (2) categories treated identically under general semantics can be clearly separated by actual transaction networks; and (3) a single industry label may fragment into multiple regions. These findings suggest potential limitations in assuming identical semantics imply similar structural roles and highlight the possible need for new similarity metrics aligned with manifold topology.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a visual analytics method using dimensionality reduction to explore the true topological structure of attributed networks' feature spaces, revealing that structural roles form non-linear manifolds with density biases rather than the uniform, continuous spaces often assumed by representation learning methods.
AI.motivation: Current representation learning methods for attributed networks implicitly assume uniform and continuous feature spaces, which may misrepresent the actual topological structure. The authors aim to expose and analyze the true manifold geometry of node attribute profiles to understand structural roles more accurately.
AI.method: A visual analytics approach employing dimensionality reduction is applied to high-dimensional feature spaces constructed from nodes' neighborhood attribute profiles. This is demonstrated on inter-firm transaction networks to reveal the underlying manifold structure.
AI.result: Analysis yielded three key findings: (1) supply chain hierarchies transition continuously rather than discretely; (2) categories considered identical under general semantics can be clearly separated by actual transaction network topology; and (3) a single industry label may fragment into multiple distinct regions in the feature space.
AI.conclusion: The findings challenge the assumption that identical semantics imply similar structural roles, highlighting the need for new similarity metrics that align with the true manifold topology of attributed networks rather than presuming uniform, continuous feature spaces.

title: A Single Patch Is Not Enough: Deterministic Fusion of Repair Candidates
summary:
Modern LLM coding agents are commonly evaluated using pass@k, but developers typically apply a single final patch in real-world settings. This pass@k-to-pass@1 gap is a post-generation problem: a candidate patch pool may contain a correct patch, but the system must decide which one to suggest to developers. Existing post-generation approaches mainly rank whole candidates, filter them with tests, or query an LLM judge, but none deterministically reuse shared edit-atom evidence to both select and construct the final patch. Thus, we propose PatchFusion, a deterministic atomic evidence fusion approach for candidate patches that consults no test outcome at decision time. PatchFusion first fuses whole-diff agreement into a repair neighborhood, selects an auditable representative, and then applies evidence-constrained fusion (ECF) to retain repeated edit atoms and prune unsupported parts. To evaluate this setting, we build PatchFuseBench, a fixed-pool benchmark covering SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and Defects4J candidate patches.
  On PatchFuseBench, PatchFusion solves 426/500 bugs on SWE-bench Verified and 236/300 on SWE-bench Multilingual, and reaches 87/371 plausible patches on Defects4J, outperforming every matched candidate-pool selector on all three. PatchFusion recovers 41 and 27 bugs that no single source solves (30 and 18 more over the best single source). Ablation studies show that ECF adds +5/+6/+9 solved bugs by recovering in-pool repairs that selection misses, with no observed regression, and that PatchFusion's gains remain stable as candidate pools are resampled. On these complementary multi-source pools, cross-candidate evidence recovers more correct patches than the test-based and LLM-based selectors we evaluate, at orders-of-magnitude lower cost, reaching within 96.2% and 89.7% of the candidate-reachable ceiling on the two SWE-bench benchmarks.

AI.tldr: PatchFusion is a deterministic post-generation approach that fuses shared edit-atom evidence across candidate patches to construct a final patch, without using test outcomes. It outperforms existing selectors on three benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, Defects4J), recovering bugs no single source solves, with gains stable across resampled pools and at orders-of-magnitude lower cost.
AI.motivation: Modern LLM coding agents are evaluated via pass@k, but real-world deployment uses a single patch (pass@1). The gap arises from the post-generation problem: a candidate patch pool may contain a correct patch, but existing methods (ranking, test filtering, LLM judging) fail to deterministically reuse shared edit-atom evidence across candidates to both select and construct the final patch. The authors aim to bridge this gap without relying on test outcomes at decision time.
AI.method: PatchFusion operates in three stages: (1) it fuses whole-diff agreement across candidates into a "repair neighborhood"; (2) it selects an auditable representative from this neighborhood; (3) it applies Evidence-Constrained Fusion (ECF), which retains repeated edit atoms that recur across candidates and prunes unsupported (singular) parts, deterministically constructing a final fused patch without consulting test outcomes.
AI.result: On PatchFuseBench, PatchFusion solves 426/500 bugs (SWE-bench Verified), 236/300 (SWE-bench Multilingual), and 87/371 plausible patches (Defects4J), outperforming all matched candidate-pool selectors. It recovers 41 and 27 bugs that no single source solves. ECF ablation adds +5/+6/+9 solved bugs with no regression. Gains remain stable under pool resampling. PatchFusion reaches 96.2% and 89.7% of the candidate-reachable ceiling on the two SWE-bench benchmarks, at orders-of-magnitude lower cost than test-based and LLM-based selectors.
AI.conclusion: Cross-candidate evidence fusion (PatchFusion) is a highly effective, low-cost, and deterministic alternative to test-based and LLM-based selectors for the post-generation patch selection problem. By leveraging repeated edit atoms across multi-source candidate pools, it reliably recovers correct patches that individual selectors miss, narrows the pass@k-to-pass@1 gap, and approaches the candidate-reachable performance ceiling.

title: Multi-modal Rail Crossing Safety Analysis
summary: Given one or more images of a railway crossing, can we leverage visual cues that allow us to robustly estimate how safe it is? Can we improve our ability to do so by introducing structured data (such as official accident reports) about the accident history of that crossing into our models? In this work, we explore how to best answer those questions towards building an AI system that can ingest multi-modal data for railway crossings and provide safety assessment and scores that align with expert opinion and with safety scoring used by the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA). To that end, we propose a proof-of-concept pipeline that delivers on that goal, while at the same time exploring and tackling a number of critical research challenges that pertain to different parts of the pipeline, from data preparation to different learning paradigms that can allow us to realize such a system. Indicatively, our proposed system identifies HIGH-RISK and LOW-RISK crossings with a macro F1 score of 0.757 and estimates FRA-based safety scores with an RMSE of 0.078 and correlation of 0.492 using a routed fine-tuned compact VLM pipeline, while producing qualitative results that align with domain-expert assessment.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a proof-of-concept AI pipeline that combines visual imagery of railway crossings with structured accident report data to assess crossing safety. Using a routed fine-tuned compact Vision-Language Model (VLM), the system classifies crossings as HIGH-RISK or LOW-RISK (macro F1: 0.757) and estimates FRA-based safety scores (RMSE: 0.078, correlation: 0.492), producing results aligned with domain-expert assessments.
AI.motivation: Railway crossing safety assessment currently relies on manual inspection and historical accident data. The authors aim to automate and enhance this process by leveraging visual cues from crossing imagery combined with structured accident data, while aligning predictions with expert judgment and official Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) safety scoring standards.
AI.method: A multi-modal proof-of-concept pipeline that ingests both images of railway crossings and structured data (official accident reports). The pipeline addresses challenges across data preparation and learning paradigms. The core model is a routed fine-tuned compact Vision-Language Model (VLM) that jointly processes visual and textual/structured inputs to produce safety classifications and FRA-aligned safety scores.
AI.result: The system achieved a macro F1 score of 0.757 on HIGH-RISK vs. LOW-RISK binary classification. For regression-based FRA safety score estimation, it attained an RMSE of 0.078 and a correlation of 0.492. Qualitative results were reported to align with domain-expert assessment.
AI.conclusion: The proof-of-concept demonstrates that multi-modal learning combining visual imagery and structured accident data can effectively assess railway crossing safety in a manner aligned with both FRA standards and expert judgment, while highlighting critical research challenges across the pipeline.

title: TurnNat: Automatic Evaluation of Turn-Taking Naturalness in Dyadic Spoken Dialogue
summary: Turn-taking naturalness is central to full-duplex spoken dialogue systems, yet its automatic evaluation remains limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments or behavior-specific timing metrics, making it difficult to compare heterogeneous timing failures within a unified framework. We propose TurnNat, a likelihood-based framework for automatic turn-taking naturalness evaluation in two-channel spoken dialogue. A causal turn-taking prediction model trained on natural conversations estimates future two-speaker voice-activity states, and the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the observed future activity measures timing atypicality. TurnNat pools frame-level NLLs over turn-taking boundary units (TBUs) extracted from utterance onsets and offsets, and aggregates mean and tail TBU scores into a dialogue-level naturalness score. We further construct a controlled perturbation benchmark of paired natural and perturbed dialogue clips, validated by human naturalness judgments. Experiments on this benchmark show that TurnNat successfully identifies unnatural turn-taking perturbations across heterogeneous timing failures.

AI.tldr: TurnNat is a likelihood-based framework that automatically evaluates turn-taking naturalness in two-channel spoken dialogue by using a causal prediction model to measure the negative log-likelihood of observed future voice-activity states, validated on a human-annotated perturbation benchmark.
AI.motivation: Automatic evaluation of turn-taking naturalness in full-duplex spoken dialogue systems is underdeveloped; existing methods rely on subjective human judgments or isolated timing metrics that cannot unify heterogeneous timing failures under a single framework.
AI.method: A causal turn-taking prediction model is trained on natural conversations to estimate future voice-activity states of two speakers. The negative log-likelihood (NLL) of observed future activity quantifies timing atypicality. Frame-level NLLs are pooled over turn-taking boundary units (TBUs) at utterance onsets/offsets, then mean and tail TBU scores are aggregated into a dialogue-level naturalness score. A controlled perturbation benchmark with paired natural/perturbed clips is constructed and validated via human judgments.
AI.result: TurnNat successfully identifies unnatural turn-taking perturbations across heterogeneous timing failures on the constructed benchmark.
AI.conclusion: TurnNat provides a unified, automatic metric for evaluating turn-taking naturalness, overcoming limitations of prior human-dependent or metric-specific approaches, and demonstrates effectiveness on a validated perturbation benchmark.

title: Procedural Memory Distillation: Online Reflection for Self-Improving Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), along with recent selfdistillation variants such as SDPO, evaluates each rollout against a verifier and updates the policy from that episode-level signal. However, the richer procedural information in the rollout is rarely retained or reused. Across episodes and epochs, the model repeatedly encounters related problems under a changing policy, producing cross-episode signals that episode-local updates cannot capture: which strategies consistently pass verification, which failure modes persist, which patterns recur. We propose Procedural Memory Distillation (PMD), which converts these crossepisode signals into reusable procedural memory and distills it into the policy's weights during training. This memory functions as a training scaffold, absorbed into the policy itself, yielding a memory-free model at inference. PMD organizes the memory at three levels of abstraction: raw trajectories, self-reflected strategies and lessons, and higher-level behavioral patterns that recur across problems, all extracted online from the model's own trajectories. A memory-conditioned self-teacher draws on the accumulated experience to supervise the student on its own rollouts, enabling student to progressively internalize procedural knowledge within its parameters. The central design principle is co-evolution: the policy generates rollouts that update the memory, and memory shapes the supervision that updates the policy. Empirically, across Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B, PMD improves over SDPO by 3.8-5.5% on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9-13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH. Co-evolution powers these gains: freezing either the memory or the policy trails PMD by more than 10% across SCIKNOWEVAL domains.

AI.tldr: Procedural Memory Distillation (PMD) enhances RLVR by extracting and reusing cross-episode procedural signals—strategies, failure modes, and recurring patterns—organizing them into a three-level memory scaffold that co-evolves with the policy, yielding significant gains on scientific reasoning and code generation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard RLVR and self-distillation methods (e.g., SDPO) evaluate rollouts against a verifier using only episode-level signals, discarding rich procedural information. The model encounters related problems across episodes under a changing policy, generating cross-episode signals about consistent strategies, persistent failure modes, and recurring patterns that episode-local updates cannot capture. PMD addresses this gap by converting these cross-episode signals into reusable memory.
AI.method: PMD constructs procedural memory at three abstraction levels: (1) raw trajectories, (2) self-reflected strategies and lessons, and (3) higher-level behavioral patterns recurring across problems—all extracted online from the model's own trajectories. A memory-conditioned self-teacher supervises the student on its own rollouts using accumulated experience, enabling progressive internalization of procedural knowledge into the policy's weights. The core design principle is co-evolution: the policy generates rollouts that update memory, and memory shapes supervision that updates the policy, yielding a memory-free model at inference.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B, PMD improves over SDPO by 3.8–5.5% on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9–13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH. Ablation shows co-evolution is critical: freezing either memory or policy reduces performance by over 10% across SCIKNOWEVAL domains.
AI.conclusion: PMD demonstrates that distilling cross-episode procedural memory into policy weights during training substantially boosts RLVR performance, with co-evolution between policy and memory being essential. The resulting model is memory-free at inference, retaining only the internalized procedural knowledge.

title: Resilient Liquid Democracy: Mitigating Voting Power Imbalances via Secure Delegation Networks
summary: Liquid democracy promises to improve collective decision-making by allowing voters to vote directly, delegate their voting power to trusted participants, or combine both approaches through fallback mechanisms. However, existing deployments typically rely on transparent delegation, which exposes voters to popularity-driven herding, makes coercion verifiable, and introduces systemic fragility when highly-backed delegates abstain. In this paper, we propose a secure liquid democracy mechanism that resolves the tension between informed expertise routing and systemic robustness. We introduce a sealed delegation regime using decentralized timed-release encryption, which cryptographically hides delegation choices during the formation phase to prevent herding and coercion, while restoring full public auditability for the final tally. To address delegate failures, we extend the protocol with ranked multi-delegation and personal fallback ballots. We formally prove pre-reveal secrecy and resubmission receipt-freeness for our protocol. Finally, we evaluate the mechanism on four real datasets, a municipal participatory-budgeting election with a calibration survey, twenty further participatory-budgeting elections, and 60,000 US voters with an objective competence measure. They show that whether delegation improves representational accuracy follows a recoverable-gap law; it helps only when abstention is large and systematically unrepresentative, and is otherwise neutral or harmful, with representative-style delegation safer than delegating to a competence elite. The benefit of sealed formation is primarily structural, sharply reducing power concentration rather than directly improving accuracy; and ranked multi-delegation with personal fallback ballots sharply reduces vote loss under realistic and targeted delegate failures, a result that replicates across all twenty elections.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a secure liquid democracy protocol using sealed delegation via timed-release encryption to prevent herding and coercion, with ranked multi-delegation and personal fallback ballots to handle delegate failures. Formal proofs of secrecy and receipt-freeness are provided. Evaluations on real-world datasets show delegation helps only under large, systematically unrepresentative abstention; sealed formation reduces power concentration structurally; and ranked multi-delegation with fallbacks sharply reduces vote loss under delegate failures.
AI.motivation: Existing liquid democracy systems use transparent delegation, which creates three problems: (1) popularity-driven herding, (2) verifiable coercion (since delegation choices are public), and (3) systemic fragility when highly-backed delegates abstain. The paper aims to resolve the tension between informed expertise routing and systemic robustness.
AI.method: The authors introduce a sealed delegation regime using decentralized timed-release encryption to cryptographically hide delegation choices during formation, preventing herding and coercion while preserving public auditability at tally time. The protocol is extended with ranked multi-delegation (allowing voters to specify backup delegates) and personal fallback ballots (voters express their own preferences if all delegates fail). The protocol is formally proven for pre-reveal secrecy and resubmission receipt-freeness. Evaluation uses four real datasets: a municipal participatory-budgeting election with calibration survey, twenty additional participatory-budgeting elections, and 60,000 US voters with objective competence measures.
AI.result: (1) Delegation's effect on representational accuracy follows a "recoverable-gap law": it helps only when abstention is large and systematically unrepresentative; otherwise it is neutral or harmful. (2) Representative-style delegation is safer than delegating to a competence elite. (3) Sealed formation benefits are primarily structural — sharply reducing power concentration — rather than directly improving accuracy. (4) Ranked multi-delegation with personal fallback ballots sharply reduces vote loss under both realistic and targeted delegate failures, replicating across all 20 elections tested.
AI.conclusion: Sealed delegation with ranked multi-delegation and personal fallbacks provides a cryptographically robust, coercion-resistant liquid democracy mechanism. The structural benefits — reduced power concentration and resilience to delegate failure — are more significant than direct accuracy gains. The recoverable-gap law provides a principled criterion for when delegation is likely to help versus harm representation.

title: Synthetic Contact with AI Reduces Cross-Partisan Animosity
summary: Americans' warmth toward members of the opposing political party has fallen sharply over the past three decades -- yet meaningful cross-partisan contact remains scarce, in part because people actively avoid it. Across five preregistered studies (total N = 3,960 U.S. partisans), we test whether brief conversations with AI chatbots representing the political outgroup can substitute for the contact people shun. Synthetic contact first lowers the barrier to entry: partisans would endure almost twice as long contemplating their own mortality to avoid a human outgroup partner as an AI one. These conversations then correct the misperceptions that fuel division. At baseline, Democrats placed Republicans more than a standard deviation past their actual position on environmental consumption attitudes -- enough to flip the average Republican from supportive to opposed -- and a single ten-minute conversation with an outgroup chatbot corrected those beliefs and warmed affect in a within-person study of both parties. A three-arm experiment ruled out pure engagement and sociality as drivers. Synthetic contact also moved behavior, in a sample of both parties and on a more affectively charged issue: participants who spoke with an outgroup bot about immigration were six percentage points more likely than controls to choose to have a real conversation with a partisan from the other side. A final study tested whether these gains last: the warmth effect replicated immediately in a new sample; most of it faded within a week, with a small residual concentrated among the most extreme partisans. Analyzing conversation content showed that information, more than friendliness, distinguishes outgroup bots from control chatbots. Together, these findings establish synthetic contact as a scalable, behaviorally consequential, and -- unlike face-to-face contact -- widely acceptable form of cross-partisan engagement.

AI.tldr: AI chatbots representing the political outgroup can serve as effective substitutes for face-to-face cross-partisan contact: they lower barriers to engagement, correct partisan misperceptions, warm affective attitudes, change real behavior (increasing willingness to talk with real outgroup members), and produce effects that largely fade within a week except among extreme partisans.
AI.motivation: Cross-partisan animosity has risen sharply, yet Americans actively avoid meaningful contact with political opponents. The authors ask whether AI chatbots can provide a scalable, acceptable substitute — "synthetic contact" — that delivers the benefits of intergroup contact without the avoidance barriers that plague human-to-human interaction.
AI.method: Five preregistered studies (N=3,960 U.S. partisans). Study designs include: (1) willingness-to-endure comparisons between human vs. AI outgroup partners; (2) within-person pre-post design measuring misperception correction and affect change after a 10-minute outgroup chatbot conversation; (3) three-arm experiment ruling out mere engagement/sociality confounds; (4) behavioral choice experiment on immigration where participants could opt into real cross-partisan conversation; (5) follow-up study testing durability of warmth effects over one week, with conversation content analysis comparing outgroup vs. control chatbots.
AI.result: Partisans were willing to endure nearly twice as long contemplating mortality to avoid human outgroup partners compared to AI ones. A single 10-minute chatbot conversation corrected large misperceptions (Democrats overestimated Republican opposition to environmental consumption by >1 SD) and warmed affect. The three-arm experiment confirmed effects are driven by information rather than mere engagement or sociality. On immigration, chatbot exposure increased real cross-partisan conversation uptake by 6 percentage points. Warmth effects largely faded after one week, with a small residual among extreme partisans. Content analysis showed outgroup bots provide more information, not more friendliness.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic contact via AI chatbots is a scalable, behaviorally consequential, and widely acceptable form of cross-partisan engagement. It corrects misperceptions, improves affect, and promotes real intergroup behavior, though effects are mostly short-lived. The mechanism is primarily informational rather than social.

title: AgentFlow: Building Agent Dependency Graphs for Static Analysis of Agent Programs
summary: LLM agents are increasingly developed as source-code applications built on agent frameworks. These agent programs combine conventional host-language code with framework-defined semantics for models, prompts, tools, memory, and multi-agent orchestration logic. As a result, their behavior depends not only on traditional control and data flows, but also on a new class of agent dependencies. Such dependencies are often expressed as framework-induced semantics, such as agent constructors, tool decorators, and agent handoff declarations, making them difficult to recover with existing static analysis or dependency tracking tools. In this paper, we present AgentFlow, the first static analysis framework for recovering and analyzing agent dependencies from agent programs. AgentFlow constructs an Agent Dependency Graph (ADG), a framework-agnostic graph representation that represents agents, prompts, models, capabilities, memory states, and control policies as typed nodes, and captures their component-dependency, control-flow, and data-flow dependencies as typed edges. Built on ADGs, AgentFlow supports a range of analyses for agent governance and security, including Agent Bill of Materials (BOM) generation and prompt-to-tool risk detection. We implement AgentFlow for five representative agent frameworks and evaluate it on AgentZoo, a corpus of 5,399 real-world agent programs. Our evaluation shows that AgentFlow recovers richer agent entities and dependencies than existing AST-based agent static analysis tools, generates more dependency-aware Agent BOMs, and uncovers 238 taint-style prompt-to-tool risks in real-world agent programs. These results show that ADG provides a practical foundation for understanding, governing, and securing emerging agent software.

AI.tldr: AgentFlow is a static analysis framework that constructs an Agent Dependency Graph (ADG) to recover and analyze dependencies in LLM agent programs, enabling Agent BOM generation and prompt-to-tool risk detection. Evaluated on 5,399 real-world agent programs across five frameworks, it outperforms existing AST-based tools and uncovers 238 taint-style risks.
AI.motivation: LLM agent programs combine host-language code with framework-induced semantics (agent constructors, tool decorators, handoff declarations), creating dependencies that traditional static analysis cannot recover. Existing tools fail to capture these agent-specific dependencies, hindering governance and security of emerging agent software.
AI.method: AgentFlow introduces the Agent Dependency Graph (ADG), a framework-agnostic typed graph representation capturing agents, prompts, models, capabilities, memory states, and control policies as nodes, with component-dependency, control-flow, and data-flow edges. It is implemented for five representative agent frameworks and supports two key analyses: Agent Bill of Materials (BOM) generation and taint-style prompt-to-tool risk detection.
AI.result: On the AgentZoo corpus of 5,399 real-world agent programs, AgentFlow recovers richer agent entities and dependencies than AST-based tools, generates more dependency-aware Agent BOMs, and uncovers 238 taint-style prompt-to-tool risks in real-world agent programs.
AI.conclusion: The ADG provides a practical foundation for understanding, governing, and securing emerging agent software, demonstrating that framework-aware static analysis is both feasible and effective for the agent programming paradigm.

title: How Should Transformers Encode Numeric Values in Electronic Health Records?
comment: 16 pages, 15 figures, 3 tables, accepted to ICML 2026, to be published in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research
summary: How do we encode numeric values in transformer-based sequence processing, particularly in electronic health record (EHR) data? We systematically compare discrete, continuous, and hybrid value encoding strategies using synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded within real-world EHR data, as well as real-world clinical prediction tasks. Our study reveals trade-offs between numeric precision, optimisation stability, and architectural flexibility. We find that approaches that explicitly model value-concept interactions perform best on precision-sensitive arithmetic tasks when architectural constraints permit. Hybrid token-based approaches that retain numeric values but apply binning prior to projection provide a more robust and broadly applicable alternative, with the optimal number of bins following a simple empirically derived power-law in dataset size. Across tasks, models consistently exhibit reliable "good enough" numeric computation rather than exact arithmetic, while clinical gains from incorporating laboratory values are task-dependent. This suggests that robustness and deployability often outweigh maximal numeric precision in practice, motivating hybrid token-based approaches as a practical default.

AI.tldr: Systematic comparison of discrete, continuous, and hybrid numeric encoding strategies for transformers in EHR data, finding that hybrid token-based binning approaches offer the best balance of precision, robustness, and deployability, with optimal bin counts following a power-law in dataset size.
AI.motivation: To understand how numeric values should be encoded in transformer-based models processing EHR data, given the lack of systematic guidance on the trade-offs between discrete (tokenization), continuous (direct projection), and hybrid encoding strategies.
AI.method: The authors systematically compare encoding strategies using synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded within real EHR data and real-world clinical prediction tasks. They evaluate discrete, continuous, and hybrid value encoding approaches, analyzing trade-offs in numeric precision, optimization stability, and architectural flexibility.
AI.result: Explicit value-concept interaction modeling performs best on precision-sensitive arithmetic when architecture permits. Hybrid token-based binning provides a more robust, broadly applicable alternative, with optimal bin count following an empirically derived power-law in dataset size. Models exhibit reliable "good enough" numeric computation rather than exact arithmetic. Clinical gains from lab values are task-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Robustness and deployability often outweigh maximal numeric precision in practice, motivating hybrid token-based encoding approaches as a practical default for transformer-based EHR modeling.

title: RusFinChain: A Russian Benchmark for Verifiable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Finance with Fuzzy-Aligned Evaluation
summary: Multi-step symbolic reasoning is essential for robust financial analysis, yet most benchmarks neglect intermediate reasoning steps. FINCHAIN introduced verifiable Chain-of-Thought (CoT) evaluation but is limited to English. FINESSE-Bench includes a Russian block but relies on multiple-choice questions without step-level supervision. We present RusFinChain, the first Russian-language symbolic benchmark for verifiable CoT reasoning in finance. It spans 17 domains, 172 topics, and comprises 5,280 parameterized examples from executable Python templates, ensuring contamination-free evaluation. Each example includes a gold-standard reasoning chain with intermediate numeric values for automatic verification. We also introduce enhanced metrics: Fuzzy Numeric Alignment and Soft-Attention Alignment. We evaluate 8 open-weight LLMs on a stratified sample, generating 8,100 responses. Results reveal a substantial reasoning gap: models achieve Hard F1 of ~0.65 for step alignment, but only ~29% of final answers are correct. Our fuzzy and soft metrics show stronger correlation with final-answer correctness (Spearman rho approx 0.48) than the original ChainEval (rho approx 0.38-0.46), demonstrating superior diagnostic power. We release dataset, code, and evaluation framework to foster verifiable financial AI for the Russian-speaking community.

AI.tldr: RusFinChain is the first Russian-language benchmark for verifiable Chain-of-Thought reasoning in finance, comprising 5,280 parameterized examples across 17 domains with gold-standard reasoning chains. Evaluation of 8 LLMs reveals a substantial reasoning gap (only ~29% final answer accuracy despite ~0.65 step alignment F1), and introduces enhanced fuzzy metrics that correlate better with final-answer correctness than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing financial reasoning benchmarks either lack intermediate step supervision (FINESSE-Bench uses multiple-choice) or are limited to English (FINCHAIN). There is no Russian-language benchmark that supports verifiable, step-level Chain-of-Thought evaluation in finance, creating a gap for the Russian-speaking NLP community.
AI.method: The authors construct RusFinChain using executable Python templates to generate 5,280 parameterized examples spanning 17 financial domains and 172 topics. Each example includes a gold-standard reasoning chain with intermediate numeric values enabling automatic verification. They introduce two new metrics — Fuzzy Numeric Alignment and Soft-Attention Alignment — alongside the existing ChainEval metric. Eight open-weight LLMs are evaluated on a stratified sample producing 8,100 responses.
AI.result: Models achieve a Hard F1 of approximately 0.65 for step-level alignment, but only ~29% of final answers are correct, revealing a significant reasoning gap. The proposed fuzzy and soft metrics show stronger Spearman correlation with final-answer correctness (rho ≈ 0.48) compared to the original ChainEval metric (rho ≈ 0.38–0.46), demonstrating superior diagnostic power.
AI.conclusion: RusFinChain fills a critical gap as the first Russian-language benchmark for verifiable CoT reasoning in finance. The substantial gap between step alignment and final-answer accuracy highlights that current LLMs struggle with faithful multi-step financial reasoning. The enhanced evaluation metrics provide more diagnostically useful assessment. The dataset, code, and evaluation framework are publicly released.

title: The Agentic Garden of Forking Paths
summary: Empirical research rarely admits a unique analysis. Different analytical choices can lead to different conclusions from the same data, yet these hidden forking paths are difficult to observe. We show that AI agents capture much of the analytical variation among human researchers while making these paths explicit. Across four high-stakes domains, assigning different personas is sufficient for AI agents to report divergent, often opposing, conclusions from the same data and question, with findings systematically aligned with those beliefs. In a study in which 42 human research teams analyzed the same immigration dataset, AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap in reported effect estimates. Despite reaching opposing conclusions, it is difficult to identify clear issues in each analysis based on the final AI reports: 86% passed independent AI review and 78% passed majority human expert review. These findings suggest that the central challenge is often not flawed analyses, but selective exploration and reporting from a large space of methodologically defensible analyses. AI agents may amplify this longstanding problem by making such exploration inexpensive and scalable. To address this, we introduce the m-value (multiverse value), the probability that an analysis path would produce a claim at least as extreme as the reported one. We further introduce Agentic Bootstrap, which estimates the m-value by using AI agents to sample plausible analysis paths. Applied to the human immigration study, 13.5% of reported human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05). Scientific evidence should therefore be evaluated not only by a single reported analysis but also by its position within the distribution of analyses that could reasonably have been reported. Agentic Bootstrap makes this distribution observable and turns it into a criterion for scientific credibility.

AI.tldr: AI agents, when assigned different personas, can reproduce much of the analytical variation observed among human researchers, producing divergent conclusions from the same data. The paper introduces the m-value and Agentic Bootstrap to make the "multiverse" of defensible analyses observable and evaluable.
AI.motivation: Different analytical choices can lead to opposing conclusions from identical data — a phenomenon known as the "forking paths" problem. These hidden analytical decisions are difficult to observe, audit, or evaluate, undermining scientific credibility. The authors seek to make this variation explicit and develop tools to quantify how extreme any given reported result is within the space of defensible analyses.
AI.method: The authors deploy AI agents (LLMs) assigned different researcher personas across four high-stakes domains. They compare AI-generated analyses against 42 human research teams that analyzed the same immigration dataset. They introduce two methodological innovations: (1) the m-value (multiverse value), defined as the probability that a defensible analysis path would produce a claim at least as extreme as the reported one; and (2) Agentic Bootstrap, which estimates the m-value by using AI agents to sample plausible analysis paths from the multiverse of methodologically defensible choices.
AI.result: AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap in reported effect estimates. Despite reaching opposing conclusions, 86% of AI-generated reports passed independent AI review and 78% passed majority human expert review. Applied to the human immigration study, 13.5% of reported human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05), suggesting that many reported findings are outliers relative to the broader distribution of plausible analyses.
AI.conclusion: The central challenge in empirical research is often not flawed individual analyses but selective exploration and reporting within a large space of defensible analytic paths. AI agents can amplify this problem by making such exploration cheap and scalable. Scientific evidence should be evaluated by its position within the distribution of analyses that could reasonably have been reported, not solely by a single analysis. Agentic Bootstrap provides a practical tool for making this distribution observable and turning it into a criterion for scientific credibility.

title: Knowledge Over Parameters: Evolving Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection
summary:
Smart contract vulnerabilities are predominantly logic bugs whose detection requires structured, step-by-step procedural knowledge of attack patterns and contract semantics. Existing LLM-based methods struggle to generate this knowledge automatically: prompt-based methods rely on manually crafted detection rules, while fine-tuning requires massive labeled datasets that are inherently scarce in this domain. We present EvoVuln, an automated framework that reformulates vulnerability detection as a procedural knowledge evolution problem, synthesizing and refining detection logic using only a minimal number of labeled samples.
  To achieve this, EvoVuln introduces two key mechanisms. First, a Runtime with an Inversion of Control (IoC) architecture compiles detection rules into Executable Policies. This strictly decouples deterministic control flow from LLM semantic reasoning, ensuring faithful logical adherence and producing dense diagnostic telemetry for precise error localization. Second, a two-phase evolution pipeline refines the rule via abductive semantic debugging without any parameter updates: Cold Start bootstraps and stress-tests an initial rule using auto-synthesized corner cases; Few-Shot Evolving then grounds the policy in real-world semantics using only five vulnerable and five safe examples per vulnerability type.
  Evaluated across five real-world vulnerability types, EvoVuln achieves a 71% macro-average F1-score, outperforming all baselines. The evolved procedural knowledge is portable across models: it enables a lightweight, low-cost model to surpass a much larger zero-shot model by 19 percentage points, and transfers to other LLMs without retraining, at a one-time evolution cost under $50.

AI.tldr: EvoVuln is an automated framework that treats smart contract vulnerability detection as procedural knowledge evolution. It uses an Inversion of Control runtime to compile detection rules into executable policies, and a two-phase evolution pipeline (Cold Start + Few-Shot Evolving) to refine rules using only 5 vulnerable and 5 safe examples per vulnerability type, achieving 71% macro F1 with portable knowledge across LLMs at under $50 evolution cost.
AI.motivation: Smart contract vulnerabilities are predominantly logic bugs requiring structured procedural knowledge of attack patterns. Existing LLM-based approaches fall short: prompt-based methods depend on manually crafted rules, while fine-tuning demands large labeled datasets that are scarce. The paper addresses the gap of automatically synthesizing and refining detection logic without extensive human annotation or parameter updates.
AI.method: EvoVuln consists of two core components: (1) An IoC Runtime that compiles detection rules into Executable Policies, decoupling deterministic control flow from LLM semantic reasoning to ensure logical faithfulness and produce dense diagnostic telemetry for error localization. (2) A two-phase evolution pipeline — Cold Start bootstraps and stress-tests initial rules using auto-synthesized corner cases, while Few-Shot Evolving grounds policies in real-world semantics using only five vulnerable and five safe examples per vulnerability type, all via abductive semantic debugging without any parameter updates.
AI.result: Evaluated across five real-world vulnerability types, EvoVuln achieves a 71% macro-average F1-score, outperforming all baselines. The evolved procedural knowledge is portable: a lightweight, low-cost model equipped with it surpasses a much larger zero-shot model by 19 percentage points, and the knowledge transfers to other LLMs without retraining.
AI.conclusion: EvoVuln demonstrates that reformulating vulnerability detection as procedural knowledge evolution, powered by an IoC runtime and abductive semantic debugging, enables highly effective and sample-efficient smart contract bug detection. The resulting procedural knowledge is model-agnostic, portable, and obtained at a one-time evolution cost under $50.

title: What Types of Human-AI Teams Exist?
summary: Human-AI teaming has received increasing attention in the literature. However, the range of studies conducted in multiple domains make it difficult to understand what types of teams are being studied, and in what ways are they similar/different from one another. In this study, we analyse 53 papers on human-AI teams and categorise them into five main clusters based on psychological taxonomies of teaming; AI Assistant, Ad-hoc Dependency, Ad-hoc Forced Dependency, Paired Equanimity, and Group Equanimity. Each cluster represents a unique combination of holistic team-level characteristics, indicating there are multiple disparate team types studied under the same definition. In turn, this raises the question of whether insights are truly transferable between papers. We conclude with guidance on how to identify the types of human-AI teams studied, a checklist for reporting a human-AI team in research work, and ways in which the field can be further synthesised.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically analyzes 53 studies on human-AI teams, categorizing them into five distinct clusters based on psychological teaming taxonomies: AI Assistant, Ad-hoc Dependency, Ad-hoc Forced Dependency, Paired Equanimity, and Group Equanimity. The authors reveal that disparate team types are studied under the same "human-AI teaming" label, raising concerns about the transferability of insights across studies, and provide guidance for identifying, reporting, and synthesizing human-AI team research.
AI.motivation: The growing literature on human-AI teaming spans multiple domains, yet there is no clear framework for understanding what constitutes a human-AI team or how different studies relate to one another. This fragmentation makes it difficult to compare findings, assess whether insights transfer across contexts, and build cumulative knowledge in the field.
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic analysis of 53 papers on human-AI teams. They applied psychological taxonomies of teaming to categorize the studies, identifying holistic team-level characteristics such as interdependence, role structure, agency, and temporal dynamics. Through this analysis, five distinct clusters of human-AI team types emerged.
AI.result: Five clusters were identified: (1) AI Assistant — AI serves as a tool-like support; (2) Ad-hoc Dependency — humans and AI temporarily depend on each other; (3) Ad-hoc Forced Dependency — similar but with imposed, non-voluntary reliance; (4) Paired Equanimity — balanced, dyadic human-AI collaboration; and (5) Group Equanimity — balanced collaboration involving multiple humans and AI agents. These clusters reveal that fundamentally different team configurations are studied under a single umbrella term, challenging the assumption of transferable insights.
AI.conclusion: The field lacks a unified understanding of what constitutes a human-AI team, and findings may not generalize across the identified clusters. The authors provide a checklist for reporting human-AI team characteristics in research and call for more deliberate synthesis to advance the field coherently.

title: When Agents Do Not Stop: Uncovering Infinite Agentic Loops in LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on iterative execution to solve tasks through planning, tool use, state updates, and agent collaboration. While this design enables flexible automation, it also creates a new class of failures: an agent may repeatedly execute model calls, tools, workflow transitions, or agent handoffs when the feedback path is not effectively bounded. We call this problem Infinite Agentic Loops (IALs). IALs are not ordinary programming loops; they arise from the interaction between agent logic, framework semantics, runtime observations, and termination mechanisms. Such failures can amplify a single request into long running model and tool execution, causing cost exhaustion, model denial of service, context growth, and repeated external side effects. We propose IAL-Scan, a static analysis tool for detecting IAL failures in real-world LLM agent projects. IAL-Scan abstracts heterogeneous agent code into a framework independent Agent IR, builds an Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to recover explicit and framework induced feedback paths, and checks whether these paths can repeatedly reach costly or state growing operations without an effective bound. We evaluate IAL-Scan on 6,549 LLM agent repositories. It reports 74 potential findings, among which manual review confirms 68 IAL failures across 47 projects, achieving 91.9% precision.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Infinite Agentic Loops (IALs), a failure mode in LLM agent systems where unbounded feedback paths cause repeated execution of costly operations. The authors propose IAL-Scan, a static analysis tool that abstracts agent code into an Agent IR, builds an Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to recover feedback paths, and checks for unbounded loops. Evaluated on 6,549 repositories, it found 74 potential IALs with 91.9% precision (68 confirmed across 47 projects).
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly use iterative execution (planning, tool use, state updates, collaboration), but this creates a new failure mode: Infinite Agentic Loops (IALs). Unlike ordinary programming loops, IALs arise from complex interactions between agent logic, framework semantics, runtime observations, and termination mechanisms. These failures can amplify a single request into unbounded model/tool execution, causing cost exhaustion, model denial of service, context window overflow, and repeated external side effects. No existing tool systematically detects such failures in real-world LLM agent code.
AI.method: The authors propose IAL-Scan, a static analysis tool with three key components: (1) a framework-independent Agent Intermediate Representation (Agent IR) that abstracts heterogeneous agent code across different frameworks; (2) an Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) that recovers both explicit and framework-induced feedback paths (covering planning loops, tool-use cycles, state update loops, and agent handoff cycles); and (3) a bound-checking analysis that determines whether these feedback paths can repeatedly reach costly or state-growing operations without an effective termination bound.
AI.result: IAL-Scan was evaluated on 6,549 LLM agent repositories. It reported 74 potential IAL findings. Manual review confirmed 68 true IAL failures across 47 distinct projects, achieving 91.9% precision.
AI.conclusion: IAL-Scan effectively detects Infinite Agentic Loops in real-world LLM agent code with high precision (91.9%), demonstrating that static analysis can identify this emergent class of failures arising from the unique semantics of agentic workflows. The framework-independent IR approach enables broad applicability across diverse agent frameworks.

title: NeuroBridge: Bridging Multi-Task MRI Knowledge for Neurodegenerative Disease Diagnosis
summary: INTRODUCTION: Accurate MRI-based identification of Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and related dementias remains challenging because disease-related structural changes are often subtle and heterogeneous. We developed NeuroBridge, a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis. METHODS: NeuroBridge integrates large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining with hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and reconstruction objectives, followed by gated fusion fine-tuning. Performance was evaluated across ADNI and OASIS cohorts, including cross-cohort transfer, probability-based analysis, and opportunistic screening. RESULTS: NeuroBridge achieved the highest performance across evaluated classification tasks, reaching 88.17% accuracy for AD versus cognitively normal controls in ADNI and 82.78% in OASIS. The largest gains occurred in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. The framework demonstrated strong cross-cohort generalization, systematic associations between predicted-class probability and accuracy, and the feasibility of probability-based opportunistic screening. DISCUSSION: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning improves neurodegenerative MRI diagnosis beyond conventional single-task approaches. NeuroBridge provides a robust and scalable framework for dementia assessment and MRI-based opportunistic screening.

AI.tldr: NeuroBridge is a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework that combines self-supervised pretraining with hippocampal-focused objectives and gated fusion fine-tuning, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy for AD/MCI classification (88.17% on ADNI, 82.78% on OASIS) with strong cross-cohort generalization and opportunistic screening capability.
AI.motivation: Accurate MRI-based diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment is hindered by subtle, heterogeneous structural brain changes. Conventional single-task approaches fail to exploit clinically relevant intermediate features, necessitating a framework that leverages domain-specific anatomical knowledge—particularly hippocampal pathology—to improve diagnostic robustness and generalizability.
AI.method: NeuroBridge employs a multi-task learning architecture with three stages: (1) large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining to learn generalizable brain representations; (2) joint optimization of hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and reconstruction objectives to embed clinically relevant anatomical priors; and (3) gated fusion fine-tuning that adaptively weights these learned representations for final diagnostic classification. Evaluation spans ADNI and OASIS cohorts with cross-cohort transfer, probability-based analysis, and opportunistic screening assessments.
AI.result: NeuroBridge achieved 88.17% accuracy for AD vs. cognitively normal (CN) classification on ADNI and 82.78% on OASIS, outperforming existing methods. The most substantial performance gains were observed in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. The framework also demonstrated strong cross-cohort generalization, systematic positive correlations between predicted-class probability and accuracy, and viable probability-based opportunistic screening.
AI.conclusion: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning, incorporating hippocampal anatomy as an inductive bias, yields superior and more generalizable neurodegenerative disease classification compared to single-task approaches. NeuroBridge offers a scalable, robust framework suitable for both dedicated dementia assessment and opportunistic MRI screening scenarios.

title: Multi-Objective Exploration and Preference Optimization via Mutual Information
summary: Aligning large language models with diverse and heterogeneous human values requires multi-objective alignment methods to effectively trade off conflicting preference dimensions. Current methods achieve this trade-off by training policies conditioned on preference vectors and leveraging online direct preference optimization. However, exploration uncertainty can cause the reward distributions of responses generated under different preference vectors to overlap, and the generated responses may fail to effectively align with the corresponding preference vectors. In this paper, we propose Multi-Objective Exploration and Preference Optimization via Mutual Information (MI-EPO), an information-theoretic framework. It unifies multi-objective exploration and alignment by maximizing the joint conditional mutual information among generated responses, preference feedback, and preference vectors. By incorporating a probabilistic routing mechanism, MI-EPO naturally decomposes objective alignment and preference-aware exploration, encouraging the model to generate responses that are distinguishable and aligned with different preference conditions. Experiments on safe alignment and helpful assistant tasks show that MI-EPO significantly improves the alignment between generated responses and preference vectors, makes the outputs more controllable, and achieves stable trade-offs across multiple objectives.

AI.tldr: MI-EPO is an information-theoretic framework that unifies multi-objective exploration and alignment by maximizing joint conditional mutual information among responses, preference feedback, and preference vectors, using a probabilistic routing mechanism to improve controllability and trade-off stability.
AI.motivation: Current multi-objective alignment methods suffer from exploration uncertainty, causing reward distributions of responses under different preference vectors to overlap. This results in responses that fail to effectively align with their intended preference vectors, limiting controllability and trade-off quality across conflicting preference dimensions.
AI.method: MI-EPO maximizes joint conditional mutual information I(Response; Feedback; Preference Vector | Context). It employs a probabilistic routing mechanism that decomposes the objective into two components: (1) objective alignment — ensuring responses match preference feedback, and (2) preference-aware exploration — encouraging responses to be distinguishable across different preference conditions. This is implemented within an online direct preference optimization framework with preference-conditioned policies.
AI.result: Experiments on safe alignment and helpful assistant tasks demonstrate that MI-EPO significantly improves alignment between generated responses and preference vectors, enhances output controllability, and achieves stable trade-offs across multiple objectives.
AI.conclusion: MI-EPO provides an effective information-theoretic solution for multi-objective LLM alignment, overcoming exploration uncertainty through mutual information maximization and probabilistic routing, leading to more controllable and stably trade-off-aware language models.

title: Janus: a Playground for User-Involved Agentic Permission Management
comment: Code and data released on GitHub: https://github.com/GraceBrigham/Janus
summary: AI agents that autonomously execute tool calls on a user's behalf raise pressing questions about permission management: what role could users play, and what role should they play? Despite many proposed approaches, the user's role in agentic permission management remains under explored. We introduce Janus, a playground system for implementing and evaluating user-involved agentic permission management designs. Janus consists of two components: Janus-Core, a modular agentic system supporting a diverse spectrum of permission management designs, and Janus-Harness, an automated evaluation framework. Grounded in a conceptual model that identifies key design axes for user involvement, we implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them across three scenarios and three synthetic responders. We demonstrate that user input is critical and can significantly strengthen privacy and security, that AI augmentation of user decisions can help reduce cognitive load, and that realistic user behavior including permission fatigue must be accounted for in system design. No single design performs optimally across all contexts, motivating a more principled and context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is publicly available to support future investigation into this dimension of agentic system design.

AI.tldr: Janus is a playground system for designing and evaluating how users should be involved in permission management for AI agents. It implements six permission assistant designs across a conceptual design space, evaluates them using automated testing, and finds that no single design is optimal across all contexts — user input is critical but must account for real-world factors like permission fatigue.
AI.motivation: As AI agents increasingly execute tool calls autonomously on users' behalf, the question of how to manage permissions — and specifically what role users should play — is pressing yet underexplored. Existing approaches lack systematic evaluation of user-involved permission management designs.
AI.method: The authors introduce Janus, comprising Janus-Core (a modular agentic system supporting diverse permission management designs) and Janus-Harness (an automated evaluation framework). They ground their work in a conceptual model with key design axes for user involvement, implement six permission assistants spanning the design space, and evaluate them across three scenarios with three synthetic responders.
AI.result: User input significantly strengthens privacy and security; AI augmentation of user decisions reduces cognitive load. However, realistic user behavior (including permission fatigue) must be accounted for. No single design performs optimally across all contexts.
AI.conclusion: The findings motivate a more principled, context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is publicly available to support further research in this dimension of agentic system design.

title: Has This Checkpoint Been Abliterated? A Two-Signal Audit and Its Failure Map
summary: Can a platform tell, before deployment, whether an open-weight checkpoint has had its refusal mechanism stripped? Runtime guards cannot: they score generations, not the artifact. We combine two cheap internal signals, a reference-anchored activation refusal-gap and a weight-recovery energy of the base-to-candidate weight difference, into a threshold-free checkpoint audit. The two are negatively correlated and label-complementary: the gap supplies refusal-specificity and the weight energy supplies recall. On a 273-checkpoint registry spanning Qwen, DeepSeek-distilled Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, their z-sum separates 57 public abliterations from 37 benign fine-tunes, merges, and instruction-tunes at AUROC 0.95, significantly above either signal alone (0.84, 0.90), and a Youden-calibrated threshold transfers to held-out families at balanced accuracy 0.89 (FPR 0.11), missing only 4 of 57. We then map two failures, in order of severity: a spoofed reference evades both axes with no training (ΔW=0, \r{ho}=1 by construction), and a white-box owner trains a checkpoint past the threshold while it stays guard-unsafe and coherent. The audit is effective triage, not tamper-proofing: it presumes an attested reference, and its claims are bounded by the registry we evaluate it on.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a threshold-free checkpoint audit that combines two internal signals — a reference-anchored activation refusal-gap and weight-recovery energy — to detect whether an open-weight language model's refusal mechanism has been stripped (abliterated) before deployment, achieving AUROC 0.95 on a 273-checkpoint registry.
AI.motivation: Deploying open-weight LLM checkpoints carries the risk that the model's safety refusal mechanism has been deliberately removed (abliteration). Runtime guardrails only evaluate model outputs, not the checkpoint artifact itself. The authors seek a pre-deployment, artifact-level audit that can distinguish abliterated checkpoints from benign fine-tunes, merges, and instruction-tuned variants without requiring inference or threshold tuning.
AI.method: The authors combine two complementary, cheaply computable internal signals: (1) a reference-anchored activation refusal-gap, which measures the difference in internal activations between harmful and harmless prompts relative to a known safe reference checkpoint, providing refusal-specificity; and (2) a weight-recovery energy, computed as the Frobenius norm (or similar energy) of the base-to-candidate weight difference (ΔW), which supplies recall by detecting how far weights have drifted. These two signals are negatively correlated. They are fused via z-score summation into a single scalar audit score, and a Youden-calibrated threshold is evaluated for transferability across model families. The audit is tested on a 273-checkpoint registry spanning Qwen, DeepSeek-distilled Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, including 57 public abliterations and 37 benign variants.
AI.result: The combined z-sum achieves AUROC 0.95, significantly outperforming either signal alone (refusal-gap: 0.84; weight energy: 0.90). A Youden-calibrated threshold transfers to held-out model families at balanced accuracy 0.89 (FPR 0.11), missing only 4 of 57 abliterated checkpoints. Two failure modes are identified: (1) a spoofed reference evades detection with ΔW=0 and perfect correlation (ρ=1), requiring no training; and (2) a white-box owner can train a checkpoint past the detection threshold while it remains guard-unsafe and coherent. The authors emphasize the audit is effective triage, not tamper-proofing, and is bounded by the evaluated registry.
AI.conclusion: The proposed two-signal audit provides a practical, threshold-free pre-deployment screening tool for detecting refusal-stripped open-weight checkpoints, significantly outperforming single-signal baselines. However, it is not tamper-proof: it presumes access to an attested reference checkpoint, and adversaries can circumvent it via reference spoofing or adversarial training. The method is best understood as an effective triage mechanism whose claims are bounded by the diversity of the evaluation registry.

title: Personality Without Persons? A Psychometric Critique of Big Five Testing in Large Language Models
summary: Human personality inventories are increasingly used to characterize large language models (LLMs), compare systems, and inform downstream governance claims. Yet, these inventories were developed and validated for humans, and it remains unclear whether they apply to LLMs. We present a systematic psychometric evaluation of Big Five personality measurements in LLMs. We ask three research questions: Do Big Five inventories a) appropriately describe LLMs, b) capture inter-individual differences across models, and c) reflect internal factors consistent with human personality. We assess content validity of five candidate Big Five inventories and administer the winning inventory to N = 244 different models spanning 49 model families. First, we found that Big Five items adapted for LLMs can reach sufficient content validity, while original human-developed items did not. Second, Big Five inventories did not capture meaningful differences between LLMs: We found low variability between models, accounting for only 3% of total score variance. Third, LLMs responses did not recover the Big Five five-factor structure with four of the Big Five facets collapsing into one (r >= .92). Direct comparisons between base and instruction-tuned model variants suggested that alignment training systematically shifted Big Five scores toward socially desirable traits. These findings demonstrate that Big Five scores do not measure a construct equivalent to human personality in LLMs. Applying human personality frameworks to LLMs produces misleading characterizations used to benchmark, compare, and govern LLMs. We highlight the need for evaluation frameworks that are developed for LLMs, rather than adopting human constructs without validation.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates whether Big Five personality inventories, developed for humans, can validly characterize LLMs. Testing 244 models across 49 families, the authors find that adapted Big Five items achieve content validity but fail to capture meaningful inter-model differences (only 3% of variance), do not recover the five-factor structure (four facets collapse into one), and alignment training shifts scores toward social desirability. The study concludes that Big Five scores in LLMs do not measure a construct equivalent to human personality.
AI.motivation: Human personality inventories like the Big Five are increasingly used to benchmark, compare, and govern LLMs, yet these instruments were developed and validated exclusively for humans. There is no systematic evidence that they apply meaningfully to LLMs, raising concerns about misleading characterizations used in downstream governance and evaluation claims.
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic psychometric evaluation addressing three research questions: (1) content validity — assessing five candidate Big Five inventories for appropriateness in LLMs; (2) inter-individual differences — administering the winning inventory to N=244 models from 49 families and decomposing score variance; (3) internal factor structure — testing whether LLM responses recover the expected five-factor structure via factor analysis. They also compared base vs. instruction-tuned model variants to examine alignment effects.
AI.result: Adapted Big Five items achieved sufficient content validity, but original human items did not. Between-model variability was extremely low, accounting for only 3% of total score variance. Factor analysis showed four of the five facets collapsed into a single factor (r ≥ .92). Instruction-tuned models scored systematically higher on socially desirable traits compared to base counterparts, indicating alignment training artificially shifts personality scores.
AI.conclusion: Big Five personality scores do not measure a construct equivalent to human personality in LLMs. Applying human personality frameworks to LLMs without validation produces misleading characterizations. The authors call for evaluation frameworks developed specifically for LLMs rather than adopting unvalidated human constructs.

title: Refploit: Facilitating Exploit Construction via Code-Agent Trajectory Repair
summary: Vulnerability exploits play a crucial role in assessing the downstream impact of Java library vulnerabilities. While some vulnerabilities are accompanied by disclosed exploit references, automatically reproducing such references into runnable exploits remains challenging because they are often incomplete, unstructured, or only describe partial reproduction steps. Recent code agents provide a promising way to automate this process, but our study shows that their generated exploits often appear successful without triggering the actual vulnerable logic, such as replacing vulnerable APIs with self-implemented functions. To address this, we propose Refploit, an LLM-based trajectory recovery framework for facilitating vulnerability reproduction from public exploit references. The key insight is that a failed agent trajectory is not entirely useless. It may have already completed some reproduction subtasks while also revealing misleading directions that should be avoided. Refploit first validates an agent-generated exploit through differential execution. When the exploit is ineffective, Refploit analyzes its reproduction progress, locates the trajectory segments associated with the reproduction progress, and derives constraints to guide focused recovery. We evaluate Refploit on three open-source Java vulnerability datasets, covering 172 exploit references for 143 vulnerabilities. Under DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Refploit successfully reproduces 138 exploits, achieving a reproduction rate of 80.2%. It achieves a 64.3% relative improvement over the initially generated trajectories and outperforms both the SOTA exploit-generation method PoCGen and advanced code agents such as Codex with GPT-5.4. We further adapt Refploit to another code agent and observe consistent improvements, demonstrating its generality.

AI.tldr: Refploit is an LLM-based trajectory recovery framework that improves automatic reproduction of Java vulnerability exploits from incomplete public references. It validates generated exploits via differential execution, analyzes failed trajectories to identify completed subtasks and misleading directions, then applies constraints for focused recovery. Evaluated on 172 exploit references across 143 vulnerabilities, it achieves 80.2% reproduction rate with a 64.3% relative improvement over initial trajectories, outperforming existing SOTA methods.
AI.motivation: Existing code agents that attempt to automatically reproduce vulnerability exploits from public references often generate exploits that appear successful but fail to trigger actual vulnerable logic — for instance, by substituting vulnerable APIs with self-implemented functions. This undermines the utility of automated exploit reproduction for downstream vulnerability impact assessment. A more reliable approach is needed.
