AI.method: Refploit uses a three-stage pipeline: (1) Differential execution validation to determine whether an agent-generated exploit actually triggers the vulnerable logic; (2) Trajectory analysis that examines failed agent trajectories, identifies which reproduction subtasks were completed and which directions were misleading; (3) Constraint-guided recovery that uses the extracted insights to steer focused re-generation of the exploit. The framework is LLM-based and designed to be agent-agnostic.
AI.result: On three open-source Java vulnerability datasets (172 exploit references, 143 vulnerabilities), Refploit with DeepSeek-V4-Flash reproduces 138 exploits (80.2% success rate), achieving a 64.3% relative improvement over initial agent-generated trajectories. It outperforms SOTA exploit-generation method PoCGen and advanced code agents like Codex with GPT-5.4. Consistent improvements are observed when Refploit is adapted to another code agent, demonstrating generality.
AI.conclusion: Refploit demonstrates that failed agent trajectories contain valuable signals — both progress and pitfalls — that can be systematically leveraged for recovery. The framework significantly advances the state of automated vulnerability exploit reproduction and is generalizable across different code agents.

title: Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics Enable Complete and Scalable $\mathrm{E}(3)$-Equivariant Networks
summary: $\mathrm{E}(3)$-equivariant networks are promising for 3D atomistic system modeling, yet their scalability is limited by the $O(L^6)$ complexity of the Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product (CGTP). The recently proposed Gaunt Tensor Product (GTP) reduces the complexity but is unable to capture the antisymmetric paths, resulting in incomplete expressivity. In this work, we present SpinGTP, an approach to overcome the GTP incompleteness by generalizing from scalar functions to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH). By relying on the algebraic properties of SWSH, SpinGTP recovers the missing antisymmetric interactions while maintaining the asymptotic efficiency of GTP. It also allows for a more expressive equivariant basis that naturally accounts for the parity-odd components of tensor products. We evaluate SpinGTP across diverse benchmarks, including Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20. Our results show that SpinGTP achieves accuracies comparable to full CGTP. Notably, by explicitly capturing antisymmetric paths, SpinGTP exhibits superior performance in tasks involving chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries. This work provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous path toward high-order equivariance in large-scale 3D atomistic system simulations.

AI.tldr: SpinGTP generalizes the Gaunt Tensor Product using Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics to recover missing antisymmetric interactions, achieving CGTP-level accuracy with GTP-level efficiency for E(3)-equivariant 3D atomistic modeling.
AI.motivation: E(3)-equivariant networks are powerful for 3D atomistic systems but suffer from the O(L^6) complexity of Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product (CGTP). The Gaunt Tensor Product (GTP) reduces complexity but cannot capture antisymmetric paths, yielding incomplete expressivity — particularly problematic for chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries.
AI.method: SpinGTP generalizes from scalar spherical harmonics to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH), leveraging their algebraic properties to recover antisymmetric interactions missing in GTP. This yields a more expressive equivariant basis that naturally incorporates parity-odd components of tensor products while maintaining GTP's asymptotic efficiency.
AI.result: SpinGTP achieves accuracy comparable to full CGTP across Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20 benchmarks. It demonstrates superior performance on tasks involving chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries by explicitly capturing antisymmetric paths.
AI.conclusion: SpinGTP provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous solution for high-order equivariance in large-scale 3D atomistic simulations, closing the expressivity gap between GTP and CGTP without sacrificing computational efficiency.

title: MultAttnAttrib: Training-Free Multimodal Attribution in Long Document Question Answering
comment: 25 pages (8 main, 17 references + appendix), 15 figures, Submitted to EMNLP 2026 Conference (Long Paper)
summary: As grounded QA systems are increasingly deployed in AI assistants, accurately attributing generated answers to evidence is critical for user trust and model safety. While unimodal attributions have been explored in depth, the multimodal setting remains relatively under-researched. As a result, we introduce MultAttnAttrib, a training-free attribution-generation method that leverages a model's prefill pass, selected attention heads, and calibrated thresholds to locate source evidence within a document. To establish baseline results for the method, we introduce MultAttrEval, a complementary benchmark dataset annotated with fine-grained, ground-truth attributions for answer components grounded in multimodal source documents. To our knowledge, this is the first evaluation dataset designed specifically for multimodal attribution in long-form documents. Experimental results show that MultAttnAttrib consistently outperforms a variety of attribution-generation methods, including several strong prompting-based approaches and matches the latest frontier models such as GPT 5.4. Our method not only substantially improves attribution accuracy for both unimodal and multimodal attribution types, but also produces attributions at up to one-seventh of the direct inference latency compared to prompting on the same base model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MultAttnAttrib, a training-free method for generating fine-grained attributions in multimodal QA by leveraging attention heads and calibrated thresholds, along with MultAttrEval, the first benchmark dataset for multimodal attribution in long-form documents. The method outperforms prompting-based approaches and matches frontier models like GPT 5.4 while achieving up to 7× faster inference.
AI.motivation: As grounded QA systems are increasingly deployed, accurate attribution of answers to source evidence is critical for trust and safety. While unimodal attribution is well-studied, multimodal attribution remains under-researched, lacking both methods and dedicated evaluation benchmarks for long-form document settings.
AI.method: The authors propose MultAttnAttrib, a training-free attribution-generation method that operates during the model's prefill pass. It uses selected attention heads and calibrated thresholds to identify which parts of a multimodal source document support each component of a generated answer. They also introduce MultAttrEval, a benchmark with fine-grained ground-truth attributions for multimodal documents.
AI.result: MultAttnAttrib consistently outperforms various attribution-generation methods, including strong prompting-based approaches, and matches the latest frontier models such as GPT 5.4. It substantially improves attribution accuracy for both unimodal and multimodal types, and produces attributions at up to one-seventh of the direct inference latency compared to prompting on the same base model.
AI.conclusion: The proposed attention-based, training-free method effectively advances multimodal attribution by being both more accurate and significantly faster than prompting-based alternatives, while the new benchmark (MultAttrEval) provides a foundation for future research in this underexplored area.

title: Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Reasoning under Limited Supervision: Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as an effective approach for activating latent reasoning capabilities in large language models. However, most existing CoT methods use reasoning chains mainly as inference-time prompts, while the generated reasoning traces are rarely reused as semi-supervised learning signals. In this report, we define \textbf{Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning} and propose \textbf{Semi-CoT}, a simple framework that uses unlabeled questions to construct pseudo reasoning supervision. Semi-CoT samples multiple pseudo-CoTs for each unlabeled question, estimates answer-level semantic entropy, and selects low-entropy reasoning chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations. This extends the self-training view of CoT from inference-time refinement to semi-supervised pseudo-supervision. Pilot experiments on AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith show that the entropy gate selects high-precision pseudo-CoTs, with pseudo-answer precision ranging from $91.36\%$ to $100\%$. Semi-CoT also gives small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, while AQuA shows negative transfer and MultiArith reaches a ceiling. These results suggest that unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo reasoning signals, but their effective use still requires stronger demonstration selection or student training.

AI.tldr: Semi-CoT introduces a framework that leverages unlabeled questions to generate pseudo chain-of-thought reasoning chains, selects reliable ones via semantic entropy filtering, and uses them as semi-supervised learning signals for LLMs, with pilot experiments showing high pseudo-answer precision (91-100%) but mixed downstream gains.
AI.motivation: Existing CoT methods use reasoning chains only as inference-time prompts and discard them afterward, wasting the potential of generated reasoning traces as semi-supervised training signals. The authors aim to extend self-training to the CoT paradigm by exploiting unlabeled questions.
AI.method: Semi-CoT operates in three steps: (1) sample multiple pseudo chain-of-thought reasoning traces for each unlabeled question from an LLM, (2) estimate answer-level semantic entropy across these traces to measure reasoning certainty, and (3) apply an entropy gate to select only low-entropy (high-consistency) chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations for subsequent student model training.
AI.result: On AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith, the entropy gate achieves pseudo-answer precision from 91.36% to 100%. Semi-CoT yields small improvements on SVAMP and GSM8K, but negative transfer on AQuA and a ceiling effect on MultiArith, indicating that stronger selection or training methods are needed for effective use.
AI.conclusion: Unlabeled questions can serve as a source of reliable pseudo reasoning signals for CoT learning, but simply filtering by entropy is insufficient; future work requires more robust demonstration selection strategies and improved student training to convert pseudo-supervision into consistent downstream performance gains.

title: Behind the Refusal: Determining Guardrail Activation via Behavioral Monitoring
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) and agentic systems become integrated into real-world applications, ensuring their safety and security is critical. Guardrail systems that detect and block malicious instructions sent to and from an LLM are an essential component of AI security. However, researchers conducting black-box adversarial emulation against production AI systems often struggle to determine whether a guardrail block or an LLM rejection has occurred. This distinction is important because the techniques used to bypass guardrails can differ substantially from those used to bypass LLM safety alignment, and has a material impact on attack technique selection and optimization. We propose the first black-box guardrail reconnaissance methodology, which detects the presence of a guardrail within a target AI system through behavioral monitoring of HTTP, lexical, and timing signals, assuming only black-box access and zero prior knowledge of the guardrail or AI system. Experiments demonstrate that our approach detects guardrail presence with 100% accuracy, with statistically significant behavioral separation between benign and malicious interactions (q < 0.001). Our approach further identifies the content categories a guardrail is designed to block, and distinguishes guardrail blocks from LLM rejection on unseen prompts with an average F1 score of 98%.

AI.tldr: A black-box methodology to detect whether a guardrail system (not the LLM itself) is blocking a malicious prompt, achieving 100% detection accuracy and 98% F1 in distinguishing guardrail blocks from LLM rejections using HTTP, lexical, and timing signals.
AI.motivation: Adversarial testers cannot easily distinguish whether a rejection originates from an external guardrail or the LLM's internal safety alignment. This distinction is critical because bypass techniques differ substantially between the two, affecting attack strategy selection and optimization.
AI.method: A black-box guardrail reconnaissance methodology that monitors HTTP response headers/status codes, lexical patterns in rejection messages, and response timing to infer guardrail presence and categorize blocked content types, requiring zero prior knowledge of the target system.
AI.result: 100% guardrail detection accuracy with statistically significant behavioral separation between benign and malicious queries (q < 0.001). The method identifies blocked content categories and distinguishes guardrail blocks from LLM rejections with an average F1 score of 98% on unseen prompts.
AI.conclusion: Guardrail presence can be reliably detected in black-box settings using passive behavioral signals, enabling more effective adversarial emulation by correctly attributing rejections and informing appropriate bypass technique selection.

title: Data Comics for Education: Evaluating Effectiveness, Benefits, and the Ethics of AI-Assisted Creation
summary: In today's data-driven world, students often struggle with interpreting visualisations due to limited visualisation literacy. Data comics have emerged as a promising medium to enhance engagement and understanding, but their educational value has seen little empirical examination, partly due to the effort required to create them. Recent advances in Generative AI (GenAI) offer a scalable solution to this challenge. We conducted a within-subjects study with 60 university students, comparing conventional visualisations with data comics, created with assistance from GenAI tools, across information retrieval and comprehension tasks. Students consistently performed better with data comics, particularly in insight comprehension tasks, independent of prior visualisation literacy. Students also commented data comics as more engaging and easier to understand, though concerns were raised about GenAI-driven misinformation and ownership. Our findings highlight the potential of data comics as a potentially effective tool for data communication in education, while underscoring the need to address ethical concerns related to AI-assisted creation.

AI.tldr: A within-subjects study with 60 university students found that GenAI-assisted data comics consistently outperformed conventional visualizations in information retrieval and comprehension tasks, particularly for insight comprehension. Students rated data comics as more engaging and understandable, though concerns about AI-driven misinformation and ownership were noted.
AI.motivation: Students often struggle with visualization literacy, and while data comics show promise as an educational medium, their empirical evaluation is lacking — partly due to the high effort required to create them. GenAI tools offer a scalable way to produce data comics, motivating this investigation into their educational effectiveness.
AI.method: A within-subjects experimental design with 60 university students comparing conventional visualizations against GenAI-assisted data comics across information retrieval and comprehension tasks. Performance metrics and subjective feedback (engagement, ease of understanding, ethical concerns) were collected.
AI.result: Students consistently performed better with data comics, especially in insight comprehension tasks, regardless of prior visualization literacy levels. Data comics were rated as more engaging and easier to understand. However, participants expressed concerns about GenAI-driven misinformation and ownership issues.
AI.conclusion: Data comics represent a potentially effective tool for data communication in education, with GenAI enabling scalable creation. However, ethical concerns — particularly around misinformation and content ownership — must be addressed to responsibly integrate AI-assisted data comics into educational contexts.

title: KRCA: An Efficient Root Cause Analysis System in Hyper-Scale Microservice Systems via Agentic AI
summary: Hyper-scale microservice systems have become the standard infrastructure for large-scale Internet companies. These systems consist of numerous loosely coupled microservices that evolve independently through continuous development and deployment. Such complexity makes failures unavoidable, necessitating efficient Root Cause Analysis (RCA) to help Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) quickly localize root cause services and classify failure types. However, existing RCA methods often struggle to adapt to the extreme dynamism and massive scale of these systems. In this paper, we present KRCA, an end-to-end RCA system designed for hyper-scale microservice systems. To manage the vast search space, KRCA employs a multi-stage pipeline that begins with an API-level drilldown to isolate suspicious services. It then instantiates a skeleton-based causal graph from anomalous metrics to serve as a high-recall structural prior, before utilizing a memory-augmented multi-agent framework to verify causality and generate the final failure report. By combining structured causal constraints with multi-agent reasoning, KRCA employs balances diagnostic accuracy with the efficiency requirements of real-time production use. Experimental results show that KRCA achieves AC@1 scores of 0.88 and 0.79 for root cause service localization and failure type classification, outperforming the strongest baseline by at lease 31% in absolute gains. KRCA has been deployed in Kuaishou's production environment for over six months, reducing the average diagnosis time by 77.3%.

AI.tldr: KRCA is an end-to-end root cause analysis system for hyper-scale microservices that uses a multi-stage pipeline (API-level drilldown, skeleton-based causal graph, and memory-augmented multi-agent reasoning) to localize root causes and classify failure types, achieving 77.3% faster diagnosis in production at Kuaishou.
AI.motivation: Hyper-scale microservice systems are highly dynamic, massive in scale, and prone to failures. Existing RCA methods fail to adapt to this extreme dynamism and scale, creating a need for an efficient, accurate system that helps SREs quickly localize root causes and classify failure types.
AI.method: KRCA employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) API-level drilldown to narrow the search space to suspicious services; (2) instantiation of a skeleton-based causal graph from anomalous metrics as a high-recall structural prior; (3) a memory-augmented multi-agent framework that verifies causality and generates the final failure report, balancing structured causal constraints with multi-agent reasoning.
AI.result: KRCA achieves AC@1 scores of 0.88 and 0.79 for root cause service localization and failure type classification, respectively, outperforming the strongest baseline by at least 31% in absolute gains. Deployed in Kuaishou's production for over six months, it reduced average diagnosis time by 77.3%.
AI.conclusion: KRCA demonstrates that combining structured causal graph constraints with multi-agent reasoning delivers both high diagnostic accuracy and real-time production efficiency, making it a practical and effective RCA solution for hyper-scale microservice environments.

title: The Rollout Infrastructure Tax in Coding-Agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: Preprint. 6 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ACM SoCC 2026
summary: Coding-agent reinforcement learning treats execution infrastructure as a background implementation detail, despite relying on large numbers of interactive software rollouts. This is a missed opportunity: measuring infrastructure overhead can reveal practical efficiency gains for RL post-training, where small per-rollout savings compound at scale. We present a comparative study of four execution substrates: single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, and cloud virtual machines. We find up to $110\times$ variation in cold-start latency and a $1.8\times$ spread in projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories. Our results suggest that future coding-agent RL systems should optimize execution substrates as part of the training system itself, not merely as deployment plumbing.

AI.tldr: This paper compares four execution substrates (containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes, and cloud VMs) for coding-agent RL, finding up to 110× variation in cold-start latency and 1.8× spread in worker-hours for large-scale training, and argues that infrastructure optimization should be treated as a first-class component of RL training systems.
AI.motivation: Existing coding-agent RL systems treat execution infrastructure as a background detail, ignoring that small per-rollout overheads compound significantly at scale during post-training with millions of interactive software rollouts. Quantifying these overheads can reveal practical efficiency gains.
AI.method: Comparative empirical study measuring cold-start latency, execution overhead, and projected total worker-hours across four execution substrates (single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, and cloud VMs) for running one million 150-step coding-agent trajectories.
AI.result: Cold-start latency varies by up to 110× across substrates. Projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories show a 1.8× spread, demonstrating substantial practical differences in total compute cost and wall-clock time at RL training scale.
AI.conclusion: Execution substrates should be optimized as an integral part of the coding-agent RL training system rather than treated as mere deployment plumbing, given the compounding efficiency implications at scale.

title: IsoSci: A Benchmark of Isomorphic Cross-Domain Science Problems for Evaluating Reasoning versus Knowledge Retrieval in LLMs
summary: We introduce ISOSCI, a benchmark of isomorphic cross-domain science problem pairs that separates reasoning ability from domain knowledge retrieval in LLM evaluation. Each pair shares identical logical structure but requires different domain-specific knowledge, enabling controlled attribution of reasoning-mode gains. Across five model pairs spanning four model families, we find that 91.3% of reasoning-mode gains are knowledge-dependent rather than structure-invariant (63/69 gains; Wilson 95% CI [82.3%, 96.0%]), directly challenging the assumption that chain-of-thought reasoning improves short-horizon procedural scientific problem-solving. Reasoning toggles on highly capable models provide less than 5 percentage points accuracy gain across all domains, and a reasoning-specialized model (o3-mini) that outperforms its standard counterpart on GPQA Diamond (+19.2 percentage points) underperforms on ISOSCI (-24.7 percentage points), showing that benchmark choice determines conclusions about reasoning utility. We release ISOSCI at https://huggingface.co/datasets/isosci/isosci

AI.tldr: ISOSCI is a benchmark of isomorphic science problem pairs that isolates reasoning from domain knowledge. The authors find that 91.3% of reasoning-mode gains depend on knowledge retrieval, not structural reasoning ability, challenging assumptions about chain-of-thought benefits for procedural science problems.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks conflate reasoning ability with domain knowledge retrieval, making it impossible to determine whether performance improvements from reasoning methods (e.g., chain-of-thought) stem from better logical reasoning or simply better knowledge access. The authors aim to disentangle these two factors.
AI.method: The authors construct ISOSCI, a benchmark of isomorphic cross-domain problem pairs — pairs that share identical logical structure but require different domain-specific knowledge. By comparing performance across such pairs with and without reasoning-mode toggles, they can control for knowledge effects and isolate reasoning-specific gains. They evaluate five model pairs across four model families.
AI.result: 91.3% of reasoning-mode gains (63/69 gains; Wilson 95% CI [82.3%, 96.0%]) are knowledge-dependent rather than structure-invariant. High-capability models gain less than 5 percentage points from reasoning. The reasoning-specialized o3-mini outperforms its standard counterpart on GPQA Diamond (+19.2 pp) but underperforms on ISOSCI (-24.7 pp), demonstrating that benchmark choice drives conclusions about reasoning utility.
AI.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning provides minimal benefits for short-horizon procedural scientific problem-solving independent of knowledge retrieval. Benchmark design critically shapes conclusions about reasoning capabilities, and ISOSCI offers a more controlled evaluation framework.

title: OPINE-World: Programmatic World Modeling with Ontology-error-Prioritized Interactive Exploration
summary: Learning how an environment behaves from interaction is central to building agents that adapt to unfamiliar tasks. World models learned with deep networks are flexible but data-hungry and transfer poorly beyond their training distribution. Program-synthesized world models, written as source code by LLMs and refined through counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), are instead data-efficient and reusable, yet they have been demonstrated mainly on structured-state worlds with a given object vocabulary, and a single program search does not scale to pixel-rendered environments whose object structure must be hypothesized flexibly. We introduce OPINE-World, an LLM agent that learns an object-centric programmatic world model online from interaction. OPINE-World couples two cooperating agents in a loop of hypothesis and test, one acting in the environment and one synthesizing the model in code with replay verification and model-based planning, and it steers exploration with a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy we call ontology error. We evaluate OPINE-World on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark for skill-acquisition efficiency in which the object vocabulary, the goal, and the action semantics are withheld. OPINE-World solves 20 of 25 games without per-game training and reaches an action-efficiency score of 78.4 against the human baseline.

AI.tldr: OPINE-World is an LLM agent that learns object-centric programmatic world models online from interaction by coupling an acting agent with a model-synthesizing agent in a hypothesis-test loop, using a Bayesian "ontology error" to steer exploration. It solves 20/25 ARC-AGI-3 games without per-game training, achieving a 78.4 action-efficiency score against human baselines.
AI.motivation: Deep-network world models are data-hungry and generalize poorly outside their training distribution. Program-synthesized world models (via LLMs + CEGIS) are data-efficient and reusable but have been limited to structured-state worlds with known object vocabularies and fail to scale to pixel-rendered environments requiring flexible object-structure discovery. The paper addresses this gap by enabling online learning of programmatic world models directly from pixel observations without a pre-given object vocabulary.
AI.method: OPINE-World employs two cooperating LLM agents in a hypothesis-and-test loop: (1) an actor agent that interacts with the environment, and (2) a synthesizer agent that writes programmatic world models in code, refined through replay verification and model-based planning. Exploration is guided by "ontology error," a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy that quantifies how well the current object vocabulary explains observations. The system iteratively proposes object types, synthesizes transition models as executable code, verifies them against replay buffers, and uses the learned model for planning.
AI.result: Evaluated on ARC-AGI-3 (a benchmark withholding object vocabulary, goal, and action semantics), OPINE-World solves 20 out of 25 games without any per-game training and achieves an action-efficiency score of 78.4 relative to a human baseline.
AI.conclusion: OPINE-World demonstrates that LLM-driven program synthesis, when coupled with online interaction and ontology-error-driven exploration, can discover object-centric world models from pixel observations efficiently. This bridges the gap between data-hungry deep world models and rigid symbolic approaches, enabling sample-efficient, reusable model learning in visually rich environments with unknown object structure.

title: Cloak and Detonate: Scanner Evasion and Dynamic Detection of Agent Skill Malware
summary:
LLM coding agents increasingly rely on third-party agent skills from public marketplaces, which execute with the agent's privileges and create a software supply-chain attack surface: a malicious skill can steal credentials, exfiltrate source code, or install backdoors. Existing defenses use static skill scanners based on pattern matching or LLM-as-judge analysis, but it remains unclear whether they withstand adaptive evasions that preserve malicious behavior while changing payload appearance.
  This paper first presents an adversarial study of existing skill scanners through SkillCloak, a payload-preserving evasion framework that keeps the attack semantics intact while transforming their visible form. SkillCloak uses two complementary strategies: Structural Obfuscation, which rewrites visible payload indicators into semantically equivalent forms, and Self-Extracting Skill (SFS) Packing, which hides malicious components from the install-time view and restores them during agent execution. Across eight scanners and 1,613 in-the-wild malicious skills, SFS Packing bypasses every scanner at over 90%, while Structural Obfuscation bypasses over 80% on most static scanners and reaches 96% on a hybrid scanner, showing that appearance-based auditing is insufficient.
  Motivated by this finding, we propose SkillDetonate, a behavior-centric runtime auditor that executes skills in a sandbox and detects malicious effects through OS-boundary information-flow evidence rather than install-time appearance. SkillDetonate combines on-demand closure lift, which observes instructions materialized during execution, with marker-based taint analysis, which tracks sensitive-data flows across the agent context, files, processes, and network operations. The results show that SkillDetonate detects 97% of attacks at a 2% false-positive rate and sustains 87% detection on real-world malicious skills.

AI.tldr: Existing LLM coding agent skill scanners relying on appearance/pattern matching are easily bypassed by adversarial evasion (SkillCloak achieves >90% bypass). The paper proposes SkillDetonate, a behavior-centric runtime auditor using sandbox execution with OS-boundary information-flow tracking, achieving 97% detection at 2% false-positive rate.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents increasingly use third-party skills from public marketplaces, creating a software supply-chain attack surface. Current defenses use static skill scanners (pattern matching or LLM-as-judge), but their resilience against adaptive, payload-preserving evasions is unknown and likely insufficient.
AI.method: The paper first introduces SkillCloak, an evasion framework with two strategies: (1) Structural Obfuscation — rewriting visible payload indicators into semantically equivalent forms; (2) Self-Extracting Skill (SFS) Packing — hiding malicious components at install time and restoring them during execution. It then proposes SkillDetonate, a runtime auditor that executes skills in a sandbox, using on-demand closure lift to observe runtime-materialized instructions, combined with marker-based taint analysis to track sensitive-data flows across agent context, files, processes, and network operations.
AI.result: SkillCloak: SFS Packing bypasses all 8 scanners at >90% on 1,613 real-world malicious skills; Structural Obfuscation bypasses >80% on most static scanners and 96% on a hybrid scanner. SkillDetonate: detects 97% of attacks at 2% false-positive rate, sustaining 87% detection on real-world malicious skills.
AI.conclusion: Appearance-based auditing is fundamentally insufficient for securing LLM agent skill marketplaces. Behavior-centric runtime auditing with OS-level information-flow tracking (SkillDetonate) provides effective and robust detection against both known and adversarially evasive malicious skills.

title: Physical surfaces make touch interactions in virtual reality precise, efficient, and bimanual
comment: This paper has been accepted by the "International Journal of Human-Computer Studies (IJHCS)" [Project Link] https://wy-blacksheep.github.io/projects/physical-surface/ [Paper Link] https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1071581926001254 [Video Link] https://youtu.be/e_nzOkZIIKA
summary:
Virtual reality (VR) systems can enable convenient hand-based interactions across diverse work scenarios. However, mid-air gestures lack tactile feedback and a physical reference surface to support the hand. This absence of haptic grounding can cause significant challenges in achieving precise and efficient touch interactions. This paper investigates the effect of different types of hand-grounded haptic feedback on the touch performance of VR tasks that demand high precision, such as selecting, tracing, and sketching. We compared three levels of haptic feedback: 1) No Haptic Feedback, where only visual feedback was provided; 2) Tactile Feedback, where users received vibrotactile and pressure feedback upon touching a virtual surface; 3) Physical Surface, where users interacted with a portable and tangible surface.
  Our study found that portable physical surfaces enabled the best selection precision, tracing efficiency, and sketch quality. Furthermore, participants showed increased bimanual hand utilization when engaging with a physical surface during tasks. These observed behaviors corresponded to participants' preference for interacting with physical surfaces, attributed to a better sense of confidence and control.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how different levels of hand-grounded haptic feedback (none, vibrotactile/pressure, and a portable physical surface) affect precision-demanding VR touch tasks. Results show that a physical surface yields superior selection precision, tracing efficiency, sketch quality, and bimanual hand use, driven by increased user confidence and control.
AI.motivation: Mid-air gestures in VR lack tactile feedback and a physical reference surface — a deficit termed absence of haptic grounding — which undermines precise and efficient touch interactions. The authors aim to systematically quantify how varying degrees of hand-grounded haptic feedback impact performance on high-precision tasks.
AI.method: A within-subjects experiment compared three haptic conditions: (1) No Haptic Feedback (visual-only), (2) Tactile Feedback (vibrotactile and pressure cues upon virtual surface contact), and (3) Physical Surface (a portable, tangible surface). Participants performed precision-demanding tasks — selecting, tracing, and sketching — while performance metrics (precision, efficiency, quality) and behavioral observations (bimanual hand utilization, subjective preference) were collected.
AI.result: The Physical Surface condition significantly outperformed the other two: it yielded the best selection precision, highest tracing efficiency, and superior sketch quality. Participants also exhibited increased bimanual hand use when a physical surface was present. These behavioral gains aligned with subjective preferences, where users attributed their improved performance to a greater sense of confidence and control.
AI.conclusion: Providing a portable physical surface as a form of hand-grounded haptic feedback substantially improves precision, efficiency, and user experience in VR touch interactions compared to vibrotactile feedback or visual-only conditions. The findings underscore the importance of haptic grounding for high-precision VR tasks and suggest that tangible surface interfaces are a promising direction for professional VR applications.

title: Archer: Towards Agentic Review for Compiler Optimizations
summary:
Modern compilers are frequently updated, but expert review capacity is highly limited, leading to delayed integration and, in some cases, subtle semantic bugs entering the compiler codebase. Automating the code review process with modern general code review agents may be feasible, but it faces critical challenges due to compiler complexity. In this paper, we use LLVM as our target compiler and present Archer, the first automated agentic code review tool for compiler optimizations. Archer constrains the agentic review process from both ends by using obligations to guide analysis and a deterministic validation guard to admit only findings backed by executable evidence.
  We evaluated Archer on 70 open PRs and 328 closed PRs in LLVM from the last two months. The review results are shocking and concerning: Archer discovers that 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs are buggy, i.e, introducing semantic bugs such as miscompilations in LLVM. Our findings expose a critical gap in the capacity for critical review in large compiler projects and demonstrate the practical value of Archer as an additional reviewer.

AI.tldr: Archer is the first automated agentic code review tool for compiler optimizations, targeting LLVM. It uses obligations to guide analysis and a deterministic validation guard to ensure findings are backed by executable evidence. Evaluation on recent LLVM PRs reveals that 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs contain semantic bugs such as miscompilations, exposing a critical gap in compiler review capacity.
AI.motivation: Modern compilers like LLVM are frequently updated, but expert review capacity is severely limited, resulting in delayed integration and subtle semantic bugs entering the codebase. Automating code review with general agents faces challenges due to compiler complexity. There is a pressing need for a specialized, automated review tool that can reliably detect semantic bugs in compiler optimizations.
AI.method: Archer is an agentic code review tool specifically designed for compiler optimizations in LLVM. It constrains the review process bidirectionally: (1) obligations are used to guide the agent's analysis, and (2) a deterministic validation guard admits only findings that are supported by executable evidence, ensuring reliability and reducing false positives.
AI.result: Evaluated on 70 open PRs and 328 closed PRs from the last two months of LLVM development, Archer found that 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs contain semantic bugs (e.g., miscompilations). These results reveal a significant gap in critical review capacity within large compiler projects.
AI.conclusion: Archer demonstrates practical value as an automated additional reviewer for compiler optimizations, uncovering a concerning rate of semantic bugs that escape both open and closed PR processes. The tool highlights the inadequacy of current human-only review pipelines in large-scale compiler projects and offers a feasible path toward augmenting review capacity with automated, evidence-backed analysis.

title: Conditional Inference Trees and Forests for Feature Selection
summary: Conditional inference trees (CIT) and conditional inference forests (CIF) reduce split-selection bias by testing features before choosing split thresholds, but repeated permutation tests and threshold searches can make these methods computationally expensive. We study CIT and CIF as top-$k$ feature-ranking methods for downstream prediction using real-data benchmarks, runtime ablations, and synthetic feature-recovery experiments. At a fixed node, if the features and permutation budget do not depend on the node responses, Bonferroni-corrected $+1$ Monte Carlo permutation $p$-values control nodewise rejection under the complete permutation null. CIF ranks 4th among 17 classification methods on 22 datasets and 3rd among 18 regression methods on 8 datasets. With Bonferroni correction held fixed, the CIF runtime ablations indicate that adaptive stopping and the number of thresholds searched have the largest measured effect on runtime: turning off adaptive stopping and using exact threshold search increase fitting time by 4.0--8.4$\times$ and 1.9--10.8$\times$, respectively, while downstream score changes are at most 0.011. Sparse high-$p$ simulations indicate that forest feature sampling can leave informative features out of many split decisions. Overall, the results support CIF as a top-$k$ feature-ranking method in the evaluated downstream prediction benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Conditional inference forests (CIF) are strong top-k feature-ranking methods for prediction, ranking 3rd–4th across benchmarks. Runtime is dominated by adaptive stopping and threshold search; sparse high-p settings reveal that feature subsampling can exclude informative features from split decisions.
AI.motivation: Conditional inference trees and forests reduce split-selection bias via permutation tests, but repeated testing and threshold optimization incur high computational cost. The authors aim to benchmark CIF as a feature-ranking method, characterize runtime bottlenecks, and examine theoretical properties of the permutation-based split selection under constrained resampling.
AI.method: The paper combines three analytic strands: (1) benchmarking CIF against 16–17 other classification/regression methods on 22/8 real-world datasets using downstream prediction scores; (2) runtime ablation experiments manipulating adaptive stopping, number of thresholds searched, and other controls to isolate cost factors; (3) synthetic high-dimensional (sparse high-p) simulations to assess how forest feature sampling affects inclusion of informative features in split decisions. A theoretical note proves that Bonferroni-corrected +1 Monte Carlo permutation p-values control nodewise type I error under the complete permutation null when features and permutation budget are independent of node responses.
AI.result: CIF ranks 4th among 17 classifiers (22 datasets) and 3rd among 18 regression methods (8 datasets). Runtime ablations show adaptive stopping and exact threshold search increase fitting time by 4.0–8.4× and 1.9–10.8× respectively, while downstream score changes remain ≤0.011. High-p synthetic experiments reveal that feature subsampling can leave informative features out of many splits. The Bonferroni-corrected +1 Monte Carlo test provides valid nodewise error control under the stated conditions.
AI.conclusion: CIF is a competitive top-k feature-ranking method. Adaptive stopping is the largest computational lever; exact threshold search is secondary. Practitioners in sparse high-dimensional settings should be mindful that feature subsampling may exclude relevant features from split decisions. The theoretical guarantee on permutation-based nodewise testing adds rigor to the framework.

title: FaithMed: Training LLMs For Faithful Evidence-Based Medical Reasoning
summary: Faithful reasoning is essential in medicine, where clinical decisions require transparent justification grounded in reliable evidence. Current medical LLMs either lack active access to evidence or use retrieved evidence without supervising how it should be appraised and applied during reasoning. To address this, we formalize evidence-based medicine principles as process-level criteria and introduce FaithMed, a framework that combines clinician-designed, automatically refined rubrics with reinforcement learning using step-level process reward assignment and advantage grouping. Across seven medical benchmarks, FaithMed improves over agentic-search baselines (+9% on average) and outcome-only RL (+5.8%), while raising average evidence-based medicine rubric scores over agentic-search Qwen3 baselines (+15.5%). This work demonstrates that explicit step-level supervision can improve both task success and the faithfulness of the reasoning process. Code is available at https://github.com/cxcscmu/FaithMed.

AI.tldr: FaithMed introduces a reinforcement learning framework with step-level process rewards grounded in evidence-based medicine rubrics to improve both task accuracy and reasoning faithfulness in medical LLMs, outperforming agentic-search and outcome-only RL baselines.
AI.motivation: Current medical LLMs either lack access to evidence or retrieve it without proper appraisal and application during reasoning, undermining faithful clinical decision-making that requires transparent, evidence-grounded justification.
AI.method: FaithMed formalizes evidence-based medicine (EBM) principles as process-level criteria using clinician-designed, automatically refined rubrics. It employs reinforcement learning with step-level process reward assignment and advantage grouping to supervise how evidence is appraised and applied throughout the reasoning chain.
AI.result: Across seven medical benchmarks, FaithMed outperforms agentic-search baselines by 9% on average, outcome-only RL by 5.8%, and improves EBM rubric scores over agentic-search Qwen3 baselines by 15.5%.
AI.conclusion: Explicit step-level supervision via EBM-aligned process rewards can simultaneously improve task success and the faithfulness of the clinical reasoning process in medical LLMs.

title: Scaling Trends for Lie Detector Oversight in Preference Learning
summary: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to monitor and prevent, motivating approaches such as Scalable Oversight via Lie Detectors (SOLiD) (Cundy & Gleave, 2025), which uses lie detectors to identify responses for review by high-cost labelers. In this paper, we scale SOLiD to larger models and evaluate it in more diverse and realistic preference-learning settings. We find favorable scaling: undetected deception drops from 34% for 1B-parameter models to 14% for 405B-parameter models at a detector true positive rate of 99%, and expensive human labelers can be removed entirely from the fine-tuning phase without a statistically significant increase in deception. However, SOLiD is sensitive to distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data, which can drive detector false positive rates to impractical levels.

AI.tldr: Scaling SOLiD (Scalable Oversight via Lie Detectors) to larger LLMs shows favorable scaling trends, with undetected deception dropping from 34% (1B) to 14% (405B) at 99% TPR. However, distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data can cause impractically high false positive rates.
AI.motivation: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to monitor and prevent. SOLiD was proposed as a scalable oversight method using lie detectors to flag responses for human review. This paper aims to scale SOLiD to larger models and evaluate it under more diverse, realistic preference-learning settings to assess its practical viability.
AI.method: The authors scale SOLiD to models up to 405B parameters and test it across diverse preference-learning settings. They train lie detectors to identify deceptive LLM outputs and measure undetected deception rates, detector true positive rates (TPR), false positive rates (FPR), and analyze sensitivity to distribution shift between detector training data and preference-training data. They also test removing human labelers from the fine-tuning phase.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Favorable scaling — undetected deception drops from 34% (1B models) to 14% (405B models) at 99% TPR; (2) human labelers can be removed from fine-tuning without statistically significant increase in deception; (3) SOLiD is sensitive to distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data, which can drive FPR to impractical levels.
AI.conclusion: SOLiD shows promise as a scalable deception mitigation strategy for larger models, but its practical deployment is threatened by vulnerability to distribution shift, which can render detector false positive rates unusably high. Addressing this sensitivity is critical for real-world application.

title: SoK: A Taxonomy for Cybersecurity Incident Response Influence Factors
comment: To be published in Proceedings of EuroS&P 2026
summary: Cybersecurity incident response has emerged as a critical area of interest for both researchers and practitioners. The corpus of literature on cybersecurity incident response is expanding, yet a unified framework for systematically organizing the accumulated knowledge remains absent. The aspects of incident response span multiple domains, including technology, human-computer interaction, organizational theory, and human factors. A comprehensive, integrative perspective on these factors can enable researchers to identify underexplored areas and more effectively target their empirical and theoretical investigations. Our study systematizes the factors that influence organizational preparedness for and response to cybersecurity incidents. Through a systematic review of academic literature (n = 417) and non-scientific publications (n = 40), we derived the "Cybersecurity Incident Response Influencing Factor Taxonomy" (\textit{CIR-IF Taxonomy}). Existing empirical findings were classified within this taxonomy, providing a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of knowledge from the period 1999 to mid-2024. The taxonomy categories were systematically compared with seven established scientific frameworks and with the \textit{NIST Cyber Security Framework} elements referenced in the \textit{NIST Special Publication 800-61r3} incident response profile. The results of this comparison show that the \textit{CIR-IF Taxonomy} delivers a richer, more rigorous, and more systematically organized view of the factors that drive and shape incident response.

AI.tldr: A systematic review of 417 academic and 40 non-scientific publications (1999–mid-2024) yields the CIR-IF Taxonomy, a unified framework classifying factors influencing organizational cybersecurity incident response preparedness and response. Comparison with seven scientific frameworks and the NIST SP 800-61r3 profile shows the taxonomy offers richer, more rigorous coverage.
AI.motivation: Despite growing literature on cybersecurity incident response spanning technology, HCI, organizational theory, and human factors, no unified framework exists to systematically organize this accumulated knowledge, hindering identification of research gaps and effective empirical investigation.
AI.method: Systematic review of academic literature (n=417) and non-scientific publications (n=40) covering 1999 to mid-2024. The derived CIR-IF Taxonomy was then systematically compared against seven established scientific frameworks and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework elements from the NIST SP 800-61r3 incident response profile.
AI.result: The CIR-IF Taxonomy was constructed, providing a comprehensive and up-to-date classification of empirical findings on incident response influencing factors. Comparative analysis demonstrated the taxonomy's superior richness, rigor, and systematic organization over existing frameworks.
AI.conclusion: The CIR-IF Taxonomy fills a critical gap by offering an integrative, multi-domain perspective on incident response factors, enabling researchers to better target underexplored areas and advance both theoretical and empirical work in cybersecurity incident response.

title: When Do LLM Personas Support Visualization Design? A Cross-Model Study of Color Assignment and Chart Choice
summary: Large language model personas are increasingly used to approximate diverse users during early-stage visualization design, but it remains unclear whether persona-conditioned outputs reflect stable personality effects or artifacts of model choice and task framing. We examine this question across two visualization-relevant tasks: color assignment for abstract and concrete concepts, and chart-idiom preference ratings across task contexts. Using 43 Big Five profiles across GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, and GPT-5-mini, we find that personality-color coupling is highly model-configuration dependent: absent in GPT-4o-mini for all six concepts, consistent in GPT-4.1-mini across all six, and partial in GPT-5-mini for two of six. Concept type further shapes the signal: for abstract concepts, personality explains more hue variance than model identity, while concrete concepts show smaller and comparable effects. In chart choice, trait-aligned cluster aggregation produces stable top-idiom rankings across all nine cluster-context combinations, but a no-persona baseline recovers the same top choice in 8 of 9 model-context cells, indicating that task context drives rank-1 selection more than personality. These findings position LLM personas as exploratory probes for visualization design, not substitutes for human participants, and motivate multi-model testing, concept-type disaggregation, and no-persona baselines in future studies.

AI.tldr: LLM personas conditioned on Big Five personality traits show inconsistent, model-dependent effects on visualization-relevant tasks: personality-color coupling varies across GPT configurations, and task context—not personality—drives chart-idiom preferences, suggesting LLM personas are exploratory probes rather than human substitutes.
AI.motivation: LLM personas are increasingly used to simulate diverse users in early-stage visualization design, but it is unknown whether persona-conditioned outputs reflect genuine, stable personality effects or are artifacts of model choice and task framing. This uncertainty threatens the validity of using LLMs as proxies for human participants in design research.
AI.method: The authors tested 43 Big Five personality profiles across three GPT model configurations (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5-mini) on two visualization-relevant tasks: (1) color assignment for six abstract and concrete concepts, and (2) chart-idiom preference ratings across task contexts. They analyzed personality-color coupling strength, variance partitioning between personality and model identity, and compared trait-aligned cluster rankings against a no-persona baseline for top idiom selection.
AI.result: Personality-color coupling was absent in GPT-4o-mini for all six concepts, fully consistent in GPT-4.1-mini across all six, and partial (2 of 6) in GPT-5-mini. For abstract concepts, personality explained more hue variance than model identity; for concrete concepts, effects were smaller and comparable. In chart choice, trait-aligned clusters produced stable top-idiom rankings, but the no-persona baseline recovered the same top choice in 8 of 9 model-context cells, indicating task context dominates rank-1 selection.
AI.conclusion: LLM personas serve as exploratory probes for visualization design rather than substitutes for human participants. Future work should adopt multi-model testing, disaggregate results by concept type, and include no-persona baselines to distinguish genuine personality signals from model and task artifacts.

title: Decoupling Code Complexity from Newcomer Participation: A Causal Study of AI Coding Agent Adoption in OSS
summary: Open-source projects depend on a steady inflow of newcomers. A growing concern is that AI coding agents (tools such as Cursor and Claude Code that write code from natural-language instructions) will crowd them out, by absorbing the simple tasks that beginners start with and by making code harder to read. We give this concern a causal answer. Using GitHub code search we identify 1,888 projects that adopted an agent, signaled by their first commit of a configuration file. We apply difference-in-differences against matched non-adopting controls, restricting the main analysis to the 603 adopters with a genuine pre-adoption period. We find no evidence of crowding-out: across estimators newcomer inflow shows no significant decline after adoption (point estimates run from a small increase to, under the most conservative trend specification, a slight and insignificant dip), onboarding and retention are unchanged, and a sparse, correlational beginner-task measure (good-first-issue labels, which we cannot test for parallel trends) shows no decline. The feared mechanism is real but decoupled: adoption raises per-function code complexity (about +11% on a cognitive metric for Python, a quarter of the prior estimate, and +3 to 4% in cyclomatic terms across all languages), yet in fixed-unit subsets where complexity rose (Python on the cognitive metric, and all languages on the cyclomatic metric), newcomer participation does not decline. These results suggest that, in established open-source projects, adopting an AI coding agent makes code modestly more complex but does not crowd out the human newcomers that a project depends on: the feared trade-off between AI assistance and human participation does not materialize.

AI.tldr: This study examines whether AI coding agents crowd out newcomers in open-source projects. Using difference-in-differences on 603 GitHub projects that adopted AI agents, the authors find no significant decline in newcomer inflow, onboarding, or retention, despite detecting modest increases in code complexity (~11% cognitive, ~3-4% cyclomatic). The feared trade-off between AI assistance and human participation does not materialize.
AI.motivation: There is growing concern that AI coding agents (e.g., Cursor, Claude Code) may crowd out newcomers from open-source projects by automating simple starter tasks and making code harder to read, thereby disrupting the pipeline of new contributors that projects depend on for sustainability.
AI.method: The authors use GitHub code search to identify 1,888 projects that adopted an AI agent (signaled by first commit of an agent configuration file). They apply difference-in-differences estimation against matched non-adopting control projects. The main analysis is restricted to 603 adopters with a genuine pre-adoption period. Outcome variables include newcomer inflow, onboarding, retention, and a correlational beginner-task measure (good-first-issue labels). They also measure code complexity changes using cognitive and cyclomatic metrics.
AI.result: No evidence of crowding-out was found: newcomer inflow showed no significant decline across estimators. Onboarding and retention were unchanged. Good-first-issue labels showed no decline (though parallel trends could not be tested). Code complexity increased: ~11% on a cognitive metric for Python and +3-4% in cyclomatic complexity across all languages. However, in subsets where complexity rose, newcomer participation did not decline, indicating a decoupling of the feared mechanism from the outcome.
AI.conclusion: In established open-source projects, adopting AI coding agents makes code modestly more complex but does not crowd out human newcomers. The feared trade-off between AI assistance and human participation does not materialize.

title: On the Utility and Factual Reliability of Pruned Mixture-of-Experts Models in the Biomedical Domain
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer inference speedups via selective activation but impose substantial memory requirements because the whole network must remain loaded. Structured expert pruning is a practical approach for reducing deployment costs in resource-constrained settings. However, prior studies primarily evaluate benchmark utility, leaving the effect of pruning on factual reliability underexplored, particularly in high-stakes domains such as biomedicine. In this paper, we investigate how domain-specific expert pruning affects both utility and reliability. We assess four MoE models, six pruning methods, and multiple pruning ratios across generation and classification tasks under in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain settings. Results reveal that moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility without immediate reliability decline, although hallucination risks increase at extreme pruning ratios. When shifting to the general domain, both utility and reliability degrade rapidly. These findings indicate that safe compression depends heavily on the task and domain. Evaluating pruned MoE models solely on utility is inadequate for high-stakes deployment without reliability assessment.

AI.tldr: Investigates how structured expert pruning in MoE models affects both utility and factual reliability, finding that moderate pruning preserves in-domain biomedical performance but hallucination risks rise at extreme ratios, while cross-domain generalization degrades rapidly — underscoring that utility-only evaluation is insufficient for high-stakes deployment.
AI.motivation: Prior work on structured expert pruning for MoE models focuses primarily on benchmark utility, neglecting the impact on factual reliability (hallucination). This gap is especially critical in high-stakes domains like biomedicine, where factual accuracy is paramount. The authors aim to fill this gap by jointly evaluating utility and reliability under pruning.
AI.method: The authors evaluate four MoE models subjected to six structured pruning methods across multiple pruning ratios. Tasks span both generation and classification, assessed under in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain (general) settings. Utility is measured via standard benchmarks, while reliability is assessed through hallucination metrics, enabling a joint analysis of the utility–reliability trade-off.
AI.result: Moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility without immediate reliability degradation. At extreme pruning ratios, hallucination risks increase notably. When shifting from biomedical to general domain, both utility and reliability degrade rapidly, indicating that safe compression is highly task- and domain-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating pruned MoE models on utility alone is inadequate for high-stakes deployment; reliability assessment (hallucination measurement) is essential. Safe compression thresholds depend on the specific task and domain, with cross-domain generalization being particularly vulnerable.

title: Grounded Optimization: A Layered Engineering Framework for Reducing LLM Hallucination in Automated Personal Document Rewriting
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure. Equal contribution by both authors. Code and data: https://github.com/shashank-indukuri/grounded-optimization
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to resume optimization for applicant tracking systems, introducing hallucination failures distinct from general text generation: anachronistic technology injection, cross-domain terminology contamination, structural mutation, and content fabrication. We present Grounded Optimization, a five-layer framework combining temporal context validation, deterministic contamination detection, structural invariant enforcement, prompt-level grounding, and an evaluator agent.
  In ablation experiments across three LLMs, four temperature settings, and six layer configurations on 25 synthetic resumes spanning 14 industries, undefended baselines produce 2.48-5.36 detected hallucinations per resume. Among detectors independent of the active defenses, temporal hallucinations are reduced by 50-95% across all conditions; overall detected hallucination rate falls to 0.04-0.24. Prompt-level grounding alone achieves zero detected hallucinations at low temperature with a capable instruction-following model; higher temperatures and weaker models reveal the need for the deterministic layers as a complement. We release the contamination taxonomy, evaluation code, and raw data.

AI.tldr: A five-layer "Grounded Optimization" framework is proposed to mitigate four distinct hallucination types in LLM-based resume optimization, reducing detected hallucinations from 2.48–5.36 per resume to 0.04–0.24, with prompt-level grounding alone achieving zero detected hallucinations under favorable conditions.
AI.motivation: LLMs used for resume optimization for applicant tracking systems (ATS) introduce unique hallucination failures—anachronistic technology injection, cross-domain terminology contamination, structural mutation, and content fabrication—that differ from general text generation hallucinations and require targeted mitigation.
AI.method: Grounded Optimization: a five-layer defense framework comprising (1) temporal context validation, (2) deterministic contamination detection, (3) structural invariant enforcement, (4) prompt-level grounding, and (5) an evaluator agent. Evaluated via ablation experiments across 3 LLMs, 4 temperature settings, and 6 layer configurations on 25 synthetic resumes spanning 14 industries.
AI.result: Undefended baselines: 2.48–5.36 detected hallucinations per resume. With defenses: temporal hallucinations reduced 50–95%; overall detected hallucination rate falls to 0.04–0.24 per resume. Prompt-level grounding alone achieves zero detected hallucinations at low temperature with a capable instruction-following model; higher temperatures and weaker models require the deterministic layers as a complement.
AI.conclusion: The Grounded Optimization framework effectively mitigates ATS-specific LLM hallucinations. Prompt-level grounding is highly effective under ideal conditions, but deterministic layers serve as essential complements for weaker models and higher-temperature settings. The authors release the contamination taxonomy, evaluation code, and raw data.

title: EO-Agents: A Three-Agent LLM Pipeline for Earth Observation Hypothesis Generation
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop
summary: Large language models have recently been explored for scientific hypothesis generation, but most prior work relies on unstructured literature and free-form textual claims. We present a pipeline for Earth observation that grounds hypothesis generation directly in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph. A heterogeneous graph neural network trained on historical co-usage relations ranks candidate dataset pairings, and a three-agent LLM pipeline filters, generates, and evaluates structured research hypotheses. Applied to 1,475 NASA datasets, the system produces 160 hypotheses spanning multiple Earth-science domains, including ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol--cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry. Model-predicted novel dataset pairings are rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages from the literature, indicating that the pipeline surfaces scientifically coherent yet unexplored combinations. A 2*2*2 factorial experiment across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 shows that hypothesis rankings remain stable, while absolute scores depend strongly on judge identity, highlighting limitations of single-judge LLM evaluation.

AI.tldr: A pipeline using a heterogeneous GNN trained on NASA's Earth Observation Knowledge Graph ranks candidate dataset pairings, then a three-agent LLM system generates and evaluates structured hypotheses. Applied to 1,475 NASA datasets, it produced 160 cross-domain hypotheses, with novel pairings rated nearly as plausible as real co-usages. A factorial experiment reveals ranking stability but judge-dependent absolute scores.
AI.motivation: Prior work on LLM-based scientific hypothesis generation relies on unstructured literature and free-form claims, lacking grounding in structured, curated knowledge bases. This limits verifiability, reproducibility, and domain specificity—particularly in Earth observation, where rich structured metadata and dataset co-usage patterns exist but remain underutilized for hypothesis discovery.
AI.method: A heterogeneous graph neural network (GNN) is trained on historical co-usage relations from the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph to rank candidate dataset pairings. The top-ranked pairings then pass through a three-agent LLM pipeline: a filtering agent screens for scientific plausibility, a generation agent formulates structured research hypotheses, and an evaluation agent scores them. The system was applied to 1,475 NASA datasets. A 2×2×2 factorial experiment across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 assessed ranking stability and judge bias.
AI.result: The system generated 160 hypotheses spanning ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol–cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry. Model-predicted novel dataset pairings were rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages from the literature. The factorial experiment showed hypothesis rankings remained stable across LLM judges, but absolute scores depended strongly on judge identity, exposing limitations of single-judge LLM evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Grounding LLM-based hypothesis generation in a structured knowledge graph (versus unstructured literature) yields scientifically coherent, cross-domain hypotheses that approximate the plausibility of real published dataset combinations. However, single-judge LLM evaluation is unreliable for absolute scoring; multi-judge or calibration strategies are needed for robust assessment.

title: Understanding Software Defect Prediction: A Large-scale Empirical Study Across Uncertainty Quantification and Performance Evaluation
summary: Software defect prediction (SDP) classifiers produce probabilities used for inspection prioritization, threshold tuning, and risk communication. Probability-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) characterizes prediction confidence, but whether common UQ metrics reliably indicate performance and calibration remains unclear. We conducted a large-scale empirical study of probability-based UQ for SDP. We evaluated five UQ metrics, six performance metrics, and three calibration metrics for 16 representative classifiers. We analyzed these relationships under two prediction settings: within-project defect prediction (WPDP), using 36 benchmark datasets, and cross-project defect prediction (CPDP), using 32 feature-compatible datasets. Results showed that UQ was highly context-dependent. Under WPDP, UQ correlated more consistently with false positive rate and AUC than with MCC, F1 score, and other metrics; these correlations also varied across classifier categories and dataset collections. Performance and calibration were related but not interchangeable; classifiers with strong discrimination could still exhibit large calibration error. Under CPDP, several UQ-performance and UQ-calibration correlations weakened or reversed, indicating that uncertainty signals do not reliably transfer across projects. Thus, UQ should be evaluated against specific performance objectives. Calibration should be assessed independently using multiple metrics. Transferred probabilities should be revalidated before guiding quality-assurance decisions.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical study shows that probability-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) in software defect prediction is highly context-dependent: UQ-performance correlations vary by metric and classifier type, performance and calibration are not interchangeable, and UQ signals do not reliably transfer across projects (CPDP). UQ should be evaluated against specific objectives, and transferred probabilities must be revalidated.
AI.motivation: SDP classifiers output probabilities for inspection prioritization and risk communication, yet it remains unclear whether common UQ metrics reliably indicate classifier performance and calibration. The authors aim to clarify the relationships among UQ, performance, and calibration under both within-project and cross-project defect prediction settings.
AI.method: An empirical study evaluating five UQ metrics, six performance metrics, and three calibration metrics across 16 representative classifiers. Two prediction settings were examined: WPDP (36 benchmark datasets) and CPDP (32 feature-compatible datasets). Correlational analyses were conducted to assess relationships among UQ, performance, and calibration.
AI.result: Under WPDP, UQ correlated more consistently with false positive rate and AUC than with MCC and F1; correlations varied by classifier category and dataset collection. Strong discrimination did not guarantee good calibration. Under CPDP, several UQ-performance and UQ-calibration correlations weakened or reversed, indicating unreliable transfer of uncertainty signals across projects.
AI.conclusion: UQ should be evaluated against specific performance objectives rather than treated as a universal surrogate. Calibration must be assessed independently using multiple metrics. Probabilities transferred across projects require revalidation before informing quality-assurance decisions.

title: Geometry-Aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
summary:
We propose a novel hybrid neural architecture, the Geometry-aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (GRS-KAN), which integrates V.L.Rvachev's R-functions into the Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) framework. The proposed approach combines two complementary modeling mechanisms: smooth nonlinear structure is learned by KAN branches, while known geometric or logical constraints are encoded analytically using differentiable R-functions. This enables explicit representation of discontinuities, feasible regions, and implicit geometric boundaries within a trainable neural architecture.
  The framework implements differentiable logical operations through R-conjunctions and R-disjunctions, allowing complex geometric supports to be represented analytically and incorporated directly into regression models. Several GRS-KAN variants are introduced, including additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted architectures.
  The method is demonstrated on regression problems involving discontinuities with circular and rectangular supports. Numerical experiments show that explicit geometric encoding substantially improves predictive accuracy and boundary localization compared with standard KANs. In the considered benchmarks, geometry-aware GRS-KAN models reduce test RMSE by up to 67% while simultaneously improving interpretability through explicit analytical representation of the learned geometric structure. The agnostic variant further demonstrates the ability to automatically determine whether geometric priors are beneficial for a given learning task.

AI.tldr: GRS-KAN integrates R-functions into KANs for explicit geometric constraint encoding, achieving up to 67% RMSE reduction on discontinuous regression tasks while improving interpretability.
AI.motivation: Standard KANs lack mechanisms to explicitly encode known geometric constraints (discontinuities, feasible regions, boundaries), relying solely on data to learn such structure. The authors aim to inject analytical geometric priors directly into the architecture.
AI.method: GRS-KAN combines KAN-learned smooth nonlinear branches with analytically encoded R-functions (R-conjunctions, R-disjunctions) for differentiable logical operations. This encodes geometric supports (circular, rectangular) explicitly within the network. Variants include additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted architectures, the latter auto-determining whether geometric priors help.
AI.result: On regression problems with circular and rectangular discontinuities, GRS-KAN reduces test RMSE by up to 67% versus standard KANs, improves boundary localization, and enhances interpretability through explicit analytical geometric representations.
AI.conclusion: Explicit geometric encoding via R-functions significantly boosts KAN performance on structured discontinuous problems. The agnostic variant offers a practical mechanism for automatically leveraging geometric priors only when beneficial.

title: Comparing Architectures for Supervised Political Scaling
summary: Text scaling, the task of positioning political actors on an ideological scale, is a fundamental task in political analysis. To ease the need for manual analysis, various NLP methods have been proposed for this task, including classification- and regression-based approaches, showing successes as well as limitations. The goal of our paper is to consolidate the state of the art in this area. We ask two questions: (a) Can the performance of scaling methods be improved by predicting scales not individually but jointly? (b) Is there a middle ground between classification and regression?

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether joint prediction of multiple ideological scales improves text scaling performance and explores a middle-ground approach between classification and regression for positioning political actors on ideological spectra.
AI.motivation: Existing NLP methods for text scaling (classifying or regressing political actors' ideological positions) have shown both successes and limitations. The authors aim to consolidate the state of the art by addressing two open questions: whether joint prediction of scales outperforms individual prediction, and whether a hybrid approach bridging classification and regression can be effective.
AI.method: The paper proposes and evaluates two methodological directions: (1) joint modeling of multiple ideological scales simultaneously rather than independently, and (2) an approach that finds a middle ground between classification-based and regression-based scaling techniques.
AI.result: Not specified in the abstract; results are to be presented in the full paper.
AI.conclusion: Not specified in the abstract; conclusions are to be presented in the full paper.

title: Hawk: Harnessing Hardware-Aware Knowledge for High-Performance NPU Kernel Generation
summary: Developing high-performance kernels for Neural Processing Units (NPUs) is a critical industry bottleneck, requiring developers to manually navigate implicit hardware constraints and strict memory hierarchies. While large language models offer immense automation potential, they fail catastrophically on NPUs due to a fundamental lack of hardware-specific priors. Naively transplanting code snippets from similar NPU kernels may pass the compiler, but it consistently triggers runtime crashes and performance degradation by blindly violating underlying hardware constraints. To overcome this, we introduce Hawk, a training-free framework that harnesses hardware-aware knowledge through three core modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module, which employs a Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation to inherently couple the error context with executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module, which implements a 2D-Retrieval paradigm to project queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; and (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module, which leverages LLM-driven semantic arbitration to continuously distill the knowledge by pruning errors and consolidating redundancies based on the empirical execution feedback. Extensive evaluations on real-world NPU workloads demonstrate that Hawk elevates generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0%, while achieving up to a 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: Hawk is a training-free framework that enables LLMs to generate correct, high-performance NPU kernels by incorporating hardware-aware knowledge through three modules: run-time knowledge synthesis, bottleneck-aware retrieval, and effect-driven distillation. It boosts generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0% and achieves up to 2.2× speedup.
