AI.motivation: Manually developing NPU kernels is a critical bottleneck because developers must navigate implicit hardware constraints and strict memory hierarchies. LLMs fail on this task due to a lack of hardware-specific priors — naively reusing code snippets from similar kernels compiles but triggers runtime crashes and performance degradation by violating hidden hardware constraints.
AI.method: Hawk introduces three training-free modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis, using a Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation that couples error context with executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval, employing a 2D-Retrieval paradigm that projects queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; and (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation, which uses LLM-driven semantic arbitration to prune errors and consolidate redundancies based on empirical execution feedback.
AI.result: On real-world NPU workloads, Hawk improves generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0% and achieves up to a 2.2× execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: Hawk demonstrates that injecting hardware-aware knowledge via a training-free, execution-feedback-driven framework can substantially close the gap between LLM-generated NPU kernels and hand-tuned implementations, addressing a critical industry bottleneck.

title: Unveiling the Non-Monotonic Effect of Privacy on Generalization under Byzantine Robustness
summary: Recent work has established a fundamental trilemma between Byzantine robustness, local differential privacy (LDP), and optimization error in distributed learning. We show that this trilemma does not universally extend to generalization error, but instead depends critically on the privacy regime. Specifically, in the high-noise regime (strong privacy), we prove that increasing privacy reduces the generalization error, i.e., there is no tension between robustness and privacy. In the low-noise regime (weaker privacy), however, the tension between robustness and privacy reappears and increasing privacy indeed degrades generalization. Our theory explains this surprising non-monotonic behavior of the generalization error via matching lower and upper bounds on the algorithmic stability of Byzantine-robust distributed learning under LDP constraints. We corroborate and further analyze these theoretical findings with empirical evaluations.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that the trilemma between Byzantine robustness, LDP, and optimization error does not uniformly apply to generalization error. In strong-privacy (high-noise) regimes, more privacy surprisingly improves generalization, while in weak-privacy (low-noise) regimes, the expected tension re-emerges. This non-monotonic behavior is explained via algorithmic stability bounds.
AI.motivation: Prior work established a fundamental trilemma among Byzantine robustness, local differential privacy (LDP), and optimization error in distributed learning. The authors aim to investigate whether this trilemma extends to generalization error, and if not, to characterize the nuanced relationship between robustness, privacy, and generalization.
AI.method: The authors derive matching lower and upper bounds on the algorithmic stability of Byzantine-robust distributed learning under LDP constraints. These stability bounds are then used to theoretically characterize generalization error across different privacy regimes (high-noise vs. low-noise), revealing non-monotonic behavior. Empirical evaluations corroborate the theoretical findings.
AI.result: In the high-noise (strong privacy) regime, increasing privacy reduces generalization error — no tension between robustness and privacy exists. In the low-noise (weak privacy) regime, the tension reappears: increasing privacy degrades generalization. This non-monotonic behavior is confirmed both theoretically via stability bounds and empirically.
AI.conclusion: The Byzantine-robustness–LDP–error trilemma is not universal for generalization error but is instead privacy-regime-dependent. The surprising beneficial effect of strong privacy on generalization is explained through the lens of algorithmic stability, providing a more nuanced understanding of the interplay between robustness, privacy, and learning performance.

title: Technical Debt Friction for Maintenance Prioritization: An Industrial Multi-Case Study
comment: Accepted for the 42nd International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (Industry Track)
summary: Software-intensive organizations need effective ways to identify where maintenance and refactoring efforts will yield the greatest practical benefit. Although software analytics such as code health, hotspots, and coupling provide valuable signals, they do not always capture the experienced burden of change that slows software evolution in practice. This paper presents a multi-case industrial study of technical debt friction as a prioritization-oriented concept for identifying where technical debt most strongly affects maintenance and evolution. We investigate how practitioners interpret the concept, whether friction-related analysis aligns with perceived maintenance pain points and refactoring needs, and what broader maintenance and evolution insights friction can provide beyond individual refactoring candidates. To this end, we conducted structured walkthrough sessions with practitioners across multiple industrial cases using analysis artifacts including code health, hotspots, coupling, refactoring targets, and socio-technical views. Our findings show that practitioners generally considered technical debt friction useful for reasoning about maintenance burden, especially when interpreted together with complementary technical and socio-technical views. At the file level, friction often aligned with known problematic areas and, in several cases, with files that later received maintenance attention, although its practical relevance depended strongly on context. In addition, our exploratory project-level analysis suggests that friction distributions may reveal broader maintenance and evolution patterns. These results indicate that technical debt friction is promising as a decision-support concept, but most effective when used with contextual knowledge and supporting evidence.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multi-case industrial study on "technical debt friction" — a prioritization-oriented concept that identifies where technical debt most severely impacts maintenance and evolution. Through structured walkthroughs with practitioners across multiple cases, the study finds that friction aligns with known problem areas and future maintenance activity, but its practical relevance is highly context-dependent and most effective when combined with complementary views and contextual knowledge.
AI.motivation: Existing software analytics (code health, hotspots, coupling) provide useful signals but fail to capture the experienced burden of change that slows evolution in practice. There is a need for a concept that better identifies where technical debt most tangibly impedes maintenance and refactoring, enabling more effective prioritization of limited resources.
AI.method: A multi-case industrial study using structured walkthrough sessions with practitioners. Participants examined analysis artifacts including code health, hotspots, coupling, refactoring targets, and socio-technical views. The study investigated three research questions: (1) how practitioners interpret technical debt friction, (2) whether friction aligns with perceived pain points and refactoring needs, and (3) what broader evolution insights friction provides at the project level beyond individual refactoring candidates.
AI.result: Practitioners found technical debt friction useful for reasoning about maintenance burden, especially when interpreted alongside complementary technical and socio-technical views. At the file level, friction frequently aligned with known problematic areas and, in several cases, with files that later received maintenance attention. Exploratory project-level analysis suggested friction distributions may reveal broader maintenance and evolution patterns. Practical relevance was strongly context-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Technical debt friction is a promising decision-support concept for prioritizing maintenance and refactoring efforts, but it is most effective when combined with contextual knowledge and supporting evidence, rather than used as a standalone metric.

title: Token Geometry
summary: Language models learn continuous programs over discrete symbols, with the embedding table and LM-head acting as the read/write interface between them. We show that this interface has gradient geometry distinct from dense hidden weights which can be exploited to improve the Pareto frontier across supervised finetuning, RL, and pretraining, while only utilizing kilobytes of optimizer state. We introduce Ember, a lightweight optimizer for embedding and LM-head matrices that utilizes O(V + D) VRAM, instead of Adam's O(2VD), and forgoes the need to shard both token table optimizer states. We provide empirical evidence that Ember scales effectively across batch size and parameter count. We show that the optimization trajectory of tokens can be well described by a simple 1D ray, counter to the popular belief that neural net parameters navigate a heavily nonconvex landscape. We provide a principled view on the surprisingly narrow space of optimizers that suffice for Transformer training. Finally, we open-source our distributed Ember implementation that merges cleanly with existing ZeRO/FSDP setups to support further research at https://github.com/katop1234/ember

AI.tldr: Ember introduces a memory-efficient optimizer specifically for embedding and LM-head matrices in Transformers, using only O(V+D) VRAM instead of Adam's O(2VD). It exploits the distinct gradient geometry of these token-related parameters to improve the Pareto frontier across training paradigms, and surprisingly shows token optimization trajectories follow a simple 1D ray.
AI.motivation: Standard optimizers like Adam allocate two momentum/variance states per parameter, costing O(2VD) memory for embedding tables (vocabulary size V × hidden dimension D). This forces model sharding of optimizer states. The authors identify that embedding/LM-head matrices have fundamentally different gradient geometry from dense hidden weights, creating an opportunity for specialized, memory-light optimization.
AI.method: Ember leverages the observation that gradient updates to token embeddings predominantly lie along a low-rank (effectively rank-1) subspace, describable as a 1D ray per token. The optimizer maintains lightweight statistics at O(V+D) cost — tracking per-token and per-dimension signals separately rather than the full O(VD) state — and applies structured updates that exploit this geometry, all while integrating cleanly with ZeRO/FSDP distributed setups.
AI.result: Ember matches or exceeds Adam's performance across supervised finetuning, RL, and pretraining while using dramatically less memory (kilobytes of optimizer state). It scales effectively across batch sizes and model sizes. The 1D ray model of token optimization trajectories is empirically validated, challenging the conventional view of highly nonconvex neural parameter landscapes.
AI.conclusion: The embedding/LM-head interface in Transformers admits a specialized optimizer (Ember) that is both principled and practical, narrowing the design space of optimizers needed for Transformer training while achieving memory efficiency and strong performance. The open-source release supports further adoption and research.

title: From Monolingual to Multilingual: Evaluating Mamba for ASR in South African Languages
summary: Recent advances in automatic speech recognition (ASR) have explored different sequence models, including Conformer-based models and newer state space models such as Mamba. Although prior work has evaluated these architectures in multiple languages, their effectiveness in African languages remains underexplored. In this work, we evaluate Mamba for ASR on seven South African languages. In monolingual experiments, each model is trained on 50 hours of speech per language, and we compare Mamba to a Conformer baseline of similar parameter scale. Mamba achieves similar recognition accuracy to Conformer while using fewer computational resources and training faster. We further evaluate generalization in this setting and find that both models struggle to generalize to speech that is much longer than what they were trained on. We then study multilingual ASR using Mamba models, where the baseline is pooling all languages together. On top of this, we tested three extensions: training with language-family information by adding both language and language-family embeddings as biases to the downsampled acoustic representations, and multitask learning with a CTC ASR objective and a language identification (LID) head. We find that multilingual training consistently improves performance over monolingual training. However, adding explicit language information does not improve in-domain performance but does improve cross-corpus robustness. We conducted ablation studies in low-resource multilingual settings using 5-hour and 10-hour per-language training data, where we observed gains from using language embeddings and further demonstrated that removing or altering them hurt model performance. Lastly, we analysed these embeddings and find that they do not capture linguistic similarity in a typological sense, but instead act as task-specific control vectors.

AI.tldr: Evaluates Mamba vs. Conformer for ASR on seven South African languages. Mamba matches Conformer accuracy with fewer resources and faster training. Multilingual training improves performance; explicit language embeddings boost cross-corpus robustness but not in-domain performance. Embeddings function as task-specific control vectors rather than capturing typological similarity.
AI.motivation: While Conformer and Mamba architectures have been evaluated across multiple languages, their comparative effectiveness for African languages—particularly South African languages—remains underexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by benchmarking Mamba against Conformer and investigating whether explicit linguistic information (language/family embeddings, multitask LID) improves multilingual ASR in low-resource settings.
AI.method: Monolingual experiments train Mamba and Conformer models (matched parameter scale) on 50 hours of speech per language across seven South African languages, comparing accuracy, compute, and generalization to long utterances. Multilingual experiments pool all languages and test three extensions: (1) language embeddings, (2) language-family embeddings added as biases to downsampled acoustic representations, and (3) multitask learning with CTC ASR + language identification (LID) head. Ablations use 5-hour and 10-hour per-language low-resource settings, with embedding removal/alteration analysis and final embedding space interpretation.
AI.result: Mamba achieves comparable recognition accuracy to Conformer with lower compute and faster training. Both models struggle to generalize to utterances significantly longer than training examples. Multilingual training consistently outperforms monolingual baselines. Explicit language/family embeddings and LID multitasking do not improve in-domain performance but enhance cross-corpus robustness. In low-resource ablations (5h, 10h per language), embeddings provide gains; removing or altering them degrades performance. Embedding analysis reveals they do not encode typological linguistic similarity but act as task-specific control vectors.
AI.conclusion: Mamba is a computationally efficient alternative to Conformer for ASR in low-resource African languages. Multilingual training is beneficial, but explicit language information primarily aids cross-domain generalization rather than in-domain accuracy. Language embeddings serve as learned task-specific control signals rather than capturing intrinsic linguistic relationships.

title: Safe and Adaptive Cloud Healing: Verifying LLM-Generated Recovery Plans with a Neural-Symbolic World Model
summary: As the scale and complexity of cloud-based AI systems continue to escalate, ensuring service reliability through rapid fault detection and adaptive recovery has become a critical challenge. While existing approaches integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) for semantic understanding and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for policy optimization, they often rely on sequential, loosely coupled architectures that underutilize the generative and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. In this paper, we propose a paradigm shift with PASE, a Planning-Aware Semantic self-healing engine, a novel fault self-healing framework that reconceptualizes recovery as a neuro-symbolic program synthesis task. PASE employs an LLM as a core Plan Synthesis Engine to generate structured recovery plans from a library of semantic primitives. A Neural-Symbolic World Model verifies plan feasibility through simulation, while a Meta-Prompt Optimizer, trained via DRL, learns to generate optimal prompts that guide the LLM's planning process. This tight reason-plan-verify-adapt loop enables dynamic, context-aware recovery strategy generation beyond predefined action spaces. Experiments on a real-world cloud fault injection dataset demonstrate that PASE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, reducing average system recovery time by over 40% and improving fault detection accuracy in unknown fault scenarios. Our framework advances autonomous system management by unifying LLM-based reasoning with model-assisted verification and meta-learned guidance.

AI.tldr: PASE introduces a neuro-symbolic self-healing engine for cloud AI systems that uses an LLM as a plan synthesis core, combined with a neural-symbolic world model for verification and a DRL-trained meta-prompt optimizer, achieving 40%+ faster recovery and improved fault detection over SOTA methods.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches that combine LLMs and DRL for cloud fault recovery rely on sequential, loosely coupled architectures that fail to fully exploit LLMs' generative and reasoning capabilities. There is a need for a tightly integrated framework that reconceptualizes fault recovery beyond predefined action spaces.
AI.method: PASE reimagines fault self-healing as neuro-symbolic program synthesis. It features: (1) an LLM-based Plan Synthesis Engine that generates structured recovery plans from semantic primitives; (2) a Neural-Symbolic World Model that simulates and verifies plan feasibility; and (3) a Meta-Prompt Optimizer trained via DRL to produce optimal prompts that guide the LLM's planning. These components form a tight reason-plan-verify-adapt loop.
AI.result: On a real-world cloud fault injection dataset, PASE reduced average system recovery time by over 40% and improved fault detection accuracy in unknown fault scenarios compared to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: PASE advances autonomous system management by unifying LLM-based reasoning, model-assisted verification, and meta-learned guidance into a cohesive self-healing framework, demonstrating significant practical gains in both recovery speed and generalization to novel faults.

title: Copewell: A Multi-Agent Swarm Architecture for Equitable Mental Wellness Support
summary: Mental health disorders affect nearly one billion people globally, yet 75% of individuals in low- and middle-income countries receive no treatment due to workforce shortages, cost barriers, and stigma. Current AI-powered wellness solutions predominantly rely on single-mode conversational interfaces that suffer high abandonment rates and fail to provide measurable, immediate relief calibrated to users' dynamic emotional states. This paper presents Copewell, a novel multi-agent swarm system designed to expand access to mental wellness support through human-centered AI principles. Our architecture introduces three technical innovations: (1) a multi-source assessment framework integrating self-reported, physiological, and contextual data to mitigate algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping using Russell's Circumplex Model of Affect to route users to specialized AI agents; and (3) dual-mode intervention delivery combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. We examine the sociotechnical design considerations underlying Copewell's development, including a privacy-first architecture, embedded ethical oversight through a dedicated Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design informed by mental health practitioners. Early practitioner engagement and beta deployment inform design decisions and identify directions for future empirical evaluation. This work contributes to responsible AI discourse by demonstrating how technical architecture can operationalize equity and safety principles from inception.

AI.tldr: Copewell is a multi-agent swarm system for mental wellness that combines multi-source assessment, emotion mapping via Russell's Circumplex Model, and dual-mode intervention (conversational + sensory) to address access gaps in low-resource settings, with embedded ethical oversight and privacy-first design.
AI.motivation: Nearly one billion people suffer from mental health disorders, with 75% untreated in low- and middle-income countries due to workforce shortages, cost, and stigma. Existing AI wellness tools rely on single-mode conversational interfaces with high abandonment rates and lack measurable, immediate, emotionally calibrated relief.
AI.method: Copewell employs a multi-agent swarm architecture with three innovations: (1) multi-source assessment fusing self-reported, physiological, and contextual data to reduce algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping via Russell's Circumplex Model to route users to specialized agents; (3) dual-mode delivery combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. The system integrates a privacy-first architecture, a dedicated Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design with mental health practitioners.
AI.result: Early practitioner engagement and beta deployment informed design decisions and surfaced directions for future empirical evaluation. The paper frames these as preliminary outcomes rather than formal efficacy results.
AI.conclusion: Copewell demonstrates how responsible AI principles — equity, safety, and ethics — can be operationalized at the architectural level from inception, contributing to discourse on sociotechnical design for accessible mental wellness support in underserved contexts.

title: Regression Accumulation in Multi-Turn LLM Programming Conversations
summary:
In LLM-assisted software development, coding is often iterative. We study regression accumulation in multi-turn LLM programming conversations, where later code suggestions may break requirements introduced in earlier turns. Reliability therefore depends not only on satisfying the current request, but also on preserving previously satisfied behavior.
  We construct 542 tasks from HumanEval+ and MBPP+ and extend each task into an 8-turn requirement-evolution chain. We evaluate six LLMs on 26,016 turn instances (542 x 6 x 8). At each turn, we test whether the current code still passes earlier benchmark tests. We also analyze 384 failure cases from the failure population and build a taxonomy of multi-turn regression bugs through independent four-annotator labeling.
  Our results show that regression accumulation appears across all six models: 40% to 73% of tasks lose previously correct behavior over the full conversation. Final-turn quality is lower than initial-turn quality across models, especially when later turns add input validation or broader input types. Manual analysis shows that Cross-Turn Conflict, where later code conflicts with earlier requirements, is the main failure class. We further find that Verification Gate, which checks new code against prior tests and triggers rollback and retry, is the only strategy that consistently improves all models, raising final-turn quality from 75.8% to 87.9% on DeepSeek-V3 and from 31.6% to 47.3% on Llama-3.1-8B.
  These findings suggest that strong single-turn performance can overestimate reliability in multi-turn coding conversations. Future evaluation and tool design should test whether later code suggestions preserve earlier requirements and should include Verification Gate mechanisms.

AI.tldr: In iterative LLM-assisted coding, models frequently regress on previously satisfied requirements as conversations progress. A study of 26,016 turn instances across six LLMs finds 40-73% of tasks lose correct behavior, with Cross-Turn Conflict as the dominant failure mode. A Verification Gate strategy — checking new code against prior tests with rollback and retry — consistently improves all models, suggesting multi-turn evaluation and preservation mechanisms are essential for reliable LLM coding assistants.
AI.motivation: LLM-assisted programming is inherently iterative, yet existing evaluations focus on single-turn code generation. The authors identify a critical gap: no prior work systematically measures whether LLMs preserve previously satisfied requirements across multi-turn conversations. This leads to overestimating real-world reliability, as strong single-turn performance may mask regression accumulation when requirements evolve turn-by-turn.
AI.method: The authors construct 542 tasks from HumanEval+ and MBPP+, extending each into an 8-turn requirement-evolution chain. Six LLMs are evaluated on 26,016 total turn instances (542 × 6 × 8). At each turn, previously passed benchmark tests are re-executed against the current code to detect regressions. Additionally, 384 failure cases undergo independent four-annotator labeling to build a taxonomy of multi-turn regression bugs. A mitigation strategy called Verification Gate is tested — it checks new code against prior tests and triggers rollback and retry upon failure.
AI.result: Regression accumulation is pervasive: 40% to 73% of tasks exhibit loss of previously correct behavior over full conversations. Final-turn quality drops below initial-turn quality across all models, particularly when later turns introduce input validation or broader input types. The failure taxonomy identifies Cross-Turn Conflict (later code conflicting with earlier requirements) as the primary failure class. The Verification Gate strategy consistently improves all models, raising final-turn quality from 75.8% to 87.9% on DeepSeek-V3 and from 31.6% to 47.3% on Llama-3.1-8B.
AI.conclusion: Strong single-turn performance is an unreliable proxy for multi-turn coding reliability. Future LLM coding benchmarks and tools should explicitly test whether later code suggestions preserve earlier requirements. Verification Gate mechanisms offer a practical, consistently effective mitigation strategy and should be incorporated into LLM-assisted development workflows.

title: Class-Grouped Normalized Momentum and Faster Hyperparameter Exploration to Tackle Class Imbalance in Federated Learning
summary: Class imbalance poses a critical challenge in federated learning (FL), where underrepresented classes suffer from poor predictive performance yet cannot be addressed by standard centralized techniques due to privacy and heterogeneity constraints. We propose FedCGNM (Federated Class-Grouped Normalized Momentum), a client-side optimizer in FL that partitions classes into a small number of groups based on minimum within-group variance, maintains a momentum per group, normalizes each group momentum to unit length, and uses the summation of the normalized group momentums as an update direction. This design both equalizes gradient magnitude across majority and minority groups and mitigates the noise inherent in rare-class gradients. We further provide a theoretical convergence analysis explicitly accounting for time-varying resampling-rates. Additionally, to efficiently optimize these rates in small-client regimes, we introduce FedHOO, an X-armed-bandit (XAB) based algorithm that exploits federated parallelism that evaluates many combinations of two candidate rates per client at linear cost. Empirical evaluation on four public long-tailed benchmarks and a proprietary chip-defect dataset demonstrates that FedCGNM consistently outperforms baselines, with FedHOO yielding further gains in small-scale federations.

AI.tldr: FedCGNM is a client-side FL optimizer that groups classes by variance, maintains normalized per-group momentum to equalize gradient magnitudes across majority/minority classes and reduce rare-class gradient noise. FedHOO, an X-armed-bandit algorithm, optimizes resampling rates in small-client settings. The approach outperforms baselines on long-tailed benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Class imbalance in federated learning leads to poor performance on underrepresented classes. Standard centralized techniques cannot be applied due to privacy and data heterogeneity constraints across clients.
AI.method: FedCGNM partitions classes into groups with minimum within-group variance, maintains one momentum buffer per group, normalizes each to unit length, and sums them as the update direction — equalizing gradient magnitudes and mitigating rare-class noise. A convergence analysis accounts for time-varying resampling rates. FedHOO uses an X-armed bandit approach exploiting federated parallelism to efficiently search resampling-rate combinations at linear cost.
AI.result: FedCGNM consistently outperforms baselines on four public long-tailed benchmarks and a proprietary chip-defect dataset. FedHOO yields further gains in small-scale federations.
AI.conclusion: Class-grouped normalized momentum effectively addresses federated class imbalance by balancing gradient magnitudes and reducing noise, with theoretical guarantees. The XAB-based FedHOO further improves performance when client counts are small.

title: Parameter Golf: What Really Works?
summary: How far can a language model improve under a strict artifact budget? Parameter Golf posed this question as an open community challenge in which participants trained the best language model, with the complete artifact (training code + compressed weights) required to fit within 16 MB and be trained in under ten minutes on 8xH100 SXM GPUs. Quality was measured in bits-per-byte (BPB), the average number of bits required to encode each byte of unseen text. We analyze 2,037 pull requests and 1,430 clean scored submissions from the contest, build a taxonomy of 84 optimization techniques, and measure each technique's contribution to BPB. The verified leaderboard score dropped from 1.2244 to 1.058 BPB across three phases -- a 13.6% reduction, despite individual techniques rarely improving BPB by more than 1%. We show that most gains in techniques shrink across competitive submissions, isolating the few methods that improve performance across stacks.

AI.tldr: Analysis of the Parameter Golf community challenge where participants optimized language models under strict constraints (16 MB artifact, <10 min training on 8×H100). The contest yielded 2,037 pull requests and 1,430 scored submissions, reducing BPB from 1.2244 to 1.058 (13.6% improvement). The authors taxonomize 84 optimization techniques, measure individual contributions, and find that most gains shrink in competitive settings — only a few methods consistently improve performance across stacks.
AI.motivation: To systematically understand how far language model performance can be pushed under extreme compute and storage constraints, and to identify which optimization techniques genuinely compound versus those whose benefits diminish in competitive, multi-technique settings.
AI.method: The authors ran a structured community challenge (Parameter Golf) with three phases, enforcing a 16 MB artifact budget and sub-10-minute training on 8×H100 SXM GPUs. They collected and analyzed 2,037 pull requests and 1,430 clean scored submissions, built a taxonomy of 84 distinct optimization techniques, and measured each technique's marginal contribution to bits-per-byte (BPB) reduction using the verified leaderboard data.
AI.result: The leaderboard BPB dropped from 1.2244 to 1.058 (13.6% reduction) across three phases. Individual techniques rarely improved BPB by more than 1%. Most techniques showed diminishing returns in competitive submissions; only a small subset of methods yielded consistent improvements when combined with other optimizations.
AI.conclusion: Extreme compression of language models under tight budgets is feasible and can yield meaningful gains, but the path is highly non-linear: most techniques do not stack additively. The few techniques that robustly improve performance across diverse stacks represent the most valuable directions for efficient LM research.

title: SemHash-LLM: A Multi-Granularity Semantic Hashing Framework for Document Deduplication
summary: Large scale document deduplication must preserve semantic equivalence while remaining efficient over massive corpora. We present SemHash LLM, a multi granularity framework that unifies semantic projection hashing, attention weighted MinHash, contrastive boundary learning, and selective LLM based adjudication. The method combines character, token, and document level signals through gated fusion, then applies a cascaded filtering pipeline for efficient candidate reduction. Semantic projection hashing learns compact binary codes in distilled LLM embedding space, while attention weighted Min- Hash suppresses boilerplate and emphasizes informative content. Adaptive decision boundaries and uncertainty estimation further improve robustness across template pollution, short text perturbation, containment, and viral fragments. Experiments show that SemHash LLM achieves strong duplicate detection quality with less than one percent neural verification cost.

AI.tldr: SemHash LLM is a multi-granularity document deduplication framework that combines semantic projection hashing, attention-weighted MinHash, contrastive boundary learning, and selective LLM adjudication to achieve high-quality duplicate detection with under 1% neural verification cost.
AI.motivation: Large-scale document deduplication must balance semantic equivalence preservation with computational efficiency over massive corpora. Existing methods struggle with template pollution, short text perturbation, containment, and viral fragments, motivating a unified multi-granularity approach with minimal reliance on expensive neural verification.
AI.method: The framework operates across character, token, and document levels with four components: (1) semantic projection hashing that learns compact binary codes in distilled LLM embedding space; (2) attention-weighted MinHash that suppresses boilerplate and emphasizes informative content; (3) contrastive boundary learning with adaptive decision boundaries and uncertainty estimation; (4) a cascaded filtering pipeline with selective LLM-based adjudication for ambiguous cases. Signals from all three granularities are combined via gated fusion.
AI.result: SemHash LLM achieves strong duplicate detection quality while requiring less than 1% neural verification cost across challenging scenarios including template pollution, short text perturbation, containment, and viral fragments.
AI.conclusion: The multi-granularity design with gated fusion and cascaded filtering enables robust, scalable document deduplication. By restricting LLM adjudication to a tiny fraction of ambiguous candidates, the framework successfully decouples detection quality from computational expense.

title: An Exploratory Study on LLM-Generated Code and Comments in Code Repositories
comment: Accepted to The Journal of Systems & Software (JSS) on 1 July 2026
summary: The use of LLMs in software development has become increasingly widespread on tasks such as code generation and summarization. Reports from large technology companies showed that around 20% to 30% of their code are generated by LLMs. However, there remains skepticism about the practical usage of LLM-generated code and comments, such as concerns on more time for debugging the generated code and the unnaturalness of the generated comments. In this paper, we study the code and comments detected as likely to be generated by LLMs and their characteristics, the differences between company- and community-maintained repositories, and how likely bugs are associated with LLM-generated code. We conduct extensive experiments on active company- and community-maintained repositories from 2021 to 2025 using various tools and techniques that detect code and comments generated by LLMs. Based on our detector-based proxy analysis, the results suggest that code detected as likely to be generated by LLMs decreased over time and appeared frequently in test cases, while that of comments remains relatively stable. Proxy results further suggest that code detected as likely to be generated by LLMs shows substantial intra-repository code clones, whereas comments exhibit a relatively low proportion of grammatically correct sentences. In addition, the company-maintained repositories show a higher percentage of code and comments detected as likely to be generated by LLMs, and only a small percentage of the human-labelled bugs are detected as being likely associated with LLM-generated code.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the prevalence, characteristics, and quality implications of LLM-generated code and comments in both company-maintained and community-maintained repositories (2021–2025). Using detector-based proxies, the authors find that LLM-generated code is declining over time and concentrated in test cases, while generated comments remain stable. LLM-generated code shows high intra-repository cloning, and generated comments exhibit poor grammatical correctness. Company repositories have higher LLM-generated content percentages, and only a small fraction of human-labeled bugs are associated with LLM-generated code.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread industry adoption of LLMs for software development (20–30% of code at large tech companies), skepticism persists regarding practical downsides — namely increased debugging effort for generated code and the unnaturalness of generated comments. The authors aim to empirically characterize LLM-generated artifacts and quantify their association with bugs and quality issues.
AI.method: The study applies LLM-generated content detection tools and techniques to active repositories from both company-maintained and community-maintained sources spanning 2021 to 2025. It performs a detector-based proxy analysis to identify code and comments likely generated by LLMs, then analyzes their temporal trends, distribution across code types (e.g., test vs. production code), code clone characteristics, grammatical quality of comments, and correlation with human-labeled bugs.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) LLM-detected code decreased over the study period and appeared disproportionately in test files; (2) LLM-detected comments remained temporally stable; (3) LLM-detected code exhibited significant intra-repository cloning; (4) LLM-detected comments had a relatively low proportion of grammatically correct sentences; (5) company-maintained repositories showed higher percentages of LLM-detected content than community ones; (6) only a small fraction of human-labeled bugs were associated with LLM-detected code.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest that while LLM-generated code is prevalent in certain contexts (especially testing), it is declining and is not a major contributor to production bugs. Quality concerns about generated comments (poor grammar) appear warranted. The higher LLM adoption in company repositories may reflect organizational incentives or tooling integration differences. The findings nuance the debate around LLM code quality and provide empirical grounding for practitioners.

title: How to Allocate Your Tokens? Scaling Laws with Training Steps and Batch Size
summary: We propose a scaling law that takes into account model size and training data while explicitly splitting the latter into training steps and batch size (called three-term law). Fitting the proposed law on a large set of training runs, we find that it correctly recovers the scaling of the optimal batch size. Moreover, because it makes use of training runs with suboptimal batch size, our proposed law can be robustly fit with a significantly smaller amount of training runs. We further show that the three-term law can be used to derive scaling laws for suboptimal batch sizes, and that it matches previous empirical findings related to the critical batch size.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a three-term scaling law that explicitly separates training data into training steps and batch size, alongside model size. It accurately recovers optimal batch size scaling, enables robust fitting with fewer training runs, and generalizes to suboptimal batch size regimes while matching prior findings on critical batch size.
AI.motivation: Existing scaling laws typically treat training data as a single quantity (number of tokens), obscuring the distinct roles of training steps and batch size. This limits their ability to predict optimal batch sizes or leverage data from suboptimally configured training runs, which are abundant in practice.
AI.method: The authors propose a three-term scaling law that decomposes training data into training steps and batch size, with model size as the third term. They fit this parametric form to a large set of neural network training runs, including those with suboptimal batch sizes, and validate its predictive accuracy for optimal batch size scaling and critical batch size behavior.
AI.result: The three-term law correctly recovers the scaling relationship of optimal batch size. It enables robust parameter fitting using significantly fewer training runs by leveraging runs with suboptimal batch sizes. It also derives scaling laws for suboptimal batch size regimes and aligns with previously reported empirical findings on critical batch size.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling batch size and training steps as separate terms yields a more data-efficient and generalizable scaling law that captures both optimal and suboptimal training configurations, offering practical benefits for scaling law estimation.

title: Can Language Models Actually Retrieve In-Context? Drowning in Documents at Million Token Scale
summary: Language models (LMs) raise an intriguing alternative to vector-based retrieval: conditioning on an in-context corpus and directly generating a relevant answer. However, prior work has largely focused on proprietary systems or the smaller-scale reranking task, leaving corpus-scale in-context retrieval largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first systematic study of in-context retrieval on two scales practical retrievers demand: million-token corpora and length-generalization far beyond training-time sizes. We first introduce BlockSearch, a 0.6B LM retriever whose architectural and training modifications improve over prior LM baselines and length-generalize up to 10 times beyond its training regime. Nevertheless, retrieval still collapses under more extreme extrapolation. We trace this failure to an attention dilution effect: as the corpus grows, irrelevant documents dominate the softmax denominator, reducing the normalized mass on the gold document even when its pre-softmax score stays high. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce length-aware adjustments to the attention softmax and document-level sparse attention. With these modifications, at the million-token scale, our model matches dense retrieval on widely studied benchmarks (e.g, MS MARCO and NQ), while outperforming the concurrent model MSA despite being 7 times smaller. Furthermore, it significantly outperforms dense retrieval on tasks requiring entirely different notions of similarity, such as LIMIT, achieving a 3 times higher score. Together, our results position in-context retrieval a promising alternative to classical retrieval while emphasizing attention control under extreme context growth as a new challenge.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic study of corpus-scale in-context retrieval using language models, introducing BlockSearch (a 0.6B retriever with architectural improvements enabling 10× length generalization). The authors diagnose a critical "attention dilution" failure mode under extreme corpus sizes and propose length-aware softmax adjustments and document-level sparse attention to fix it, achieving performance matching dense retrieval on standard benchmarks while significantly outperforming on tasks requiring different similarity notions.
AI.motivation: Prior work on LM-based in-context retrieval has been limited to proprietary systems or small-scale reranking. The authors aim to explore whether LMs can serve as practical retrievers at corpus scale (million-token corpora) with length generalization far beyond training-time sizes — a largely unexplored regime.
AI.method: (1) BlockSearch: a 0.6B LM retriever with architectural/training modifications that length-generalizes up to 10× beyond training. (2) Analysis tracing collapse under extreme extrapolation to "attention dilution" — irrelevant documents dominating the softmax denominator. (3) Two fixes: length-aware adjustments to the attention softmax and document-level sparse attention. Evaluated on MS MARCO, NQ, and LIMIT benchmarks at million-token scale.
AI.result: At million-token scale, the modified model matches dense retrieval on MS MARCO and NQ, outperforms the concurrent MSA model despite being 7× smaller, and achieves 3× higher scores than dense retrieval on LIMIT (a benchmark requiring different similarity notions).
AI.conclusion: In-context retrieval is a promising alternative to classical vector-based retrieval. The key challenge going forward is attention control under extreme context growth, which the proposed length-aware adjustments and sparse attention mechanism effectively address.

title: Profit-Based Counterfactual Explanations for Product Improvement: A Case Study of Manga Sales in Japan
summary: Counterfactual explanation (CE) is widely used to enhance the interpretability of machine learning models and support data-driven decision-making based on model predictions. However, existing CE methods typically require two exogenously specified inputs: a desired output value (target) and a distance function that quantifies changes in explanatory variables. In regression settings, neither the validity of target specification nor the practical interpretation of the distance metric has been sufficiently addressed. Furthermore, most existing CE methods focus on altering predictions rather than optimizing a decision objective, even though real-world decision-making often requires explicit objective maximization. To address these limitations, we formulate CE as a profit maximization problem in management and marketing contexts and propose a framework termed profit-based counterfactual explanation (PBCE). PBCE eliminates the need for exogenous target specification by directly maximizing profit as the primary optimization objective. Concurrently, the distance term is reinterpreted as the cost of modifying product attributes, providing a clear and economically grounded interpretation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Profit-Based Counterfactual Explanation (PBCE), a framework that reformulates counterfactual explanations as a profit maximization problem, eliminating the need for exogenously specified target outputs and reinterpretating distance as the cost of modifying product attributes.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual explanation methods suffer from two key issues in regression contexts: (1) they require an exogenously specified target output value whose validity is questionable, and (2) the distance function lacks practical economic interpretation. Moreover, current CE methods focus on prediction alteration rather than objective-driven decision-making, which misaligns with real-world decision needs.
AI.method: The authors formulate counterfactual explanation as a profit maximization problem within management and marketing domains. The PBCE framework directly maximizes profit as the primary optimization objective, thereby removing the need for target specification. The distance function is reinterpreted as the economic cost of modifying product attributes, providing grounded interpretation.
AI.result: The abstract does not specify quantitative or empirical results. The contribution is the novel PBCE framework itself, which addresses the identified limitations of existing CE methods in regression settings.
AI.conclusion: The PBCE framework offers a more practical and economically meaningful approach to counterfactual explanations in regression, better aligning CE with real-world decision-making by focusing on profit maximization rather than mere prediction alteration.

title: ElephantAgent: Contextual State Continuity in Agentic Systems
summary: Agentic systems enhance their capabilities by invoking external tools and maintaining persistent memory. However, these external dependencies introduce novel attack surfaces. Recent tool and memory poisoning attacks show that maliciously crafted tool descriptors and poisoned memory can covertly bias agent behavior. These threats reflect a deeper issue: the lack of verifiable continuity in the agent's contextual state for planning and execution. We present ElephantAgent, a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity to defend against contextual state poisoning. Inspired by prior state-continuity mechanisms (e.g., Nimble), ElephantAgent extends this protection to the evolving contextual state of agentic systems. We define the contextual state as the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's entire context (e.g., tool state and memory). Before processing each query, ElephantAgent recomputes the digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest. Using replicated trusted hardware, ElephantAgent maintains a linearizable ledger of authorized contextual state transitions and detects out-of-band state tampering. To handle in-band semantic abuse, ElephantAgent additionally provides Historical Traceability, enabling conditional post-hoc audit and recovery to a known-good prior state.

AI.tldr: ElephantAgent is a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity for agentic systems, using replicated trusted hardware and digest verification to defend against tool and memory poisoning attacks, while also providing historical traceability for post-hoc audit and recovery.
AI.motivation: Agentic systems rely on external tools and persistent memory, which introduce new attack surfaces. Recent tool and memory poisoning attacks demonstrate that malicious tool descriptors and poisoned memory can covertly bias agent behavior. The core problem is the lack of verifiable continuity in the agent's contextual state during planning and execution.
AI.method: ElephantAgent defines the contextual state as the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's context (tool state and memory). Before each query, it recomputes a digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest. It employs replicated trusted hardware to maintain a linearizable ledger of authorized contextual state transitions, detecting out-of-band state tampering. For in-band semantic abuse, it provides Historical Traceability, enabling conditional post-hoc audit and recovery to a known-good prior state.
AI.result: The paper presents a protocol design (no empirical evaluation is described in the abstract).
AI.conclusion: Contextual State Continuity, enforced through digest verification, a linearizable ledger on trusted hardware, and historical traceability, provides a systematic defense against contextual state poisoning in agentic systems, addressing both out-of-band tampering and in-band semantic abuse.

title: Understanding Build Reproducibility in the F-Droid Ecosystem
comment: 2026 ACM Conference on Reproducibility and Replicability, Jul 2026, Delft, Netherlands
summary: The security of open source applications benefits considerably from the possibility of rebuilding their source and verifying the output. F-Droid, a prominent distribution for open source Android applications, systematically rebuilds them from source and tests their bitwise reproducibility at app publishing time. However, F-Droid offers no guarantee that app reproducibility will continue to hold in the future. As software ecosystems evolve, reproducibility may degrade, with potential negative consequences for software preservation and security. We present the first empirical study of build reproducibility in the F-Droid app ecosystem. Analyzing historical reproducibility logs, we find that the overall bitwise reproducibility rate has been steadily increasing over time (as new versions of apps are published). We then evaluate how reproducibility holds in time for fixed app versions, by attempting to rebuild 18 904 app versions that F-Droid had previously confirmed bitwise reproducible, published between September 2018 and February 2026, achieving an 83% rebuild success rate, and identify missing dependencies as the dominant cause of failure, accounting for 76% of non-rebuildable cases. Among successfully rebuilt apps, 94% are also bitwise reproducible-i.e., they still yield bitwise identical artifacts upon rebuild. Together, these results show that while bitwise reproducibility largely holds for apps that can be rebuilt, rebuildability itself is highly sensitive to temporal decay.

AI.tldr: First empirical study of build reproducibility degradation over time in the F-Droid Android app ecosystem. While 94% of successfully rebuilt apps remain bitwise reproducible, rebuildability itself decays significantly over time — 17% of previously reproducible app versions could not be rebuilt, with missing dependencies accounting for 76% of failures.
AI.motivation: F-Droid verifies bitwise reproducibility at app publishing time but offers no guarantees that reproducibility persists. As software ecosystems evolve, this reproducibility may degrade, threatening software preservation and security. No prior empirical study had quantified this temporal decay.
AI.method: Two-phase empirical analysis: (1) longitudinal analysis of F-Droid's historical reproducibility logs to track overall reproducibility rates over time; (2) a large-scale rebuild experiment attempting to rebuild 18,904 previously confirmed bitwise-reproducible app versions (published Sept 2018 – Feb 2026), measuring both rebuild success rate and continued bitwise reproducibility.
AI.result: Overall bitwise reproducibility rates have steadily increased over time for newly published app versions. However, for fixed historical versions: 83% rebuild success rate; missing dependencies dominate failures (76% of non-rebuildable cases); among successfully rebuilt apps, 94% remain bitwise reproducible.
AI.conclusion: Bitwise reproducibility, once achieved, largely persists for rebuildable apps. However, rebuildability is highly sensitive to temporal decay due to dependency rot, suggesting that F-Droid and similar ecosystems should invest in dependency archival and long-term rebuild infrastructure to preserve verifiability.

title: Don't Let Gains FADE: Breaking Down Policy Gradient Weights in RL
summary: Reinforcement learning post-training dramatically improves LLM reasoning, but suffers from training instability and diversity collapse. Advantage functions offer an appealing fix: they reshape the training objective, reweight which rollouts drive learning, and are trivial to implement. Yet a proliferation of methods makes it unclear which advantage to use and when. We cut through the confusion with a unifying framework that decomposes any advantage into its positive and negative gradient mass along two orthogonal axes. On the sign axis, imbalanced updates collapse either entropy or weight geometry. On the difficulty axis, hard-problem focus sharpens signal but costs sample size. Both trade-offs shift during training: exploration favors balance and hard focus; exploitation favors suppression and medium focus. This motivates FADE (Focal Advantage with Dynamic Entropy), a self-adapting advantage that reads training dynamics to schedule the gradient weight automatically. FADE reaches peak pass@1 20k steps earlier than the best static baseline at the 7B scale and 2k steps earlier at the 32B , while achieving the best accuracy-diversity trade-off across all pass@k on LiveCodeBench and AIME.

AI.tldr: FADE (Focal Advantage with Dynamic Entropy) is a self-adapting advantage function for RL post-training of LLMs that automatically schedules gradient weights by reading training dynamics, achieving faster convergence and better accuracy-diversity trade-offs than static baselines.
AI.motivation: RL post-training for LLM reasoning suffers from training instability and diversity collapse. While advantage functions can reshape training objectives and reweight rollouts, the proliferation of methods creates confusion about which advantage to use and when, as trade-offs between exploration/exploitation and hard/medium problem focus shift during training.
AI.method: A unifying framework that decomposes any advantage function into positive and negative gradient mass along two orthogonal axes: (1) the sign axis, where imbalanced updates collapse entropy or weight geometry; (2) the difficulty axis, where hard-problem focus sharpens signal but costs sample size. Based on this analysis, FADE dynamically schedules gradient weight by adapting to training dynamics, shifting from balance and hard focus (exploration) to suppression and medium focus (exploitation).
AI.result: FADE reaches peak pass@1 20,000 steps earlier than the best static baseline at 7B scale and 2,000 steps earlier at 32B scale, while achieving the best accuracy-diversity trade-off across all pass@k on LiveCodeBench and AIME benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Advantage function trade-offs are not static; they shift during training. FADE demonstrates that a self-adapting advantage that reads training dynamics can significantly accelerate convergence and improve the accuracy-diversity Pareto frontier compared to any fixed advantage formulation.

title: DiPS: Dialogue Policy Selection for High-Stakes Persuasion Agents
comment: Proceedings of the 27th Annual Meeting of the Special Interest Group on Discourse and Dialogue (SIGDIAL 2026)
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with persuasion in high-stakes scenarios. People's individual personalities and concerns require tailored strategies rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. To address this challenge, we focus on a fire-rescue scenario in which an operator must persuade a resident to evacuate as a high-stakes persuasion domain and propose Dialogue Policy Selection (DiPS), a Q-learning framework to dynamically select persuasion strategies adapted to the evolving conversational context. Specifically, we train a critic, trained to maximize the chance of evacuation success, to select a persuasion policy at each turn based on the resident's recent utterances.We then evaluate DiPS against multiple baselines in both simulated and real human interactions. We find that DiPS achieves higher evacuation success than a zero-shot LLM and generic RAG-augmented approach.

AI.tldr: DiPS is a Q-learning framework that dynamically selects persuasion strategies in a fire-rescue evacuation scenario, outperforming zero-shot LLM and RAG-augmented baselines in both simulated and real human interactions.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with high-stakes persuasion because a one-size-fits-all approach fails to account for individual personalities and concerns. A dynamic, context-adaptive strategy selection mechanism is needed.
AI.method: DiPS employs a Q-learning framework where a critic is trained to maximize evacuation success probability. At each conversational turn, the critic selects a persuasion policy based on the resident's recent utterances, enabling dynamic adaptation to the evolving dialogue context. The system is evaluated in a fire-rescue operator-resident scenario.
AI.result: DiPS achieves higher evacuation success rates compared to a zero-shot LLM and a generic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach, validated through both simulated and real human interaction experiments.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, reinforcement learning-based policy selection (DiPS) effectively tailors persuasion strategies to individual interlocutors in high-stakes scenarios, surpassing static and generic approaches.

title: Scaling with Confidence: Calibrating Confidence of LLMs for Adaptive Test Time Scaling
summary: Training large language models (LLMs) with reinforcement learning (RL) has significantly advanced their performance on reasoning and question-answering tasks. However, prevailing RL reward designs typically prioritize response correctness, neglecting to incentivize models to express their confidence accurately. This leads to a critical problem: performance gains are often accompanied by poor calibration between confidence and accuracy, misleading models to overconfidently hallucinate when uncertain. To address this limitation, we propose $\textbf{C}$orrectness and $\textbf{C}$onfidence $\textbf{C}$alibration $\textbf{R}$einforcement $\textbf{L}$earning ($\textbf{C3RL}$), a novel RL algorithm integrating correctness, calibration and dataset-informed reference accuracy rewards together. Comprehensive evaluation across 8 text and multimodal datasets demonstrates that C3RL enhances calibration without sacrificing accuracy, outperforming the current state-of-the-art method in both performance and calibration metrics. Utilizing the well-calibrated verbalized confidence from C3RL, we further introduce $\textbf{C}$onfidence-based $\textbf{A}$daptive Test Time $\textbf{S}$caling ($\textbf{CAS}$), an adjustable inference-time strategy that allocates computational resources based on response confidence. Experiments show that CAS surpasses majority voting on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets while reducing the inference budget by up to 12.33 times. We believe the synergy of C3RL and CAS paves the way for deploying more reliable and resource-efficient LLMs. The code, data and models will be released.

AI.tldr: C3RL is a reinforcement learning algorithm that jointly optimizes LLMs for response correctness and confidence calibration, outperforming SOTA on both metrics. The authors further propose CAS, which adaptively allocates inference compute based on calibrated confidence, achieving superior accuracy over majority voting with up to 12.33× less inference budget.
AI.motivation: Current RL for LLMs prioritizes answer correctness while ignoring confidence calibration, causing models to become overconfident and hallucinate when uncertain. There is a need for RL methods that simultaneously improve accuracy and calibration.
AI.method: C3RL incorporates three reward signals into RL training: (1) a correctness reward for answer accuracy, (2) a calibration reward that penalizes mismatches between verbalized confidence and actual accuracy, and (3) a dataset-informed reference accuracy reward. The well-calibrated confidence from C3RL then enables CAS, an inference-time strategy that allocates computational resources adaptively based on response confidence levels.
AI.result: Across 8 text and multimodal datasets, C3RL improves calibration without sacrificing accuracy and beats SOTA in both performance and calibration metrics. CAS surpasses majority voting on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets while reducing inference budget by up to 12.33×.
AI.conclusion: The synergy between C3RL and CAS enables more reliable, well-calibrated, and resource-efficient LLM deployment, with code and models to be publicly released.

title: kNNGuard: Turning LLM Hidden Activations into a Training-Free Configurable Guardrail
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in domains requiring guardrails to detect unsafe, off-topic, or adversarial prompts. Existing guardrails predominately rely on fine-tuning to build classifiers, which often suffer from low generalization and high inference latency. We present kNNGuard, a training-free guardrail that utilizes the activation space of an off-the-shelf LLM. Given a small bank of 50 safe and unsafe prompts, kNNGuard extracts hidden activations and performs multi-layer kNN fusing activation-space and embedding-space scores for classification. Across six domains spanning topical and security prompts, kNNGuard achieves competitive or superior F1 compared to fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails while running 2.7x faster than the best comparable guardrail, and 10x faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier without gradient updates or fine-tuning. Domain adaptation requires only updating the labeled bank, which can be constructed in under 10 seconds and several orders of magnitude faster than established guardrails. We also analyze the impact of system prompts, layer selection, and integration into production LLM pipelines as a configurable, low-latency guardrail.

AI.tldr: kNNGuard is a training-free safety guardrail for LLMs that uses nearest-neighbor classification in activation space, achieving competitive F1 scores against fine-tuned baselines while being 2.7–10× faster and enabling sub-10-second domain adaptation by simply updating a small labeled prompt bank.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM guardrails rely on fine-tuned classifiers, which suffer from poor generalization to new domains, high inference latency, and costly retraining. There is a need for a low-latency, easily adaptable, training-free alternative for detecting unsafe, off-topic, or adversarial prompts.
AI.method: kNNGuard operates by: (1) maintaining a small bank of ~50 labeled safe/unsafe prompts; (2) extracting hidden activations from multiple layers of an off-the-shelf LLM for both the bank and incoming queries; (3) performing multi-layer k-nearest-neighbor classification that fuses activation-space similarity scores with embedding-space similarity scores; (4) classifying prompts without any gradient updates or fine-tuning. Domain adaptation is achieved by simply swapping the labeled bank.
AI.result: Across six domains (topical and security prompts), kNNGuard matches or exceeds the F1 scores of fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails. It runs 2.7× faster than the best comparable guardrail and 10× faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier. Domain adaptation requires constructing a new labeled bank in under 10 seconds — orders of magnitude faster than retraining existing guardrails.
AI.conclusion: kNNGuard demonstrates that activation-space nearest-neighbor classification is a viable, training-free paradigm for LLM guardrailing, offering strong detection performance, significant latency improvements, and rapid domain adaptability suitable for production deployment.

title: AI Writes Faster Than Humans Can Review: A Longitudinal Study of an Enterprise 2x Mandate
summary: Enterprises increasingly mandate AI coding tools and report large productivity gains, yet longitudinal evidence on how such a mandate unfolds is scarce. In this paper, we present a quantitative case study of a documented enterprise "2x" mandate at a mid-sized, AI-forward company that has been committed to doubling merged pull requests per engineer since mid-2025. In a panel of 802 developers and 196,212 pull requests (January 2024-April 2026), per-capita throughput eventually doubled, reaching 2.09x the pre-mandate baseline in April 2026, among the largest gains reported from a field deployment of AI coding tools to our knowledge. A staggered difference-in-differences design links the within-developer share of this gain to AI adoption and to a further gain that grows with accumulated use, with the mandate acting as a catalyst rather than a direct driver. Because adoption and usage intensity were not randomly assigned, we read this evidence as strongly implicating an adoption-and-use channel rather than as exact causal attribution. The gain is broadly shared across seniority yet concentrated in newer code and not separable across model generations. Adoption also restructured code review around automation: per-reviewer load roughly doubled and automated review overtook human review, while merge and revert rates held steady.

AI.tldr: A longitudinal case study at a mid-sized company shows that an enterprise "2x" mandate for AI coding tools led to per-capita pull request throughput reaching 2.09x baseline by April 2026. Gains are linked to AI adoption and accumulated use via staggered difference-in-differences, with the mandate acting as a catalyst. Benefits are broadly shared across seniority, concentrated in newer code, and accompanied by a restructuring of code review toward automation.
AI.motivation: Despite enterprises increasingly mandating AI coding tools and reporting large productivity gains, there is scarce longitudinal evidence on how such mandates actually unfold in practice over time.
AI.method: The authors conduct a quantitative case study using a panel of 802 developers and 196,212 pull requests spanning January 2024 to April 2026. They employ a staggered difference-in-differences design to link within-developer productivity gains to AI adoption and accumulated usage intensity, treating the mandate as a catalyst rather than a direct causal driver.
AI.result: Per-capita merged pull requests doubled, reaching 2.09x the pre-mandate baseline by April 2026. The gain is associated with AI adoption and grows with accumulated use. Benefits are broadly shared across seniority levels but concentrated in newer code and not separable across model generations. Additionally, per-reviewer code review load roughly doubled, automated review overtook human review, while merge and revert rates remained stable.
AI.conclusion: The evidence strongly implicates an adoption-and-use channel — rather than the mandate itself — as the mechanism driving productivity gains. The mandate acted as a catalyst. The restructuring of code review around automation, with stable merge/revert rates, suggests that throughput gains did not come at the expense of code quality.

title: Beyond Skepticism: Evaluating LLMs Pedagogical Intent Reasoning with the Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance Framework
summary: The capacity of Large Language Models (LLMs) to reason about pedagogical intent within instructional communication remains underexplored, particularly in educational domains such as translation pedagogy. To address this, we propose the \textbf{Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance (APV)} framework, a novel computational formalism that reframes communicative vigilance as an adaptive mechanism for optimizing learning through intent inference. APV formalizes the problem via a Bayesian Pedagogical Intent Inference Engine (PIIE), which models how instructors select content to maximize pedagogical utility and how vigilant learners should inversely reason about latent instructional configurations -- encompassing genre, stance, and incentives. We evaluate APV through a three-tier hierarchy: distinguishing instructional genre, reasoning about structured pedagogical setups, and generalizing to authentic educational discourse. Experiments on leading LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude 3.5) show that APV substantially improves model vigilance. It achieves the strongest discrimination between pedagogical and exposure-based content, correlates highly with human judgments ($r=0.958$), and maintains robust performance on naturalistic data where baseline methods degrade. This work establishes a unified framework for assessing and enhancing LLMs' understanding of pedagogical motives, advancing the development of more reliable AI-assisted learning systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance (APV) framework, which uses a Bayesian Pedagogical Intent Inference Engine to help LLMs infer instructors' latent pedagogical goals (genre, stance, incentives). Tested on GPT-4o and Claude 3.5, APV significantly improves models' ability to distinguish instructional from non-instructional content, correlates strongly with human judgment (r=0.958), and generalizes well to naturalistic data.
AI.motivation: LLMs currently lack the ability to reason about pedagogical intent — the underlying instructional goals behind educational communication. This gap is especially critical in domains like translation pedagogy, where understanding why an instructor selects certain content is essential. Existing communicative vigilance research has not been adapted to educational contexts.
AI.method: The authors propose the Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance (APV) framework centered on a Bayesian Pedagogical Intent Inference Engine (PIIE). The PIIE formalizes instruction as a utility-maximization process where instructors select content to optimize pedagogical outcomes, and learners (or models) perform inverse Bayesian reasoning to infer latent instructional configurations: genre, stance, and incentives. Evaluation follows a three-tier hierarchy: (1) distinguishing instructional vs. exposure-based genre, (2) reasoning about structured pedagogical setups, and (3) generalizing to authentic educational discourse.
AI.result: APV achieves strong discrimination between pedagogical and exposure-based content, correlates highly with human judgments at r=0.958, and maintains robust performance on naturalistic data where baseline methods degrade. Leading LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5) show substantially improved vigilance under the framework.
AI.conclusion: APV provides a unified, principled framework for both assessing and enhancing LLMs' understanding of pedagogical motives, contributing to more reliable AI-assisted learning systems in educational domains.

title: Spatial Support Matters: Geometry-Aware Graph Fusion for Rainfall Field Reconstruction
summary: Fine-scale rainfall reconstruction is critical for urban flood modeling, but real rainfall sensing systems observe the field through incompatible spatial supports: gauges measure points, microwave links measure paths, and radar/satellite products measure gridded areas. These differences in measurement support impose geometrically distinct constraints on the rainfall field, yet existing heterogeneous graph approaches reconcile such sources in feature space, giving each its own embedding while discarding the geometry of its support. We propose a geometry-aware multi-support heterogeneous graph neural network that represents each observation according to its support type (0D point, 1D line, or 2D grid) as a distinct node layer, and fuses them through cross-support message passing into a point-support prediction layer from which the field is reconstructed. An inductive masked-node formulation decouples prediction resolution from sensing resolution, allowing the same trained model to reconstruct the field at user-defined target locations or display grids. On Singapore data, the proposed method reduces RMSE by 23.2\% over the classical interpolation baseline, inverse-distance weighting, and consistently outperforms other neural architectures such as convolutional fusion and support-agnostic heterogeneous graph baselines. A generalization study using data from Sydney, Australia lets us characterize when multi-support fusion helps: the available skill appears to depend on gauge spacing relative to the spatial correlation length of the field, so fusion delivers the largest gains where the field is under-sampled relative to its correlation length and little when it is already resolved. Code and models will be open-sourced upon paper acceptance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a geometry-aware heterogeneous graph neural network for rainfall reconstruction that fuses point (gauge), line (microwave link), and grid (radar/satellite) observations through cross-support message passing, achieving 23.2% RMSE improvement over IDW baseline on Singapore data, with generalization analysis on Sydney data revealing fusion benefits depend on gauge spacing relative to spatial correlation length.
AI.motivation: Existing rainfall sensing systems provide observations with incompatible spatial supports (0D points from gauges, 1D paths from microwave links, 2D grids from radar/satellite). Current heterogeneous graph approaches reconcile these in feature space while discarding the geometry of each measurement's support, limiting their ability to properly fuse multi-support observations for fine-scale rainfall reconstruction critical to urban flood modeling.
AI.method: A geometry-aware multi-support heterogeneous graph neural network with distinct node layers per support type (0D point, 1D line, 2D grid). Cross-support message passing fuses information across layers into a point-support prediction layer for field reconstruction. An inductive masked-node formulation decouples prediction resolution from sensing resolution, enabling reconstruction at arbitrary user-defined target locations without retraining.
AI.result: On Singapore data, the method achieves 23.2% RMSE reduction over inverse-distance weighting and consistently outperforms convolutional fusion and support-agnostic heterogeneous graph baselines. A generalization study on Sydney data reveals that multi-support fusion benefits are largest when gauge spacing exceeds the spatial correlation length (under-sampled regime) and negligible when the field is already well-resolved.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware heterogeneous graph fusion effectively reconciles multi-support rainfall observations. The practical value of fusion depends on the relationship between sensor density and the inherent spatial correlation structure of the rainfall field. Code and models will be open-sourced.

title: HaloGuard 1.0: An Open Weights Constitutional Classifier for Multilingual AI Safety
summary: We present HaloGuard 1.0, an open-weights implementation of the constitutional-classifier paradigm for input safety. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on English and multilingual prompt-safety benchmarks at roughly one-tenth the model size of current leading open guard models. The safety constitution is the organising structure of the corpus: a natural-language constitution of 46 policies and 2,940 subcategories drives synthetic data generation, with exhaustive one-to-one paired counterfactuals that hold topic and vocabulary fixed while flipping intent, a two-tier harmless design that separately targets boundary and baseline false positives (FPs), and balanced multilingual materialisation across 46 languages that treats language as a surface form appearing on both sides of the boundary rather than as an adversarial signal. Across seven prompt-safety benchmarks, HaloGuard 1.0-0.8B attains the best average F1 (90.9) of any open guard we evaluate, outperforming baselines up to 27B parameters (over 30 times larger) while holding false-positive rate (FPR) to 4.3 and false-negative rate (FNR) to 9.5. The HaloGuard 1.0-4B variant reaches average F1 of 92.1 and FPR of 3.5, spending its extra capacity on precision rather than recall. A structured adjudication of the remaining failures indicates that most apparent missed-harm cases are benchmark mislabels rather than genuine model misses.
