An always-on adversarial red-teaming protocol continuously hardens the guard against both content-level and agentic attacks. We release the models as open weights.

AI.tldr: HaloGuard 1.0 is an open-weights input safety classifier that achieves state-of-the-art prompt-safety performance at a fraction of the size of competing models (0.8B–4B params). It uses a constitutional-classifier approach with 46 safety policies, 2,940 subcategories, paired counterfactual data, and balanced multilingual coverage across 46 languages.
AI.motivation: Current open guard models for prompt safety are large (often 8B–27B parameters) and struggle with multilingual performance, false positives, and adversarial robustness. There is a need for a smaller, more efficient guard model that maintains or exceeds SOTA performance while being openly available.
AI.method: HaloGuard employs a constitutional-classifier paradigm: (1) a natural-language safety constitution of 46 policies and 2,940 subcategories drives synthetic data generation; (2) exhaustive one-to-one paired counterfactuals hold topic/vocabulary constant while flipping intent (safe ↔ unsafe); (3) a two-tier harmless design separately targets boundary false positives and baseline false positives; (4) balanced multilingual materialisation across 46 languages treats language as a surface form on both sides of the safety boundary; (5) an always-on adversarial red-teaming protocol continuously hardens the guard against content-level and agentic attacks.
AI.result: On seven prompt-safety benchmarks, HaloGuard 1.0-0.8B achieves the best average F1 (90.9) among evaluated open guards, outperforming models up to 27B parameters (30× larger), with FPR of 4.3 and FNR of 9.5. The 4B variant reaches F1 of 92.1 and FPR of 3.5. Structured adjudication of remaining failures indicates most apparent missed-harm cases are benchmark mislabels rather than genuine model misses.
AI.conclusion: The constitutional-classifier paradigm enables compact, efficient, and highly accurate input safety guard models. HaloGuard demonstrates that a 0.8B model can surpass much larger alternatives, and that careful data design (counterfactuals, two-tier harmless filtering, balanced multilingualism) is more impactful than scale alone. The models are released as open weights.

title: Beyond Textual Repository Exploration: Dual-Modal Structural Reasoning for Agentic Issue Resolution
summary: Recent advances in agentic program repair have significantly improved issue resolution by enabling iterative repository exploration. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on sequential, text-based code navigation, which fundamentally limits their ability to reason over large-scale long-horizon repositories with complex and long-range dependencies. As issue-resolution agents traverse repositories through fragmented textual observations, structural information such as module organization, call relationships, and dependency chains must be repeatedly reconstructed across interaction steps, often leading to exploration drift and incomplete localization. We present DUALVIEW, a dual-modal structural scaffolding framework that brings visual reasoning into repository exploration for issue-resolution agents. DUALVIEW represents repository structure through four complementary graph views: Module Coupling Graph (MCG), Function Call Graph (FCG), Class Hierarchy Graph (CHG), and Program Dependence Graph (PDG), and exposes them through a queryable interface with visual and textual responses. Rather than reconstructing repository structure from a sequence of textual observations, agents can directly reason over persistent visual representations of code dependencies, enabling more effective exploration and understanding of long-horizon codebases. We evaluate DUALVIEW on SWE-bench Pro and Verified. Results show that DUALVIEW consistently improves issue-resolution performance across different agent architectures and model families. Further ablation studies demonstrate that the gains arise not only from textual structural information but also from visual externalization of repository dependencies, which better supports long-horizon repository exploration.

AI.tldr: DUALVIEW introduces a dual-modal structural scaffolding framework that augments agentic program repair with visual repository representations (four graph views: MCG, FCG, CHG, PDG), enabling agents to reason over persistent visual dependency structures instead of reconstructing them from sequential text, leading to consistent improvements on SWE-bench Pro and Verified across multiple agent architectures and model families.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic program repair systems rely on sequential, text-based code navigation, which forces agents to repeatedly reconstruct structural information (module organization, call relationships, dependency chains) across interaction steps. This leads to exploration drift, incomplete localization, and fundamentally limits reasoning over large-scale, long-horizon repositories with complex long-range dependencies.
AI.method: DUALVIEW provides a dual-modal structural scaffolding framework with four complementary graph views: Module Coupling Graph (MCG), Function Call Graph (FCG), Class Hierarchy Graph (CHG), and Program Dependence Graph (PDG). These are exposed through a queryable interface that returns both visual and textual responses, allowing agents to directly reason over persistent visual representations of code dependencies rather than reconstructing structure from sequential textual observations.
AI.result: DUALVIEW consistently improves issue-resolution performance on SWE-bench Pro and Verified across different agent architectures and model families. Ablation studies confirm that gains stem from both the textual structural information and the visual externalization of repository dependencies, with the latter particularly benefiting long-horizon repository exploration.
AI.conclusion: Visual reasoning over persistent structural representations significantly enhances agentic program repair by mitigating exploration drift and improving localization in large codebases. DUALVIEW demonstrates that dual-modal scaffolding is a broadly applicable and effective paradigm for repository-level issue resolution.

title: Towards Learning Representations of Policies in Two-Player Zero-Sum Imperfect-Information Games
summary:
We investigate the problem of learning useful policy representations (embeddings) in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games. We make three contributions: First, we introduce methods of creating datasets of policies for a given game. Second, we propose methods to learn policy representations. Third, we introduce downstream tasks to evaluate the effectiveness of such representations.
  We evaluate each dataset method, embedding method, and downstream task on Kuhn and Leduc Poker. Although our methods are very basic, we demonstrate that useful behavioral representations are present in the learned embeddings. To our knowledge, this work is among the first to systematically compare self-supervised learning techniques for learning policy representations in games. Our code is available at https://github.com/VitamintK/ssl-project for others to extend.

AI.tldr: This paper explores self-supervised learning for generating policy embeddings in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games, proposing dataset creation methods, embedding techniques, and downstream evaluation tasks, and validating them on Kuhn and Leduc Poker.
AI.motivation: Learning useful representations (embeddings) of policies is crucial for generalization, transfer learning, and analysis in multi-agent settings, yet systematic approaches for imperfect-information games remain underexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a framework and baseline comparison.
AI.method: The paper contributes three components: (1) methods for constructing policy datasets from a given game; (2) self-supervised learning techniques to embed policies into compact vector representations; and (3) downstream tasks to quantitatively assess the quality and utility of the learned embeddings. Experiments are conducted on Kuhn Poker and Leduc Poker.
AI.result: Even with basic methods, the learned embeddings capture meaningful behavioral information about policies. The work provides a systematic comparison of self-supervised techniques for policy representation learning in games, establishing baselines for future research.
AI.conclusion: Useful policy representations can be learned via self-supervised methods in imperfect-information games. This foundational work opens avenues for more sophisticated embedding techniques and broader game domains, with code publicly released to facilitate extensions.

title: ProWAFT: A ROMA-LPD Instance for Workload-Aware and Dynamic Fault Tolerance in FPGA-Based CNN Accelerators
summary: SRAM-based FPGAs provide an attractive platform for energy- and latency-constrained CNN inference at the network edge, yet transient faults can lead to silent errors that compromise reliability. Always-on redundancy (e.g., full TMR) improves correctness but incurs substantial performance and energy overhead, while reactive recovery may introduce unacceptable latency on the critical path. We propose \textbf{ProWAFT}, a proactive workload-aware fault-tolerance framework for FPGA-based CNN accelerators that uses partial reconfiguration to selectively apply TMR across reconfigurable partitions. ProWAFT quantifies workload criticality, models fault propagation and reconfiguration overhead, and selects configurations that minimize a composite objective over latency, energy, and reliability risk. Implemented on a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU104 platform with six reconfigurable regions and evaluated on a 500-task trace derived from ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNet-Lite under time-varying SEU injection, ProWAFT achieves lower composite cost than static TMR and reactive reconfiguration while maintaining high task success rate and near-baseline throughput with low online decision overhead.

AI.tldr: ProWAFT is a proactive fault-tolerance framework for FPGA-based CNN accelerators that uses partial reconfiguration to selectively apply TMR based on workload criticality, balancing latency, energy, and reliability.
AI.motivation: SRAM-based FPGAs are attractive for energy- and latency-constrained CNN inference at the edge, but transient faults (SEUs) can cause silent errors. Static full TMR incurs high overhead, while reactive recovery adds unacceptable latency on the critical path. A more intelligent, selective approach is needed.
AI.method: ProWAFT quantifies workload criticality, models fault propagation and reconfiguration overhead, and formulates a composite optimization objective over latency, energy, and reliability risk. It uses partial reconfiguration to selectively apply TMR across reconfigurable FPGA partitions. The framework is implemented on a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU104 with six reconfigurable regions and evaluated using a 500-task trace (ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet-Lite) under time-varying SEU injection.
AI.result: ProWAFT achieves lower composite cost compared to static TMR and reactive reconfiguration baselines, maintains high task success rate and near-baseline throughput, and incurs low online decision overhead.
AI.conclusion: Proactive, workload-aware selective TMR via partial reconfiguration is an effective strategy for balancing reliability, performance, and energy in FPGA-based CNN inference at the edge, outperforming both always-on and reactive fault-tolerance approaches.

title: Autonomous discovery of traffic laws with AI traffic scientists
summary: Universal traffic laws describe recurrent patterns in congestion, mobility and driving behavior across cities, providing a scientific basis for transportation planning, management and control. Their discovery, however, remains expert-driven, requiring candidate regularities to be identified from heterogeneous observational evidence or validated through intervention experiments. Although autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems have advanced scientific discovery in controlled laboratory settings, extending them to complex transportation domains remains a challenge. Here we present TrafficSci, an agentic AI system that formulates traffic-law discovery as an iterative, auditable workflow integrating evidence scoping, critic-judge hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation. Across four case studies spanning population, network, control and trajectory scales, TrafficSci autonomously rediscovers three established traffic laws and identifies an unreported intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior, statistically consistent across eight cities and two trajectory datasets. TrafficSci provides a route for extending AI-driven scientific discovery from controlled domains to complex urban systems.

AI.tldr: TrafficSci is an agentic AI system that autonomously discovers traffic laws by integrating evidence scoping, hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation. It rediscovers three established laws and identifies a new intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior across eight cities.
AI.motivation: Traffic law discovery remains expert-driven and manual, requiring candidate regularities to be identified from heterogeneous data or validated through costly intervention experiments. While AI has advanced scientific discovery in controlled lab settings, extending it to complex, open-ended transportation domains remains an open challenge.
AI.method: TrafficSci formulates traffic-law discovery as an iterative, auditable workflow with three stages: (1) evidence scoping across heterogeneous transportation data, (2) critic-judge hypothesis induction to propose candidate laws, and (3) observational-interventional validation to rigorously test hypotheses. The system operates across four scales: population, network, control, and trajectory.
AI.result: TrafficSci autonomously rediscovered three established traffic laws and identified an unreported intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior. This new finding was statistically consistent across eight cities and two independent trajectory datasets.
AI.conclusion: TrafficSci demonstrates a viable pathway for extending AI-driven scientific discovery from controlled laboratory domains to complex urban systems, enabling autonomous, auditable, and reproducible traffic-law discovery at scale.

title: Privacy-Preserving and Verifiable Approximate Distributed Coded Computing
summary: Distributed machine learning enables collaborative model training without centralizing data, but it also exposes learning processes to privacy leakage and malicious manipulation. Existing defenses typically address these threats in isolation and are often tailored to specific learning paradigms or model architectures, limiting their applicability in realistic deployments. In particular, federated learning and decentralized learning exhibit distinct adversarial surfaces that are rarely addressed within a unified framework. In this paper, we present a model-agnostic framework for adversary-resistant distributed learning that jointly addresses privacy preservation and malicious behavior across both federated and decentralized settings. Our approach combines paradigm-specific defense mechanisms with GPBACC, a privacy-enhancing coded computing technique applicable to arbitrary machine learning models. For federated learning, we integrate robust aggregation strategies to mitigate the impact of malicious participants, while for decentralized learning we employ approximate decode-and-compare and group testing techniques to enable lightweight verification and adversary isolation without relying on a trusted aggregator. Crucially, we evaluate the proposed framework through an explicit, attack-driven analysis. We implement representative privacy attacks and malicious behaviors, and empirically demonstrate that the combination of GPBACC with robust aggregation and verification mechanisms significantly reduces privacy leakage and improves resilience against active adversaries. These results suggest that privacy-enhancing coded computing, when combined with appropriate adversary-resistance strategies, provides a practical and deployable foundation for secure distributed machine learning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified, model-agnostic framework for adversary-resistant distributed learning that jointly addresses privacy leakage and malicious manipulation across both federated and decentralized settings. It combines GPBACC (a privacy-enhancing coded computing technique) with robust aggregation (for federated learning) and lightweight verification via approximate decode-and-compare with group testing (for decentralized learning). Empirical attack-driven evaluation shows significant reductions in privacy leakage and improved resilience against active adversaries.
AI.motivation: Existing defenses for distributed machine learning address privacy and malicious manipulation in isolation, are tailored to specific paradigms or architectures, and fail to provide a unified framework covering both federated and decentralized learning's distinct adversarial surfaces. This limits deployability in realistic settings.
AI.method: A model-agnostic framework integrating: (1) GPBACC — a privacy-enhancing coded computing technique applicable to arbitrary ML models; (2) robust aggregation strategies to counter malicious participants in federated learning; (3) approximate decode-and-compare combined with group testing for lightweight verification and adversary isolation in decentralized learning without a trusted aggregator. Evaluation is attack-driven, implementing representative privacy attacks and malicious behaviors.
AI.result: The combination of GPBACC with robust aggregation and verification mechanisms empirically demonstrates significantly reduced privacy leakage and improved resilience against active adversaries compared to isolated defenses.
AI.conclusion: Privacy-enhancing coded computing (specifically GPBACC), when paired with appropriate adversary-resistance strategies, provides a practical and deployable foundation for secure distributed machine learning across both federated and decentralized paradigms.

title: Underspecification does not imply Incoherence: The Risks of Semantic Collapse in Coding Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly effective at generating code when task descriptions are clear and precise. Yet, in practice, user-provided task descriptions are often ambiguous, incomplete, or contradictory, leaving critical aspects of the intended program behavior underspecified. In such cases, multiple behaviorally distinct interpretations may satisfy the description equally well, yet semantically differ in ways that matter/affect the user intent. A natural expectation, often assumed by researchers, is that prompt underspecification manifests as incoherence: When asked multiple times, an LLM produces multiple semantically distinct implementations reflecting the ambiguity of the task description. In this paper, we challenge this assumption. We find that LLMs frequently collapse onto a single incorrect interpretation of the task description, consistently generating coherent but behaviorally misaligned code. We term this failure mode detrimental semantic collapse and find that it affects over 10% of tasks in MBPP, 3% in HumanEval, and 32% of LiveCodeBench, all benchmarks assumed to be well-specified. By deliberately injecting underspecification issues in the benchmark prompts, the rate rises to over 5 times, exposing a fundamental blind spot in disambiguation and correctness estimation techniques that rely on incoherence as a proxy for prompt underspecification.

AI.tldr: LLMs often produce coherent but behaviorally incorrect code when prompts are underspecified—a failure mode called "detrimental semantic collapse"—rather than exhibiting incoherence (multiple distinct outputs). This affects 10%+ of standard benchmarks and rises 5× with deliberately injected ambiguity, undermining methods that use incoherence as a proxy for detecting underspecification.
AI.motivation: The prevailing assumption in LLM research is that underspecified prompts lead to incoherent outputs—sampling multiple times yields semantically diverse implementations. The authors challenge this, hypothesizing that LLMs instead frequently collapse onto a single, coherent but incorrect interpretation, creating a blind spot for disambiguation and correctness estimation techniques.
AI.method: The authors analyze three standard code generation benchmarks (MBPP, HumanEval, LiveCodeBench) by repeatedly sampling LLMs on each task and measuring semantic diversity of outputs. They introduce deliberately underspecified variants of benchmark prompts to quantify the rate of detrimental semantic collapse—where outputs are semantically consistent across samples yet behaviorally misaligned with the intended specification.
AI.result: Detrimental semantic collapse occurs in over 10% of MBPP tasks, 3% of HumanEval, and 32% of LiveCodeBench tasks. When underspecification is deliberately injected, the collapse rate increases more than fivefold. This demonstrates that coherence is an unreliable proxy for prompt well-specifiedness.
AI.conclusion: Detrimental semantic collapse is a significant and previously overlooked failure mode in LLM code generation. Methods relying on output incoherence to detect underspecification are fundamentally flawed, and new approaches are needed to identify and mitigate semantically collapsed but incorrect generations.

title: The risk of KV cache compression
summary: Transformer inference on long sequences is expensive because softmax attention repeatedly reads from a large KV cache. The prevalent approach to this bottleneck is KV cache compression, which replaces the full cache with a compact summary. Despite its practical importance, the design of such summaries is largely driven by empirical experimentation. On the theoretical side, existing results show that KV cache compression can be impossible in the worst case, but offer little systematic guidance for designing algorithms in regimes where accurate compression is possible. We bridge this gap by characterizing the minimax risk of KV cache compression in terms of the intrinsic compressibility of a cache, revealing when and how accurate compression is possible. These results yield novel design principles for KV cache compression under causal masking that map efficiently to prefill and autoregressive decoding while achieving minimax-optimal risk. We instantiate these principles in a practical algorithm and report promising performance on LongBench in targeted experiments. Overall, our results provide a principled avenue for practical KV cache compression with theoretical guarantees.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically characterizes the minimax risk of KV cache compression, revealing when accurate compression is possible and deriving design principles that lead to a practical algorithm with theoretical guarantees.
AI.motivation: Transformer inference on long sequences is bottlenecked by repeatedly reading from a large KV cache. While KV cache compression is the prevalent remedy, its design is mostly empirical, and existing theory only offers worst-case impossibility results without constructive guidance for regimes where compression is feasible.
AI.method: The authors characterize the minimax risk of KV cache compression as a function of the cache's intrinsic compressibility. From this analysis, they derive design principles tailored to causal masking that map efficiently to both prefill and autoregressive decoding stages, and instantiate these principles in a practical algorithm.
AI.result: The derived design principles yield a KV cache compression algorithm that achieves minimax-optimal risk and shows promising performance on the LongBench benchmark in targeted experiments.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a principled, theoretically-grounded framework for KV cache compression, bridging the gap between worst-case impossibility results and practical algorithm design, and demonstrating that theoretical guarantees can coexist with strong empirical performance.

title: When Does Generating More Help? Disentangling Fixed-Source Synthesis from Source Expansion in Synthetic Data Scaling
summary: Synthetic data can be scaled along two routes: Source Expansion (SE), which enlarges the source by adding seed materials or generators, and Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS), which holds the source fixed and scales the generation budget. Existing scaling studies typically expand the source as the data grows, conflating SE with FSS and leaving FSS underexplored. We isolate FSS by holding the seed-question pool and teacher model fixed, varying only the per-question response budget under Rejection Sampling (RS). We adapt the rectified scaling law to FSS, deriving it from how repeated sampling covers a fixed source. Empirically, the derived form, fit on low budgets, predicts performance at the held-out highest budget for every evaluated teacher--student pair. At matched total-sample budgets, SE and FSS are comparable at small budgets; at large budgets, adding seed questions outperforms spending the same budget on more responses. Within FSS, however, neither synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds nor varying the synthesis protocol outperforms plain RS at matched budgets. FSS is thus a bounded scaling axis and a controlled setting for comparing synthesis protocols. We will release our code and data to facilitate further research.

AI.tldr: This paper isolates Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS) — scaling synthetic data by increasing the per-question response budget while holding the source fixed — from the commonly conflated Source Expansion (SE). Using a derived rectified scaling law, the authors show FSS is a bounded scaling axis where plain Rejection Sampling matches or outperforms more elaborate protocols at matched budgets, and at large budgets, adding seed questions (SE) outperforms adding more responses per question (FSS).
AI.motivation: Prior work on scaling synthetic data conflates two distinct axes: expanding the source (adding seeds/generators) versus increasing the generation budget per source item. This conflation leaves Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS) underexplored as an isolated phenomenon. The authors aim to disentangle these two routes to understand their individual scaling properties and to provide a controlled setting for fairly comparing synthesis protocols.
AI.method: The authors isolate FSS by fixing both the seed-question pool and the teacher model, then vary only the per-question response budget under Rejection Sampling (RS). They adapt the rectified scaling law to the FSS setting, deriving it from how repeated sampling covers a fixed source. The derived functional form is fit on low-budget data and extrapolated to predict held-out high-budget performance. They also conduct controlled comparisons between FSS, SE, and variants such as synthesizing additional questions from existing seeds or altering the synthesis protocol.
AI.result: The rectified scaling law fit on low budgets accurately predicts performance at the held-out highest budget across all evaluated teacher–student pairs. At small total-sample budgets, SE and FSS perform comparably; at large budgets, SE (adding seed questions) significantly outperforms FSS (spending budget on more responses). Within FSS, neither synthesizing additional questions from existing seeds nor varying the synthesis protocol outperforms plain Rejection Sampling at matched budgets.
AI.conclusion: FSS is a bounded scaling axis — performance saturates as the per-question budget increases — and serves as a principled, controlled setting for comparing synthesis protocols. The findings caution against conflating SE and FSS in scaling studies and highlight that source diversity (more seeds) ultimately matters more than response multiplicity when budgets are large.

title: Diverse Evidence, Better Forecasts: Multi-Agent Deliberation Under Information Asymmetry
summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used for forecasting future events, as deliberation among multiple LLMs is believed to improve reasoning and calibration. Yet existing approaches overlook a critical design choice: what information each agent receives. When all agents are given identical evidence, deliberation collapses into herding rather than genuine belief revision, leaving multi-agent systems little better than a single agent. We identify this as a fundamental gap and propose designed information asymmetry to close it: by partitioning evidence into shared public and disjoint private subsets, each agent holds exclusive knowledge that can only reach others through deliberation. We theoretically show that this decomposition reduces inter-agent error correlation, and instantiate it in InfoDelphi, a framework combining relevance-aware evidence routing, rationale-based iterative deliberation, and confidence-weighted aggregation. On PolyGym, a benchmark of 375 binary forecasting questions derived from real-world prediction markets, InfoDelphi outperforms the strongest single-agent and multi-agent baselines by 12--18% in Brier score and 4--8 percentage points in accuracy. More detailed experiments confirm that removing information asymmetry eliminates most deliberation gains, establishing diversity of input as the key enabler of effective multi-agent reasoning.

AI.tldr: InfoDelphi introduces designed information asymmetry in multi-agent LLM forecasting by partitioning evidence into shared public and disjoint private subsets, preventing herding and enabling genuine deliberation. The framework outperforms baselines by 12–18% in Brier score on the PolyGym benchmark, demonstrating that input diversity — not deliberation alone — drives effective multi-agent reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM systems for forecasting give all agents identical evidence, causing deliberation to collapse into herding rather than genuine belief revision. This eliminates the potential benefits of multi-agent reasoning, making such systems little better than a single agent. The authors identify this as a fundamental gap: the lack of input diversity across agents.
AI.method: The paper proposes designed information asymmetry, where evidence is partitioned into shared public and disjoint private subsets so each agent holds exclusive knowledge. This is instantiated in InfoDelphi, a framework with three components: (1) relevance-aware evidence routing to assign private evidence, (2) rationale-based iterative deliberation where agents exchange and update beliefs, and (3) confidence-weighted aggregation for final predictions. The authors also provide theoretical analysis showing that information decomposition reduces inter-agent error correlation.
AI.result: On PolyGym, a benchmark of 375 binary forecasting questions from real-world prediction markets, InfoDelphi outperforms the strongest single-agent and multi-agent baselines by 12–18% in Brier score and 4–8 percentage points in accuracy. Ablation experiments confirm that removing information asymmetry eliminates most deliberation gains.
AI.conclusion: Diversity of input — achieved through designed information asymmetry — is the key enabler of effective multi-agent reasoning. Deliberation alone, without private information, yields negligible benefits. The work establishes that how information is distributed across agents is a critical and previously overlooked design choice in multi-agent LLM systems.

title: Steerability via constraints: a substrate for scalable oversight of coding agents
comment: Accepted to the Deep Learning for Code Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
summary: Coding agents are capable; human oversight is the bottleneck. Unconstrained agents introduce security risks, erode codebase scalability, and make human review increasingly costly. We argue that the same methods used for decades to manage large human engineering teams: access control, network policies, strict coding conventions enforced by tooling; transfer directly to coding agents, and are cheaper (in token) than recent agentic scaffolding. We sketch a start-to-end system on this principle, and report a controlled experiment in scalable oversight: a small reviewer (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase containing 11 inserted backdoors. Recall rises from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC `docs` CLI), with substrate and tools contributing independently. We choose Python deliberately: substrate-level oversight gains are largest where the language gives the fewest guarantees by default; the principles extend to languages like Rust.

AI.tldr: Coding agents are powerful but introduce security and scalability risks; applying traditional software engineering governance (access control, policies, tooling) to agents improves oversight. A controlled experiment shows that constraining agents with a substrate and CLI tools boosts a small reviewer's backdoor detection recall from 54.5% to 90.9% in a Python codebase.
AI.motivation: Unconstrained coding agents create security vulnerabilities, harm codebase scalability, and overwhelm human reviewers. The authors argue that rather than complex agentic scaffolding, established organizational controls from managing human teams can be directly and cheaply applied to coding agents.
AI.method: The paper proposes a start-to-end system applying access control, network policies, and tooling-enforced coding conventions to coding agents. A controlled experiment tests scalable oversight: a small reviewer model (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase with 11 hidden backdoors, comparing unconstrained versus constrained-substrate conditions with a ~200-line `docs` CLI tool.
AI.result: Recall improved from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus `docs` CLI). The substrate and tools contributed independently to the gain. Python was chosen deliberately because its weak default guarantees maximize the benefit of substrate-level oversight.
AI.conclusion: Traditional software engineering governance mechanisms transfer effectively to coding agents, providing cheaper and more effective oversight than recent agentic scaffolding approaches. These principles generalize beyond Python to languages like Rust.

title: Epic-Organized vs. Requirement-Aligned Gherkin: An Empirical Evaluation of LLM-Based Acceptance Criteria Generation
comment: Accepted for publication at the International Conference on Software Engineering of Emerging Technologies (SEET 2026)
summary: Automated authoring of Gherkin Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) acceptance criteria remains a manual bottleneck in requirements engineering. This study investigates whether epic-organized LLM-generated Gherkin produces higher quality and coverage than requirement-aligned generation. We compare our Timeless (an epic-organized LLM pipeline) approach against a naive large language model (LLM) baseline on four requirements documents (107 requirements) from the PURE dataset. Evaluation covers structural metrics, automated requirement coverage via TF-IDF and dense embeddings, and blind expert assessment by four researchers. In our evaluation, the JSON-constrained pipeline produced structurally valid scenarios across all generated outputs, while the zero-shot baseline achieved 99% structural validity. Semantic coverage was comparable to the baseline, with Timeless achieving 94.3% semantic Requirement Coverage Rate compared with 92.9% for the baseline. TF-IDF produced lower coverage scores for the epic-organized output, suggesting that lexical metrics may miss coverage when scenarios paraphrase requirements at a higher level of abstraction. Expert raters prefer the epic-organized strategy on Correctness (4.61 vs 4.14), Executability (4.61 vs 4.07), and Completeness (4.31 vs 3.50). Overall, the results suggest that epic-organized generation can improve perceived Gherkin quality while maintaining comparable semantic coverage, although broader replication is needed before generalizing this finding.

AI.tldr: This paper compares an epic-organized LLM pipeline ("Timeless") against a naive requirement-aligned LLM baseline for generating Gherkin BDD acceptance criteria. Results show the epic-organized approach yields comparable semantic coverage but significantly higher expert-rated quality on correctness, executability, and completeness.
AI.motivation: Manual authoring of Gherkin acceptance criteria in Behavior-Driven Development is a bottleneck in requirements engineering. Current LLM-based generation typically aligns scenarios directly to individual requirements, but the authors hypothesize that organizing generation around higher-level epics may produce better quality and coverage.
AI.method: The authors implement "Timeless," a JSON-constrained LLM pipeline that organizes Gherkin scenario generation around epics rather than individual requirements. They compare this against a zero-shot LLM baseline using four requirements documents (107 requirements) from the PURE dataset. Evaluation includes structural validity, automated requirement coverage (TF-IDF and dense embeddings), and blind expert assessment by four researchers rating correctness, executability, and completeness.
AI.result: Timeless achieved 100% structural validity vs. 99% for the baseline. Semantic Requirement Coverage Rate was comparable (94.3% for Timeless vs. 92.9% baseline). TF-IDF scores were lower for the epic-organized output, suggesting lexical metrics underestimate coverage when scenarios paraphrase at higher abstraction levels. Expert raters preferred the epic-organized strategy across all subjective measures: Correctness (4.61 vs 4.14), Executability (4.61 vs 4.07), and Completeness (4.31 vs 3.50).
AI.conclusion: Epic-organized LLM generation improves perceived Gherkin quality while maintaining comparable semantic coverage to requirement-aligned approaches. However, the authors caution that broader replication across more diverse datasets is needed before generalizing the findings.

title: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents
summary: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors--memory capture and memory retention--and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.

AI.tldr: Recurrent memory agents suffer from catastrophic retention failure over long contexts because monolithic memory overwrites prior content. The authors propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a training-free architecture that partitions memory into independent heads with a select-then-update strategy, and demonstrate substantial improvements in retention and accuracy across 100K–1M token benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing recurrent memory agents degrade systematically as context length grows. The authors decompose this failure into memory capture and memory retention, identifying retention—specifically the overwriting problem in monolithic memory designs—as the dominant bottleneck.
AI.method: The authors propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, only one head is updated while others are structurally shielded from overwriting. They introduce MHM-LRU (Least-Recently-Updated) as a lightweight instantiation that guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead.
AI.result: MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K–1M token range. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, memory retention rate improved from under 30% to 73.96%. Gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types.
AI.conclusion: Architectural optimization of memory structure, rather than relying solely on model behavior, offers a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory agents.

title: Rethinking Speech-LLM Integration for ASR: Effective Joint Speech-Text Training by Interleaving
summary: Speech-LLM integration has shown promising results by leveraging extensive textual pretraining, yet its specific benefits for automatic speech recognition (ASR) remain unclear. We observe that as supervised ASR training data increases, the contribution of LLM priors becomes less evident, and simple speech-text joint training under-utilizes textual knowledge. We therefore propose Joint Speech-Text Interleaved Pretraining (JSTIP), an ASR-oriented pretraining strategy that constructs word-level and segment-level interleaved speech-text sequences within aligned pairs for speech-LLM architectures that accept continuous inputs. Experiments on 38k hours of ASR data show consistent entity accuracy improvement compared to ASR-only and joint speech-text training baselines. JSTIP achieves on-par entity recognition performance using domain transcription text compared to synthetic speech-text pairs, simplifying domain adaptation. Benefiting from textual pretraining and domain text data, JSTIP is competitive with open-source ASR and Speech-LLM systems in medical entity recognition. The zero-shot speech question answering behaviors further suggest that interleaving reduces the speech-text modality gap and preserves the LLM generative prior, which is likely the reason for the entity improvements on the ASR task.

AI.tldr: JSTIP proposes word/segment-level speech-text interleaved pretraining for speech-LLM architectures, improving ASR entity recognition by better leveraging LLM priors and reducing the speech-text modality gap.
AI.motivation: Supervised ASR training with increasing data diminishes the contribution of LLM priors, and simple joint speech-text training under-utilizes textual knowledge. The authors aim to better exploit LLM pretrained knowledge for ASR, especially for entity recognition.
AI.method: JSTIP constructs word-level and segment-level interleaved speech-text sequences from aligned pairs, designed for speech-LLM architectures accepting continuous inputs. Pretraining is conducted on 38k hours of ASR data, and domain adaptation uses transcription text rather than synthetic speech-text pairs.
AI.result: JSTIP shows consistent entity accuracy improvements over ASR-only and joint speech-text baselines. It achieves on-par entity recognition using domain text versus synthetic pairs, simplifying domain adaptation. It is competitive with open-source ASR and Speech-LLM systems on medical entity recognition. Zero-shot speech QA indicates reduced modality gap and preserved LLM generative prior.
AI.conclusion: Interleaved speech-text pretraining effectively reduces the modality gap and preserves LLM generative priors, leading to improved ASR entity recognition. The approach simplifies domain adaptation by enabling effective use of plain domain text data.

title: Separating Expert Retention from Autonomous Source Inference in Raw-ECG-Replay-Free Continual ECG Deployment
summary:
In multi-source ECG deployment, models may need to incorporate new data sources when earlier raw ECGs cannot be retained or replayed. Freezing a pretrained backbone and assigning each source an isolated classifier prevents parameter interference, but deployment still requires selecting an expert when source metadata are unavailable. We study this distinction through \ours{}, an incremental expert bank built on frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features. Each arriving domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert, while a lightweight router is fitted only on retained training features and domain labels from sources observed so far. A validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the two most likely experts instead of committing to a single routed expert.
  On CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing, source-aware expert selection reaches $0.7915\pm0.0036$ Macro-F1 and a matched offline independent-head reference reaches $0.7885\pm0.0009$, supporting strong source-aware expert retention. Without source IDs, an MLP router reaches $0.7756\pm0.0027$ and top-2 margin fusion reaches $0.7782\pm0.0022$. The top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small ($+0.0026$), with a 95\% confidence interval from paired bootstrap that includes zero. Across three domain orders, the top-2-to-oracle gap remains $0.0111$--$0.0133$, identifying autonomous source inference as the main remaining bottleneck. No raw ECGs are replayed, but frozen training features are retained for router updates; the method is therefore not memory-free.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an incremental expert bank for multi-source ECG classification where frozen ECGFounder features are paired with per-source classifiers. When source metadata is unavailable at deployment, a lightweight router (trained only on retained feature embeddings, not raw ECGs) selects experts, with a top-2 margin fusion rule slightly improving over hard routing. The main finding: source-aware selection nearly matches an offline upper bound, but autonomous source inference without metadata remains the key bottleneck.
AI.motivation: In multi-source ECG deployment scenarios, new data sources must be incorporated incrementally, but raw ECGs from earlier sources often cannot be retained or replayed (e.g., due to privacy or storage constraints). While freezing a pretrained backbone and using per-source classifiers avoids catastrophic forgetting, a practical challenge arises: at deployment, the correct expert must be selected, yet source metadata (domain IDs) may be unavailable. The paper studies this autonomous source inference problem and whether router-based expert selection can close the gap to source-aware (oracle) selection.
AI.method: The method, called an "incremental expert bank," uses frozen 1024-dimensional features from a pretrained ECGFounder backbone. Each new source adds a balanced-softmax linear expert classifier without modifying prior experts. A lightweight router (MLP) is fitted solely on retained training features and domain labels from sources seen so far — raw ECGs are never replayed, only feature vectors are stored. At inference, instead of committing to a single routed expert, a validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the predictions of the top-2 most likely experts. Experiments span three domain arrival orders across four ECG datasets: CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing.
AI.result: Source-aware expert selection achieves 0.7915 ± 0.0036 Macro-F1, closely matching an offline independent-head reference (0.7885 ± 0.0009), confirming strong expert retention. Without source IDs, an MLP router reaches 0.7756 ± 0.0027 and top-2 margin fusion yields 0.7782 ± 0.0022. The top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is only +0.0026, with a 95% paired bootstrap CI that includes zero — indicating marginal benefit. Across three domain orders, the top-2-to-oracle gap is 0.0111–0.0133, identifying autonomous source inference as the primary remaining bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: Frozen-backbone expert banks with per-source classifiers achieve strong incremental performance comparable to offline models, but the main bottleneck is autonomous source inference when domain metadata are unavailable. The proposed top-2 margin fusion provides only negligible improvement over hard routing. The method is not memory-free, as frozen training features must be retained for router updates, but it avoids replaying raw ECG signals.

title: HTTP REST API Structure Learning
summary: Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) are essential in software development, enabling web services, mobile apps, and microservices. However, their widespread use introduces significant security risks, highlighting the importance of API security. This paper presents HTTP REST API Learning (HRAL), a novel unsupervised anomaly detection approach that models the structure and behavior of API endpoints directly from network traffic, without relying on predefined rules or documentation. HRAL enables robust detection of malicious activity by understanding how APIs behave and flagging deviations as potential threats. We evaluate HRAL across varying levels of OpenAPI documentation detail and compare it with existing techniques. HRAL achieves strong performance, with an average recall of 82.07% and an F1-score of 87.24%, significantly outperforming alternatives when API documentation is limited. Moreover, our results approach the effectiveness of full API document definitions. When combined with signature-based rules such as the OWASP ModSecurity CRS, our system achieves 100% detection. These results highlight HRAL's effectiveness in real-world, partially documented API environments and its potential as a foundational layer for modern API security solutions.

AI.tldr: HRAL is an unsupervised anomaly detection system that learns API endpoint structures and behaviors from network traffic, achieving strong threat detection (82.07% recall, 87.24% F1) without predefined rules, and reaches 100% detection when combined with OWASP ModSecurity CRS.
AI.motivation: APIs are ubiquitous in modern software but introduce significant security risks. Existing detection methods often rely on predefined rules or full documentation (e.g., OpenAPI specs), which are frequently incomplete or unavailable in practice. There is a need for an approach that works effectively without such prerequisites.
AI.method: HRAL (HTTP REST API Learning) — an unsupervised anomaly detection approach that models API endpoint structure and behavior directly from observed network traffic. It learns normal API usage patterns and flags deviations as potential threats. The system is evaluated under varying levels of OpenAPI documentation detail, compared against existing techniques, and tested in combination with signature-based rules (OWASP ModSecurity CRS).
AI.result: HRAL achieves an average recall of 82.07% and F1-score of 87.24%, significantly outperforming alternatives when API documentation is limited. Its performance approaches that of systems using full API document definitions. When combined with OWASP ModSecurity CRS, detection reaches 100%.
AI.conclusion: HRAL demonstrates strong effectiveness in real-world, partially documented API environments and shows significant potential as a foundational layer for modern API security solutions, particularly where documentation is sparse or absent.

title: Benchmarking Quantum Software Testing with Scalable Quantum Programs
summary: Quantum software testing (QST) checks whether quantum programs behave according to their intended specifications. A key requirement for QST research is a benchmark that supports rigorous empirical evaluation on programs that are testable and better reflect current software development practices. However, existing studies heavily rely on small hard-coded or circuit-level benchmarks, while available quantum programs are scattered across repositories without clear selection criteria, which limits fair comparison and systematic reproducibility. To this end, we present Qolumbina, a benchmark infrastructure for controlled QST experiments on scalable quantum programs. Qolumbina curates 40 programs from open-source repositories, turns them into test-ready subjects through systematic selection, refactoring, specifications, test case examples, unit tests, and standardized interfaces. We also propose QST-oriented criteria to characterize quantum programs along functionality, output behavior, development complexity, and quantum-specific execution complexity. Using these criteria, our empirical study shows that Qolumbina covers diverse testing-relevant properties and supports scalability analysis beyond fixed-size circuit benchmarks. Through controlled experiments with two recent QST approaches, we demonstrate the feasibility of using Qolumbina for execution-cost and fault-detection studies, and highlight backend-dependent effects that can influence QST result interpretation.

AI.tldr: Qolumbina is a benchmark infrastructure for quantum software testing (QST) that curates 40 real-world quantum programs from open-source repositories, standardizes them with specifications and unit tests, and characterizes them along multiple testing-relevant dimensions, enabling rigorous, reproducible, and scalable empirical evaluation of QST approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing QST research lacks a standardized benchmark for fair comparison and systematic reproducibility. Current studies rely on small, hard-coded or circuit-level benchmarks, while real-world quantum programs scattered across repositories have no clear selection criteria. This hinders rigorous empirical evaluation reflective of actual software development practices.
AI.method: The authors built Qolumbina by curating 40 quantum programs from open-source repositories and transforming them into test-ready subjects through systematic selection, refactoring, adding specifications, test case examples, unit tests, and standardized interfaces. They proposed QST-oriented criteria to characterize programs along four dimensions: functionality, output behavior, development complexity, and quantum-specific execution complexity. They then conducted an empirical study to assess diversity and scalability, and performed controlled experiments with two recent QST approaches for execution-cost and fault-detection evaluation.
AI.result: The empirical study demonstrated that Qolumbina covers diverse testing-relevant properties and supports scalability analysis beyond fixed-size circuit benchmarks. Controlled experiments with two recent QST approaches confirmed the benchmark's feasibility for execution-cost and fault-detection studies, while also revealing backend-dependent effects that can influence QST result interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Qolumbina provides a much-needed standardized, scalable benchmark infrastructure for quantum software testing, enabling fair comparison, reproducibility, and more realistic empirical evaluation that reflects current quantum software development practices.

title: Wind-Aware Reinforcement Learning Control of a Small Quadrotor Using Learned Onboard Wind Estimation in Simulated Atmospheric Turbulence
summary: Small multirotor aircraft are increasingly tasked with operations in the atmospheric boundary layer, where turbulent winds comparable to the vehicle's airspeed degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback control. This work illustrates a two-stage learning pipeline that first estimates the local wind from onboard kinematics and dynamics and then exploits that estimate inside a reinforcement learning (RL) flight controller. The wind estimator, an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with power-law shear and veer, recovers the horizontal wind vector with a per-flight root-mean-square error of 0.40 m/s and a direction error of 3.2 degrees on unseen wind regimes, an accuracy near the floor imposed by unresolved turbulence, and generalizes to vertical ascent profiles with a skill score of 0.861 over a constant-wind reference. A proximal policy optimization controller receiving the frozen estimator's output reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% relative to a wind-blind proportional-derivative baseline across mean winds of 4 m/s to 12 m/s, winning on 100% of evaluation episodes. A three-way ablation decomposes this improvement into a kinematic component, available without wind information, and a wind-perception component; the perception share rises with wind speed, from small in light winds toward roughly half the total benefit in strong winds, consistent with the quadratic scaling of aerodynamic drag. The controller degrades gracefully on out-of-distribution winds of 13 m/s to 15 m/s, where the baseline fails catastrophically.

AI.tldr: A two-stage learning pipeline combining a wind estimator (attention-augmented gated recurrent network) with a PPO-based RL flight controller reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% for small multirotors in turbulent boundary-layer winds, with the perception benefit growing as wind speed increases.
AI.motivation: Small multirotor aircraft operating in the atmospheric boundary layer face turbulent winds comparable to their airspeed, which severely degrades trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback controllers. Existing methods lack effective integration of wind perception into flight control.
AI.method: A two-stage pipeline: (1) a wind estimator — an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Kármán turbulence with power-law shear and veer — recovers the horizontal wind vector from onboard kinematics and dynamics; (2) a proximal policy optimization (PPO) RL flight controller uses the frozen estimator's output for control. A three-way ablation separates kinematic and wind-perception contributions.
AI.result: The wind estimator achieves 0.40 m/s RMSE and 3.2° direction error on unseen wind regimes, with a skill score of 0.861 on vertical ascent profiles. The PPO controller reduces horizontal tracking error by 48% versus a wind-blind PD baseline across 4–12 m/s mean winds, winning 100% of evaluation episodes. The perception share of improvement rises with wind speed, consistent with quadratic drag scaling. The controller degrades gracefully on out-of-distribution winds (13–15 m/s) where the baseline fails catastrophically.
AI.conclusion: Wind perception via learned estimation significantly improves RL-based trajectory tracking for small multirotors in turbulent conditions. The approach generalizes to unseen wind regimes and vertical ascent profiles, with perception benefits scaling with wind speed, and exhibits graceful degradation beyond the training distribution.

title: PARTREP: Learning What to Repeat for Decoder-only LLMs
summary: While decoder-only LLMs excel at a vast array of natural language tasks, it suffers from an asymmetric information flow induced by causal attention: later tokens are richer in contextual grounding than earlier ones. A simple and effective remedy is prompt repetition -- just appending a second copy of prompt before generation can redistribute grounding across positions and improve reasoning performance. However, full repetition of the original prompt doubles the KV cache footprint and quadruples attention cost during prefill, making it impractical for long-context settings. We propose PartRep, a selective augmentation method that appends only the most informative tokens -- rather than the entire prompt. We use token-wise negative log-likelihood (NLL) as a selection signal, motivated by the hypothesis that less predictable tokens are less recoverable from surrounding context and therefore benefit more from late-position repetition. To avoid the heavy cost of a full forward pass for scoring, we train a lightweight gate that predicts high-NLL tokens from early-layer hidden states, enabling token selection during mid-prefill via early exit. Across eight benchmarks (including MMLU, GSM8K, and RULER) and three model families (Qwen2.5, Llama3.2, Gemma4), PartRep retains most of the gains of full repetition while using only 59.4\% of its KV cache and 79.0\% of its prefill FLOPs.

AI.tldr: PartRep selectively repeats only high-NLL (less predictable) tokens using early-exit gating, retaining most reasoning gains of full prompt repetition while using ~59% KV cache and ~79% prefill FLOPs.
AI.motivation: Decoder-only LLMs suffer from asymmetric information flow due to causal attention, where later tokens have richer context than earlier ones. Full prompt repetition mitigates this but doubles KV cache and quadruples prefill attention cost, making it impractical for long contexts.
AI.method: PartRep uses token-wise negative log-likelihood (NLL) to identify less predictable tokens that benefit most from late-position repetition. A lightweight gating network trained to predict high-NLL tokens from early-layer hidden states enables token selection during mid-prefill via early exit, avoiding full forward pass cost.
AI.result: Across 8 benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, RULER) and 3 model families (Qwen2.5, Llama3.2, Gemma4), PartRep retains most reasoning gains of full repetition while using only 59.4% of KV cache and 79.0% of prefill FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: Selective token repetition guided by NLL-based importance scoring is an efficient alternative to full prompt repetition for mitigating causal attention asymmetry in decoder-only LLMs.

title: Epistemic Goggles: A Pretrained Module that Induces an Epistemic Frame via Gradient Editing
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Code at https://github.com/JoshuaSP/epistemic-goggles and generated documents, questions, and teacher rollouts at https://huggingface.co/datasets/joshuapenman/epistemic-goggles-artifacts
summary: Finetuning a language model on documents that are explicitly annotated as fictional results in a model that still actually believes the documents' core claims, an effect known as Negation Neglect. In our evaluations, models trained on documents prefixed and suffixed with such annotations correctly identify the relevant claims as fictional only about 9% of the time. To address this, we introduce Goggles, a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient rather than the data. During supervised finetuning, a Goggles module edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives, imparting a chosen epistemic frame (the stance the model takes toward the nature of what it reads) to whatever the documents teach. A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to documents it was never trained on. Trained through Goggles on those same documents, now carrying no fictional annotation, the model flags the content as fictional roughly 91% of the time, while preserving capability (GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline). The same architecture supports other frames: a Goggles instance can be trained to treat documents as "part of an AI safety evaluation by Redwood Research" rather than simply as fiction. The imparted frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, where prior interventions revert. Goggles suggests a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates.

AI.tldr: Language models finetuned on documents explicitly labeled as fictional still absorb their claims (Negation Neglect). The authors introduce Goggles, a gradient-level intervention module that imparts an epistemic frame during LoRA finetuning, enabling models to learn from documents while treating their content as fictional ~91% of the time, without degrading general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Language models suffer from Negation Neglect: even when documents are explicitly annotated as fictional, the model still internalizes the core claims. This poses a problem for training on potentially misaligned or untrusted data. The authors seek a method to train on such documents while having the model adopt a specified epistemic stance (e.g., treating content as fictional) rather than believing it.
AI.method: Goggles is a learned gradient-intervention module applied during LoRA-based supervised finetuning. Rather than modifying the training data, Goggles edits the gradients flowing into the LoRA parameters, imparting a pre-chosen epistemic frame (e.g., "this is fiction," "this is an AI safety evaluation"). A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then frozen and applied to unseen documents. The method is evaluated against baselines including data-level annotation approaches.
AI.result: Baseline models with annotated fictional documents correctly identify claims as fictional only ~9% of the time. With Goggles, the model flags untagged fictional content as fictional ~91% of the time. GPQA and TruthfulQA performance matches or exceeds baseline. The imparted frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, whereas prior interventions revert.
AI.conclusion: Goggles demonstrates that gradient-level epistemic framing can enable language models to learn from known-misaligned or untrusted data without absorbing undesirable behaviors, offering a path toward safer training on problematic corpora.

title: Mitigating Package Hallucinations in Large Language Models via Model Editing
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in software engineering tasks, such as code generation, library recommendation, and dependency configuration. However, recent studies show that LLMs may suffer from package hallucination, where they generate non-existent or invalid package names. These hallucinations can be exploited in software supply chain attacks, as attackers may register malicious packages under hallucinated names. Therefore, mitigating package hallucination is important for improving the reliability and security of LLM-assisted software development. In this paper, we introduce BOUND, a lightweight localized model editing framework for mitigating package hallucinations in LLMs. BOUND formulates package hallucination mitigation as a package-validity boundary editing problem, where the boundary refers to the model's ability to distinguish valid packages from hallucinated package names under a given task context. It first locates modules related to package hallucination through a risk-aware localization strategy, and then edits these modules with lightweight LoRA adapters using a boundary-aware objective that reinforces valid packages, suppresses hallucinated packages, and preserves locality behavior. Experimental results show that BOUND effectively reduces package hallucinations while preserving valid package recommendations. In the package recommendation task, BOUND reduces package-level hallucination rate (Package-HR) by 79.9% on edit prompts and by 65.4% on unseen prompts. The learned package-validity boundary further generalizes to other package-related tasks, reducing Package-HR by 12.8% in code generation and by 34.0% in pip install recommendation. These results show that BOUND refines the package-validity boundary of LLMs and improves the reliability of package-related outputs.

AI.tldr: BOUND is a lightweight model editing framework that mitigates LLM package hallucinations by localizing hallucination-related modules and applying LoRA adapters with a boundary-aware objective, achieving up to 79.9% reduction in package hallucination rates while preserving valid recommendations.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from package hallucination — generating non-existent package names — which poses software supply chain security risks since attackers can register malicious packages under hallucinated names. Existing mitigation approaches are insufficient, motivating a targeted model editing solution.
AI.method: BOUND formulates mitigation as a package-validity boundary editing problem. It employs: (1) a risk-aware localization strategy to identify hallucination-related modules; (2) lightweight LoRA adapters trained with a boundary-aware objective that reinforces valid packages, suppresses hallucinated ones, and preserves locality; applied to targeted model modules.
AI.result: On package recommendation, BOUND reduces Package-HR by 79.9% on edit prompts and 65.4% on unseen prompts. Generalization to other tasks: 12.8% reduction in code generation and 34.0% reduction in pip install recommendation.
AI.conclusion: BOUND effectively refines the package-validity boundary of LLMs, significantly reducing package hallucinations across multiple tasks while preserving valid package outputs, thereby improving reliability and security of LLM-assisted software development.

title: Certified World Models as Sensing Clocks: Drift-Aware Deadlines for Active Perception
summary: Certified world models estimate how long their predictions remain valid. We turn this validity horizon into an operational sensing clock: a rule for when an agent should stop coasting and re-sense. Starting from an audited equivariant world model, we derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals and show that deployable deadlines in learned world models must be drift-aware: on-manifold Lyapunov rates alone overestimate coasting validity, while calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes carry the deployed guarantee. On a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model, the resulting clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards. In a cue-conditioned theorem-bed (a synthetic bench where all schedulers share the exact model, isolating the scheduling rule), the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. We also report limits: in the short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock on validity and budget, and a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term. Thus the contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, not a claim that spectral clocks empirically dominate all non-spectral schedulers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a certified sensing clock derived from world models that tells an agent when to stop coasting on predictions and re-sense the environment. Using drift-aware deployment with learned world models, the method provides guaranteed validity horizons, outperforming naive Lyapunov-based estimates and reducing tail violations compared to belief-based scheduling, though it does not universally dominate all non-spectral schedulers.
AI.motivation: Agents operating with learned world models can "coast" on predictions between sensing observations, but knowing how long predictions remain valid is critical for safety and efficiency. Existing approaches lack certified, deployable deadlines for when to re-sense. The paper aims to turn certified validity horizons from world models into an operational sensing clock with formal guarantees that hold at deployment.
AI.method: Starting from an audited equivariant world model (frozen 3D VN-JEPA), the authors derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals using drift-aware deployment. They show that on-manifold Lyapunov rates alone overestimate coasting validity, so they calibrate native rollout-drift envelopes to carry the deployed guarantee. The method is evaluated on both a frozen VN-JEPA model and a cue-conditioned theorem-bed (a synthetic benchmark where all schedulers share the exact same model, isolating the scheduling rule). They compare against exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budgets and test empirical conformal horizons as a baseline.
AI.result: On the frozen 3D VN-JEPA model, the derived clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards. In the theorem-bed, the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. However, limits are reported: in the short-horizon VN-JEPA regime, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock on validity and budget, and a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term.
AI.conclusion: The core contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and a drift-aware deployment method for learned world models, not a claim that spectral clocks empirically dominate all non-spectral schedulers. The method provides formal deployment guarantees for when to re-sense, with particular strength in reducing tail violations.

title: On the Limits of Steering Vectors for Preference-Aligned Generation
summary: Steering vectors have emerged as a promising approach to controlled text generation, offering interpretable, training-free mechanisms for shaping model outputs. However, their practical generality remains poorly understood. We study the limits of steering vector generalization along three dimensions: trait expressibility, task transfer, and multi-trait composition. Using the PLUME writing personalization benchmark, we extract steering vectors for a range of preferences and evaluate them on summarization and email-writing tasks across two open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct). We find that steering effectiveness varies substantially across traits. We further show that steering effectiveness can degrade when vectors extracted from positive and negative style examples are transferred to downstream writing personalization tasks. Finally, we compare common methods for composing multiple steering vectors and find that all methods suffer significant drops in trait expression as more vectors are added, with a tradeoff between coherence and expressibility that requires per-setting hyperparameter tuning. Taken together, our results suggest that steering vectors face meaningful limits as a general-purpose tool for preference alignment.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates the generalization limits of steering vectors across three dimensions—trait expressibility, task transfer, and multi-trait composition—finding that steering effectiveness varies by trait, degrades upon task transfer, and suffers significant expressibility loss in multi-trait composition, suggesting fundamental limits to their utility as a general-purpose preference alignment tool.
AI.motivation: Steering vectors are increasingly popular for controlled text generation due to their interpretability and training-free nature, but their practical generality—how well they work across different traits, tasks, and in combination—remains poorly understood and underexplored.
AI.method: The authors use the PLUME writing personalization benchmark to extract steering vectors for a range of stylistic preferences. They evaluate these vectors on summarization and email-writing tasks using two open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct). They test three dimensions: (1) trait expressibility by measuring variation across traits, (2) task transfer by applying vectors derived from positive/negative style examples to downstream tasks, and (3) multi-trait composition by comparing common vector composition methods while monitoring coherence and expressibility.
AI.result: Steering effectiveness varies substantially across traits. Task transfer leads to degraded steering performance. In multi-trait composition, all composition methods exhibit significant drops in trait expression as more vectors are added, revealing a coherence–expressibility tradeoff that demands per-setting hyperparameter tuning.
AI.conclusion: Steering vectors face meaningful limitations as a general-purpose tool for preference alignment, with their effectiveness constrained by trait specificity, limited cross-task transferability, and poor scalability in multi-trait composition.

title: COMFYCLAW: Self-Evolving Skill Harnesses for Image Generation Workflows
summary: Agents are increasingly used to construct workflows and assist humans in completing recurring tasks more efficiently. As these workflows become repeated and domain-specific, agent memory and reusable skills become increasingly important: agents should be able to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs. We study this problem in workflow-based image generation and introduce COMFYCLAW, an agentic skill evolution harness for controlling ComfyUI workflows. COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes tools organized by construction stage, automatically reverts invalid edits, and uses a region-level vision-language model (VLM) verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The framework further evolves a progressively disclosed skill library, where trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs are distilled into reusable Agent Skills. Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotations further show that annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution. Our results suggest that skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

AI.tldr: COMFYCLAW introduces an agentic framework for ComfyUI workflow construction that uses typed graph editing, a VLM verifier for visual feedback, and a progressively disclosed skill library where past trajectories and errors are distilled into reusable Agent Skills, achieving superior image-generation scores across multiple benchmarks and models.
AI.motivation: As agent-based workflows become recurrent and domain-specific, agents need memory mechanisms to recall workflow patterns, constraints, and user preferences from prior runs. Existing approaches lack effective skill evolution — the ability to learn from past execution errors and verifier feedback to improve reliability in repeated visual workflow construction tasks.
AI.method: COMFYCLAW formulates ComfyUI workflow construction as typed graph editing with stage-organized tools and automatic rollback of invalid edits. A region-level VLM verifier translates visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The core innovation is a progressively disclosed skill library: trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs are distilled into reusable Agent Skills that evolve over time.
