AI.result: Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotators also prefer COMFYCLAW over variants lacking skill evolution.
AI.conclusion: Skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction, demonstrating that distilling past execution experience into reusable skills enhances both automated metrics and human preference.

title: Prompt Coverage Adequacy
summary: In recent years, it has become increasingly evident that large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents raise the level of abstraction in software development by shifting the focus from writing precise procedures to expressing intents and goals. This paradigm shift introduces new challenges, particularly in how testing should be guided when prompts, rather than code, become primary development artifacts. To address this challenge, we propose Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a novel coverage criterion designed to support the testing of code generated from task descriptions. Prompt Coverage Adequacy serves as an analog to traditional code coverage, but operates at the level of prompts used in LLM and agent-based programming. Specifically, it measures how well a given test suite satisfies the requirements expressed in a prompt by leveraging the attention mechanisms of LLMs. We evaluate a simple instantiation of this criterion, based on attention boosting, across two datasets and multiple LLMs. Our results demonstrate that Prompt Coverage is associated with fault-detection effectiveness and can uncover over 30+% more faults than traditional code coverage when used to guide test generation. These findings suggest that Prompt Coverage Adequacy can serve as a foundation for developing testing metrics better suited to the emerging paradigm of LLM-driven software development, addressing the limitations of classical coverage criteria in this new context.

AI.tldr: Proposes Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a novel testing metric for LLM-generated code that measures how well test suites satisfy prompt requirements using attention mechanisms, showing 30%+ improvement in fault detection over traditional code coverage.
AI.motivation: As LLMs shift software development from writing code to expressing intents via prompts, traditional code coverage criteria become inadequate. There is a need for testing metrics that operate at the prompt level to ensure generated code faithfully satisfies task descriptions.
AI.method: Introduces Prompt Coverage Adequacy, which uses LLM attention mechanisms to quantify how well a test suite covers requirements expressed in a prompt. A simple instantiation based on attention boosting is evaluated across two datasets and multiple LLMs.
AI.result: Prompt Coverage correlates with fault-detection effectiveness and uncovers over 30% more faults than traditional code coverage when guiding test generation.
AI.conclusion: Prompt Coverage Adequacy provides a foundation for testing metrics suited to LLM-driven development, addressing limitations of classical coverage criteria in the emerging intent-based programming paradigm.

title: Evolutionary Feature Engineering for Structured Data
comment: 9 page main content, 41 pages in total
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as open-ended search operators in evolutionary optimization. We introduce Evolutionary Feature Engineering (EFE), a framework for using LLM-based evolution to discover preprocessing transformations for structured data. EFE represents transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface, allowing them to be inserted directly into existing machine learning pipelines. During evolution, candidate programs are refined using dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream performance feedback on validation set. We instantiate EFE in two settings. For time-series forecasting, EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations that improve off-the-shelf time-series foundation models. It reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) 3% or more when averaged across datasets and improvements are as much as 19% on the COVID-Deaths dataset. Notably, these improvements occur with recent TSFMs such as Chronos-2. For tabular prediction, EFE-Tab evolves compact feature programs that add useful interpretable features and remove redundant ones, improving or matching existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods. We found EFE-Tab to be particularly effective on classical decision trees, where small sets of evolved features yield competitive accuracy while preserving interpretability. Overall, EFE demonstrates that LLM-based evolution can improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically tackling structured data.

AI.tldr: EFE uses LLM-based evolution to discover preprocessing transformations (Python programs with fit/transform interfaces) for structured data, improving forecasting accuracy for time-series foundation models by up to 19% and enhancing interpretable feature engineering for tabular prediction, particularly with decision trees.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as search operators in evolutionary optimization. The authors aim to leverage this capability for automated feature engineering — discovering dataset-specific preprocessing transformations that improve downstream model performance while maintaining interpretability. Existing automated feature engineering methods often lack flexibility, interpretability, or integration with modern ML pipelines.
AI.method: The Evolutionary Feature Engineering (EFE) framework represents candidate transformations as Python programs with standardized fit/transform interfaces. Evolution proceeds by iteratively refining these programs using dataset context, summary statistics, and validation-set performance feedback from downstream models. Two instantiations are proposed: (1) EFE-Time, which learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations to boost off-the-shelf time-series foundation models (e.g., Chronos-2); and (2) EFE-Tab, which evolves compact feature programs that add interpretable features and remove redundant ones for tabular prediction.
AI.result: EFE-Time reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) by ≥3% on average across datasets, with up to 19% improvement on COVID-Deaths when paired with models like Chronos-2. EFE-Tab matches or outperforms existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods, and is especially effective with decision trees — small sets of evolved features yield competitive accuracy while preserving interpretability.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based evolution can simultaneously improve accuracy and interpretability for structured data preprocessing. EFE provides a flexible, pipeline-compatible framework that yields significant gains in both time-series forecasting and tabular prediction tasks.

title: PairCoder++: Pair Programming as a Universal Paradigm for Verified Code-Driven Multimodal and Structured-Artifact Generation
comment: Accepted by ACL 2026. Project Page: https://yisuanwang.github.io/PairCoder/
summary: Code is the medium through which large language models generate structured artifacts: charts, scientific figures, vector graphics, CAD models, 3D scenes, and hardware designs are all produced by writing programs. In this regime single pass inference is brittle, because the compiler, renderer, or simulator that decides whether the artifact exists is invisible to the model. We present PairCoder, which grounds review in the toolchain and realizes it as two agent pair programming: a Driver agent writes the program, a Navigator agent reviews it against verification evidence (diagnostics, execution results, and renderings of the current artifact beside the target), and the two switch roles when errors persist. Across 17 public benchmarks and seven models from three vendors, PairCoder improves essentially every benchmark whose artifact is verifiable, on full official metric suites rather than execution alone (for example, Blender scene executability 0.20 to 0.78; TikZ compile rate up 10 to 30 points on every model), at 2.9 to 9.2 times single model cost (about 7 times overall). The improvements concentrate where the toolchain provides an informative oracle and the baseline leaves headroom, and the method ties or mildly regresses where the oracle is weak; we frame pair programming as a reliable recipe for verified code driven generation.

AI.tldr: PairCoder introduces a two-agent pair-programming framework (Driver writes code, Navigator reviews against toolchain verification evidence) that substantially improves verifiable code generation across 17 benchmarks and 7 models, with gains of up to 58 points on executability and 30 points on compile rate, at roughly 7× cost.
AI.motivation: Single-pass LLM inference for code-driven artifact generation (charts, CAD, 3D scenes, etc.) is brittle because the model cannot see compiler/renderer/simulator feedback — it has no access to whether the generated artifact is valid. This motivates a verification-grounded approach.
AI.method: PairCoder implements two-agent pair programming: a Driver agent generates the program, while a Navigator agent reviews it against verification evidence from the toolchain (diagnostics, execution results, renderings of current vs. target artifacts). When errors persist, the agents swap roles. The method treats the toolchain as an informative oracle.
AI.result: Across 17 public benchmarks and 7 models (3 vendors), PairCoder improves nearly every verifiable benchmark. Key results: Blender scene executability from 0.20 to 0.78; TikZ compile rate up 10–30 points per model. Cost is 2.9–9.2× single-model cost (~7× overall). Gains concentrate where toolchain oracles are informative and baseline headroom exists; ties or mild regression occurs where the oracle is weak.
AI.conclusion: Pair programming with toolchain-grounded review is a reliable recipe for verified code-driven generation. The Driver–Navigator structure, with role-switching on persistent errors, consistently improves performance wherever the toolchain provides meaningful verification signals.

title: Generic Expert Coverage for Pruning SparseMixture-of-Experts Language Models
summary: Sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models contain substantial structured redundancy among routed experts, but pruning them without downstream calibration data remains challenging. Existing expert-pruning methods typically rely on a single aggregated importance score, which can bias the retained set toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. We propose \textbf{Generic TB-Coverage}, a coverage-aware expert pruning method that uses only generic text corpora (WikiText2 and C4) for calibration. Instead of collapsing expert utility into one score, our method profiles per-expert utility separately on each corpus and enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. Across Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25\%, 50\%, and 75\% retention budgets, our method improves average accuracy on six common zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while also reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. The gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25\% and 50\% retain), suggesting that preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. Our improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.

AI.tldr: Generic TB-Coverage proposes a coverage-aware pruning method for MoE models that preserves experts important across multiple generic corpora (WikiText2, C4), outperforming single-score methods like REAP and ExpertSparsity, especially under aggressive pruning budgets, without needing downstream calibration data.
AI.motivation: MoE language models contain structured redundancy among routed experts. Existing pruning methods rely on a single aggregated importance score biased toward dominant calibration patterns, risking the loss of experts that are critical for certain corpora but undervalued in aggregate. The authors aim to solve expert pruning using only generic text corpora, without downstream calibration data.
AI.method: The method profiles per-expert utility separately on each generic corpus (WikiText2, C4). It then enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule: high-utility experts from each corpus are preserved before constructing the final pruning mask. This ensures cross-corpus coverage rather than collapsing utility into a single aggregated score.
AI.result: Evaluated on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25%, 50%, and 75% retention budgets. The method improves average accuracy on six zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. Gains are largest at aggressive pruning levels (25% and 50% retain).
AI.conclusion: Preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. The approach holds under fixed pruning budgets and requires no downstream calibration data, making it a practical and robust solution for reducing MoE model redundancy.

title: File-Level Copying Is an Implicit Dependency in Open Source
summary: File-level copying is a widespread but ungoverned form of software reuse. Copying files across repositories reduces supply-chain visibility: it removes the four observable signals a package manager provides for a declared dependency (provenance, maintenance, security, and compliance) with no mechanism to restore them. To characterize the scale and consequences of this unmanaged reuse, we present a mixed-method study of copying across the entire open-source ecosystem using World of Code (WoC). From a 0.1% commit sample, we extract 690,500 copy events and retain 3,912 rationale-bearing copy commits for intent labeling. We show that the 13 axial copy forms, spanning vendored dependencies, hardware/driver synchronization, scaffolding, UI assets, and direct source-code reuse, are unreliable proxies for developer intent: among rationale-bearing commits, hardware/driver copies are predominantly fork-maintenance work (78%), while dependency-vendoring copies more often signal upstream bypass (70%) than offline availability. These visibility gaps are form-specific: security and license risk concentrate in complementary copy forms. Copied sources are frequently stale (median 155 days; 38.5% over one year old) and seldom record a recoverable origin (4.3% documented), let alone a checkable version (2.0% versioned); even vendored copies record where they came from only 10% of the time. Security risk concentrates in vendored dependencies: 17,314 CVE-risk copy commits in the full-WoC graph, 88% in the dependency-vendoring form; 80% score CVSS >= 7.0 and upstream-fix adoption is only 47%-84%. License risk concentrates in direct source-code reuse: 41,777 pre-validation candidates, 66% in the source-code form, with 39 verified high-star violations (kappa = 0.752). Both risks reach packaged software and are invisible to dependency scanners operating on declared metadata alone.

AI.tldr: File-level copying is a widespread but invisible form of software reuse that undermines supply-chain visibility. Analyzing 690K copy events across open-source, the study identifies 13 copy forms, reveals their unreliability as intent proxies, and quantifies concentrated security (vendored deps) and license (direct source-code reuse) risks invisible to package-manager-based scanners.
AI.motivation: File-level copying across repositories eliminates the four key signals that package managers provide for declared dependencies: provenance, maintenance, security, and compliance. Despite being widespread, this practice lacks governance and quantitative characterization, leaving supply-chain risks invisible to existing dependency scanning tools.
AI.method: A mixed-method study using the World of Code (WoC) infrastructure. From a 0.1% commit sample across the entire open-source ecosystem, the authors extract 690,500 copy events and retain 3,912 rationale-bearing commits for manual intent labeling. They classify copies into 13 axial forms (vendored dependencies, hardware/driver sync, scaffolding, UI assets, direct source-code reuse, etc.) and analyze staleness, origin documentation, version tracking, CVE-risk exposure, and license violations, with inter-rater reliability measured via Cohen's kappa.
AI.result: The 13 copy forms are unreliable proxies for developer intent: 78% of hardware/driver copies are fork-maintenance work; 70% of dependency-vendoring copies signal upstream bypass rather than offline availability. Copied sources are stale (median 155 days; 38.5% >1 year old), rarely document origin (4.3%), and almost never include a checkable version (2.0%); even vendored copies record provenance only 10% of the time. Security risk concentrates in vendored dependencies (17,314 CVE-risk commits, 88% in dependency-vendoring form; 80% score CVSS ≥ 7.0; upstream-fix adoption 47–84%). License risk concentrates in direct source-code reuse (41,777 pre-validation candidates, 66% source-code form; 39 verified high-star violations, κ = 0.752). Both risks propagate to packaged software and evade metadata-based dependency scanners.
AI.conclusion: File-level copying constitutes a significant, ungoverned supply-chain attack surface. Copy-form-based heuristics are inadequate for inferring intent or risk. The concentrated but complementary nature of security and license risks across different copy forms, combined with near-total absence of provenance metadata, demands new tooling and practices that operate at the file/commit level rather than relying solely on declared package-manager dependencies.

title: X-LogSMask: Expand Transformer for Graph-Structured Data
summary: Transformers have become general-purpose architectures, but their all-to-all self-attention is poorly matched to graph data, whose interactions are sparse, structured and multi-scale. Existing Graph Transformers address this mismatch through structural encodings, hybrid message-passing modules or learned attention constraints, often introducing additional complexity and limited interpretability. Here we introduce X-LogSMask, an explainable multi-head logarithmic structural mask that injects symmetrically normalized graph topology directly into attention logits. The logarithmic transform converts structural connectivity into a topology-aware gating signal, suppressing unsupported node interactions while preserving feature-dependent attention. By assigning different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix to different attention heads, X-LogSMask gives each head a defined structural radius and supports multi-hop information propagation within a single layer. We further show that a standard Transformer encoder can be interpreted as one-step message passing on a complete graph, motivating X-LogSMask as a topology-constrained alternative to unrestricted self-attention. Across 20 node-, edge- and graph-level benchmarks, Transformers equipped with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remain competitive in a lightweight one-layer configuration. These results show that simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without changing the Transformer architecture. The code is available at https://github.com/LiLeyan-0120/X-LogSMask.

AI.tldr: X-LogSMask introduces a logarithmic structural mask that directly injects normalized graph topology into Transformer attention logits, enabling multi-scale graph learning without architectural modifications. The method achieves SOTA on 13 of 20 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard Transformers use all-to-all self-attention, which poorly matches graph data characterized by sparse, structured, multi-scale interactions. Existing Graph Transformers address this via structural encodings, hybrid message-passing, or learned constraints, but these add complexity and reduce interpretability. The authors seek a simple, interpretable way to make self-attention graph-aware without altering the Transformer architecture.
AI.method: X-LogSMask applies a logarithmic transformation to symmetrically normalized adjacency matrix powers and injects the result as an additive mask into attention logits. Different attention heads receive different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix, giving each head a defined structural radius for multi-hop propagation within a single layer. The approach is motivated by reframing standard self-attention as one-step message passing on a complete graph, with the mask serving as a topology-constrained alternative.
AI.result: Transformers with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art performance on 13 out of 20 node-, edge-, and graph-level benchmarks and remain competitive even in a lightweight one-layer configuration.
AI.conclusion: Simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without modifying the Transformer architecture, matching or exceeding more complex Graph Transformer designs.

title: The Grammar Does the Work: Functional vs. Lexical Dependency Length Minimization Across Universal Dependencies
summary: Dependency length minimization (DLM) is a well-documented processing universal, but previous studies report a single mean dependency distance (MDD) per language, obscuring variation across syntactic relation types. We analyze 122 languages in UD and SUD (version 2.17), showing that DLM operates on two distinct levels. Grammar-driven optimization targets functional dependencies (det, case, aux), which are universally short (mean 1.71, $σ$ = 0.33) and invariant across typologically diverse languages. Processing-driven optimization operates on lexical dependencies (nsubj, obj, obl), which are longer (mean 2.87), highly variable ($σ$ = 0.63), and constrained by word-order typology. This asymmetry holds in SUD despite reversed head direction (r = 0.92). We conclude that ''the grammar does the work'' of minimization by scaffolding sentences with local functional attachments, leaving processing pressures to determine the ordering of lexical heads.

AI.tldr: Dependency length minimization operates on two distinct levels: grammar-driven optimization keeps functional dependencies universally short and invariant, while processing-driven optimization governs lexical dependencies, which are longer, more variable, and constrained by word-order typology.
AI.motivation: Previous DLM studies report only a single mean MDD per language, obscuring variation across syntactic relation types. The authors aim to disentangle whether minimization is a uniform phenomenon or operates differently across functional vs. lexical dependencies.
AI.method: Analysis of 122 languages from UD and SUD (v2.17), comparing mean dependency distances for functional dependencies (det, case, aux) versus lexical dependencies (nsubj, obj, obl), assessing universality, variability, and typological constraints; cross-framework validation using SUD with reversed head direction.
AI.result: Functional dependencies are universally short (mean 1.71, σ = 0.33) and invariant across typologically diverse languages. Lexical dependencies are longer (mean 2.87), highly variable (σ = 0.63), and constrained by word-order typology. The asymmetry holds in SUD despite reversed head direction (r = 0.92).
AI.conclusion: Grammar does the work of minimization by scaffolding sentences with local functional attachments, while processing pressures determine the ordering of lexical heads — a two-level DLM architecture.

title: Distributionally Robust Listwise Preference Optimization
summary: Existing robust preference optimization for language-model alignment mainly studies pairwise supervision and places robustness at the dataset, prompt, or preference-pair level. We instead study listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty: given a prompt and a candidate list, the observed ranking over that list may be ambiguous due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise. We propose a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett--Luce objective that directly robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss admits an exact decomposition into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, and the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing the inner maximization from $K!$ enumeration to $O(K\log K)$. This tractable structure yields strong offline and online optimization guarantees. In the offline fixed-list setting, the robust objective is convex and projected stochastic subgradient reaches global $ε$-suboptimality with $O(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity. In the online policy-induced setting, where candidate lists are generated by the current policy, we establish weak convexity and $\widetilde O(ε^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments in offline LLM alignment show that the proposed robust correction largely preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. In online alignment, it makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable and improves both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.

AI.tldr: Proposes a computationally tractable robust Plackett-Luce objective for listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty. The worst-case ranking reduces from factorial enumeration to $O(K\log K)$ sorting, yielding strong offline convex and online weakly-convex convergence guarantees, with empirical gains in LLM alignment under noisy and clean conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing robust preference optimization focuses on pairwise supervision and dataset/prompt-level robustness, leaving listwise ranking-label uncertainty (from annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy feedback, reward-model noise) unaddressed. The authors aim to provide robustness directly at the ranking-label level within the Plackett-Luce framework.
AI.method: A pointwise total-variation robust Plackett-Luce objective is constructed. The robust loss decomposes into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case correction term, where the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order — collapsing the inner maximization from $K!$ to $O(K\log K)$. Analysis covers both offline fixed-list (convex, projected stochastic subgradient with $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity) and online policy-induced settings (weak convexity, $\widetilde O(\epsilon^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity).
AI.result: Offline experiments show the robust correction preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. Online alignment experiments demonstrate that reward-model-ranked candidate expansion becomes more reliable, improving both reward-model metrics and external GPT-4 judge evaluations.
AI.conclusion: The tractable robust Plackett-Luce objective effectively handles ranking-label uncertainty in both offline and online LLM alignment settings, offering theoretical guarantees and practical improvements in robustness without sacrificing clean-label performance.

title: Coding Agents Are Guessing: Measuring Action-Boundary Violations in Underspecified DevOps Instructions
summary:
LLM coding agents are increasingly deployed to act autonomously on real production infrastructure. They execute shell commands, modify repositories, and call operational APIs. However, completing a task is not sufficient for safety. A wrong action can cause severe consequences. Existing agent benchmarks largely emphasize task completion, leaving open how agents behave under benign but underspecified instructions.
  We present UnderSpecBench, a benchmark for measuring action-boundary violations in coding agents (i.e., Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode) on DevOps tasks. UnderSpecBench includes 69 task families grounded in documented incidents, CVEs, or tool behavior and organized across four DevOps capability domains and nine operational control surfaces. To isolate underspecification from task difficulty, each task keeps the same environment and ground-truth safe action while varying the instruction along three axes: intent clarity, target certainty, and blast radius. The resulting 2,208 prompt variants are evaluated with deterministic, side-effect-based oracles that separate Safe Success, Wrong Target, and OverScope outcomes; non-action runs are further classified as clarification, refusal, or deferment.
  Across five agent x model configurations using OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex, the evaluation results show that underspecification does not mainly make agents fail; it makes them guess. 55.8-67.8% of runs violate at least one boundary. Target underspecification sharply degrades action quality, while blast-radius cues barely reduce action propensity. These findings show that completion-centric evaluation can overstate safe autonomy and motivate mitigations at the model, harness, and system layer.

AI.tldr: UnderSpecBench is a benchmark evaluating how LLM coding agents behave under underspecified DevOps instructions. Across 2,208 prompt variants, 55.8–67.8% of agent runs violated action boundaries, with target ambiguity being the primary driver of unsafe behavior rather than task failure.
AI.motivation: Existing coding agent benchmarks emphasize task completion but neglect safety under underspecification. Agents deployed on production infrastructure can cause severe damage from wrong actions, yet it is unknown how they behave when instructions lack clarity on intent, target, or blast radius.
AI.method: The authors constructed UnderSpecBench with 69 task families across four DevOps capability domains and nine operational control surfaces, grounded in real incidents, CVEs, and tool behaviors. Each task preserves the same environment and ground-truth safe action while varying instructions along three axes: intent clarity, target certainty, and blast radius, yielding 2,208 prompts. Evaluation uses deterministic, side-effect-based oracles to classify outcomes as Safe Success, Wrong Target, OverScope, or non-action (clarification, refusal, deferment). Five agent × model configurations were tested: OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex.
AI.result: Underspecification does not primarily cause agents to fail but to guess. 55.8–67.8% of runs violated at least one action boundary. Target underspecification sharply degraded action quality, while blast-radius cues barely reduced action propensity. Completion-centric evaluation was shown to overstate safe autonomy.
AI.conclusion: Completion-centric evaluation inflates perceived safe autonomy in coding agents. Mitigations are needed at the model, harness, and system layers to prevent boundary-violating actions under underspecification.

title: Geometric Signatures of Reasoning: A Spectral Perspective on Task Hardness
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex problems by generating intermediate reasoning steps. While much attention has been paid to the length and content of these reasoning chains, far less is known about their internal geometry. We study the \emph{geometry} of CoT trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer models, formalizing each reasoning chain as a discrete curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and characterizing it through spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. We introduce the effective dimension $d_ρ$ as a measure of trajectory complexity and show theoretically that trajectories with flatter eigenvalue spectra correspond to harder tasks, as they explore more of the hidden dimensions. Lastly, we explore how kinematic features of the trajectory, mean position, positional dispersion, initial and current hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion, can be used to predict solution correctness before generation is complete, and may inform future early-stopping strategies. Experimentally, on mathematical reasoning problems from the MATH500 dataset, $d_ρ$ achieves $0.93$ AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems, while kinematic features potentially can predict correctness from only the first $20\%$ of generated tokens. These correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty, establishing that the shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory is a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the geometric properties of chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer LLMs. It introduces effective dimension as a measure of trajectory complexity, shows flatter eigenvalue spectra correlate with harder tasks, and demonstrates that kinematic features can predict solution correctness from only the first 20% of generated tokens, achieving 0.93 AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems on MATH500.
AI.motivation: While prior work has focused on the length and content of chain-of-thought reasoning chains, the internal geometric structure of these trajectories in hidden state space remains unexplored. Understanding this geometry could reveal principled signatures of task difficulty and solution quality, enabling early-stopping strategies and deeper insight into how LLMs navigate reasoning.
AI.method: The authors formalize each CoT reasoning chain as a discrete curve in ℝᵈ and characterize it using three categories of geometric functionals: (1) spectral — effective dimension d_ρ derived from the eigenvalue spectrum of the trajectory's covariance matrix, (2) positional — mean position and positional dispersion of hidden states, and (3) kinematic — mean velocity, mean speed, speed dispersion, plus initial and current hidden states. They provide theoretical analysis linking flatter eigenvalue spectra (higher d_ρ) to harder tasks and experimentally evaluate on MATH500 mathematical reasoning problems.
AI.result: Effective dimension d_ρ achieves 0.93 AUC in discriminating easy from hard problems on MATH500. Kinematic features can predict solution correctness using only the first 20% of generated tokens. These correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty, demonstrating that trajectory shape is a robust indicator of both task hardness and solution quality.
AI.conclusion: The geometry of internal CoT trajectories provides a principled, content-agnostic window into task difficulty and solution correctness. Spectral complexity (effective dimension) reliably separates easy from hard tasks, while early-trajectory kinematic features enable correctness prediction well before generation completes, holding promise for early-stopping mechanisms in LLM inference.

title: TUDUM: A Turkish-Thinking Reasoning Pipeline for Qwen3.5-27B
summary: This paper presents TUDUM (Türkçe Düşünen Üretken Model), a project pipeline for adapting a Qwen-family 27B thinking model toward Turkish reasoning. The central problem is not only to answer Turkish prompts in Turkish, but to make the explicit reasoning trace itself Turkish. A thinking model may translate a Turkish prompt into an English-centered internal or visible scratchpad, solve the problem mostly in English, and only localize the final answer. TUDUM instead treats the generated <think>...</think> block as a trainable behavior. The pipeline starts from the project base checkpoint unsloth/Qwen3.5-27B, applies supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on 15,991 Turkish reasoning examples using LoRA adapters, and then applies GRPO-family reinforcement learning on a proxy-filtered Turkish mathematics environment. The results are mixed. SFT made the model shorter and more consistently Turkish in its reasoning behavior, with large reductions in average response length and thinking exhaustion, but reduced benchmark accuracy. RL recovered some mathematical performance, especially AIME24 at the best early checkpoint, yet did not uniformly improve all benchmarks and did not exceed the base model on the reported Macro-6 average. The contribution is therefore best framed as a technically honest Turkish-thinking reasoning pipeline and evaluation, not as a claim of state-of-the-art Turkish reasoning. The released step-50 model is publicly available.

AI.tldr: TUDUM adapts a Qwen-27B thinking model to produce reasoning traces directly in Turkish via SFT and GRPO-based RL, achieving consistent Turkish-language reasoning but with mixed benchmark results compared to the base model.
AI.motivation: Existing multilingual thinking models tend to internally translate non-English prompts into English, reason in English within the think block, and only localize the final answer. The goal is to make the explicit `<think>` reasoning trace itself natively Turkish, which requires treating the reasoning block as a trainable behavior rather than merely localizing output.
AI.method: A pipeline starting from `unsloth/Qwen3.5-27B`: (1) supervised fine-tuning on 15,991 Turkish reasoning examples using LoRA adapters to instill Turkish-language reasoning in the `<think>` block; (2) GRPO-family reinforcement learning on a proxy-filtered Turkish mathematics environment to recover and enhance mathematical reasoning performance post-SFT.
AI.result: SFT successfully shortened response length, reduced thinking exhaustion, and made reasoning consistently Turkish, but decreased benchmark accuracy. RL partially recovered mathematical performance (notably AIME24 at the best early checkpoint) but did not uniformly improve all benchmarks and failed to surpass the base model on the Macro-6 average.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is a technically honest Turkish-thinking reasoning pipeline and evaluation, publicly releasing the step-50 model, without claiming state-of-the-art Turkish reasoning.

title: DRL-CLBA: A Clean Label Backdoor Attack for Speech Classification via DDPG Reinforcement Learning
summary: Deep learning models for speech classification are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where malicious triggers cause misclassification at inference time. While sample-specific attacks can bypass many defenses, they often rely on poisoned label attack, making them detectable via manual data defense. In this paper, we propose DRL-CLBA, a novel clean label backdoor attack for speech classification that leverages Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) reinforcement learning. We also utilize deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers into source audio, creating feature-space anchors. The proposed reinforcement learning framework effectively optimizes target samples toward trigger-bearing anchor points in the model's deep latent space, enabling label-migration-free poisoning of target samples. Experimental results across three datasets and four different DNNs demonstrate that DRL-CLBA achieves a high attack success rate, effectively bypassing some backdoor defenses. The attack demonstrates strong resistance against fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature defenses, exposing critical vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems.

AI.tldr: A clean-label backdoor attack using DDPG reinforcement learning and audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers into speech, achieving high attack success while evading multiple defenses.
AI.motivation: Existing sample-specific backdoor attacks rely on poisoned labels, making them detectable by manual inspection. A clean-label attack—where poisoned samples retain correct labels—is needed to subvert both automated and human defenses in speech classification systems.
AI.method: DRL-CLBA uses Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) to optimize target samples toward trigger-bearing anchor points in the model's latent space. Deep audio steganography embeds sample-specific triggers into source audio, creating feature-space anchors. During inference, trigger-bearing inputs are pulled toward poisoned anchor representations, inducing misclassification without label tampering.
AI.result: Evaluated across three datasets and four DNN architectures, DRL-CLBA achieves high attack success rates and demonstrates strong resistance to fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature defenses.
AI.conclusion: Clean-label backdoor attacks via reinforcement learning and steganography pose a serious threat to speech classification systems, exposing critical vulnerabilities that existing defenses fail to adequately address.

title: Guiding Human Validation of LLM-Generated Code via Verifiable Literate Programming
summary:
Vibe coding democratizes software development by allowing users to generate code via natural-language (NL) interaction with large language models (LLMs). However, the code is reliable only when it faithfully implements the user's intent, which is difficult and labor-intensive for users to validate. Existing validation methods either rely on LLM-assisted automated testing, which suffers from prompt ambiguity and model fallibility, or involve users only in partial software artifacts such as prompts and test cases, which may overlook corner cases and program details. Motivated by a bug study of LLM-generated code, we find that detailed human feedback is essential, as failures often stem from underspecified requirements or subtle semantic deviations.
  This paper presents verifiable literate programming (VLP), a human-in-the-loop framework designed to make the review/validation process of LLM-generated code accessible to users at all programming levels. At its core, VLP proposes unambiguous NL-based documentation as a readable intermediate layer between prompts and code. The documentation demonstrates concrete program semantics and enables users to provide feedback on potential intent-code mismatches. It supports human-involved, end-to-end repair and validation via three techniques: (i) an NL-style literate language with unambiguous syntax and mostly deterministic code-to-documentation translation, (ii) LLM-based fine-grained mismatch detection that uses trace links between prompts and documentation to focus users' review effort on suspicious documentation lines, and (iii) a verification module that leverages user-validated documentation to derive API-usage checks and formal properties, which are then verified against the generated code using model checking. Our evaluation shows that VLP improves code pass@1 from 28.7%-73.2% to 65.4%-93.5% with reasonable user effort.

AI.tldr: Vibe coding lets users generate code via natural language, but verifying that the code matches user intent is hard. This paper proposes Verifiable Literate Programming (VLP), a human-in-the-loop framework that uses unambiguous NL documentation as an intermediate layer between prompts and code, enabling users to review suspicious parts, provide feedback, and formally verify intent-code alignment, improving pass@1 from 28.7–73.2% to 65.4–93.5%.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated code from natural-language prompts often contains subtle semantic deviations and underspecified requirements that are difficult for users to detect. Existing validation methods (LLM-assisted testing or partial user involvement) suffer from prompt ambiguity, model fallibility, and missed corner cases. A bug study reveals that detailed human feedback is essential because failures frequently arise from intent-code mismatches that only humans can identify.
AI.method: VLP introduces three core techniques: (1) a literate NL-style language with unambiguous syntax and mostly deterministic code-to-documentation translation, producing readable documentation that captures concrete program semantics; (2) LLM-based fine-grained mismatch detection using trace links between prompts and documentation to spotlight suspicious lines for user review; and (3) a verification module that derives API-usage checks and formal properties from user-validated documentation and verifies them against the generated code via model checking, enabling end-to-end human-involved repair and validation.
AI.result: VLP improves code pass@1 from a baseline of 28.7%–73.2% to 65.4%–93.5% with reasonable user effort, demonstrating significant gains in code reliability across the evaluated scenarios.
AI.conclusion: VLP demonstrates that a human-in-the-loop approach centered on unambiguous NL documentation can effectively bridge the gap between user intent and LLM-generated code, making validation accessible to users at all programming levels while substantially improving code correctness.

title: BOUNDARY_SYNC: Measuring Communication-Induced Representational Coupling in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as communicating agents, does inter-agent communication cause outputs to converge? We introduce BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol measuring representational coupling via the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline), where CAF < 1 indicates homogenization and CAF > 1 indicates diversification. In controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls), we measure coupling in text and image communication. Key findings: (1) text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803 [0.740, 0.873], d=1.30, p<0.001), confirmed by no-communication ablation and prompt-perturbation controls; (2) image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834 [0.811, 0.858]), with comparable proportional effect; (3) group size moderates coupling direction -- K=5 produces homogenization while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (point estimates 1.14 and 1.06, CI pending), suggesting a directional shift toward diversification; (4) cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034-0.803), with DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts; (5) coupling is stateless -- driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence. These results establish LLM agent coupling as real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with direct implications for multi-agent system design.

AI.tldr: LLM agents communicating with each other exhibit measurable representational coupling: text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF < 1), group size moderates the effect (smaller groups diversify), coupling is stateless and prompt-driven rather than cumulative, and cross-model results vary widely.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed as communicating agents in multi-agent systems, it is critical to understand whether inter-agent communication drives their outputs to converge (homogenization) or diverge (diversification), and what factors govern this coupling.
AI.method: The authors introduce BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol that measures representational coupling using the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline), where JSD is Jensen-Shannon Divergence. CAF < 1 indicates homogenization, CAF > 1 indicates diversification. Controlled experiments use GPT-4o (N=30, ~9,900 API calls) across text and image communication modalities, with no-communication ablations, prompt-perturbation controls, group-size manipulation (K=3 vs K=5), cross-model replication, and analyses of statefulness vs. prompt-driven effects.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Text communication produces significant homogenization (CAF=0.803, d=1.30, p<0.001). (2) Image communication also homogenizes (CAF=0.834). (3) Group size moderates coupling direction—K=5 homogenizes while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (point estimates 1.14, 1.06), suggesting diversification. (4) Cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034–0.803), with DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts. (5) Coupling is stateless, driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating; continuous consensus produces monotonic convergence.
AI.conclusion: LLM agent coupling is real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level. These findings have direct implications for multi-agent system design, particularly regarding group size, modality choice, and model selection to either promote or mitigate representational convergence.

title: AIriskEval-edu: New Dataset for Risk Assessment in AI-mediated K-12 Educational Explanations
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the IEEE International Carnahan Conference on Security Technology (ICCST 2026), October 14, 2026
summary: This work introduces AIriskEval-edu-db2, a new dataset designed to train and evaluate auditors based on LLMs for an explainable pedagogical risk assessment in instructional content for grades K-12. The dataset comprises 1,639 explanations from 170 curated ScienceQA questions, covering science, language arts, and social sciences. For each question, the dataset includes an explanation written by a human teacher alongside 11 explanations generated by LLM-simulated teacher profiles associated with distinct pedagogical risks. We propose a comprehensive risk rubric aligned with established educational standards that covers five complementary dimensions: factual precision, depth and completeness, focus and relevance, student-level appropriateness, and ideological bias. A key contribution is the addition of 785 explanations with structured explainability annotations, including risk localization and risk description. The annotations are produced through a semi-automatic process with expert teacher validation. Finally, we present validation experiments comparing state-of-the-art proprietary models with a lightweight local Llama 3.1 8B model in both the pedagogical risk detection and the explainability assessment. These experiments evaluate whether supervised fine-tuning on AIriskEval-edu-db2 enables a locally deployable model to approach or outperform stronger frontier models while preserving privacy in educational auditing and assessment tasks.

AI.tldr: AIriskEval-edu-db2 is a dataset of 1,639 explanations (from 170 ScienceQA questions) for training LLM-based auditors to perform explainable pedagogical risk assessment in K-12 instructional content, covering five risk dimensions and featuring 785 explanations with structured explainability annotations validated by expert teachers.
AI.motivation: The need for LLM-based auditing tools that can detect pedagogical risks in K-12 instructional content in a privacy-preserving, explainable manner, enabling locally deployable models to match or exceed proprietary frontier models.
AI.method: Construction of a dataset with 1,639 explanations (human-written + 11 LLM-simulated teacher profiles with distinct risks) across 170 ScienceQA questions. A five-dimension risk rubric is proposed (factual precision, depth/completeness, focus/relevance, student-level appropriateness, ideological bias). 785 explanations receive structured explainability annotations (risk localization + description) via semi-automatic process with expert teacher validation. Validation experiments compare proprietary models against a fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B on both risk detection and explainability tasks.
AI.result: Validation experiments demonstrate that supervised fine-tuning on the dataset enables a lightweight local Llama 3.1 8B model to approach or outperform stronger proprietary frontier models on pedagogical risk detection and explainability assessment tasks.
AI.conclusion: AIriskEval-edu-db2 provides a valuable resource for developing privacy-preserving, locally deployable LLM-based auditors capable of explainable pedagogical risk assessment in K-12 education, with the fine-tuned small model showing competitive performance against larger proprietary alternatives.

title: Reformalization of the Jordan Curve Theorem
summary: We present a case study in reformalization, a variant of autoformalization in which the input proof is not natural language but a formal development in a different proof assistant. Concretely, we report three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. We analyse the results and identify pipeline design choices that matter for practical reformalization tasks.

AI.tldr: A case study on reformalization—translating formal proofs between proof assistants—applied to the Jordan Curve Theorem across three pairs: Mizar→Lean, HOL Light→Lean, and HOL Light→Agda, analyzing pipeline design choices.
AI.motivation: Formal proof libraries are fragmented across different proof assistants, creating duplication of effort. Reformalization offers a way to reuse existing formal developments by automatically translating them between systems, but the practical design choices for such pipelines are underexplored.
AI.method: The authors perform three concrete reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem bridging different proof assistants (Mizar, HOL Light, Lean, Agda). They analyze the resulting translations and identify key pipeline design decisions that affect the feasibility and quality of reformalization.
AI.result: The paper reports on the outcomes of three cross-system translations and distills practical insights about pipeline design choices that significantly impact reformalization success.
AI.conclusion: Reformalization is a viable strategy for proof reuse across assistants, but careful attention must be paid to pipeline architecture choices to achieve practical results.

title: Developers' Experience with Generative AI Beyond Productivity Assessment -- Insights from an Empirical Mixed-Methods Field Study
summary: With the growing adoption of AI-powered coding assistants, organizations and developers are increasingly seeking to optimize their interaction with these tools. Prior research has largely focused on output quality and productivity gains, with limited attention paid to developers' well-being and interaction experiences. This paper presents a developer-centered empirical mixed-methods study to investigate how professional developers engage with Generative AI (GenAI) in their natural work environment. Controlled data collection sessions are combined with natural work periods. Results show that developers are generally satisfied with GenAI, particularly for monotonous, repetitive, and structured tasks, and report perceived efficiency and productivity gains. Copilot interaction type preferences differ by task type and complexity: While both in-code suggestions and chat-based prompting independently improve task efficiency and reduce perceived workload, combining these interaction types within a single task diminishes benefits. We propose a rule-of-thumb for selecting an interaction type based on task characteristics. During development-heavy tasks, results indicate that perceived cognitive load arises from AI interaction, while perceived productivity depends on AI output quality. Participation in this study positively influenced developers' awareness and intentional use of GenAI tools. These findings demonstrate the value of real-world, mixed-methods study designs to understand GenAI tools and developers' experiences with them.

AI.tldr: A mixed-methods study of professional developers using GenAI coding assistants in natural work settings reveals that while both in-code suggestions and chat-based prompting independently improve efficiency and reduce workload, combining them in a single task diminishes benefits. Task characteristics should guide interaction type selection, and cognitive load stems from AI interaction itself while productivity depends on output quality.
AI.motivation: Prior research on AI-powered coding assistants has focused narrowly on output quality and productivity gains, neglecting developers' well-being and interaction experiences. This study addresses the gap by centering on how professional developers actually experience GenAI tools in their natural work environment.
AI.method: A developer-centered empirical mixed-methods study combining controlled data collection sessions with natural work periods, involving professional developers using GenAI tools (specifically GitHub Copilot) in their authentic work contexts.
AI.result: Developers are generally satisfied with GenAI, especially for monotonous, repetitive, and structured tasks. In-code suggestions and chat-based prompting independently improve efficiency and reduce perceived workload, but combining both in the same task diminishes these benefits. Perceived cognitive load arises from AI interaction itself, while perceived productivity depends on AI output quality. Study participation increased developers' awareness and intentional use of GenAI tools.
AI.conclusion: A rule-of-thumb for selecting interaction type based on task characteristics is proposed. Real-world, mixed-methods study designs are valuable for understanding GenAI tools and developer experiences. Interaction modality should be chosen deliberately rather than combined indiscriminately to maximize benefits.

title: SINA: A Fully Automated Circuit Schematic Image to Netlist Generator Using Artificial Intelligence
summary: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have revolutionized Electronic Design Automation (EDA), particularly through Large Language Models (LLMs) for circuit design tasks. However, their application to analog and mixed-signal domains remains limited by the lack of machine-readable representations of existing circuit design knowledge. Circuit schematic images found in research manuscripts, textbooks, and websites constitute a vast repository of validated designs; however, these visual representations cannot be directly processed by EDA tools. Converting them into machine-readable netlists is essential for enabling simulation, verification, and building comprehensive databases for AI-based models. Current conversion methods lack generalization across both Integrated Circuit (IC) and Printed Circuit Board (PCB) level schematics. Moreover, they struggle with component recognition and connectivity inference, and fail to distinguish between connected junctions and crossing wires. In this paper, we propose SINA, an open-source circuit schematic image-to-netlist generator. SINA is a fully automated pipeline that integrates deep learning for robust component detection, connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for component reference designator extraction, and a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment. SINA handles both IC- and PCB-level schematics and incorporates dedicated crossing-wires detection to differentiate wire intersections from connections. We validate the correctness of the generated netlists using graph isomorphism techniques. Our experiments demonstrate an overall netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, which is 2.72x higher compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: SINA is an open-source, fully automated pipeline that converts circuit schematic images (both IC and PCB level) into machine-readable netlists using deep learning for component detection, connected-component labeling for connectivity inference, OCR for designator extraction, and a VLM for designator assignment, achieving 96.67% netlist generation accuracy — 2.72× higher than prior state-of-the-art.
AI.motivation: LLMs have advanced digital EDA, but analog/mixed-signal domains lack machine-readable circuit design knowledge. Vast repositories of schematic images exist in papers, textbooks, and websites, yet they cannot be directly processed by EDA tools. Existing conversion methods fail to generalize across IC and PCB schematics, struggle with component recognition and connectivity inference, and cannot reliably distinguish connected junctions from crossing wires.
AI.method: SINA is a fully automated pipeline comprising: (1) deep learning-based component detection, (2) connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, (3) Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for extracting component reference designators, (4) a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment to detected components, and (5) a dedicated crossing-wires detection module to disambiguate wire intersections from electrical connections. Netlist correctness is validated via graph isomorphism techniques.
AI.result: SINA achieves 96.67% overall netlist generation accuracy, representing a 2.72× improvement over state-of-the-art approaches. It successfully handles both IC-level and PCB-level schematics.
AI.conclusion: SINA provides a robust, generalizable, and open-source solution for converting schematic images to netlists, bridging a critical gap in analog/mixed-signal EDA and enabling the construction of machine-readable design databases for AI-driven circuit design tools.

title: NAVER LABS Europe Submission to the Instruction-following 2026 Short Track
summary: In this paper, we describe NAVER LABS Europe's submission to the instruction-following speech processing short track at IWSLT 2026. We participate again in the constrained setting, developing systems capable of jointly performing ASR, ST, and SQA from English speech into Chinese, Italian, and German. Building on our previous submission, ranked first in last year's short track, we update our multi-stage training pipeline by replacing the speech projector with SpeechMapper, a method for learning a speech-to-LLM embedding projector using only ASR data. In addition, we introduce a synthetic SQA dataset, fakACL, composed of artificially generated scientific presentations. This dataset is built by prompting the LLM backbone, segmenting the generated talks, and synthesizing speech with SeamlessM4T-large-v2. The combination of an improved speech projection mechanism and domain-specific synthetic data allows our model to outperform last year's best short-track system, while being considerably more compact and relying on a weaker LLM backbone. This year's results place our system tied for first place in the overall short track ranking.

AI.tldr: NAVER LABS Europe presents an improved multi-stage training pipeline for joint ASR, ST, and SQA, featuring SpeechMapper for speech-to-LLM projection and a synthetic SQA dataset (fakACL). The system ties for first place in the IWSLT 2026 short track while being more compact and using a weaker LLM backbone than the prior year's winning entry.
AI.motivation: Improving upon their first-place submission from the previous year's IWSLT short track, the authors aim to build a more compact yet higher-performing system for joint automatic speech recognition (ASR), speech translation (ST), and speech question answering (SQA) under constrained settings, without relying on a powerful LLM backbone.
AI.method: The system employs a multi-stage training pipeline with two key innovations: (1) SpeechMapper — a speech-to-LLM embedding projector trained using only ASR data, replacing the previous speech projector; (2) fakACL — a synthetic SQA dataset of artificially generated scientific presentations, created by prompting the LLM backbone to generate talks, segmenting them, and synthesizing speech via SeamlessM4T-large-v2.
AI.result: The combination of SpeechMapper and the fakACL synthetic dataset yields a system that outperforms the previous year's best short-track system, despite being considerably more compact and using a weaker LLM backbone. The system ties for first place in the overall IWSLT 2026 short track ranking.
AI.conclusion: Improved speech projection (SpeechMapper) and domain-specific synthetic data (fakACL) are effective strategies for advancing instruction-following speech processing, enabling state-of-the-art joint ASR/ST/SQA performance with a smaller, more efficient architecture.

title: Meta-Benchmarks for Financial-Services LLM Evaluation
summary: Public LLM leaderboards optimise for global average performance and do not capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work: a model that leads on MMLU-Pro may underperform on document-grounded compliance reasoning, and a coding leader may handle multi-turn customer interactions poorly. We present a meta-benchmarking framework that organises 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregates those into 38 BIAN banking business domains spanning sales, operations, risk, and support work. A multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination x coverage x recency), computed over a rolling model window, rewards benchmarks that still separate the best models, are widely reported, and remain in active use, suppressing saturated legacy tests automatically. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, producing cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalisation; business-domain scores are weighted averages of the constituent work-activity Elos. We demonstrate the framework on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organisations as of June 2026, and describe the methodology, full taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations with the aim of making the approach reproducible for institutions facing similar selection and governance challenges.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a meta-benchmarking framework that maps 452 public benchmarks to work activities and banking business domains, using a multiplicative weighting scheme and pairwise Elo tournament to produce cross-benchmark-comparable scores for financial-services model selection, demonstrated on 288 models from 25 organizations.
AI.motivation: Public LLM leaderboards prioritize global average performance and fail to capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work, such as document-grounded compliance reasoning or multi-turn customer interactions. Institutions lack systematic, domain-relevant methods for model selection and governance.
AI.method: A meta-benchmarking framework that: (1) maps 452 publicly reported benchmarks to 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities, then aggregates these into 38 BIAN banking business domains (sales, operations, risk, support); (2) applies a multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination × coverage × recency) over a rolling model window to suppress saturated legacy tests and reward benchmarks that still separate top models; (3) uses these weights to scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, yielding cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalization; (4) computes business-domain scores as weighted averages of constituent work-activity Elos.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organizations as of June 2026, producing work-activity and business-domain Elo scores that enable domain-relevant model comparison.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a reproducible, governance-oriented methodology for financial institutions to evaluate LLMs against domain-specific cognitive work demands, addressing limitations of generic leaderboards. The authors disclose the full taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations to facilitate adoption by institutions with similar selection challenges.

title: SkillFuzz: Fuzzing Skill Composition for Implicit Intents Discovery in Open Skill Marketplaces
summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents increasingly automate software engineering tasks through reusable skills, natural-language instruction documents that guide planning and execution. Open skill marketplaces enable users to assemble agents by co-activating community-contributed skills, but marketplace operators typically audit skills in isolation. As a result, individually benign skills may interact to redirect an agent toward unintended objectives, which we term implicit intents. Detecting such intents is challenging because the effect emerges only through skill composition, execution environments are often unavailable at admission time, and the space of possible co-activations grows exponentially with marketplace size. In this paper, we formulate implicit-intent discovery as a fuzzing problem over skill compositions, where skill compositions are the unit under test, planning artifacts expose agent intent before execution, and deviations from a skill-free baseline serve as a differential oracle. Based on this formulation, we propose skillfuzz, the first execution-free testing approach that extracts structured skill contracts and uses contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to prioritize potentially conflicting compositions. Across representative skill-marketplace workloads, skillfuzz discovers over 1,000 distinct implicit intents under a fixed query budget, confirms more than 80% of the highest-risk flagged compositions during execution-time validation, and identifies substantially more high-severity implicit intents than alternative search strategies while exploring only a fraction of the pairwise interaction space they require.

AI.tldr: SkillFuzz is an execution-free fuzzing approach that discovers implicit intents in LLM agent skill marketplaces by using contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to find skill compositions where individually benign skills combine to redirect agents toward unintended objectives.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents increasingly use reusable skills from open marketplaces, but operators audit skills in isolation. Individually benign skills can interact to produce "implicit intents" — emergent behaviors that redirect agents toward unintended objectives. Detecting these is hard because: (1) the harmful effect only emerges through composition, (2) execution environments are often unavailable at admission time, and (3) the composition space grows exponentially with marketplace size.
AI.method: SkillFuzz formulates implicit-intent discovery as a fuzzing problem over skill compositions. It extracts structured skill contracts from natural-language skill descriptions and uses contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to prioritize potentially conflicting compositions. It employs a differential oracle: deviations from a skill-free baseline in planning artifacts expose agent intent before execution, making the approach execution-free.
AI.result: On representative skill-marketplace workloads, SkillFuzz discovers over 1,000 distinct implicit intents under a fixed query budget, confirms >80% of the highest-risk flagged compositions during execution-time validation, and identifies substantially more high-severity implicit intents than alternative search strategies while exploring only a fraction of the pairwise interaction space those alternatives require.
AI.conclusion: Skill composition introduces a previously overlooked safety risk in LLM agent ecosystems. Contract-guided search with MCTS effectively discovers emergent harmful interactions without requiring execution, offering a scalable auditing mechanism for skill marketplace operators.

title: MKGR: Multimodal Knowledge-Graph Representation Learning for Cold-Start Protein-Protein Interaction Prediction
summary: Accurate protein-protein interaction (PPI) prediction is central to functional genomics, disease mechanism discovery, and drug development. A difficult setting arises when candidate interactions include proteins that have no observed PPI edges during training, where models relying on network topology alone often lose useful context. This paper presents \method, a multimodal representation framework for cold-start PPI prediction. \method\ combines region-aware protein sequence encoding with four protein-centered biomedical knowledge graphs, including protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, and protein-lncRNA associations. The sequence branch extracts contextual representations from structurally informed sequence regions, while graph attention encoders learn modality-specific protein embeddings from sparse biomedical associations. A bridge reconstruction objective regularizes graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations, and a pair-level gating module adaptively integrates sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair. Experiments on two benchmark datasets under novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings show that \method\ consistently outperforms competitive sequence, network, and knowledge-graph baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC.

AI.tldr: A multimodal framework for cold-start PPI prediction that combines region-aware protein sequence encoding with four biomedical knowledge graphs (protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, protein-lncRNA), using a bridge reconstruction objective and pair-level gating to adaptively integrate sequence and graph evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics.
AI.motivation: Cold-start PPI prediction — where candidate proteins lack observed interaction edges during training — is challenging because topology-based models lose useful context. Existing methods fail to adequately leverage multimodal biomedical knowledge to compensate for absent network information.
AI.method: The proposed framework has three main components: (1) a region-aware protein sequence encoder that extracts contextual representations from structurally informed sequence regions; (2) four protein-centered biomedical knowledge graphs (protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, protein-lncRNA) processed via graph attention encoders to learn modality-specific embeddings; (3) a bridge reconstruction objective that regularizes graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations, plus a pair-level gating module that adaptively fuses sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair.
AI.result: The method consistently outperforms competitive sequence-based, network-based, and knowledge-graph baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC on two benchmark datasets under both novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings.
AI.conclusion: Integrating region-aware sequence features with diverse biomedical knowledge graphs via adaptive gating and bridge reconstruction offers a robust solution for cold-start PPI prediction, significantly outperforming unimodal and existing multimodal approaches.

title: Beyond Supervised Clarification: Input Rewriting with LLMs for Dialogue Discourse Parsing
summary: Rewriting inputs to improve frozen downstream models has become a common strategy in modern NLP pipelines. Prior work on incremental dialogue discourse parsing (DDP) shows that supervised clarification models can rewrite fragmentary or underspecified utterances, such as resolving ellipsis or references, to improve parsing accuracy. In this work, we revisit this idea under realistic deployment conditions, where no clarification supervision is available and the clarifier must rely on zero-shot prompting or feedback from a frozen parser. Across three Segmented Discourse Representation Theory (SDRT) datasets and multiple parsers, we find that last-utterance clarification is far less reliable than suggested by supervised settings. Parser-agnostic rewriting often introduces more regressions than repairs, as edits that enable fixes also disrupt discourse cues relied upon by the parser. A best-of-8 rewriting analysis further reveals a practical ceiling: a large fraction of errors are not repairable through input rewriting alone. A parser-aware clarifier trained with GRPO reduces regressions by up to 37% by learning conservative abstention, yet still fails to produce selectivity-aware clarifications that consistently improve parsing. Together, these findings recast clarification as a selective intervention problem. We identify rewritability prediction, deciding whether an utterance is repairable before intervention, as the key missing capability for input-side optimization of frozen discourse parsers, and a critical direction for improving agentic pipelines more broadly.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates utterance clarification for frozen discourse parsers under realistic zero-shot conditions. It finds that parser-agnostic rewriting often causes more regressions than improvements, that many errors are fundamentally unrepairable via input rewriting alone, and that even parser-aware clarifiers with GRPO training struggle to produce selective, beneficial edits. The authors reframe clarification as a selective intervention problem and identify rewritability prediction as the critical missing capability.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed supervised clarification models improve incremental dialogue discourse parsing (DDP) by rewriting fragmentary utterances. However, real-world deployment lacks clarification supervision, requiring zero-shot prompting or parser feedback. The paper aims to test whether input rewriting remains viable under these realistic constraints.
AI.method: The authors evaluate last-utterance clarification across three SDRT datasets and multiple parsers under zero-shot and parser-feedback conditions. They conduct a best-of-8 rewriting analysis to estimate the ceiling of repairability. They also train a parser-aware clarifier using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to reduce regressions via conservative abstention.
AI.result: Parser-agnostic rewriting introduces more regressions than repairs. A best-of-8 analysis reveals a large fraction of errors cannot be repaired through input rewriting. The GRPO-trained clarifier reduces regressions by up to 37% through learned abstention but still fails to produce selectivity-aware clarifications that consistently improve parsing.
AI.conclusion: Clarification should be recast as a selective intervention problem. The key missing capability is rewritability prediction — deciding whether an utterance is repairable before intervening. This is critical not only for frozen discourse parsers but for improving agentic pipelines more broadly.

title: Path-level Hindsight Instructions for Semantic Exploration in Vision-Language Navigation
summary: On-policy exploration is a crucial component for training robust Vision-Language Navigation agents, as it exposes the policy to a broader state distribution. However, such exploration inevitably leads to trajectories that deviate from expert demonstrations, resulting in a semantic mismatch between the executed visual stream and the original language instruction. In this work, we address this challenge by introducing Phi-Nav, a unified on-policy framework that leverages hindsight reasoning to align instructions with the agent's actual exploratory journey. Specifically, Phi-Nav operates through a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: 1) the agent performs oracle-guided on-policy exploration, sampling a trajectory while learning from expert action feedback, 2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level hindsight instruction grounded in the collected visual observations, and 3) the agent conducts a second imitation pass, treating the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration. Through this process, Phi-Nav bridges the critical semantic supervision gap inherent in on-policy methods, transforming semantically unlabeled movement into dense training signals. Evaluations on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks show that Phi-Nav yields competitive performance while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines. These results underscore the necessity of semantic exploration in VLN, positioning Phi-Nav as an effective solution for training embodied agents with limited data.

AI.tldr: Phi-Nav introduces a three-stage on-policy framework that uses hindsight reasoning to align language instructions with exploratory trajectories, bridging the semantic supervision gap in VLN and achieving competitive performance with far fewer expert demonstrations.
