AI.motivation: On-policy exploration in VLN exposes agents to broader state distributions but creates a semantic mismatch between the executed visual trajectory and the original language instruction, resulting in a supervision gap — exploratory paths lack corresponding expert-aligned instructions.
AI.method: Phi-Nav employs a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: (1) oracle-guided on-policy exploration where the agent samples trajectories with expert action feedback; (2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a new language instruction grounded in the actual collected visual observations; (3) the agent performs a second imitation pass using the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration.
AI.result: Phi-Nav achieves competitive performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines.
AI.conclusion: Semantic exploration is essential for VLN, and hindsight-based instruction alignment offers an effective strategy for training embodied agents under limited data regimes.

title: Understanding Agent-Based Patching of Compiler Missed Optimizations
summary: Compiler missed optimizations refer to cases in which compilers failed to optimize certain code. It takes many compiler developers' efforts to implement or patch such missed optimizations. In this paper, we present a systematic study of how well agents patch compiler missed optimizations. We identify a significant challenge that patching a missed optimization requires more than just fixing the reported case, and instead requires generalizing to similar cases. We construct a benchmark of real-world LLVM missed optimization issues and compare agent-generated patches with patches from developers in terms of optimization scope. Our results show that coding agents often optimize the given examples, but many generated patches either cover only part of the developer-intended scope or partially overlap with it; in some cases, they further generalize beyond the reference patch. We further introduce historical-knowledge augmentation techniques that leverage prior LLVM optimization pull requests through retrieval and distillation, showing that they improve developer-aligned generalization and yield practical benefits when applied to real-world IR.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates how well coding agents (e.g., LLM-based systems) can automatically patch compiler missed optimizations in LLVM. The key finding is that while agents can fix reported cases, they struggle to generalize correctly to similar cases—often producing patches with narrower, overlapping, or overly broad scope compared to human developer patches. The authors introduce historical-knowledge augmentation via retrieval and distillation of prior LLVM optimization PRs, which improves developer-aligned generalization.
AI.motivation: Implementing patches for compiler missed optimizations is labor-intensive for compiler developers. Automating this with AI agents could reduce effort, but the core challenge is that a patch must not merely fix the specific reported case—it must generalize appropriately to similar code patterns. Prior work has not systematically studied whether agents can achieve this generalization.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark from real-world LLVM missed optimization issues. They compare agent-generated patches against developer-written reference patches, evaluating them along the dimension of optimization scope (narrower, matching, overlapping, or broader than the reference). They also propose historical-knowledge augmentation: retrieving and distilling information from prior LLVM optimization pull requests to guide agents toward developer-aligned generalization.
AI.result: Coding agents frequently optimize the given test cases but produce patches whose scope only partially matches developer intent—covering only a subset, overlapping partially, or sometimes over-generalizing beyond the reference patch. Historical-knowledge augmentation improves alignment with developer patches and yields practical benefits on real-world LLVM IR.
AI.conclusion: Automated patching of compiler missed optimizations requires generalization beyond the reported case, which remains a significant challenge for current coding agents. Leveraging historical LLVM optimization data through retrieval and distillation is a promising direction to improve patch quality and scope alignment with developer intentions.

title: DeadPool: Resilient LLM Training with Hot-Swapping via Zero-Overhead Checkpoint
summary: State-of-the-art large language model (LLM) training takes tens of thousands of graphics processing units (GPUs) for months and encounters failures across the software and hardware stack. Existing fault-tolerance mechanisms either impose non-trivial overhead during failure-free execution or suffer from prolonged recovery latency, particularly under scenarios where a small subset of compute nodes experience permanent failures. %The tradeoff between failure-free overhead and recovery latency forms a space forms a Pareto frontier We present DeadPool to simultaneously address both optimization objectives. DeadPool incorporates a fault-tolerance mechanism that restores LLM training via hot-swapping, namely by replacing failed nodes with spare nodes without terminating the complete job. The hot-swapping of DeadPool is enabled by two ideas: First, it exploits an off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing mechanism for spatial redundancy. Second, it introduces a communicator reconstruction protocol that replaces failed nodes with spare nodes at runtime. DeadPool efficiently overlaps the in-memory checkpointing with computation, thus introducing zero overhead during error-free execution. Upon permanent node failures, DeadPool can rebuild memory states with minimal recomputation by leveraging in-memory checkpoints. We evaluate DeadPool across scales (up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs) and LLMs (up to 65B parameters), and observe zero checkpoint overhead with hot-swapping recovery completing in under 40 seconds. These results show that DeadPool simultaneously achieves both zero-overhead error-free execution and extremely low recovery cost.

AI.tldr: DeadPool introduces a zero-overhead fault-tolerance mechanism for LLM training that uses hot-swapping of failed nodes with spare nodes, leveraging off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing and runtime communicator reconstruction to achieve recovery in under 40 seconds without impacting error-free execution.
AI.motivation: LLM training spans tens of thousands of GPUs over months and inevitably encounters hardware/software failures. Existing fault-tolerance mechanisms force a tradeoff between non-trivial overhead during normal execution and prolonged recovery latency, especially when a small subset of nodes suffer permanent failures. DeadPool aims to simultaneously optimize both objectives — eliminating failure-free overhead while minimizing recovery time.
AI.method: DeadPool employs two core techniques: (1) off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing that exploits spatial redundancy by overlapping checkpoint writes with computation, yielding zero overhead during error-free execution; and (2) a communicator reconstruction protocol that dynamically replaces failed nodes with spare nodes at runtime without terminating the entire job. Upon permanent node failures, memory states are rebuilt with minimal recomputation using the in-memory checkpoints.
AI.result: Evaluated at scales up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs and LLMs up to 65B parameters, DeadPool achieves zero checkpoint overhead during error-free execution and completes hot-swapping recovery in under 40 seconds.
AI.conclusion: DeadPool successfully achieves both zero-overhead error-free execution and extremely low recovery latency, breaking the traditional tradeoff between these two objectives in fault-tolerant LLM training.

title: Towards a Phonology-Informed Evaluation of Multilingual TTS
summary: Neural TTS systems can sound natural across languages, but naturalness does not guarantee the preservation of sound contrasts that distinguish words from their grammatical forms. Standard metrics like MOS do not test for this. We propose a classifier-based framework that audits TTS output against language-specific phonological patterns using human speech as a benchmark. Testing Assamese advanced tongue root (ATR) vowel harmony with Meta's MMS TTS, we show that a classifier trained on human speech transfers to synthesized speech with minimal loss. The faithfulness audit reveals that [+ATR] mid vowels are realized as [-ATR] in 1/3 tokens despite an underlying [+ATR] specification, a bias absent in human speech. At the word level, predicted ATR labels classify harmony more accurately than transcription labels, indicating a gap between intended and produced phonology. The framework offers task-specific diagnostics and generalizes to other phonological contrasts with measurable acoustic cues.

AI.tldr: A classifier-based audit framework reveals that Meta's MMS TTS fails to faithfully reproduce Assamese ATR vowel harmony, with ~33% of [+ATR] mid vowels incorrectly realized as [-ATR] despite correct underlying specification, exposing a gap between intended and produced phonology in neural TTS.
AI.motivation: Standard TTS evaluation metrics (e.g., MOS) assess naturalness but fail to verify whether systems preserve linguistically meaningful sound contrasts — specifically, phonological patterns like vowel harmony that distinguish words and grammatical forms. This motivates a diagnostic framework that audits phonological faithfulness.
AI.method: A classifier trained on human speech to detect Assamese advanced tongue root (ATR) vowel harmony is applied to synthesized speech from Meta's MMS TTS. The classifier's transfer performance (minimal loss) validates it as an audit tool. ATR predictions are compared at both the segment and word levels between human and TTS output, and predicted labels are contrasted with underlying transcription specifications.
AI.result: The classifier transfers to TTS output with minimal loss. The audit shows [+ATR] mid vowels surface as [-ATR] in ~1/3 of TTS tokens — a systematic bias absent in human speech. At the word level, ATR labels predicted by the classifier classify harmony more accurately than the intended transcription labels, revealing a mismatch between intended and actual phonological output.
AI.conclusion: The classifier-based faithfulness audit provides a task-specific, generalizable diagnostic for evaluating phonological contrast preservation in TTS. The framework can be extended to other phonological contrasts with measurable acoustic correlates, offering a principled complement to subjective naturalness ratings.

title: Mastermind: Strategy-grounded Learning for Repository-Scale Vulnerability Reproduction
summary: Repository-level vulnerability reproduction is a demanding software engineering (SE) task: an agent must inspect a codebase, infer the input grammar that reaches a vulnerable path, construct a proof-of-conceptv(PoC), and verify that the crash disappears on the patched build. Recent LLM agents can often execute these steps when the approach is correct, yet they still fail by choosing the wrong strategy. This paper argues that strategy, rather than the full action trajectory, is the right learning unit for such SE agents: it is compact enough to optimize, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough to store and reuse across attempts. We present Mastermind, a dual-loop framework that separates transferable strategy learning from task-specific experience. A trainable planner learns reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies through SFT and milestone-based GRPO, while an experience loop maintains task-local strategy records that guide subsequent attempts. The planner is trained independently of the executor, allowing strategy learning to improve multiple frozen executors without modifying their action-generation capability. We evaluate Mastermind on CyberGym using 260 training tasks and 200 held-out evaluation tasks. With GPT-5.5 as the frozen executor, Mastermind achieves an 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner also improves GPT-5.4 mini and GLM~5.1 from 45.0% and 58.5% to 60.0% and 71.0%. These results demonstrate that learning high-level strategies is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale SE agents.

AI.tldr: Repository-level vulnerability reproduction is challenging for LLM agents due to strategic errors rather than execution failures. Mastermind introduces a dual-loop framework that separates reusable strategy learning from task-specific experience, training a planner via SFT and milestone-based GRPO. The planner improves multiple frozen executors (GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4 mini, GLM 5.1), achieving 84.5% pass rate on CyberGym, demonstrating that high-level strategy learning is an effective, transferable mechanism.
AI.motivation: LLM agents fail at repository-level vulnerability reproduction not due to incorrect action execution but due to choosing the wrong strategy. Existing approaches conflate strategy with action trajectories, making learning inefficient. The authors argue that strategy is the optimal learning unit: compact enough to optimize, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough for reuse across attempts.
AI.method: Mastermind is a dual-loop framework. The strategy learning loop trains a planner via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and milestone-based Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to learn reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies. The experience loop maintains task-local strategy records to guide subsequent attempts. Critically, the planner is trained independently of the executor, enabling strategy improvements to benefit multiple frozen executors without modifying their action-generation capabilities.
AI.result: Evaluated on CyberGym with 260 training and 200 held-out test tasks: Mastermind with GPT-5.5 executor achieves 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner improves GPT-5.4 mini from 45.0% to 60.0% and GLM 5.1 from 58.5% to 71.0%, demonstrating cross-model transferability.
AI.conclusion: Learning high-level strategies rather than full action trajectories is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale SE agents. The decoupled planner-executor architecture allows strategy knowledge to generalize across different executor models without retraining them.

title: Reasoning effort, not tool access, buys first-try reliability in agentic code generation: an observational study
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Dataset and evaluation artifacts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21134406
summary: Agentic coding assistants are increasingly given extra capabilities, such as browser based testing tools and design oriented system prompts, on the assumption that more capability yields better software. This study tested that assumption directly. Ninety independent agent runs built the same application, a real time retrospective board, from one detailed specification, each scored on a fixed 14 criterion functional rubric (42 point maximum) and a visual quality review. The runs spanned several model generations, two agent harnesses, two reasoning effort levels, a testing tool, and two design oriented prompts. Capability tier dominated: frontier models clustered near the ceiling while a low cost local model fell to 24 to 37 points. A criterion level analysis revealed what run totals conceal. Container deployment was the dominant defect, failing first try in 44 percent of runs, with its failure rate shifting sharply across model generations while mean totals moved less than a point. The testing tool raised cost by 42 to 68 percent without improving functional score or reliability, even on interface visible criteria. Raising reasoning effort from High to xHigh lifted first try perfect runs from 28 percent to 89 percent and cut corrective prompts about five fold, for 9 to 29 percent more cost. A design oriented prompt raised visual quality, 4.5 versus 3.0 on a 5 point scale, without lifting function, and a one paragraph paraphrase of its directive reproduced the entire lift. The practical lesson is to match the fix to the failure: most first run failures came from weak reasoning, which a stronger model or more effort prevents, not from visible flaws a checking tool would catch.

AI.tldr: A study of 90 independent agentic coding runs building the same application found that frontier model capability dominates functional scores, container deployment is the dominant failure mode, testing tools increase cost without improving outcomes, higher reasoning effort dramatically improves first-try success, and a simple design-oriented prompt reliably boosts visual quality without affecting function.
AI.motivation: To empirically test the assumption that giving agentic coding assistants more capabilities (browser-based testing tools, design-oriented system prompts, higher reasoning effort) yields better software. Prior work lacked rigorous, controlled comparisons isolating these individual capability dimensions.
AI.method: Ninety independent agent runs built an identical real-time retrospective board application from a single detailed specification. Each run was scored on a fixed 14-criterion functional rubric (42-point maximum) and a visual quality review. The runs systematically varied: model generation, agent harness, reasoning effort level (High vs. xHigh), presence/absence of a testing tool, and presence/absence of design-oriented prompts. A criterion-level analysis decomposed aggregate scores to identify where failures actually occur.
AI.result: Frontier models clustered near the score ceiling while a low-cost local model scored 24-37 points. Container deployment was the dominant defect, failing first-try in 44% of runs, with failure rates shifting sharply across model generations even when mean totals moved less than a point. The testing tool raised cost 42-68% without improving functional scores or reliability. Raising reasoning from High to xHigh lifted first-try perfect runs from 28% to 89% and cut corrective prompts ~5×, at only 9-29% more cost. A design-oriented prompt raised visual quality from 3.0 to 4.5 (5-point scale) without affecting function; a one-paragraph paraphrase reproduced the entire lift.
AI.conclusion: More capability is not uniformly better. The practical lesson is to match the fix to the failure: most first-run failures stem from weak reasoning, which stronger models or higher reasoning effort prevent, not from visible flaws a checking tool would catch. Scaffolding should target the dominant failure modes — deployment failures and reasoning gaps — rather than adding cost-ineffective tools.

title: CALM: Interpretable Cross-Modal Alignment for Biomarker Discovery from Unpaired Data
summary: The interaction between brain structure and genetic influences is key to understanding neuropsychiatric disorders. However, most large-scale datasets are unimodal, providing either neuroimaging or genetics data. We propose CALM, a framework that learns interpretable associations between brain ROIs and genetic pathways from completely disjoint populations. CALM aligns the two modalities in a shared latent space via linear projections that simultaneously match the class-conditional latent distributions and ensure group separability. These projections provide interpretable pathway--ROI associations. When trained on unimodal imaging and genetics datasets, CALM generalizes to an unseen paired dataset, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines. We also demonstrate stability of the learned associations against a paired baseline. Our experiments on autism spectrum disorder reveal immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions and are consistent with established literature. Thus, CALM opens the door to leveraging large unimodal repositories for studying cross-modal interactions in brain disorders across disparate datasets.

AI.tldr: CALM aligns brain ROI and genetic pathway data from disjoint unimodal populations into a shared latent space using linear projections, enabling interpretable cross-modal associations. It outperforms baselines and recovers known autism-linked pathway–region relationships.
AI.motivation: Most large-scale datasets are unimodal (imaging-only or genetics-only), preventing direct study of brain–gene interactions. There is a need for methods that can discover interpretable associations between brain regions and genetic pathways without requiring paired multimodal data.
AI.method: CALM uses linear projections to embed brain ROI features and genetic pathway features into a shared latent space, jointly optimizing for (1) matching class-conditional distributions across modalities and (2) ensuring group separability. The linear projection weights directly yield interpretable pathway–ROI association scores. Training uses only unimodal datasets; evaluation includes generalization to held-out paired data.
AI.result: CALM generalizes to unseen paired datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines. Learned associations are stable against a paired baseline. On autism spectrum disorder data, it identifies immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions, consistent with prior literature.
AI.conclusion: CALM enables leveraging large unimodal repositories to study interpretable cross-modal brain–gene interactions, opening new avenues for understanding neuropsychiatric disorders without requiring costly paired multimodal data collection.

title: Object Aligner: A Configurable JSON Schema Similarity Score for Graphs, Applied to LLM Prompt Optimization
comment: 28 pages, This is a submitted version of a manuscript under review at IEEE Access; it has not been peer reviewed
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are often asked to produce JSON conforming to a fixed schema, powering information extraction, tool calling, agentic planning, and knowledge-graph construction. Measuring how closely an output matches a gold reference is essential yet surprisingly hard: exact match is brittle, text similarity ignores structure, and an LLM judge is expensive, opaque, and non-deterministic. We address this with Object Aligner (OA), an open-source Python library that scores two JSON objects deterministically by recursively aligning their trees (the Hungarian algorithm for unordered collections, sequence alignment for ordered ones) and awarding partial credit at the granularity the schema declares. The Object Aligner is configured entirely through a set of JSON Schema extensions, so adapting it to a new task involves annotating a schema rather than writing code. Complex structured data, however, are rarely flat trees: records may form graphs or hypergraphs keyed by arbitrary identifiers, breaking the assumptions of prior similarity metrics. Our central contribution, referential alignment, closes this gap by inferring a bijection between gold and candidate identifiers and scoring every reference through it, so the score is invariant to relabeling. Since recovering this bijection exactly is graph isomorphism, the Object Aligner approximates it with Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement. An order-sensitive sequence regime targets ranking and planning. Since the same alignment localizes every mismatch, the Object Aligner emits ranked repair suggestions at no extra cost. Used as a reward inside the GEPA prompt optimizer, Object Aligner helps or stays neutral across all datasets.

AI.tldr: Object Aligner (OA) is an open-source Python library that deterministically scores JSON objects against a gold reference by recursively aligning their trees using the Hungarian algorithm and sequence alignment. Its key innovation, referential alignment, handles graph-structured data by inferring a bijection between identifiers via Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement, making scores invariant to relabeling. The tool also emits ranked repair suggestions and can serve as a reward for prompt optimization.
AI.motivation: Evaluating how closely an LLM-generated JSON output matches a gold reference is difficult: exact match is too brittle, text similarity metrics ignore structural constraints, and LLM-based judges are expensive, opaque, and non-deterministic. Furthermore, complex structured data often forms graphs or hypergraphs keyed by arbitrary identifiers, which breaks existing tree-based similarity metrics.
AI.method: Object Aligner scores two JSON objects deterministically through recursive tree alignment: the Hungarian algorithm handles unordered collections, while sequence alignment handles ordered ones. Partial credit is awarded at the granularity declared by JSON Schema extensions, so adapting to new tasks requires only schema annotation, not code. The central contribution — referential alignment — infers a bijection between gold and candidate identifiers using Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement, approximating graph isomorphism and ensuring score invariance to relabeling. An order-sensitive sequence regime targets ranking and planning tasks. Mismatch localization enables OA to emit ranked repair suggestions at no extra cost.
AI.result: When used as a reward signal inside the GEPA prompt optimizer, Object Aligner either improves performance or remains neutral across all datasets tested.
AI.conclusion: Object Aligner provides a deterministic, schema-configurable, and structurally-aware alternative for scoring LLM-generated JSON, addressing both flat-tree and graph-structured data. Its referential alignment with Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement is the key contribution enabling robust handling of identifier-keyed records, and its utility extends to repair suggestion generation and prompt optimization.

title: SimWorlds: A Multi-Agent System for Dynamic 3D Scene Creation
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used to translate natural language into 3D scenes in a procedural way, but existing systems focus on static output. Dynamic 4D scenes from text alone, in which liquids flow, particles emit, rigid bodies cascade, and articulated mechanisms move, remain largely unexplored despite their value as editable content and as physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. Two challenges set the dynamic case apart from static text-to-scene work: an agent must jointly coordinate spatial layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting in a single coherent scene, and verifying motion correctness from rendered video is fundamentally harder than judging a single image. We present SimWorlds: a multi-agent framework that produces dynamic, editable 4D scenes from text, with Blender-specific procedural knowledge, a planner-coder-reviewer workflow driving a fixed ordered sequence of construction stages, a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier, and a runtime-state inspection tool suite that catches mechanism failures the rendered image cannot reveal. We also introduce 4DBuildBench, a benchmark for assessing both visual fidelity and physical consistency of the procedural dynamic 3D scenes generated from text prompts. Experiments show that SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines.

AI.tldr: SimWorlds is a multi-agent framework that generates dynamic, editable 4D scenes (3D + time) from text prompts using a planner-coder-reviewer workflow with deterministic verification and runtime-state inspection, outperforming prior baselines on a new benchmark called 4DBuildBench.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-3D scene systems focus on static output. Dynamic 4D scenes — involving liquids, particles, rigid body cascades, and articulated mechanisms — remain largely unexplored despite their value for editable content creation and as physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. Two key challenges differentiate the dynamic case: (1) agents must jointly coordinate spatial layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting in a coherent scene; (2) verifying motion correctness from rendered video is fundamentally harder than judging a single static image.
AI.method: SimWorlds employs a multi-agent framework with several core components: (a) Blender-specific procedural knowledge for scene construction; (b) a planner-coder-reviewer workflow that drives a fixed, ordered sequence of construction stages; (c) a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier to ensure structural correctness; and (d) a runtime-state inspection tool suite that detects mechanism failures invisible in rendered images. The authors also introduce 4DBuildBench, a benchmark for evaluating both visual fidelity and physical consistency of procedurally generated dynamic 3D scenes.
AI.result: SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines on the 4DBuildBench benchmark across metrics assessing both visual fidelity and physical consistency.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent approach with layered verification and runtime inspection effectively addresses the unique challenges of text-to-4D scene generation, enabling coherent, physically plausible dynamic scenes that prior static-focused systems cannot produce.

title: Message Passing Based Two-Timescale Bayesian Learning for Joint Channel and Memory Hardware Impairments Tracking
summary: Hardware impairments in massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) receivers introduce inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling, severely degrading channel estimation. This paper employs a residual recurrent gated unit (RGRU) to model the intra-slot memory of the hardware impairments and proposes a message-passing-based two-timescale Bayesian deep learning (MP-TTBDL) framework for joint channel and impairment tracking. Owing to small-scale fading, the wireless channel varies rapidly across slots, whereas hardware impairments drift slowly due to hardware aging and environmental variations. To capture these distinct physical timescales, a fastvarying Markov prior and a slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior are assigned to the sparse channel and the network parameters, respectively. Based on a multi-slot factor graph formulation, a message-passing algorithm is developed. Specifically, the inter-slot messages admit closed-form updates, while the intra-slot factor graph, due to its complex recurrent structure, is partitioned into a channel tracking module and an impairments calibration module. The channel tracking module performs sparse channel estimation via turbo orthogonal approximate message passing (Turbo-OAMP), and the impairments calibration module updates the impairment parameters via a specially designed deep approximate message passing (DAMP) procedure, with the two modules iteratively exchanging extrinsic information through expectation propagation (EP) until convergence. Simulation results show that the proposed framework robustly achieves lower channel estimation error than conventional compensators followed by channel estimation across different online impairment scenarios and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an MP-TTBDL framework using RGRU-based modeling and message-passing algorithms to jointly track fast-varying wireless channels and slow-drifting hardware impairments in massive MIMO receivers, achieving robust channel estimation via iterative exchange between Turbo-OAMP channel tracking and DAMP impairment calibration modules.
AI.motivation: Hardware impairments in massive MIMO receivers introduce inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling that severely degrade channel estimation. Existing approaches fail to adequately address the distinct physical timescales: wireless channels vary rapidly across slots due to small-scale fading, while hardware impairments drift slowly due to aging and environmental changes.
AI.method: The authors employ a Residual Recurrent Gated Unit (RGRU) to model intra-slot impairment memory. They propose a message-passing-based two-timescale Bayesian deep learning (MP-TTBDL) framework with a multi-slot factor graph. Fast-varying Markov priors are assigned to sparse channels, while slow-varying Gaussian Markov priors are assigned to network parameters. The intra-slot factor graph is partitioned into: (1) a channel tracking module using Turbo-OAMP for sparse channel estimation, and (2) an impairments calibration module using a specially designed DAMP procedure. Both modules iteratively exchange extrinsic information via Expectation Propagation (EP) until convergence.
AI.result: Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed MP-TTBDL framework robustly achieves lower channel estimation error compared to conventional compensators followed by channel estimation, across various online impairment scenarios and SNR conditions.
AI.conclusion: The MP-TTBDL framework effectively captures the two distinct physical timescales of channel variation and hardware impairment drift, enabling robust joint tracking and superior channel estimation performance in hardware-impaired massive MIMO systems.

title: Using embeddings to predict spoken word duration and pitch in Mandarin monosyllabic words
summary: Time-normalized f0 contours of Mandarin words in conversational speech have been shown to be predictable in part from their contextualized embeddings (CEs). The present study investigates whether CEs also predict spoken word duration for 7470 tokens of Mandarin monosyllabic CV words extracted from a Mandarin corpus of spontaneous speech. We show that CEs indeed are predictive for duration, above chance level, not only at the type level, but also at the level of individual tokens, as indicated by the results obtained with the type-wise and token-wise permutation baselines. We also show that the predicted durations are sufficiently precise to back-transform predicted f0 contours in [0,1] normalized time to contours on the ms time scale. The resulting predicted contours approximate empirical contours and also outperform a permutation baseline.

AI.tldr: Contextualized embeddings (CEs) from NLP models can predict not only Mandarin word f0 contours but also spoken word duration at both type and token levels, enabling accurate back-transformation of time-normalized f0 contours to absolute time scales.
AI.motivation: Prior work established that CEs partially predict time-normalized f0 contours of Mandarin words. However, to map these normalized contours onto absolute time (milliseconds), duration information is essential. This study investigates whether CEs also encode duration information for spontaneous Mandarin speech.
AI.method: The authors extracted 7,470 tokens of Mandarin monosyllabic CV words from a spontaneous speech corpus. They tested whether CEs predict spoken word duration using type-wise and token-wise permutation baselines to assess above-chance performance. Predicted durations were then used to back-transform normalized f0 contours from [0,1] time to millisecond-scale contours, comparing the results against empirical contours and a permutation baseline.
AI.result: CEs significantly predict word duration above chance at both the type level and the token level, as confirmed by permutation baselines. The predicted durations were sufficiently accurate to back-transform normalized f0 contours to absolute time, yielding contours that approximate empirical f0 contours and outperform a permutation baseline.
AI.conclusion: Contextualized embeddings encode not only prosodic contour shape (f0) but also temporal information (duration) for Mandarin words in spontaneous speech, enabling integrated prediction of both dimensions and faithful reconstruction of absolute-time prosodic contours.

title: Repair the Amplifier, Not the Symptom: Stable World-Model Correction for Agent Rollouts
summary: As agent planning moves from short tool chains toward persistent workflows with thousands or tens of thousands of steps, failures will occur inside large planning graphs rather than in isolated predictions. Replanning the entire graph after every mistake is neither computationally realistic nor desirable: full-graph replay consumes large context budgets, exposes the LLM to many irrelevant symptoms, and can degrade long-context retrieval. This paper studies the missing component in such systems: a world-model corrector that repairs the failed planning graph in place. We compare two families of correctors. The first is the common engineering approach: scan nodes and edges, choose a suspicious local region, and ask an LLM to repair it. We implement strong engineering LLM correctors and find that they can help, especially when given very large contexts. The second family is our approach, WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair): instead of scanning for visible symptoms, it works backward from subgraph amplification, identifies the nodes and edges that keep re-amplifying error, and sends only that causal subgraph to the LLM. Across graph simulations and LLM repair experiments, WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact region, and gives the LLM a cleaner repair target.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces WM-SAR, a world-model corrector that repairs failed planning graphs in place by identifying and sending only the causal error-amplifying subgraph to an LLM, outperforming conventional engineering correctors under realistic token budgets.
AI.motivation: As agent planning scales to persistent workflows with thousands of steps, failures occur within large planning graphs rather than in isolated predictions. Full-graph replanning is computationally prohibitive, consumes excessive context, and degrades long-context retrieval. A targeted repair mechanism is needed.
AI.method: The paper compares two corrector families: (1) engineering correctors that scan nodes/edges, select a suspicious local region, and ask an LLM to repair it; (2) WM-SAR, which works backward from subgraph amplification to identify nodes and edges that persistently re-amplify error, sending only that causal subgraph to the LLM for repair.
AI.result: WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization using only a compact region, and provides LLMs with a cleaner repair target.
AI.conclusion: Targeted causal-subgraph repair via WM-SAR is a more efficient and effective strategy than broad local-region scanning for correcting failures in large-scale agent planning graphs.

title: TestEvo-Bench: An Executable and Live Benchmark for Test and Code Co-Evolution
comment: TestEvo-Bench leaderboard and data explorer are hosted at https://www.testevo-bench.com
summary:
Software tests and code evolve together: a code change should be followed by new or updated tests that record the new software behavior. Yet existing test generation and update benchmarks often isolate the test from the code change, and rely on static metadata that does not verify whether a test is executable or semantically tied to the code change. This makes it difficult to evaluate whether a test automation agent understands how a code change should propagate into the test suite.
  We introduce TestEvo-Bench, a benchmark of test and code co-evolution tasks mined from software repositories, with two tracks: in test generation, the agent shall write new tests to capture the new software behavior; in test update, the agent shall adapt failing existing tests to the changed software behavior. Each task is anchored to a real commit history and packaged with environment configuration to support execution-grounded metrics such as pass rate, coverage, and mutation score. TestEvo-Bench is also a live benchmark: each task records the timestamp of the test and code changes, and new tasks are periodically mined by our automated pipeline, so evaluation can be restricted to tasks postdating a model's training cutoff to reduce data leakage risk. The current snapshot contains 746 test generation and 509 test update tasks, curated from 59,950 candidate co-evolution records across 152 open-source Java projects. We experiment with four state-of-the-art agents that combine strong harnesses (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and SWE-Agent) with strong foundation models (Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro). Results show that they achieve up to 77.5% success rate on test generation and 74.6% on test update. However, success rate is materially lower on the most recent benchmark tasks and drops significantly under limited per-task cost.

AI.tldr: TestEvo-Bench is a live, execution-grounded benchmark for test-code co-evolution with 746 generation and 509 update tasks mined from 152 Java projects. SOTA agents achieve up to 77.5% success on generation and 74.6% on update, but performance degrades on recent tasks and under cost constraints.
AI.motivation: Existing test generation/update benchmarks isolate tests from code changes and rely on static metadata, failing to verify executability or semantic relevance. This makes it hard to evaluate whether test automation agents truly understand how code changes should propagate to tests.
AI.method: TestEvo-Bench is constructed by mining real commit histories from 152 open-source Java projects (59,950 candidate co-evolution records), yielding two tracks: (1) test generation — writing new tests for new behavior, and (2) test update — adapting failing tests to changed behavior. Tasks are packaged with environment configs enabling execution-grounded metrics (pass rate, coverage, mutation score). The benchmark is live: timestamps are recorded and an automated pipeline periodically mines new tasks, allowing restriction to post-cutoff tasks to mitigate data leakage. Four SOTA agents (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, SWE-Agent paired with Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro) are evaluated.
AI.result: Agents achieve up to 77.5% success rate on test generation and 74.6% on test update. However, success rates are materially lower on the most recent benchmark tasks and drop significantly under limited per-task cost budgets.
AI.conclusion: TestEvo-Bench provides a more realistic, execution-verified evaluation framework for test-code co-evolution. While SOTA agents show promising results, their brittleness on recent tasks and under cost constraints highlights remaining challenges for practical test automation.

title: Revisiting Decentralized Online Convex Optimization with Compressed Communication
summary: Decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) is a popular framework for distributed applications with streaming data. To tackle the communication bottleneck, previous studies have investigated D-OCO with compressed communication and proposed several algorithms that are variants of online gradient descent (OGD). However, for D-OCO with exact communication, the best existing algorithms are variants of follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL). In this paper, for the first time, we propose two FTRL-type algorithms for D-OCO with compressed communication. Compared with OGD-type algorithms, our algorithms are more elegant in both algorithmic design and theoretical analysis. The key insight is that the dual update mechanism of FTRL allows us to make a simple application of the technique for average consensus with communication compression. More specifically, our first algorithm considers the full-information setting, and can match the existing regret bounds. Our second algorithm is designed for the bandit setting, and can significantly improve both the regret bounds and communication costs of existing algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the first FTRL-type algorithms for decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication, addressing both full-information and bandit settings. The FTRL dual update mechanism elegantly integrates with average consensus under communication compression, matching existing regret bounds in the full-information case and significantly improving both regret and communication costs in the bandit setting.
AI.motivation: Existing D-OCO with compressed communication relies exclusively on OGD-type algorithms, while the best algorithms for exact-communication D-OCO are FTRL-type. There is a gap: no FTRL-based algorithms exist for the compressed communication setting. The authors aim to fill this gap, leveraging FTRL's dual update structure for more elegant integration with compressed average consensus.
AI.method: The authors propose two FTRL-type algorithms for D-OCO with compressed communication. The core insight is that FTRL's dual update mechanism naturally accommodates the average consensus technique with communication compression. The first algorithm addresses the full-information setting, while the second targets the bandit setting with improved design.
AI.result: The full-information algorithm matches existing regret bounds of OGD-type methods. The bandit algorithm significantly improves both regret bounds and communication costs compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: FTRL-type algorithms are not only viable but advantageous for D-OCO with compressed communication, offering more elegant algorithmic design and theoretical analysis, with particularly strong gains in the bandit setting.

title: EduArt: An educational-level benchmark for evaluating art history knowledge in large language models
summary: Large language models now score near ceiling on general benchmarks, but these aggregate measures reveal little about how models behave within single disciplines. Existing art-focused evaluations rely on synthetic questions and rarely report item-level properties. This paper introduces EduArt, an educational-level benchmark for art-historical knowledge and visual reasoning in multimodal LLMs. EduArt comprises 871 human-authored questions from Italian secondary-school exercises and US Advanced Placement Art History exams, spanning two languages and seven formats from multiple choice to in-text word placement and error identification. Twelve models from six provider families were evaluated under a default answer-only condition and a motivation condition requiring written justification, and characterized using Classical Test Theory and a logistic regression isolating the effects of format, language, image presence, and model. The benchmark showed strong psychometric properties (mean discrimination 0.514, 82.3 percent good discriminators), while multiple-choice accuracy saturated near ceiling for six models, showing recognition formats alone cannot distinguish frontier models. Format was a strong independent predictor of accuracy: models exceeding 94 percent on multiple choice fell to 23.9 percent on open completion (Claude Opus 4.6) and 6.2 percent on error identification (Claude Sonnet 4.6). The motivation condition changed accuracy in a predominantly negative, family-dependent direction. These dissociations indicate that art-historical knowledge and the ability to deploy it are distinct capabilities, and that single-format benchmarks overestimate what models can reliably do. Mapping this capability profile is a precondition for responsible use of multimodal LLMs in art-historical scholarship, where tasks demand producing and manipulating content rather than selecting from fixed options.

AI.tldr: EduArt is a bilingual, multi-format benchmark of 871 art-history questions revealing that while frontier models saturate on multiple-choice, they collapse on generative formats like open completion (23.9%) and error identification (6.2%), demonstrating that recognition-based benchmarks overestimate multimodal LLM capabilities in art-historical scholarship.
AI.motivation: General LLM benchmarks obscure domain-specific behavior. Existing art-focused evaluations rely on synthetic questions, lack item-level psychometric reporting, and fail to capture how models perform across different task formats. The authors aim to provide a rigorous, educationally grounded benchmark that reveals capability dissociations in art-historical knowledge and visual reasoning.
AI.method: EduArt consists of 871 human-authored questions drawn from Italian secondary-school exercises and US AP Art History exams, covering two languages and seven formats (multiple choice, open completion, error identification, in-text word placement, etc.). Twelve multimodal LLMs from six providers were tested under two conditions: answer-only and answer-with-motivation. Data were analyzed using Classical Test Theory (discrimination, difficulty indices) and logistic regression to isolate effects of format, language, image presence, and model.
AI.result: The benchmark showed strong psychometric properties (mean discrimination 0.514, 82.3% good discriminators). Six models saturated near ceiling on multiple-choice accuracy. Format was a strong independent predictor: models achieving >94% on multiple choice dropped to 23.9% on open completion (Claude Opus 4.6) and 6.2% on error identification (Claude Sonnet 4.6). The motivation condition produced predominantly negative, model-family-dependent accuracy shifts.
AI.conclusion: Art-historical knowledge and the ability to deploy it are distinct, dissociable capabilities. Single-format (recognition-only) benchmarks systematically overestimate what models can reliably do. Responsible use of multimodal LLMs in art-historical scholarship requires mapping these capability profiles, particularly for tasks demanding content production and manipulation rather than selection.

title: Verifiable Knowledge Expansion through Retrieval-Grounded Formal Concept Analysis
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, Accepted to the 8th epiDAMIK ACM SIGKDD International Workshop on Epidemiology meets Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery (epiDAMIK 2026)
summary: Ontology construction requires deciding which objects, attributes, and structural relations should be accepted as valid knowledge. Language models can propose such structures from text, but their outputs can still be unsupported or inconsistent. This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented small language model (SLM) framework that uses formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop for knowledge expansion. Starting from seed attributes, FCA proposes implications over a growing formal context. A retrieval-grounded SLM oracle then validates each implication or returns a counterexample. The oracle also supports incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals, making accepted implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections inspectable. In a rare ataxia setting constructed from Orphadata resources, retrieval-grounded 10-seed runs obtain relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22-0.30. Larger seed sets increase the number of evaluated implications and often improve implication F1. The lower implication scores reflect a stricter evaluation of derived implications, where one missed or extra relation can affect several implication judgments. Ablations show that incidence judgments in a fixed object-attribute setting can improve closure-based implication scores. However, identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult even when the candidate objects and attributes are fixed.

AI.tldr: A retrieval-augmented small language model framework with FCA-based symbolic verification is proposed for ontology construction, achieving inspectable knowledge expansion with relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and implication F1 of 0.22-0.30 in a rare ataxia domain.
AI.motivation: Language models can propose ontological structures from text, but their outputs are often unsupported or inconsistent. There is a need for a verifiable, inspectable knowledge expansion method that combines the generative capacity of LMs with formal, symbolic guarantees.
AI.method: The framework uses Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop: starting from seed attributes, FCA proposes implications over a growing formal context. A retrieval-grounded small language model (SLM) oracle validates each implication or returns a counterexample. The oracle also handles incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals, ensuring all accepted implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections remain inspectable.
AI.result: In a rare ataxia setting built from Orphadata, retrieval-grounded 10-seed runs achieved relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22-0.30. Larger seed sets increased evaluated implications and often improved implication F1. Ablations showed that incidence judgments in a fixed object-attribute setting can improve closure-based implication scores, though identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult.
AI.conclusion: The retrieval-augmented SLM with FCA verification enables inspectable, formally grounded ontology construction. The lower implication F1 scores reflect stricter evaluation of derived implications, and while incidence judgments help, the core challenge of identifying positive object-attribute pairs persists.

title: UniWind: Toward Unified Day-Ahead Wind Power Forecasting via Physics-Informed State Routing
summary: Day-ahead wind power forecasting is essential for cost-effective power-system operation. It is primarily driven by future meteorological conditions while retaining temporal dependencies in power generation. In practice, observed wind-farm power often entangles physically available power with local environmental effects and latent operational states, such as shutdowns and curtailment. Existing physical models provide useful constraints but adapt poorly across wind farms, whereas data-driven models can capture rich correlations but often conflate meteorological effects with state-induced deviations. In this study, we propose UniWind, a wind power forecasting model based on physics-informed state routing. UniWind first employs a Physical Prior Estimator to construct a site-calibrated physical prior by combining site-conditioned monotonic warping with a shared physical power curve. It further applies a physical upper-bound constraint to shape this prior as a soft envelope of available wind power generation. UniWind then proposes a Latent State Encoder to model operating-state embeddings and transforms the physical prior into final power forecasts through a State-aware Power Corrector, which uses knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction. Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of UniWind.

AI.tldr: UniWind is a day-ahead wind power forecasting model that combines a physics-informed prior (site-calibrated power curve with upper-bound constraints) with latent operational state modeling and state-specific corrections, achieving strong accuracy and zero-shot transfer across 20+ real-world wind farms.
AI.motivation: Observed wind farm power data entangles physically available wind power with local environmental effects and latent operational states (shutdowns, curtailment). Physical models adapt poorly across sites, while data-driven models conflate meteorological effects with state-induced deviations. A hybrid approach is needed that leverages physical constraints while explicitly modeling operational states.
AI.method: UniWind consists of three components: (1) a Physical Prior Estimator that creates a site-calibrated physical prior via site-conditioned monotonic warping and a shared physical power curve, shaped by a physical upper-bound constraint as a soft envelope; (2) a Latent State Encoder that learns operating-state embeddings; and (3) a State-aware Power Corrector that uses knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction to transform the physical prior into final forecasts.
AI.result: Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of UniWind, including strong zero-shot transfer performance across wind farms.
AI.conclusion: Integrating physics-informed priors with explicit latent state modeling and state-aware correction yields a wind power forecasting model that is both accurate and generalizable, effectively disentangling meteorological availability from operational state effects across diverse wind farms.

title: OpenSafeIntent: Evaluating Intent-Calibrated Safe Completion Across Dual-Use Prompt Sets
summary: Safe completion requires models to provide useful assistance without enabling harm, but this behavior is difficult to evaluate with isolated prompts. We introduce OpenSafeIntent, a benchmark of controlled prompt-sets that vary intent while holding the underlying task fixed. Each datapoint contains benign, dual-use, and malicious variants of the same task. This design lets us evaluate whether models calibrate assistance across intent shifts, rather than merely appearing safe on average. Across a broad model suite, we find that prompt-level safety hides important failures: models often fail to remain safe across matched intent variants, dual-use behavior is brittle under paraphrase, high-level answers on risky topics are not reliably safe, and responses that reframe ambiguous requests into safer tasks are substantially less likely to cross the safety boundary. Our results suggest that safe completion should be evaluated as intent-calibrated behavior over controlled task variants, not as a single safety-helpfulness tradeoff over independent prompts.

AI.tldr: OpenSafeIntent is a benchmark that evaluates model safety by testing matched benign, dual-use, and malicious variants of the same task, revealing that prompt-level safety metrics hide failures in intent-calibrated behavior.
AI.motivation: Current safety evaluations rely on isolated prompts, making it difficult to assess whether models truly calibrate their assistance based on intent. The authors argue that safe completion should be measured as intent-conditional behavior, not as an average safety-helpfulness tradeoff over independent examples.
AI.method: The authors construct OpenSafeIntent, a benchmark where each datapoint consists of controlled prompt-sets sharing the same underlying task but varying in intent: benign, dual-use, and malicious. This design enables direct comparison of model responses across intent shifts while controlling for task content. They evaluate a broad suite of models on their ability to calibrate assistance appropriately.
AI.result: Prompt-level safety aggregates mask critical failures: models inconsistently maintain safety across matched intent variants; dual-use behavior is fragile under paraphrase; high-level answers on risky topics are not reliably safe; and responses that reframe ambiguous requests into safer tasks are significantly less likely to violate safety boundaries.
AI.conclusion: Safe completion evaluation should shift from aggregating over independent prompts to measuring intent-calibrated behavior across controlled task variants, as the latter reveals nuanced safety failures that average-case metrics conceal.

title: Subliminal Clocks: Latent Time Modelling in Diffusion Language Models
comment: Equal contribution: Thomas Fontanari and Simone Petruzzi
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models. Unlike standard diffusion-based approaches, DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on a timestep, raising a natural question: do these models internally represent denoising progress, and how is such information used downstream? In this work, we show that DLMs do in fact encode a latent representation related to the diffusion timestep within their residual streams. We find that this signal can be reliably extracted using probes across layers, indicating that denoising progress is decodable from internal activations. We further demonstrate that steering the model along a low-dimensional subspace associated with the inferred timestep allows us to systematically modulate its notion of denoising progress, leading to predictable changes in model confidence and entropy. Finally, we analyse the geometry of the identified representation, showing that it exhibits structured and interpretable properties in activation space, and shedding light on how such a signal is processed by these models.

AI.tldr: Diffusion Language Models encode a latent timestep signal in their residual streams, which can be probed, steered, and geometrically analyzed — revealing structured representations of denoising progress that influence model confidence and entropy.
AI.motivation: Unlike standard diffusion models, Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) are not explicitly conditioned on a timestep, raising the question of whether and how they internally represent denoising progress.
AI.method: The authors use linear probes trained on residual stream activations across layers to decode timestep information; apply steering vectors along a low-dimensional timestep-associated subspace to modulate denoising progress; and perform geometric analysis of the identified representation in activation space.
AI.result: Probes reliably extract timestep information across layers. Steering along the timestep subspace predictably alters model confidence and entropy. The representation exhibits structured, interpretable geometric properties.
AI.conclusion: DLMs internally represent denoising progress as a latent, decodable signal that is functionally consequential — it can be manipulated to control model behavior, and its geometry offers insight into how these models process the denoising process.

title: SCAPE: Accurate and Efficient LLM Training with Extreme Sparse Communication
summary: Communication increasingly dominates the cost of Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, especially under data-parallel and sharded training schemes, where gradient synchronization and parameter reconstruction overhead increase with model size and system scale. Existing communication-reduction methods either sparsify raw gradients, which can be unstable for modern Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, or quantize communication, whose savings are fundamentally bounded by bit width and often incur additional runtime overhead. We present SCAPE, a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM training that exploits the stability of AdamS's first-moment to enable aggressive sparsification without loss of LLM quality. Instead of constructing masks from raw gradients, SCAPE derives them from first-moment-based statistics, partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, and delays mask usage by one step so that mask synchronization can overlap with computation. SCAPE also reconstructs the quantities required for second-moment updates from a single synchronized sparse buffer, avoiding an additional collective. We implement SCAPE in Megatron-LM and evaluate its convergence by pre-training GPT-345M on OpenWebText and Llama-500M on SlimPajama-6B using 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs on TACC Vista. In both models, SCAPE preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream task accuracy under 90\% and 99\% sparsity. For Llama-500M, SCAPE reduces end-to-end pre-training wall-clock time by up to 43.3\% while maintaining model quality comparable to dense AdamW and AdamS. For Llama-1.8B, SCAPE achieves up to 3.26$\times$ speedup per step compared to dense AdamS.

AI.tldr: SCAPE is a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM pre-training that uses AdamS first-moment statistics for stable gradient sparsification at 90–99% sparsity, achieving up to 43.3% wall-clock reduction and 3.26× per-step speedup without degrading model quality.
AI.motivation: Communication dominates LLM pre-training costs in data-parallel and sharded settings. Existing solutions are limited: raw-gradient sparsification is unstable with Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, and quantization savings are bounded by bit-width with additional runtime overhead. A method is needed that achieves aggressive communication reduction while preserving training stability.
AI.method: SCAPE exploits AdamS first-moment stability to derive sparsity masks from first-moment statistics rather than raw gradients. It partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, delays mask usage by one step so mask synchronization overlaps with computation, and reconstructs second-moment update quantities from a single synchronized sparse buffer to avoid an extra collective communication.
AI.result: Evaluated on GPT-345M (OpenWebText) and Llama-500M (SlimPajama-6B) with 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs, SCAPE maintained training stability, validation loss, and downstream accuracy under 90% and 99% sparsity. For Llama-500M, end-to-end wall-clock time dropped up to 43.3% versus dense AdamW/AdamS. For Llama-1.8B, per-step speedup reached 3.26× over dense AdamS.
AI.conclusion: SCAPE demonstrates that first-moment-guided sparsification enables aggressive, stable communication reduction in distributed LLM training, outperforming both raw-gradient sparsification and quantization-based approaches while preserving model quality across scales.

title: SPLIT: Cross-Lingual Empathy and Cultural Grounding in English and Ukrainian LLM Responses
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Benchmark paper introducing SPLIT for evaluating empathy, linguistic naturalness, and cultural grounding in English and Ukrainian LLM responses
summary: Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in emotional-support contexts and crisis-related situations. Nevertheless, their cross-lingual abilities in these circumstances remain underexplored. Existing benchmarks emphasize multilingual performance but rarely examine crisis-related empathy and cultural grounding in low-to-mid-resource languages. We introduce SPLIT, a 500-prompt benchmark designed to evaluate LLM consistency in generating emotionally grounded responses across five categories: Stress, Panic, Loneliness, Internal Displacement, and Tension. We evaluate three technically diverse LLMs across three dimensions: Empathetic Accuracy, Linguistic Naturalness, and Contextual & Cultural Grounding. The framework aims to assess and compare the quality of LLM responses in both English and Ukrainian languages, as well as to explore the reliability of the LLM-as-a-jury paradigm. Our findings reveal that Gemini-2.5-Flash and LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct degrade when transitioning to Ukrainian, while DeepSeek-V3 remains comparatively stable within our benchmark. We additionally find that human and AI evaluators agree weakly on empathy and naturalness but diverge on cultural grounding. We further argue that producing Ukrainian text is not equivalent to producing Ukrainian emotional support. Our findings may assist in the future development of more culturally tailored benchmark designs, as well as encourage a stronger emphasis on human-centered evaluation.

AI.tldr: SPLIT is a 500-prompt benchmark evaluating LLMs on emotionally grounded crisis responses in English and Ukrainian across five stress categories. Three LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Flash, LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, DeepSeek-V3) were assessed on Empathetic Accuracy, Linguistic Naturalness, and Contextual & Cultural Grounding. Results show degradation in non-English performance for most models, weak human-AI evaluator agreement (especially on cultural grounding), and that language production does not equate to culturally competent emotional support.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in emotional-support and crisis contexts, yet their cross-lingual capabilities—particularly in low-to-mid-resource languages—remain underexplored. Existing multilingual benchmarks overlook crisis-related empathy and cultural grounding, creating a gap in understanding whether LLMs can provide culturally appropriate emotional support beyond English.
AI.method: The authors introduce SPLIT, a 500-prompt benchmark covering five emotional categories: Stress, Panic, Loneliness, Internal Displacement, and Tension. Three LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Flash, LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, DeepSeek-V3) are evaluated along three dimensions: Empathetic Accuracy, Linguistic Naturalness, and Contextual & Cultural Grounding. Evaluation is conducted in both English and Ukrainian, incorporating both human evaluators and an LLM-as-a-jury paradigm to assess reliability.
AI.result: Gemini-2.5-Flash and LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct exhibit performance degradation when transitioning from English to Ukrainian, while DeepSeek-V3 remains comparatively stable. Human and AI evaluators show weak agreement on empathy and naturalness, with notable divergence on cultural grounding. The study further demonstrates that producing grammatically correct Ukrainian text is not equivalent to delivering culturally appropriate Ukrainian emotional support.
AI.conclusion: Cross-lingual emotional-support capabilities of LLMs are inconsistent and culturally shallow. The findings call for more culturally tailored benchmark designs and stronger emphasis on human-centered evaluation, rather than relying solely on automated or LLM-as-a-jury approaches—particularly for low-to-mid-resource languages in crisis contexts.

title: Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale: From Risk Discovery to Evidence-Grounded Verification
summary: LLM agents increasingly perform autonomous actions through external tools, leading to complex and evolving safety risks. However, existing safety testing targets expert-designed safety violations, and the corresponding outcomes are evaluated by hard-coded rules, making them costly to extend as agents evolve. To this end, we present Vera, an end-to-end automated safety testing framework that instantiates software engineering testing principles for non-deterministic agents through a three-stage, self-reinforcing pipeline. First, a literature-driven exploration continuously discovers and structures emerging risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments. Second, combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions produces executable safety cases, each specifying a concrete safety goal, a programmatically constructed initial state, and a deterministic verification predicate grounded in observable artifacts. Third, adaptive execution runs heterogeneous agents in isolated sandboxes where a control agent steers multi-turn interaction based on runtime observations, while evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence rather than model self-report. We evaluate Vera on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code), revealing substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates reaching 93.9\% under multi-channel attacks; we also release Vera-Bench, comprising 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings. These results indicate that modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Yunhao-Feng/Vera.

AI.tldr: Vera is an automated safety testing framework for LLM agents that uses a three-stage pipeline (risk exploration, combinatorial test case composition, and adaptive sandbox execution) to discover vulnerabilities. Evaluated on four production agent frameworks, it achieved up to 93.9% attack success rates and produced Vera-Bench, a benchmark of 1600 executable safety cases.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent safety testing relies on expert-designed violation scenarios evaluated by hard-coded rules, making it expensive and non-scalable as agents rapidly evolve. There is a need for automated, extensible safety evaluation infrastructure that adapts to emerging risks.
AI.method: Vera employs a three-stage self-reinforcing pipeline: (1) Literature-driven exploration that continuously discovers risks and organizes them into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and execution environments; (2) Combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions to generate executable safety cases with concrete safety goals, programmatic initial states, and deterministic verification predicates grounded in observable artifacts; (3) Adaptive execution in isolated sandboxes using a control agent for multi-turn interaction steering and evidence-grounded verifiers that judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence rather than model self-reports.
AI.result: Evaluated on OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, and Claude Code, Vera revealed substantial safety weaknesses with average attack success rates reaching 93.9% under multi-channel attacks. Vera-Bench, containing 1600 executable safety cases across 124 risk categories and three execution settings, was released.
AI.conclusion: Modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. Vera demonstrates the viability of automating safety testing by adapting software engineering testing principles for non-deterministic LLM agents.

title: WARP: Weight-Space Analysis for Recovering Training Data Portfolios
comment: This work appears in the ICML 2026 Workshop on Weight-Space Symmetries (WSS): from Foundations to Practical Applications. Our source code is available at github.com/SprocketLab/WARP
summary: Foundation models are routinely released to the public, yet the data recipes used to train them -- such as domain mixture weights that determine how different sources are sampled -- are rarely disclosed. This creates an access asymmetry: researchers study the resulting models but lack visibility into the training distribution that produces them. Prior works for inferring training data, such as membership inference, detect at the level of individual samples and thus cannot characterize the global composition of the training corpus. We introduce WARP, a framework that recovers a fine-tuned model's training mixtures directly from its released weights. WARP interpolates between the base and fine-tuned models using model merging, generating pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory and expose a geometric footprint of the training data in the weight space. From these simulated footprints, WARP extracts geometric features and maps them to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures. In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with an average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.

AI.tldr: WARP recovers the domain mixture weights of a fine-tuned model's training data directly from its released weights by merging base and fine-tuned models to simulate the training trajectory, then mapping geometric features in weight space to domain proportions.
AI.motivation: Foundation model data recipes (e.g., domain mixture weights) are rarely disclosed, creating an access asymmetry where researchers can study models but not the training distributions that produced them. Existing methods like membership inference operate at the sample level and cannot characterize global corpus composition.
AI.method: WARP interpolates between base and fine-tuned model weights via model merging to generate pseudo-checkpoints approximating the training trajectory. These simulated trajectories produce geometric footprints in weight space. WARP then extracts geometric features from these footprints and maps them to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures.
AI.result: In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP achieved average MAE of 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming both membership inference baselines and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.
AI.conclusion: Training data composition leaves a recoverable geometric signature in model weights, and model merging can serve as an effective proxy for the missing training trajectory, enabling accurate inference of domain mixtures without access to the original training data.

title: MMIR-TCM: Memory-Integrated Multimodal Inference and Retrieval for TCM Clinical Decision Support
summary: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) diagnosis, particularly through tongue inspection, faces persistent challenges in subjectivity and reproducibility. The application of multimodal artificial intelligence to TCM clinical tasks, such as syndrome differentiation and prescription generation, is significantly hampered by the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, as well as the lack of large-scale, standardized datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce MMIR-TCM, a novel framework that emulates the diagnostic process of TCM experts by integrating multimodal large language model(MLLM) with memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Employing a three-stage architecture, MMIR-TCM integrates a training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue extraction, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL model for structured tongue diagnosis generation, and a Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support generation. The framework was developed and validated using MedTCM, a new large-scale multimodal dataset that we introduce specifically for advanced TCM research. To properly evaluate our framework's clinical accuracy, which existing metrics fail to capture, we also developed TDEU, a domain-specific evaluation metric incorporating semantic understanding and diagnostic importance. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.

AI.tldr: MMIR-TCM is a multimodal AI framework for TCM tongue diagnosis that combines a training-free segmentation module, a fine-tuned MLLM for structured diagnosis, and a RAG component for clinical decision support, trained/evaluated on a new dataset (MedTCM) with a novel domain-specific metric (TDEU), outperforming GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.
AI.motivation: TCM tongue diagnosis suffers from subjectivity and poor reproducibility. Multimodal AI applications in TCM are hindered by (1) the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual clinical reasoning, and (2) the absence of large-scale, standardized multimodal datasets.
AI.method: The MMIR-TCM framework uses a three-stage architecture: (1) Memory-SAM, a training-free memory-augmented segmentation module for robust tongue extraction; (2) a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL MLLM for structured tongue diagnosis generation; (3) a Qwen3-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support. The framework was trained on MedTCM, a newly introduced large-scale multimodal dataset. A new metric, TDEU (TCM Diagnostic Evaluation Unit), was developed to capture semantic understanding and diagnostic importance that existing metrics miss.
AI.result: MMIR-TCM significantly outperformed leading models including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash on clinical accuracy as measured by the TDEU metric.
