AI.conclusion: The MMIR-TCM framework effectively bridges the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual TCM reasoning, offering a reproducible, high-accuracy solution for tongue-inspection-based diagnosis and clinical decision support, validated by both the MedTCM dataset and the TDEU evaluation metric.

title: Rethinking Complexity Metrics for LLM-Integrated Applications: Beyond Source Code
summary: LLM-integrated applications blend natural language prompts with program code, and much of their runtime behavior originates in the prompt layer rather than in the code itself. Existing complexity metrics, however, operate solely at the code level and therefore overlook this behavioral logic entirely. We present HECATE, the first tool designed to assess complexity in both the prompt and code layers of such applications. Central to HECATE is Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism that interprets every prompt as a specification of intended behavior. Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions identified across published taxonomies, the tool generates 52 candidate metrics. We assess each metric against 118 components collected from 18 open-source repositories, relying on maintenance activity derived from version history as an empirical proxy for complexity, and discard any metric that loses significance once code size is accounted for. Only ten metrics withstand this test. Seven belong to our newly introduced set; rather than measuring sheer volume, each tallies structurally distinct elements, such as LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates, an attribute we call structural breadth. Of the three surviving conventional metrics, RFC exhibits a similar breadth-oriented character, while Halstead N and V survive only as a residual effect of size; our top-performing metrics exceed all three. Crucially, the prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric is added as a covariate, establishing prompt complexity as a dimension in its own right. A final validation on 20 components spanning six held-out repositories shows that the two best-performing metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, supporting their generalizability beyond the training set.

AI.tldr: HECATE introduces the first dual-layer complexity assessment tool for LLM-integrated applications, measuring both prompt and code complexity. From 52 candidate metrics, only 10 survive empirical validation against maintenance activity. Seven are novel "structural breadth" metrics counting distinct elements rather than volume; prompt-layer metrics independently predict maintenance effort beyond code-level metrics.
AI.motivation: LLM-integrated applications embed substantial behavioral logic within natural language prompts, yet existing complexity metrics operate exclusively at the code level, completely overlooking the prompt layer. This creates a blind spot in software quality assessment for an emerging class of applications.
AI.method: The authors develop HECATE with a formalism called Prompt-as-Specification, inspired by Hoare logic, treating each prompt as a behavioral specification. They identify 25 complexity dimensions from published taxonomies, generate 52 candidate metrics, and validate them against 118 components from 18 open-source repositories using version-history maintenance activity as an empirical proxy for complexity. Metrics are discarded if they lose significance after controlling for code size. A final held-out validation uses 20 components from 6 repositories.
AI.result: Only 10 of 52 metrics survive: 7 are novel "structural breadth" metrics (counting distinct elements like LLM call sites, memory attributes, prompt templates), and 3 are conventional (RFC, Halstead N, Halstead V). The novel metrics outperform conventional ones. Prompt-layer metrics retain significance even with the strongest code-level metric as a covariate. The two best-performing metrics generalize to held-out repositories.
AI.conclusion: Prompt complexity constitutes an independent dimension of software complexity in LLM-integrated applications. Structural breadth—counting distinct structural elements rather than volume—is a more effective complexity measure than traditional size-based metrics. HECATE provides the first validated tool for comprehensive complexity assessment across both layers.

title: Model Merging as Probabilistic Inference in Fine-Tuning Parameter Space
comment: Accepted for Publication at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI), 2026
summary: Model merging aims to combine existing single-task solutions into a multi-task solution without additional data-driven fine-tuning.~Most existing approaches achieve this using geometric properties of local solution spaces. However, such geometric views provide limited guidance for scoring how statistically useful each task-specific update direction is across tasks during merging. To address this, we formulate model merging from a new perspective of probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) scenario where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over the merged parameters. We show that several existing model merging methods arise as special cases of our framework under energy designs that impose implicit Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals between merged and task-specific models. Empirically, we find that these residuals are often heavy-tailed which exposes a mismatch with the imposed light-tailed Gaussian structures. We address this with a heavy-tailed PoE design based on Cauchy experts, which better captures the observed residual behavior while admitting a provably convergent inference procedure. Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures show significant improvements over state-of-the-arts baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/MinhLong210/PoE-EBM-Merging.git.

AI.tldr: Model merging is reframed as probabilistic inference under a Product-of-Experts framework, where each single-task model defines an energy-based model. Existing methods implicitly assume Gaussian residuals, but empirical evidence shows heavy-tailed residuals, motivating a Cauchy-based expert design that outperforms state-of-the-art merging methods.
AI.motivation: Existing model merging methods rely on geometric properties of local solution spaces, which offer limited guidance on statistically scoring how useful each task-specific update direction is across tasks. There is a need for a principled statistical framework that better captures the empirical behavior of parameter residuals between merged and task-specific models.
AI.method: The paper formulates model merging as probabilistic inference under a Product-of-Experts (PoE) scenario, where each single-task solution defines an energy-based model (EBM) over merged parameters. It shows that several existing merging methods are special cases with implicit Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals. Observing that residuals are empirically heavy-tailed, the authors propose a heavy-tailed PoE design using Cauchy experts, which admits a provably convergent inference procedure.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: The probabilistic PoE-EBM framework provides a unified statistical lens for model merging. Replacing implicit Gaussian assumptions with Cauchy experts yields better alignment with empirical residual distributions and superior merging performance.

title: Unlocking Speech-Text Compositional Powers: Instruction-Following Speech Language Models without Instruction Tuning
summary: Instruction tuning for speech language models (SLMs) is substantially more challenging than for text-based large language models (LLMs), as it requires learning a new modality and a wide range of speech-specific instructions in addition to those supported by text LLMs. Existing SLM training approaches largely replicate the text LLM training paradigm by synthesizing large-scale speech pre-training and instruction-tuning datasets. However, this strategy is difficult to scale, since speech sequences are significantly longer than text sequences. In this paper, we propose SpeechCombine, an instruction-following speech language model trained without any instruction tuning, using only a single round of speech pre-training on 30k hours of data. Starting from a text LLM base model, we perform continuous pre-training on speech utterances to obtain a speech-adapted model, and then directly combine its weights with the weight difference between the instruction-tuned and base versions of the text LLM. Our results show that this simple combination strategy not only preserves the knowledge and capabilities of the original text LLM, but also effectively transfers them to the speech domain. These findings suggest a new direction for SLM training that avoids reliance on massive speech data.

AI.tldr: SpeechCombine proposes training a speech language model without any speech instruction tuning. It works by continuously pre-training a text LLM on speech data, then combining its weights with the weight delta between the instruction-tuned and base text LLM. This simple weight-merging approach transfers instruction-following capabilities to speech using only 30k hours of pre-training data, avoiding massive speech instruction datasets.
AI.motivation: Instruction tuning for speech language models is extremely challenging because it requires learning a new modality plus speech-specific instructions, and speech sequences are far longer than text, making large-scale dataset synthesis difficult to scale. Existing methods that replicate text LLM training paradigms are thus impractical.
AI.method: SpeechCombine starts from a text LLM base model and performs a single round of continuous pre-training on 30k hours of speech utterances to produce a speech-adapted model. Then, it directly combines the speech-adapted model's weights with the weight difference (delta) between the instruction-tuned and base versions of the text LLM — no speech instruction tuning involved.
AI.result: The weight-combination strategy preserves the original text LLM's knowledge and capabilities while effectively transferring them to the speech domain, enabling instruction-following speech behavior without any speech-specific instruction tuning.
AI.conclusion: This work suggests a new direction for SLM training that avoids reliance on massive speech data, demonstrating that instruction-following can be transferred from text to speech through simple weight-space arithmetic rather than expensive speech instruction tuning.

title: Pre-Flight: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Aviation Operational Knowledge
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Benchmark available in inspect_evals (UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_evals)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations, from documentation and training generation to customer facing assistants. General purpose benchmarks do not measure whether a model reasons safely and correctly about aviation specific operational knowledge, and the high stakes, regulated nature of the domain makes that gap consequential. We present Pre-Flight, an open source benchmark of 300 multiple choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with experience in air traffic management, ground operations and commercial flying. We evaluate a range of contemporary commercial and open weight models using the Inspect evaluation framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol, and we maintain the leaderboard on a rolling basis as new models are released. Against an informal expert reference of around 95%, obtained from a low sample quiz of aviation professionals at a conference, even the strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved only gradually from roughly 75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert level reliability therefore remains. We release the dataset, the evaluation harness and the results, and the benchmark is available within the community evaluations package distributed with inspect_evals. We argue that domain specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non safety critical aviation operations.

AI.tldr: Pre-Flight is an open-source benchmark of 300 multiple-choice questions on aviation operational knowledge, created by domain practitioners. Evaluating contemporary LLMs reveals a persistent gap: the best model scores 82.7% against an expert baseline of ~95%, indicating current models remain insufficiently reliable for even non-safety-critical aviation deployment.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLM benchmarks fail to measure domain-specific reasoning about aviation operations. Given aviation's high-stakes, regulated nature, this gap is consequential. Domain-specific evaluation is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in aviation, even for non-safety-critical tasks.
AI.method: The authors created Pre-Flight, a benchmark of 300 multiple-choice questions covering ICAO and FAA regulations, international airport ground operations, aviation general knowledge, and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with air traffic management, ground operations, and commercial flying experience. Models were evaluated using the Inspect evaluation framework under standard multiple-choice protocol, with accuracy as the scoring metric. An informal expert reference (~95%) was established via a quiz at an aviation conference. A rolling leaderboard is maintained as new models release.
AI.result: The strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) achieves 82.7% accuracy, improving only gradually from ~75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap of over 12 percentage points remains below the expert reference of ~95%.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific benchmarks like Pre-Flight are essential for assessing LLM readiness in aviation. The persistent expert-level gap indicates that current models are not yet reliable enough for responsible deployment, even in non-safety-critical aviation operations. The dataset, evaluation harness, and results are publicly released within the inspect_evals community package.

title: A Mathematical Introduction to Diffusion Models
comment: Lecture notes for the John Tukey Summer Graduate School on Mathematics of Generative Models at SLMath (June 22nd, 2026 -- July 2nd, 2026)
summary: These notes give a proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from the viewpoint of sampling, tracing a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, their error analysis, and inference-time control. Throughout, the material is layered into core definitions and identities proved in full, representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and research-level theorems stated with a proof roadmap. The intended audience is beginning graduate students with a background in probability but no prior exposure to stochastic differential equations, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.

AI.tldr: A pedagogical introduction to diffusion models from a sampling perspective, covering classical sampling dynamics, modern diffusion samplers, error analysis, and inference-time control, aimed at graduate students with probability background.
AI.motivation: To provide a proof-oriented, self-contained educational resource that makes diffusion models accessible to beginning graduate students who have probability knowledge but no prior exposure to SDEs, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.
AI.method: The material is layered into three levels of depth: (1) core definitions and identities with full proofs, (2) representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and (3) research-level theorems stated with proof roadmaps. The exposition traces a single conceptual arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers.
AI.result: These are pedagogical lecture notes rather than a research paper presenting novel results; thus they synthesize and explain existing results across classical and modern diffusion sampling, error analysis, and inference-time control techniques.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion models can be coherently understood through the lens of sampling theory, and a carefully scaffolded proof-oriented approach can make this advanced topic accessible to students with foundational probability training.

title: Challenges and Recommendations for LLMs-as-a-Judge in Multilingual Settings and Low-Resource Languages
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm for many natural language generation tasks, due to shortcomings of conventional metrics and high correlations with human judgment, albeit mostly in English. There are now attempts to extend LLM-as-a-Judge to multilingual settings including low-resource languages. However, LLMs have limited proficiency in low-resource languages, and there is often no adequate human validation in these settings. To highlight the scope of the problem and current practices, we explore the use of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators in ACL Anthology papers focusing on multilingual settings and low-resource languages across a diverse set of tasks. Out of 650 papers mentioning LLM-as-a-judge, only 33 of them focus on low-resource or multilingual settings. Our in-depth analysis of these papers indicates inconsistent evaluation outcomes, a tendency to overtrust LLM judgments in multilingual settings, and the widespread reliance on a single judge model per study. To help the NLP community further, we conclude with recommendations about how to use LLM-as-a-Judge in multilingual and low-resource settings.

AI.tldr: A systematic review of 650 ACL Anthology papers reveals that only 33 address LLM-as-a-Judge in multilingual/low-resource settings, exposing widespread overtrust in LLM judgments, inconsistent evaluation outcomes, and over-reliance on single judge models. The authors provide recommendations for improved practice.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-a-Judge has become dominant for NLG evaluation in English, but its extension to multilingual and low-resource settings is problematic: LLMs have limited proficiency in low-resource languages, and there is often no adequate human validation. The authors aim to quantify the scope of this problem and audit current practices.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic literature survey of ACL Anthology papers that mention LLM-as-a-Judge, identifying 650 such papers. From these, they filter down to 33 papers that specifically focus on multilingual or low-resource language settings. They then perform an in-depth qualitative analysis of these 33 papers, examining evaluation outcomes, judge model selection practices, and validation protocols.
AI.result: Only 33 out of 650 LLM-as-a-Judge papers (≈5%) address multilingual/low-resource settings. The analysis reveals three key problems: (1) inconsistent evaluation outcomes across studies, (2) a widespread tendency to overtrust LLM judgments without adequate human validation in multilingual contexts, and (3) heavy reliance on a single judge model per study rather than using ensembles or multiple evaluators.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes with actionable recommendations for the NLP community on how to responsibly deploy LLM-as-a-Judge in multilingual and low-resource settings, emphasizing the need for human validation, multi-model evaluation, and greater methodological rigor.

title: Actual causality in fault trees
summary: Fault trees are a widely used as effective risk models for complex systems, answering the question "what can go wrong?", especially through minimal cut set analysis. We study fault trees from the perspective of Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality. This allows us to use fault trees to answer the question "why has it gone wrong?", which is fundamental to failure diagnostics. We give a complete classification of each of the different notions of actual causality in terms of the fault tree's graph structure and logical structure, and show how minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.

AI.tldr: This paper bridges fault tree analysis with Halpern & Pearl's actual causality theory. It provides a complete classification of causality notions (but-for, sufficient, actual) in terms of fault tree graph/logical structure, and demonstrates how minimal cut sets correspond to actual causes, enabling fault trees to answer both "what can go wrong?" and "why has it gone wrong?" for failure diagnostics.
AI.motivation: Fault trees are well-established for prospective risk analysis (what can go wrong?) via minimal cut sets, but lack a formal framework for retrospective failure diagnostics (why did it go wrong?). The authors seek to unify these two perspectives by grounding fault tree analysis in a rigorous theory of actual causality.
AI.method: The authors apply Halpern & Pearl's formal theory of actual causality to fault tree models. They systematically map the structural (graph) and logical (Boolean) properties of fault trees onto the different causality notions defined by Halpern & Pearl, providing a complete classification. They further establish the formal relationship between minimal cut sets and actual causes.
AI.result: A complete classification is achieved: each notion of actual causality (but-for cause, sufficient cause, actual cause under the HP definition) is characterized in terms of fault tree structure. Minimal cut sets are shown to systematically give rise to actual causes, providing a direct bridge between the two frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Fault trees, traditionally used for forward-looking risk assessment, can be endowed with retrospective diagnostic power through the lens of actual causality. The correspondence between minimal cut sets and actual causes provides a principled mechanism for answering "why has it gone wrong?" within the same modeling formalism.

title: Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine for Solving High-Frequency Partial Differential Equations
summary: Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency solutions remains a central challenge in physics-informed machine learning due to spectral bias -- the tendency of neural networks to learn low-frequency components preferentially. This paper proposes a Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (FS-PIELM) framework that addresses this limitation through an additive mechanism for weight initialization. Rather than multiplying random weights by a scaling factor, the method translates the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping the variance fixed at unity, thereby avoiding the variance amplification inherent in scaling-based methods. Two variants are developed: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes to individual neurons, while FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for improved robustness. Theoretical analysis shows that the frequency variance under the proposed framework remains bounded and approaches unity regardless of target frequency, in contrast to the quadratic growth of conventional approaches. The method preserves the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines, requiring only a single linear solve. Experiments on seven benchmark problems spanning six equation types -- Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, and advection-diffusion -- on both regular and complex geometries show that the linear variant achieves the best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of one to nearly five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. The code and data accompanying this manuscript will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xgxgnpu/Physics-informed-vibe-coding/tree/main/FS-PIELM.

AI.tldr: FS-PIELM addresses spectral bias in physics-informed neural networks by shifting the mean of Gaussian weight initialization (rather than scaling variance), keeping variance bounded near unity regardless of target frequency. The linear variant achieves 1–5 orders of magnitude accuracy improvement over existing PIELM methods across seven benchmark PDE problems.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed machine learning struggles with high-frequency PDE solutions due to spectral bias—neural networks preferentially learn low-frequency components. Existing approaches that scale random weights to target higher frequencies suffer from variance amplification, which destabilizes training and limits accuracy.
AI.method: The authors propose Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (FS-PIELM), which uses an additive frequency shift mechanism: the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution is translated (shifted) while keeping variance fixed at unity, avoiding variance inflation. Two variants are introduced: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes per neuron; FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for robustness. The method retains the single linear solve efficiency of extreme learning machines.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis proves frequency variance remains bounded and approaches unity under FS-PIELM, contrasting with quadratic growth in scaling-based methods. Experiments on seven benchmarks across six equation types (Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, advection-diffusion) on regular and complex geometries show the linear variant achieves best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of 1–5 orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants.
AI.conclusion: FS-PIELM effectively mitigates spectral bias through a simple yet principled shift-based initialization, delivering substantial accuracy gains for high-frequency PDE solutions without sacrificing the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines.

title: BamiBERT: A New BERT-based Language Model for Vietnamese
summary: In this paper, we introduce BamiBERT, a new BERT-based pre-trained language model for Vietnamese that addresses key limitations of PhoBERT -- the current de facto Vietnamese text encoder. Trained from scratch on a 129GB corpus of general-domain Vietnamese text for 20 epochs, BamiBERT supports an extended context length of up to 2048 tokens and operates directly on raw input, eliminating the need for external word segmentation. Across 8 Vietnamese benchmarks, it achieves the best score on 11 of 15 metrics and the second-best on 3 others, setting a new state of the art among "base"-sized Vietnamese encoders and demonstrating strong cross-domain generalization. We release BamiBERT at: https://huggingface.co/Qualcomm-AI-Research/BamiBERT

AI.tldr: BamiBERT is a new BERT-based pre-trained language model for Vietnamese that outperforms PhoBERT by supporting longer context (2048 tokens), operating without external word segmentation, and achieving state-of-the-art results across 8 Vietnamese benchmarks.
AI.motivation: PhoBERT, the current standard Vietnamese text encoder, has key limitations including reliance on external word segmentation and restricted context length. The authors aim to address these shortcomings with a from-scratch pre-trained model that handles raw input and longer sequences.
AI.method: BamiBERT is a BERT-based encoder trained from scratch on a 129GB general-domain Vietnamese corpus for 20 epochs. It supports an extended context window of up to 2048 tokens and processes raw text directly without requiring a separate word segmentation step.
AI.result: BamiBERT achieves the best score on 11 out of 15 metrics across 8 Vietnamese benchmarks and the second-best on 3 others, establishing a new state of the art among base-sized Vietnamese encoders with strong cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: BamiBERT successfully addresses PhoBERT's limitations and sets a new SOTA for base-sized Vietnamese text encoders. The model is publicly released on HuggingFace for further research and application.

title: CLAP: Closed-Loop Training, Evaluation, and Release Control for Domain Agent Post-training
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Accepted to CRAE 2026; to appear in SPIE Proceedings. Best Poster Award
summary: Domain agents often face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk. This paper presents CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training), a closed-loop method that converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. CLAP combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide whether an adapter is suitable for the target application chain. On five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches, QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT yields modest average gains: overall score increases by 0.0098, pass rate by 0.0240, and evidence accuracy by 0.0280, while hallucination and wrong facts decrease. Yet only 3 of 5 batches improve, some batches regress, and GRPO exposes high KL risks. Application-chain replay further shows that RAG is necessary for factual extraction; under the same 3B backbone and 100 replay cases, an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but increases latency. These results support managing domain-agent post-training through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying on training completion or a single offline score.

AI.tldr: CLAP is a closed-loop post-training framework for domain agents that transforms noisy business data into structured samples with diagnostic gates and application-chain replay to evaluate adapter suitability. Experiments show LoRA-SFT yields mixed gains across manufacturing batches, GRPO introduces high KL risks, and RAG-oriented adapters improve factual extraction at latency cost — supporting the need for integrated data-training-evaluation-release loops over single-score offline evaluation.
AI.motivation: Domain agents deployed in industrial settings suffer from noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, mismatches between offline evaluation and real applications, and risks when releasing adapters. Existing approaches lack an integrated mechanism to validate data quality, diagnose training outcomes (e.g., KL divergence), and gate adapter releases based on application-level replay — motivating a closed-loop methodology.
AI.method: CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training) converts business data into five structured artifacts: SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. The pipeline integrates: (1) data validation, (2) target/evidence normalization, (3) reward/KL diagnosis, (4) offline evaluation gates, and (5) application-chain replay. Adapters are assessed via QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT and GRPO; application-chain replay tests RAG-oriented vs. base configurations under a 3B backbone across 100 replay cases.
AI.result: On five anonymized manufacturing batches, LoRA-SFT yields modest average improvements: overall score +0.0098, pass rate +0.0240, evidence accuracy +0.0280, with reductions in hallucination and wrong facts. However, only 3 of 5 batches improve; some regress. GRPO exposes high KL risks. Application-chain replay reveals RAG is necessary for factual extraction; a RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value extraction, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but increases latency.
AI.conclusion: Post-training for domain agents should be governed by an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying solely on training completion signals or single offline metrics. The CLAP framework demonstrates that batch-level regressions, KL risks, and application-level trade-offs (e.g., accuracy vs. latency) are only visible through closed-loop diagnostics with replay-based gating.

title: Predicting Closed-Loop Performance of Latent World Models: Offline Checkpoint Selection for MPC and Model-Based RL Under Non-Markovian Rewards in LunarLander
comment: Preprint, 19 pages (16 main text + 3 pages appendix), 7 figures, 4 tables. Video: https://youtu.be/4PxHFW_TYUw , Code: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM
summary: We study how to predict the downstream closed-loop performance of a learned latent world model from validation-time diagnostics alone. Choosing the right checkpoint from a world-model training run is difficult: validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE keep improving long after closed-loop performance has collapsed. We present a suite of structural validation-time diagnostics drawn from optimal-control theory and apply them to Gymnasium's LunarLander v3, which features shaped rewards. We train an RSSM [5, 4] world model on it and treat per checkpoint CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. By evaluating 40 metrics against this oracle, we find that the strongest single predictor is the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF), which measures the reward predictor's dependence on the observable subspace. We combine ROF with three structural regularizers into a single-number offline checkpoint selection score, the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF). The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that beats a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions, and the same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy. Code and data: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces validation-time diagnostics from optimal-control theory to predict closed-loop world model performance without online evaluation. The key contribution is the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) and its composite variant (CROF), which identify checkpoints that generalize well for downstream control tasks, demonstrated on LunarLander with RSSM-based models achieving superior sample efficiency.
AI.motivation: Selecting the right checkpoint during world-model training is challenging because validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE continue improving even after closed-loop control performance collapses. There is a need for offline metrics that reliably predict downstream policy performance without costly online evaluation.
AI.method: The authors train an RSSM world model on Gymnasium's LunarLander v3. For each checkpoint, they compute CEM-MPC return as the ground-truth closed-loop oracle. They evaluate 40 structural diagnostics from optimal-control theory against this oracle. The Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) — measuring the reward predictor's dependence on the observable subspace — emerges as the strongest single predictor. ROF is combined with three structural regularizers into the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF) for offline checkpoint selection. The selected model is used for model-based A2C and zero-shot CEM-MPC.
AI.result: ROF is the strongest single predictor of closed-loop performance among 40 metrics tested. The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that outperforms a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions. The same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy.
AI.conclusion: Structural diagnostics from optimal-control theory, particularly ROF and CROF, provide reliable offline signals for checkpoint selection in world-model training. This enables sample-efficient model-based RL without requiring online evaluation for model selection, validated on LunarLander.

title: CheckRLM: Effective Knowledge-Thought Coherence Checking in Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning
summary: Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) have significantly improved performance on complex tasks by extending the reasoning chain. However, these chains are prone to containing factual errors, particularly in knowledge-intensive tasks. To address this issue, we propose CheckRLM, a framework that improves the reliability of the reasoning process through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by timely checking and correcting factual errors. Specifically, CheckRLM extracts factual claims from the reasoning chain to identify and localize subtle knowledge inconsistencies during inference. Upon detection of errors, a refinement mechanism performs minimal-cost yet precise corrections by leveraging external knowledge, ensuring coherence between the reasoning chain and correct knowledge. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CheckRLM substantially outperforms existing baselines, exhibiting a strong capability to mitigate error accumulation in long-horizon reasoning with lower costs. The code and data are available at https://github.com/AI9Stars/CheckRLM.

AI.tldr: CheckRLM is a framework that improves reasoning reliability by integrating RAG-based factual checking and correction into the reasoning chain, outperforming baselines in mitigating error accumulation in long-horizon reasoning.
AI.motivation: Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) extend reasoning chains for complex tasks but frequently introduce factual errors, especially in knowledge-intensive scenarios. Existing approaches lack mechanisms to detect and correct subtle factual inconsistencies during inference.
AI.method: CheckRLM extracts factual claims from the reasoning chain during inference to identify knowledge inconsistencies. Upon detecting errors, a refinement mechanism performs minimal-cost, precise corrections using external knowledge retrieved via RAG, preserving coherence between the reasoning chain and verified facts.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show CheckRLM substantially outperforms existing baselines, demonstrating strong capability in reducing error accumulation during long-horizon reasoning while maintaining lower computational costs.
AI.conclusion: CheckRLM offers an effective, cost-efficient solution for improving factual reliability in RLMs by combining real-time fact-checking with targeted knowledge refinement.

title: Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement
summary: Safety training for large language models (LLMs) is conducted predominantly in English, leaving uncertain how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and mixed-language code-switching. We show that this creates an epistemic gap in which models confidently generate harmful responses for inputs that fall outside the distribution of their safety training. To study this phenomenon, we introduce STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most strongly to the model's refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Across six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER achieves attack success rates of up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG). The resulting prompts also transfer to GPT-4o-mini, achieving a 35.5% attack success rate without requiring access to the target model, suggesting that the underlying weakness is not specific to a single architecture. These findings demonstrate that safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. We argue that improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

AI.tldr: LLM safety training, predominantly in English, fails to generalize to low-resource languages and code-switching. The authors introduce STEER, a gradient-guided attack that iteratively translates refusal-triggering words into low-resource languages, achieving up to 96.7% ASR on AdvBench and transferring to GPT-4o-mini, exposing a fundamental multilingual safety gap.
AI.motivation: LLM safety alignment is conducted almost exclusively in English, creating an epistemic gap where models confidently produce harmful responses for out-of-distribution multilingual or code-switched inputs. The authors aim to systematically demonstrate and exploit this vulnerability to highlight the inadequacy of current safety mechanisms across languages.
AI.method: STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement): a gradient-guided attack that (1) computes token-level gradients with respect to a refusal loss function to identify words most responsible for triggering model refusal, (2) iteratively translates these high-contribution words into low-resource languages to suppress the refusal signal, and (3) preserves harmful intent in the prompt. Evaluated on six 8B-parameter open-source models using JailbreakBench and AdvBench, with transfer attacks on GPT-4o-mini.
AI.result: STEER achieves up to 93.0% ASR on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench across six open-source 8B models, significantly outperforming random code-switching and GCG baselines. Transferred prompts achieve 35.5% ASR on GPT-4o-mini (black-box), indicating the vulnerability is architecture-independent.
AI.conclusion: Safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English do not generalize across multilingual inputs. The authors argue for broader multilingual coverage during safety alignment and explicit out-of-distribution detection/abstention mechanisms to close this gap.

title: Finite-Lag Operator Geometry of Recurrent Representations
summary: Recurrent representations are trajectories, but representation geometry is often measured from static snapshots. We develop finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states from observed source-successor pairs $(X_t,X_{t+Δ})$. The primitive is the conditional transport law $Q_Δ(dy\mid x)$, estimated by a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator. From this directed finite-lag law we derive a source-centered transport tensor $G_Δ$, which decomposes exactly into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and an antisymmetric coordinate circulation $W_Δ^ρ$, which summarizes directed lagged flow. We prove affine covariance with explicit metric dependence of scalar summaries, dense estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation result showing that source-centered transport detects deterministic recurrent motion not recorded by infinitesimal carre-du-champ geometry. A linear-Gaussian closed form calibrates the quantities in terms of the update $A_Δ$, source covariance, and innovation covariance. Controlled experiments validate the decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In performance matched repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while coherent displacement fraction is metric and resolution dependent.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces finite-lag operator geometry for analyzing recurrent neural representations by treating hidden states as trajectories. It develops source-centered transport tensors and antisymmetric coordinate circulation derived from conditional transport laws, providing affine-covariant summaries that detect deterministic recurrent motion beyond what infinitesimal carré-du-champ geometry captures. Validated on controlled experiments and repeat-copy networks.
AI.motivation: Recurrent network representations are inherently trajectories evolving over time, yet existing representation geometry methods typically rely on static snapshots, failing to capture the directed, lagged structure of these dynamics. The authors aim to bridge this gap by developing geometric tools that operate directly on finite-lag source-successor pairs, revealing dynamical properties invisible to instantaneous analyses.
AI.method: The core primitive is the conditional transport law Q_Δ(dy|x), estimated via a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator from observed (X_t, X_{t+Δ}) pairs. From this, the authors derive: (1) a source-centered transport tensor G_Δ that decomposes exactly into conditional spread and coherent displacement components; (2) an antisymmetric coordinate circulation W_Δ^ρ summarizing directed lagged flow. They prove affine covariance with explicit metric dependence, dense estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation result. A linear-Gaussian closed form provides calibration.
AI.result: Controlled experiments validate the decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In performance-matched repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture-dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while coherent displacement fraction proves metric- and resolution-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Finite-lag operator geometry provides a principled, affine-covariant framework for analyzing recurrent dynamics that captures directed motion invisible to static or infinitesimal methods. Architecture-dependent transport signatures can be disentangled from metric- and resolution-dependent quantities, offering a new lens for understanding recurrent network internals.

title: On the Role of Directionality in Structural Generalization
summary: Several SLOG test categories explicitly involve directional distinctions (modifier position shifts, argument extraction positions), yet AM-Parser, the previous SOTA, uses an AM algebra whose operations do not encode direction. We redesign the symbolic backend around CCG directed types (deterministic CKY + single linear decoder, 30K learnable parameters). Under the same BERT-base encoder, the system achieves 75.9$\pm$6.4% LF exact match, surpassing AM-Parser (70.8$\pm$4.3%). Per SLOG's own category groupings, gains are highly directional: the CCG system outperforms AM-Parser on all 5 position-shift categories (+29.9pp), while AM-Parser outperforms on all 6 recursive-depth categories. Replacing the encoder with DeBERTa-v3-large yields 90.7$\pm$4.9%, with the largest encoder gains in recursive-depth categories, complementary to directionality's gains. Directional representations shift the bottleneck from the symbolic layer (AM-Parser's 0% category ceiling) to the neural layer, which improves with encoder upgrades.

AI.tldr: Redesigning the symbolic backend of a semantic parser using CCG directed types achieves substantial gains on directional SLOG categories, shifting the bottleneck from the symbolic layer to the neural encoder.
AI.motivation: AM-Parser, the previous SOTA on SLOG benchmarks, uses an AM algebra whose operations lack directional encoding, despite several SLOG test categories explicitly requiring directional distinctions (e.g., modifier position shifts, argument extraction positions). This representational mismatch limits performance on directionally-sensitive phenomena.
AI.method: The authors replace AM-Parser's symbolic backend with one grounded in Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) directed types, implementing a deterministic CKY parser coupled with a single linear decoder (~30K learnable parameters). The neural encoder (BERT-base or DeBERTa-v3-large) remains unchanged, isolating the contribution of the symbolic layer.
AI.result: Under BERT-base, the CCG system achieves 75.9±6.4% LF exact match vs. AM-Parser's 70.8±4.3%. Gains are concentrated in SLOG's 5 position-shift categories (+29.9pp), while AM-Parser retains superiority on 6 recursive-depth categories. With DeBERTa-v3-large, performance reaches 90.7±4.9%, with encoder gains primarily benefiting recursive-depth categories — complementary to the directional gains from the CCG backend.
AI.conclusion: Directional representations in the symbolic layer resolve a critical bottleneck: AM-Parser faced a 0% ceiling on certain categories, which the CCG backend eliminates. The bottleneck consequently shifts from the symbolic layer to the neural layer, where further gains can be achieved simply by upgrading the encoder.

title: CamoNAS: Neural Architecture Search for Enhanced Camouflaged Object Detection
comment: Published in The Visual Computer. Author manuscript version
summary: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to locate and segment objects that blend into their surroundings, presenting challenges due to weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries. Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion, which are often guided by intuition rather than systematic search. This paper introduces CamoNAS, a frequency-aware multi-resolution Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework for COD. CamoNAS automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, forming a hierarchical search space tailored to detect camouflaged objects. Additionally, it adopts an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture, where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream. CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON), highlighting the effectiveness of NAS for COD. Our code is available at https://github.com/rendaweiSIMIT/CamoNAS.

AI.tldr: CamoNAS introduces a neural architecture search framework for camouflaged object detection that jointly searches cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, augmented with a learnable wavelet-based frequency stream, achieving SOTA on four COD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional COD models rely on manually designed architectures and heuristic multi-scale feature fusion, which may be suboptimal. There is a need for automated, systematic architecture design tailored to the unique challenges of detecting camouflaged objects (weak edges, ill-defined boundaries).
AI.method: CamoNAS proposes a frequency-aware multi-resolution NAS framework with: (1) a hierarchical search space covering both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths; (2) an RGB-frequency dual-stream architecture where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream; (3) automatic joint search over both cell and network structure.
AI.result: CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four standard COD benchmarks: CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, and CHAMELEON.
AI.conclusion: NAS is highly effective for COD, and jointly searching operations and downsampling paths with a frequency-aware dual-stream design yields superior performance over hand-crafted alternatives.

title: Efficient Temporal Point Processes via Monotone Alternating Splines
summary: Temporal point processes (TPPs) have widespread applications across various domains. Compared to modeling the conditional intensity of a TPP, modeling its cumulative conditional intensity function (CCIF) improves computational efficiency and eliminates numerical approximation errors. However, current CCIF parameterizations uniformly rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs), which we identify as suffering from three structural deadlocks--convexity restrictions, saturation limits, and violations of CCIF modeling requirements--that fundamentally restrict their representational capacity for complex temporal dynamics. To resolve these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a novel framework called Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS). By leveraging distinct interpolation and extrapolation components, MAS provides a flexible and efficient framework for modeling CCIFs. Theoretically, MAS's interpolation provides strong fitting accuracy, while its extrapolation supports robust generalization, reducing the irreducible approximation gaps of MNNs. Extensive experiments show that MAS achieves superior performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies three structural limitations of Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs) for modeling cumulative conditional intensity functions (CCIFs) in temporal point processes, and proposes Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS)—a flexible framework combining interpolation and extrapolation components—that achieves superior fitting accuracy and generalization.
AI.motivation: Current CCIF parameterizations uniformly rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs), which suffer from three structural deadlocks: (1) convexity restrictions, (2) saturation limits, and (3) violations of CCIF modeling requirements. These fundamentally restrict their representational capacity for complex temporal dynamics, motivating the need for a more flexible alternative.
AI.method: The authors propose Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS), a framework that decouples CCIF modeling into distinct interpolation and extrapolation components. The interpolation component provides strong fitting accuracy, while the extrapolation component supports robust generalization beyond observed data ranges.
AI.result: MAS achieves superior performance compared to existing MNN-based approaches on both synthetic and real-world datasets, with theoretical guarantees that its interpolation reduces irreducible approximation gaps inherent to MNNs.
AI.conclusion: MAS effectively resolves the three structural bottlenecks of MNNs, providing a more flexible and efficient framework for CCIF modeling in temporal point processes, with both theoretical and empirical advantages over existing methods.

title: World Wide Models: Literary Tools for Cultural AI
summary: LLMs stage a new form of cultural encounter that is massive, automated, and monolingual. Literary disciplines have always negotiated cultural struggles with comparative reading of literature, narratological and poetic analysis, critical theory, world literature, and translation. These tools have now become indispensable for building culturally literate AI. The essay develops a layered framework toward more nuanced textual models and pluralistic interpretations of AI, emphasizing the natural intersections of literature and AI development, connecting current debates in critical theory with structural monolingualism, and suggesting a new application of world literature approaches to address global AI textuality through macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework leveraging literary disciplines—comparative reading, narratology, critical theory, and world literature—to address the cultural limitations of LLMs, particularly their structural monolingualism, and to build more pluralistic, culturally literate AI systems.
AI.motivation: LLMs embody a massive, automated, and monolingual form of cultural encounter that risks flattening cultural diversity. Literary scholarship has long developed tools for navigating cultural struggles, and these tools are now urgently needed to inform AI development and critique its monocultural tendencies.
AI.method: The essay constructs a layered conceptual framework that connects critical theory debates on structural monolingualism with world literature methodologies—specifically macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability—to analyze and reimagine global AI textuality.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates natural intersections between literary analysis and AI development, showing how narratological, poetic, and comparative approaches can yield more nuanced textual models and pluralistic AI interpretations.
AI.conclusion: Literary disciplines offer indispensable tools for building culturally literate AI. Applying world literature approaches to AI textuality can counteract structural monolingualism and foster genuinely pluralistic machine understanding of global cultural production.

title: SkillCoach: Self-Evolving Rubrics for Evaluating and Enhancing Agentic Skill-Use
summary: Skills are becoming a reusable operational layer for LLM agents, encoding SOPs, domain rules, tool workflows, scripts, and validation routines. In realistic skill repositories, overlapping skills make reliable skill-use difficult. Final verifier success is too coarse for both evaluation and training, since an agent may pass through trial and error while selecting distractor skills, skipping required steps, composing workflows incorrectly or omitting final checks. We introduce SkillCoach, a self-evolving rubric framework for evaluating and enhancing agentic skill-use. SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts and evaluates trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. It keeps the external verifier as a separate outcome signal, allowing process quality to be distinguished from accidental task success. The evolved rubrics further serve as process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories. Experiments show that evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.

AI.tldr: SkillCoach introduces self-evolving process rubrics for evaluating LLM agent skill-use along four dimensions (selection, following, composition, reflection), distinguishing process quality from accidental task success. The evolved rubrics improve evaluation quality and serve as supervision for training trajectory selection, outperforming outcome-only filtering.
AI.motivation: In realistic skill repositories, overlapping skills cause agents to select distractors, skip steps, compose workflows incorrectly, or omit checks. Final verifier success is too coarse — agents can pass via trial-and-error while exhibiting poor skill-use. There is a need for fine-grained, process-level evaluation and training signals that distinguish genuine skill mastery from accidental success.
AI.method: SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real agent rollouts, evaluating trajectories across four dimensions: (1) skill selection, (2) skill following, (3) skill composition, and (4) skill-grounded reflection. The framework self-evolves rubrics iteratively and retains the external verifier as a separate outcome signal. Evolved rubrics then provide process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories.
AI.result: Evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy alone, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.
AI.conclusion: Process-level evaluation via self-evolving rubrics is both feasible and beneficial: it reveals nuanced skill-use failures that outcome-based metrics miss and yields higher-quality training data, ultimately strengthening LLM agent reliability in skill-rich environments.

title: Role-Aware Neural Convex Divergence Heads for Asymmetric Representation Learning
summary: Many representation learning problems involve directed relations, such as lexical entailment, sentence entailment, ontology hierarchy, and citation links. Standard Euclidean, cosine, and Mahalanobis heads are symmetric, while generic neural scorers can model directionality but provide limited geometric structure. This paper proposes a role-aware neural convex divergence head for asymmetric representation learning. The head applies source- and target-role projections before evaluating an input-convex neural Bregman divergence, yielding a nonnegative structured score in the role-projected space. We characterize its projected-space identity, source-role convexity, directional-gap decomposition, and Hessian-based local curvature. Experiments on lexical, sentence, ontology, and directed graph benchmarks compare symmetric distances, unstructured asymmetric scorers, order/hyperbolic baselines, plain ICNN-Bregman heads, and the proposed role-aware variant. Across ten random seeds on the main semantic and ontology benchmarks, role-aware projections consistently improve directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads while preserving zero observed negative divergence rate. The results also identify a boundary case: on large fixed-feature citation prediction, specialized symmetric or hyperbolic baselines remain stronger in ranking accuracy. Overall, the proposed head is best understood as a structured and interpretable plug-in distance module for tasks where directional relations matter.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a role-aware neural convex divergence head for asymmetric representation learning, which applies source/target projections before an input-convex neural Bregman divergence, consistently improving directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads on semantic and ontology benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard symmetric distance heads (Euclidean, cosine, Mahalanobis) cannot model directed relations like lexical entailment or ontology hierarchies, while generic neural scorers lack geometric interpretability. There is a need for a structured, asymmetric distance module with clear geometric properties.
AI.method: The authors propose a role-aware neural convex divergence head combining: (1) source-role and target-role projections that embed inputs into a shared space, and (2) an input-convex neural network (ICNN) that computes a Bregman divergence over the projected representations. The framework is analyzed through projected-space identity, source-role convexity, directional-gap decomposition, and Hessian-based local curvature properties.
AI.result: Across ten random seeds on semantic and ontology benchmarks, role-aware projections consistently improve directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads while maintaining zero negative divergence rate. However, on large fixed-feature citation prediction tasks, specialized symmetric or hyperbolic baselines still outperform in ranking accuracy, revealing a boundary condition.
AI.conclusion: The role-aware neural convex divergence head serves as a structured, interpretable plug-in distance module best suited for tasks where directional relations are central, though it may not replace specialized symmetric/hyperbolic methods on all large-scale fixed-feature problems.

title: HULAT2 at MER-TRANS 2026: Governed Multi-Agent Simplification for Spanish Easy-to-Read Generation
summary: This paper describes the participation of HULAT2-UC3M in the Spanish track of MER-TRANS 2026, a shared task on multilingual Easy-to-Read translation. Three fully automatic Spanish runs were submitted. RUN1 and RUN2 used a LangGraph-based multi-agent workflow combining Gemini 2.5 Flash and RigoChat-7B-v2, parallel generation strategies, internal quality signals, Event-Condition-Action routing, controlled editing and traceable decisions. RUN1 used the base workflow, while RUN2 activated an additional lexical-support layer based on a glossary and lexical resources. RUN3 was a RigoChat-based generate-evaluate-regenerate baseline with prompt engineering and LoRA-based adaptation. The official leaderboard reports BLEU-Orig, BLEU-Gold, SARI and BERTScore. During development, additional internal signals were also inspected, including semantic fidelity, readability, lexical simplicity, syntactic clarity and factual consistency. According to official SARI, RUN1 was the best HULAT2 run, with 44.0543 points, followed by RUN2 with 43.1049 and RUN3 with 38.5136. These results indicate that, in this task setting, signal-guided multi-agent routing outperformed the linear regeneration baseline. They also show that adding lexical support did not automatically improve reference-based scores. Further segment-level and document-level analysis are required to assess readability, factual consistency and user-oriented adequacy.

AI.tldr: The paper presents HULAT2-UC3M's three submissions to the MER-TRANS 2026 Spanish Easy-to-Read translation task. The best-performing system (RUN1, SARI 44.05) used a LangGraph-based multi-agent workflow with signal-guided routing, outperforming both a lexical-augmented variant (RUN2, SARI 43.10) and a generate-evaluate-regenerate baseline (RUN3, SARI 38.51).
AI.motivation: Participation in the MER-TRANS 2026 shared task on multilingual Easy-to-Read (E2R) translation, aiming to automatically simplify Spanish texts while preserving meaning, with an emphasis on exploring whether multi-agent orchestration and internal quality signals can improve over linear regeneration approaches.
AI.method: Three fully automatic Spanish systems were submitted: (1) RUN1 — a LangGraph multi-agent workflow using Gemini 2.5 Flash and RigoChat-7B-v2 with parallel generation, Event-Condition-Action routing, controlled editing, and traceable decisions; (2) RUN2 — same as RUN1 but with an additional lexical-support layer (glossary + lexical resources); (3) RUN3 — a RigoChat-based generate-evaluate-regenerate baseline with prompt engineering and LoRA adaptation. Internal signals monitored included semantic fidelity, readability, lexical simplicity, syntactic clarity, and factual consistency.
AI.result: Official SARI scores: RUN1 = 44.0543, RUN2 = 43.1049, RUN3 = 38.5136. Signal-guided multi-agent routing (RUN1) significantly outperformed the linear regeneration baseline (RUN3). Adding lexical support (RUN2) did not improve reference-based metrics and slightly degraded SARI.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent routing guided by internal quality signals is more effective than a linear generate-evaluate-regenerate pipeline for E2R translation in this task setting. Lexical support layers do not automatically yield better reference-based scores. Further segment- and document-level analysis is needed to assess readability, factual consistency, and user-oriented adequacy beyond automatic metrics.

title: Spec-AUF: Accept-Until-Fail Training under Train-Inference Misalignment for Masked Block Drafters
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting a block of tokens that the target model verifies left-to-right, committing only the longest accepted prefix. Block (DLM-style) drafters predict the whole block in parallel, which is fast but trained with a full-block cross-entropy that supervises every position against the gold continuation -- even though inference discards every token after the first rejection. Recent acceptance-aware objectives patch this by reweighting the full-block loss; we instead use teacher-forced learning as a motivation for how supervision should concentrate on the accepted prefix. A mask-only block drafter has no input-side channel for gold-prefix conditioning, so AUF approximates that prefix-sensitive supervision on the loss side by keeping the cross-entropy support only through the drafter's first predicted failure. AUF is a single, detached change to the CE support -- no auxiliary objective, no verifier rollouts, and no change to the inference pipeline or the exactness contract. Within fixed drafter backbones and serving settings on Qwen3-8B, AUF raises the DFlash drafter's average emitted length $τ$, averaged over six benchmarks, from 2.40 to 2.61, with a gain on every benchmark, and transfers to Domino's two-branch head (2.56 to 2.68). Two findings sharpen the picture: the decay-only baseline reaches higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse, and on DFlash, once AUF truncates the support, the standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.

AI.tldr: AUF (Accepted Until Failure) improves block drafters for speculative decoding by truncating the cross-entropy loss support at the first predicted rejection, aligning training supervision with the inference-time acceptance behavior — yielding consistent gains in emitted length across benchmarks without changing the inference pipeline.
AI.motivation: Standard block drafters are trained with full-block cross-entropy that supervises all positions uniformly, but at inference time, only the prefix up to the first rejection is used. This misalignment wastes training signal on tokens that will be discarded. Recent acceptance-aware objectives try to fix this via reweighting; this paper instead proposes directly truncating supervision to match the accepted prefix, motivated by teacher-forced learning principles.
AI.method: AUF modifies the cross-entropy loss support for mask-only block drafters (like DFlash): it identifies the first position where the drafter's predicted token differs from the gold token, and truncates the loss to only supervise positions up to that failure point. This is a single, detached change — no auxiliary objectives, no verifier rollouts, no inference pipeline changes. The method also extends to two-branch architectures like Domino.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B across six benchmarks, AUF raises DFlash's average emitted length τ from 2.40 to 2.61 (gains on every benchmark) and improves Domino from 2.56 to 2.68. A decay-only baseline paradoxically achieves higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse. Once AUF truncates the support, standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.
AI.conclusion: Training supervision for block drafters should concentrate on the accepted prefix rather than the full block. AUF provides a minimal, effective implementation of this principle, and its success suggests that token accuracy on the full block is not a reliable proxy for decoding performance — prefix-aligned training matters more.

title: Denser $\neq$ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training
summary: Continual post-training enables foundation models to acquire new knowledge while preserving existing capabilities. Recent work suggests that on-policy learning can mitigate forgetting, with on-policy self-distillation emerging as a particularly attractive approach. In this work, we revisit this optimistic view through self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO). Our experiments show that SDPO can accelerate in-domain specialization when teacher signals are stable and well aligned, but it struggles to generalize to out-of-distribution scenarios. In continual post-training, SDPO exhibits stronger forgetting and can even collapse, whereas on-policy reinforcement learning methods such as GRPO adapt more conservatively and better preserve prior capabilities. Further analyses reveal that denser self-distillation induces larger drift in both parameter space and response space, and can amplify high-frequency formatting artifacts through a self-reinforcing teacher--student loop. These findings suggest that on-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning. Dense self-distillation can accelerate specialization when teacher targets are stable and token-level supervision is reliable, but it should not be treated as a default stabilizer for continual post-training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Moenupa/SDPO-CL.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the optimistic view of on-policy self-distillation for continual post-training. Through experiments with Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO), the authors show that while SDPO accelerates in-domain specialization under stable teacher signals, it causes stronger forgetting and even collapse in continual settings. Denser self-distillation induces larger parameter/response drift and amplifies formatting artifacts via a self-reinforcing loop. The conclusion: on-policy data alone is insufficient, and dense self-distillation should not be a default stabilizer for continual learning.
AI.motivation: Recent work has suggested that on-policy learning, particularly on-policy self-distillation, can mitigate catastrophic forgetting during continual post-training of foundation models. The authors seek to rigorously test this optimistic view and determine whether self-distillation truly serves as a reliable stabilizer or whether it introduces hidden failure modes.
AI.method: The authors employ Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) as their primary framework, contrasting it with on-policy reinforcement learning methods like GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). They conduct controlled experiments in continual post-training settings, analyzing parameter-space drift, response-space drift, and high-frequency formatting artifacts. They examine both in-domain specialization and out-of-distribution generalization, and investigate the effects of distillation density on model stability.
AI.result: SDPO accelerates in-domain specialization when teacher signals are stable and well-aligned. However, in continual post-training, SDPO exhibits stronger forgetting and can collapse, whereas GRPO adapts more conservatively and preserves prior capabilities. Denser self-distillation causes larger drift in both parameter and response spaces and amplifies high-frequency formatting artifacts through a self-reinforcing teacher-student loop.
AI.conclusion: On-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning. Dense self-distillation can accelerate specialization when teacher targets are stable and token-level supervision is reliable, but it should not be treated as a default stabilizer for continual post-training. More conservative on-policy RL methods like GRPO offer better preservation of prior capabilities.

title: Know Your Source: A Public Knowledge Store for Media Background Checks
summary: LLM-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is increasingly used for automated fact-checking (AFC) and related tasks. By grounding LLM outputs in retrieved evidence, RAG-based systems provide transparent justifications while allowing external information to be updated independently of the underlying model. However, existing approaches often assume retrieved evidence is reliable, although real-world information may be conflicting, outdated, and can originate from unreliable or biased sources. Recent work on *source-critical reasoning* addresses this challenge through media background checks (MBCs) (Schlichtkrull, 2024), which assess the credibility of evidence sources to support downstream fact verification. However, generating MBCs relies on costly proprietary search APIs, limiting reproducibility. To mitigate this issue, we introduce MEDIAREF, a publicly available knowledge store of web-sourced documents that enables reproducible, low-cost evaluation of MBC generation across 200 media sources. We describe a reproducible methodology for constructing and updating the collection, assess widely used LLMs on the MBC generation task, and demonstrate that MEDIAREF supports higher-quality MBC generation through both automatic and qualitative evaluation.

AI.tldr: MEDIAREF is a publicly available knowledge store enabling reproducible, low-cost evaluation of media background check (MBC) generation for source-critical reasoning in retrieval-augmented fact-checking systems, addressing reliance on costly proprietary APIs.
AI.motivation: RAG-based fact-checking systems assume retrieved evidence is reliable, but real-world sources may be conflicting, outdated, or biased. Source-critical reasoning via MBCs addresses this, but current methods rely on expensive proprietary search APIs, limiting reproducibility. There is a need for a reproducible, low-cost, publicly available resource for evaluating MBC generation.
AI.method: The authors introduce MEDIAREF, a publicly available knowledge store of web-sourced documents covering 200 media sources. They describe a reproducible methodology for constructing and updating the collection, and evaluate widely used LLMs on the MBC generation task using both automatic and qualitative metrics.
AI.result: MEDIAREF supports higher-quality MBC generation compared to baselines, as demonstrated through both automatic and qualitative evaluation. It provides a reproducible, low-cost alternative to proprietary search APIs for source-critical reasoning.
AI.conclusion: MEDIAREF enables reproducible and cost-effective evaluation of MBC generation, advancing source-critical reasoning for automated fact-checking by providing open access to structured knowledge about media source credibility.

title: Set Diffusion: Interpolating Token Orderings Between Autoregression and Diffusion for Fast and Flexible Decoding
comment: ICML 2026. We provide the code at https://github.com/kuleshov-group/setdlms
summary: Discrete diffusion models have steadily improved in quality relative to autoregressive (AR) models. However, these models are normally constrained to fixed-length generation and do not support key-value (KV) caching. Block diffusion partially bridges diffusion and AR by generating token blocks left-to-right, but its fixed-size sequential blocks limit decoding flexibility and parallelism. Here, we present a new class of language models, set diffusion, comprised of (i) a likelihood parameterization that factorizes over flexible-position, flexible-length token sets and (ii) a set-causal diffusion architecture that supports KV cache updates after every inference step. By factorizing over token sets instead of fixed-size blocks, tokens can be decoded in arbitrarily-ordered sets, including sliding-window sets, enabling faster inference and support for any-order decoding. Set diffusion achieves better speed-quality tradeoffs on mathematical reasoning, summarization, and unconditional generation compared to prior diffusion language models while offering stronger infilling performance than block diffusion. We provide the code, along with the model weights and blog post on the project page: https://m-arriola.com/setdlms/

AI.tldr: Set diffusion introduces a new language model class that factorizes over flexible-position, flexible-length token sets with a set-causal architecture supporting KV caching, enabling arbitrary-order decoding (including sliding-window) with better speed-quality tradeoffs than prior diffusion LMs and stronger infilling than block diffusion.
AI.motivation: Discrete diffusion models are constrained to fixed-length generation and lack KV caching support. Block diffusion partially addresses this via left-to-right sequential blocks, but its fixed-size blocks limit decoding flexibility and parallelism. The authors aim to overcome these limitations with a more flexible set-based formulation.
AI.method: The method comprises two components: (1) A likelihood parameterization that factorizes over token sets with flexible positions and flexible lengths, rather than over fixed-size blocks; (2) A set-causal diffusion architecture that enables KV cache updates after every inference step. Tokens are decoded in arbitrarily-ordered sets (e.g., sliding-window sets), supporting any-order generation.
AI.result: Set diffusion achieves superior speed-quality tradeoffs on mathematical reasoning, summarization, and unconditional generation compared to prior diffusion language models, and offers stronger infilling performance than block diffusion.
AI.conclusion: Set diffusion represents a new class of language models that combines the strengths of diffusion and autoregressive approaches, overcoming key limitations of both discrete diffusion (fixed-length, no KV caching) and block diffusion (fixed-size sequential blocks) through flexible set-based factorization and set-causal architecture.

title: The Future of NLP may not be at NLP Conferences: Scholarly Migration Patterns in Natural Language Processing
summary: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has traditionally been published in its core disciplinary venues like ACL. However, advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) has led to a blurring of the disciplinary lines between NLP and general Machine Learning (ML), with authors regularly publishing in venues from both fields. Here, we ask whether the disciplinary center of gravity is shifting. Using NLP research published from 2010 to 2026 and studies of both established and new authors, we find that a migration is taking place.
