First, comparing the pre- and post-LLM eras, established authors lost 19.2pp of share at flagship *ACL main-conference tracks while gaining 14.8pp in the newer Findings tracks, and general ML venues rose 8.6pp, even when adjusting for parallel growth in the fields. Second, among newer authors who debut with at least three first-author NLP-topic papers, the share whose work appears mostly at *ACL venues fell from 84% (2019) to 74% (2024), while the share appearing mostly at general ML venues rose from 5% to 21%. Using causal inference techniques, we estimate that these general ML venues confer a significant citation premium, which influences venue selection. Together, these results point to a significant shift in where NLP research is published.

AI.tldr: NLP research is migrating away from traditional ACL venues toward general ML venues, driven partly by a citation premium at ML venues. Established authors lost ~19pp share at flagship ACL tracks while newer authors increasingly publish at ML venues (from 5% to 21%, 2019–2024).
AI.motivation: The blurring of disciplinary boundaries between NLP and general ML, accelerated by LLM advances, raises the question of whether the center of gravity for NLP research publication is shifting away from traditional NLP venues.
AI.method: The authors analyze NLP publications from 2010–2026, examining both established and new authors across ACL and general ML venues. They track venue share changes pre- and post-LLM eras, cohort-level publication behavior of debut authors, and apply causal inference techniques to estimate the citation premium of general ML venues.
AI.result: Established authors lost 19.2 percentage points of share at flagship *ACL tracks while gaining 14.8pp in Findings tracks and 8.6pp at general ML venues. Among newer authors, those publishing mostly at ACL venues fell from 84% (2019) to 74% (2024), while those at ML venues rose from 5% to 21%. A significant citation premium at general ML venues was identified, influencing venue selection.
AI.conclusion: A significant and measurable shift is underway in where NLP research is published, with general ML venues gaining ground at the expense of traditional ACL venues, partially driven by citation incentives.

title: ContextSniper: AntTrail's Token-Efficient Code Memory for Repository-Level Program Repair
summary: Large language model agents can repair real repository issues, but they often spend large context budgets on whole-file reads, broad searches, and long terminal outputs where useful evidence is mixed with irrelevant code and logs. This paper presents ContextSniper, AntTrail's token-efficient code memory layer for repository-level program repair. As the coding specialization of AntTrail's broader agent memory engine, ContextSniper implements the Sniper feature for precision evidence selection: it retrieves candidate code and runtime evidence, ranks it with hybrid retrieval signals, filters long outputs through an intention-aware context gate, and returns compact evidence packets while preserving recoverable source context outside the prompt. We evaluate ContextSniper on SWE-bench Lite with OpenClaw and Claude Code, using 50 task runs per host-agent condition. ContextSniper reduces total token use by 51.5% and logged cost by 36.4% for OpenClaw, and reduces total token use by 38.9% and estimated cost by 27.3% for Claude Code. Submitted-resolution rates decrease slightly, from 26.0% to 24.0% for OpenClaw and from 32.0% to 30.0% for Claude Code. ContextSniper's pilot testing scripts are open-sourced at https://github.com/Calluking/ContextSniper

AI.tldr: ContextSniper is a token-efficient code memory layer that reduces LLM agent token usage in repository-level program repair by 39–52% with only a 2% drop in resolution rates, using precision evidence selection with hybrid retrieval and intention-aware context gating.
AI.motivation: LLM agents for program repair waste large context budgets on whole-file reads, broad searches, and verbose terminal outputs where relevant evidence is buried in irrelevant code and logs. This inefficiency increases cost and limits scalability.
AI.method: ContextSniper, part of the AntTrail agent memory engine, implements the Sniper feature with four components: (1) retrieval of candidate code and runtime evidence, (2) ranking via hybrid retrieval signals, (3) filtering long outputs through an intention-aware context gate, and (4) returning compact evidence packets while preserving recoverable source context externally. Evaluated on SWE-bench Lite with OpenClaw and Claude Code across 50 task runs per host-agent condition.
AI.result: ContextSniper reduces total token use by 51.5% and logged cost by 36.4% for OpenClaw; for Claude Code, token use drops 38.9% and estimated cost drops 27.3%. Resolution rates decrease marginally: OpenClaw from 26.0% to 24.0%, Claude Code from 32.0% to 30.0%.
AI.conclusion: ContextSniper demonstrates that precision evidence selection can dramatically cut token consumption and cost in LLM-based program repair with minimal impact on repair efficacy, representing a practical efficiency improvement for repository-level coding agents.

title: EHHN: An Event-driven Heterogeneous Hypergraph Network for Object-Centric Next Activity Prediction
summary: Next activity prediction helps service-oriented processes anticipate upcoming steps before delays, exceptions, or service-level risks occur. Most existing methods assume classical single-case event logs, whereas real service processes often involve events shared by multiple typed business objects. Object-centric event logs (OCELs) capture such interactions, but current predictors remain limited. Flattening-based approaches lose cross-object context, and native OCEL graph-based approaches encode multi-object events through pairwise relations. Existing models also do not jointly capture event-driven object state changes, inter-event timing, and global execution patterns. We propose EHHN, an Event-driven Heterogeneous Hypergraph Network for object-centric next activity prediction. EHHN represents each prediction prefix as a heterogeneous hypergraph, where event--object hyperedges bind retained co-participating objects and a lifecycle hyperedge groups the primary object's observed lifecycle events. Based on this representation, EHHN uses a dual-stream architecture in which a micro-spatial stream models event-driven object-state evolution and a macro-evolution stream captures temporal dynamics using retrieved global prototypes. The two streams are fused to predict the next activity. Experiments on four public OCEL benchmarks against nine baselines show that EHHN achieves the best accuracy and macro F1-score on all datasets, with improvements of up to 8.1 and 12.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines. Compared with the strongest OCEL-native graph baseline, EHHN also reduces peak GPU memory by up to 24 times. Code is available at https://github.com/chenkaitao1112/EHHN.

AI.tldr: EHHN proposes a heterogeneous hypergraph network for next activity prediction in object-centric event logs, using a dual-stream architecture (micro-spatial for object state evolution and macro-evolution for temporal dynamics with global prototypes), achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with up to 24× GPU memory reduction.
AI.motivation: Existing next activity prediction methods either flatten object-centric event logs (OCELs) losing cross-object context, or use native OCEL graph approaches limited to pairwise relations. No current method jointly captures event-driven object state changes, inter-event timing, and global execution patterns.
AI.method: EHHN represents prediction prefixes as heterogeneous hypergraphs with two hyperedge types: event-object hyperedges binding co-participating objects, and lifecycle hyperedges grouping the primary object's observed events. A dual-stream architecture processes these: a micro-spatial stream models event-driven object-state evolution, while a macro-evolution stream captures temporal dynamics via retrieved global prototypes. The streams are fused for final prediction.
AI.result: On four public OCEL benchmarks against nine baselines, EHHN achieved best accuracy and macro F1-score on all datasets, with improvements up to 8.1 and 12.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines. Peak GPU memory reduced up to 24× compared to the strongest OCEL-native graph baseline.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous hypergraph representations with dual-stream micro-macro modeling effectively capture the complex relational and temporal dynamics in object-centric processes, outperforming both flattening-based and pairwise graph-based approaches significantly in both accuracy and efficiency.

title: Language Models as Measurement Apparatus for Culture
comment: Accepted to the Big Picture workshop co-located with ACL 2026. This version expands the camera-ready (adding Fig. 3 and section 6.3, as well as correcting minor typos) in Proceedings of The Big Picture v2: Crafting a Research Narrative, pp. 131--143, San Diego, CA, USA. Association for Computational Linguistics
summary: Language models are increasingly used to quantify cultural phenomena, but what makes such measurement distinctively cultural? This paper argues that NLP work on culture is a material-discursive practice: the apparatus -- model, data, annotation, evaluation -- participates in constituting the cultural reality it measures, rather than passively recording it. Drawing on Karen Barad's concept of the agential cut -- the contingent boundary between phenomenon and instrument -- I show that the apparatus's substantive design choices draw such boundaries, and that the boundary is entangled from the start because language models have already internalized much of the cultural material they measure. I illustrate this through three case studies on television and film dialogue (measuring structure, interaction, and deviation) and three examinations of the apparatus itself (erasure of cultural markers, attunement to historical material, and agency in an agentic workflow). This big picture analysis proposes a research program that is theory-driven, empirically rigorous, and culturally contingent, treating each agential cut as a conscious commitment, at once methodological and ethical.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that NLP-based cultural measurement is a "material-discursive practice" where the apparatus (model, data, annotation, evaluation) actively shapes the cultural reality it purports to measure. Drawing on Barad's "agential cut," the author illustrates through case studies on film/TV dialogue that design choices create contingent boundaries between instrument and phenomenon, and that language models are always already entangled with the cultural material they analyze.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by a need to theorize what makes cultural measurement via NLP distinctively cultural. Rather than treating language models as neutral instruments that passively record pre-existing cultural phenomena, the author seeks to expose how methodological choices in model design, data curation, and annotation practices co-constitute the very cultural realities under investigation.
AI.method: The paper employs a theoretical-philosophical framework grounded in Karen Barad's agential realism, specifically the concept of the "agential cut." It presents three illustrative case studies on television and film dialogue (measuring structure, interaction, and deviation) alongside three reflexive examinations of the apparatus (erasure of cultural markers, attunement to historical material, and agency in agentic workflows). The analysis is conceptual rather than experimental.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that: (1) design choices in the NLP apparatus draw contingent boundaries between phenomenon and instrument; (2) language models are always already entangled with cultural material, undermining any claim to objective exteriority; (3) cultural markers can be erased, historical material can be differently attuned to, and agency operates within agentic workflows — all shaped by the apparatus. The paper proposes a research program that is theory-driven, empirically rigorous, and culturally contingent.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that every "agential cut" in NLP-based cultural measurement is simultaneously a methodological and ethical commitment. It calls for treating these cuts as conscious, reflexive choices and proposes a research program that integrates theoretical sophistication with empirical rigor while remaining attuned to cultural contingency.

title: EPnG: Adaptive Expert Prune-and-Grow for Parameter-Efficient MoE Fine-tuning
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale efficiently but remain costly to adapt due to redundant experts and uniform parameter allocation. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA ignore MoE routing dynamics, leading to suboptimal resource use. We propose EPnG, an adaptive prune-and-grow framework that reallocates LoRA capacity based on expert importance derived from router gate probabilities. EPnG prunes under-utilized experts and expands high-importance experts via rank growth with orthogonal initialization, while maintaining a fixed parameter budget. Across OLMoE and Qwen1.5-MoE, EPnG consistently outperforms LoRA under the same budget and achieves performance comparable to full fine-tuning while updating only 0.55%-0.72% of parameters (up to 140x-180x fewer). These results demonstrate that aligning PEFT with MoE routing yields a more effective and scalable fine-tuning strategy.

AI.tldr: EPnG is an adaptive prune-and-grow LoRA framework for Mixture-of-Experts models that reallocates capacity based on router-gate importance, outperforming LoRA and matching full fine-tuning while updating only 0.55–0.72% of parameters.
AI.motivation: MoE models suffer from redundant experts and uniform parameter allocation during fine-tuning. Existing PEFT methods like LoRA ignore MoE routing dynamics, leading to suboptimal resource utilization. There is a need for a method that aligns fine-tuning capacity with actual expert importance.
AI.method: EPnG uses router gate probabilities to derive expert importance scores, then adaptively prunes LoRA modules from under-utilized experts and grows (expands rank with orthogonal initialization) LoRA modules on high-importance experts, all within a fixed total parameter budget.
AI.result: On OLMoE and Qwen1.5-MoE benchmarks, EPnG consistently outperforms standard LoRA under identical budgets and achieves performance comparable to full fine-tuning while updating only 0.55%–0.72% of parameters (up to 140×–180× fewer).
AI.conclusion: Aligning PEFT strategies with MoE routing dynamics via adaptive prune-and-grow yields a more effective and scalable fine-tuning strategy, matching full fine-tuning quality at a fraction of the parameter cost.

title: Will Scaling Improve Social Simulation with LLMs?
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) social simulations are a promising research method, but they are not yet faithful enough to be adopted widely. In this work, we investigate whether the current scaling paradigm in language modeling is likely to close these gaps, or whether simulation fidelity is orthogonal to general capabilities and therefore deserving of more research attention. We use scaling laws to study the relationship between LLMs' compute scale, general capability benchmarks, and the fidelity of social simulation in three representative sub-domains: opinion modeling, behavioral simulation, and longitudinal forecasting. Surprisingly, we discover strong compute scaling in all three settings, using a suite of 85 transformer LLMs with the Qwen3 architecture pre-trained on the DCLM web text corpus under fixed-compute budgets from $10^{18}$ to $10^{20}$ FLOPs. Then we evaluate 35 larger and more capable open-weight models up to 70B parameters, allowing us to predict downstream accuracy from loss. This reveals that the majority of behavioral and opinion simulation tasks will rapidly improve with scale, particularly when they involve populations that are well-represented in English web corpora. Longitudinal forecasting and underrepresented opinions scale more slowly, especially when they are less correlated with general knowledge and reasoning benchmarks like MMLU. In behavior simulation, scaling fails to improve model calibration with human cognitive biases like risk aversion, as well as human heuristics like learning correlated rewards from related tasks. On these tasks, even fine-tuned models fail to noticeably scale up performance from 0.5B to 8B parameters. Taken together, we conclude that scale will improve social simulations in most settings, but outliers exist, and improvements will be less reliable in low-resource domains.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether scaling laws in LLMs improve social simulation fidelity across three domains (opinion modeling, behavioral simulation, longitudinal forecasting). Using 85 Qwen3 models and 35 larger open-weight models, the authors find strong compute scaling in most tasks, but scaling fails to improve calibration on human cognitive biases and forecasting in underrepresented domains. They conclude scale helps broadly but leaves important gaps requiring dedicated research.
AI.motivation: LLM-based social simulations are promising but not yet faithful enough for widespread adoption. The authors aim to determine whether simply scaling models (the dominant paradigm) will close fidelity gaps, or whether simulation fidelity is orthogonal to general capabilities and thus requires independent research attention.
AI.method: The study employs scaling laws methodology across two model suites: (1) 85 transformer LLMs with the Qwen3 architecture pre-trained on DCLM corpus under fixed compute budgets from 10^18 to 10^20 FLOPs, and (2) 35 larger open-weight models up to 70B parameters. They evaluate social simulation fidelity across three sub-domains — opinion modeling, behavioral simulation, and longitudinal forecasting — and use downstream accuracy predicted from loss to assess scaling trends.
AI.result: Strong compute scaling emerges in all three settings. Most behavioral and opinion simulation tasks improve rapidly with scale, especially for populations well-represented in English web corpora. However, longitudinal forecasting and underrepresented opinions scale more slowly, particularly when weakly correlated with benchmarks like MMLU. Critically, scaling fails to improve model calibration on human cognitive biases (e.g., risk aversion) and heuristics (e.g., learning correlated rewards), with even fine-tuned models showing negligible gains from 0.5B to 8B parameters.
AI.conclusion: Scaling will improve social simulations in most settings, but outliers persist. Improvements will be less reliable in low-resource domains, and certain human-like cognitive biases remain resistant to scaling. These gaps merit dedicated research attention beyond the scaling paradigm.

title: A-TMA: Decoupling State-Aware Memory Failures in Long-Term Agent Memory
summary: Long term memory lets LLM agents act as persistent assistants, but user facts change. A useful memory system must know what is true now, what used to be true, and what changed. We study \emph{ghost memory}, a state coordination failure in which old, current, and transition facts coexist in the memory bank, remain mixed during retrieval, and mislead the answer model. We argue that memory systems should be understood and optimized from three levels: bank maintenance, retrieval, and answer time resolution. We propose ATMA, a state aware overlay for existing memory systems. ATMA keeps superseded and transition records in the bank, builds evidence packets for the query's requested state view, and exposes current, historical, and transition labels to QA. We further call for decoupled evaluation of bank, retrieval, and answer level failures, since final QA accuracy can hide where ghost memory occurs. To make this failure measurable, we build LTP (LoCoMo Temporal Plus), a conflict heavy benchmark for ghost memory, and evaluate on LoCoMo for long conversation generalization. On LTP, Graphiti+ATMA improves conflict accuracy by 0.240 absolute over Graphiti. On LoCoMo, Graphiti+ATMA raises temporal F1 from 0.0295 to 0.1705. The gains are host dependent, but they indicate that explicit state roles can reduce memory failures hidden by final QA accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper studies "ghost memory" — a failure mode in LLM agent memory systems where outdated, current, and transitional facts coexist and confuse retrieval/QA. The authors propose ATMA, a state-aware overlay that labels records by temporal state (current, historical, transition) and builds evidence packets per query. They also introduce LTP, a conflict-heavy benchmark, showing significant accuracy gains when ATMA is added to existing memory systems like Graphiti.
AI.motivation: LLM agents need persistent long-term memory, but user facts evolve over time. Existing memory systems suffer from "ghost memory": a state coordination failure where old, current, and transitional facts mix during retrieval and mislead the answer model. Current evaluation also obscures where failures occur (bank, retrieval, or answer level), necessitating both a solution and decoupled evaluation.
AI.method: The authors propose ATMA (A State-Aware Overlay) operating at three levels: (1) bank maintenance — retaining superseded and transition records with explicit state labels; (2) retrieval — building evidence packets tailored to the query's requested state view (current, historical, transition); (3) answer-time resolution — exposing state labels to the QA model. They also construct LTP (LoCoMo Temporal Plus), a conflict-heavy benchmark for measuring ghost memory, and introduce decoupled evaluation across bank, retrieval, and answer levels.
AI.result: On the LTP benchmark, Graphiti+ATMA improved conflict accuracy by 0.240 absolute over Graphiti alone. On the LoCoMo long-conversation benchmark, Graphiti+ATMA raised temporal F1 from 0.0295 to 0.1705. Gains are host-system-dependent but demonstrate that explicit state roles reduce memory failures otherwise hidden by final QA accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Memory systems should be understood and optimized across three levels: bank maintenance, retrieval, and answer-time resolution. ATMA shows that explicit state-aware labeling and evidence packet construction can meaningfully reduce ghost memory failures. Decoupled evaluation is essential, as aggregate QA metrics mask where failures originate.

title: Single-Channel EEG-Based Cognitive Load Assessment in Online Learning: A Hybrid Deep Learning Approach
summary: Monitoring cognitive load during online learning could help instructors identify content that learners find difficult, but remote settings remove the visual cues that support this judgement in a classroom. We study whether a single-channel, consumer-grade EEG device (the NeuroSky MindWave Mobile 2) can distinguish easy from difficult educational-video content, using the publicly available dataset of Wang et al. [24] (ten learners, one excluded for excessive noise, leaving nine). We implement a hybrid CNN+LSTM+Attention model that combines the raw waveform with band-power features. In a within-subject setting, the model reaches up to 78.5% accuracy, compared with 55% for conventional feature-based classifiers; regularization (dropout and L2) closes the large gap between training and validation accuracy that we observe without it, keeping validation accuracy stable at roughly 68-73%. We are deliberately cautious about these numbers: with only nine subjects, within-subject evaluation is optimistic, and we argue that subject-independent evaluation -- in which no learner appears in both training and test data -- should be the standard for this task. To that end we release a reproducible evaluation pipeline. We frame the work as a feasibility study rather than a deployable system, and pair it with an open, notebook-based tool that records EEG, runs inference, and visualizes estimated cognitive load as a heatmap over the video timeline to help educators locate potentially challenging segments.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether a low-cost, single-channel consumer EEG device can detect cognitive load differences when learners watch easy vs. difficult educational videos. Using a hybrid deep learning model (CNN+LSTM+Attention), they achieve up to 78.5% within-subject classification accuracy on a public 9-subject dataset, but emphasize that subject-independent evaluation should be the standard for this task and caution against overinterpretation given the small sample size.
AI.motivation: In remote/online learning environments, instructors lose the visual cues (facial expressions, body language) traditionally used to gauge learner difficulty. An unobtrusive, affordable physiological sensing approach using consumer EEG could help automatically identify challenging educational content, enabling instructors to adapt materials accordingly.
AI.method: The authors use the NeuroSky MindWave Mobile 2 (single-channel, dry-electrode, consumer-grade EEG) and the public dataset from Wang et al. with 9 subjects after exclusion. They implement a hybrid CNN+LSTM+Attention architecture that fuses raw waveform data with band-power features. Regularization (dropout + L2) is applied to close train-validation accuracy gaps. They also develop an open, notebook-based tool that records EEG, runs inference, and visualizes estimated cognitive load as a heatmap over video timelines for educators.
AI.result: Within-subject classification accuracy reaches 78.5% with the hybrid model vs. ~55% for conventional feature-based classifiers. Regularization stabilizes validation accuracy at approximately 68-73% and mitigates overfitting. However, the authors stress these results are optimistic due to the small sample (n=9) and within-subject evaluation design.
AI.conclusion: Consumer-grade single-channel EEG shows promise as a feasibility-level tool for distinguishing cognitive load during video-based learning, but subject-independent evaluation should become the standard benchmark. The work is framed as a feasibility study paired with a reproducible pipeline and an educator-facing visualization tool, rather than a deployable system.

title: Audio-Based Understanding of Audiobook Narration Appeal
summary: Narration is central to the audiobook listening experience, shaping how listeners engage with and understand the content. This work explores how narration qualities shape an audiobook's appeal, noting that their effects can vary by genre, title, and audience. We extract vocal and acoustic features (e.g., tone, pace, loudness) from LibriVox using pre-trained audio models and analyse their relationship with consumption data (specifically, view-rate) and their interplay with genre and title. Despite limited consumption data, we find that acoustic information alone has a robust association with appeal, even after accounting for title effects. We further validate these findings using more nuanced proprietary engagement metrics. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic computational study linking narration qualities, genre, title, and audiobook consumption, highlighting the potential of data-driven insights to improve audiobook personalisation and narrator casting.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic computational study linking acoustic features of audiobook narration (tone, pace, loudness) to listener consumption metrics, finding that narration qualities robustly predict appeal even after controlling for title effects, with implications for personalization and narrator casting.
AI.motivation: Narration is central to the audiobook experience, yet no prior work has systematically and computationally studied how specific vocal and acoustic narration qualities influence audiobook consumption and appeal across different genres, titles, and audiences.
AI.method: The authors extract vocal and acoustic features (tone, pace, loudness) from LibriVox audiobooks using pre-trained audio models. These features are then analyzed for their relationship with consumption data (view-rate), examining interactive effects with genre and title. Findings are further validated using proprietary engagement metrics from a commercial platform.
AI.result: Acoustic information alone shows a robust association with audiobook appeal, significant even after statistically controlling for title-level effects. The relationship between narration qualities and appeal is moderated by genre and title, and results are corroborated by finer-grained proprietary engagement data.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates the feasibility and value of using computational audio analysis to understand audiobook consumption, opening avenues for data-driven improvements in audiobook personalization systems and more informed narrator casting decisions.

title: Atomic Task Graph: A Unified Framework for Agentic Planning and Execution
summary: LLM-based agents have shown strong potential for solving complex multi-step tasks, yet existing performance improvements often rely on either scaling to larger backbone models or task-specific fine-tuning. The former incurs substantial computational costs, while the latter typically generalizes poorly across different tasks. Although prompt-based control is training-free and broadly applicable, existing methods still leave input-output dependencies between subtasks implicit in textual trajectories, making verified intermediate results difficult to reuse. To address these limitations, we propose Atomic Task Graph (ATG), a unified control framework for planning and execution. Specifically, ATG maintains an explicit graph to expose dependencies and support reuse. During planning, it recursively decomposes a high-level task into subtasks, forming a sequence of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) whose evolution can be traced. During execution, the dependencies exposed by ATG allow independent branches to be executed in parallel, thereby improving execution efficiency. When failures are detected, ATG leverages the graph evolution history to localize the error source and repair only the affected region, preserving validated regions unchanged. Experiments show that ATG consistently outperforms strong baselines in success rate and execution efficiency across three interactive benchmarks using only 7B-8B backbones.

AI.tldr: ATG is a graph-based control framework that decomposes tasks into directed acyclic graphs, enabling parallel execution, result reuse, and localized failure repair, achieving strong performance with only 7B-8B models.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents either rely on costly large models or task-specific fine-tuning that generalizes poorly. Prompt-based methods are training-free but leave subtask dependencies implicit, hindering reuse of verified intermediate results.
AI.method: ATG explicitly maintains a task graph as DAGs. During planning, it recursively decomposes high-level tasks into subtask DAGs with traceable evolution. During execution, independent branches run in parallel. Upon failure, it localizes errors via graph history and repairs only affected regions.
AI.result: ATG consistently outperforms strong baselines in success rate and execution efficiency across three interactive benchmarks, using only 7B-8B backbone models.
AI.conclusion: Explicit dependency modeling via ATG enables smaller LLMs to achieve superior multi-step task performance through parallel execution, intermediate result reuse, and targeted failure recovery.

title: Expander Sparse Autoencoders: Parameter-Efficient Dictionaries for Mechanistic Interpretability
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose internal activations of neural networks into sparse linear combinations of learned features by fitting an overcomplete dictionary $\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ with $m<n$, and inferring a sparse code $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ from $\mathbf{h}\approx\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$. This inference problem closely resembles the canonical setup of compressed sensing, but dense decoders requires $O(mn)$ learned values, which becomes costly at large feature counts. We introduce Expander SAEs: TopK SAEs whose decoder and tied encoder are supported on a left-$d$-regular expander mask with $d\ll m$, learning only $dn$ decoder values while keeping the sparse-coding problem $(m,n,k)$ fixed. The same structure reduces storage and turns the matching-pursuit correlation step $\mathbf{W}^\top \mathbf{r}$ in OMP into an $O(dn)$ gather-and-reduce operation. Our experiments show that across Pythia-70M/160M, Qwen2.5-3B, and Llama-3.2-1B residual-stream activations, varying $d$ traces a consistent storage--fidelity frontier, and that at the most compressed modern-LM setting, Qwen2.5-3B with $d=7$ uses $293\times$ fewer learned decoder values than the full dense decoder while retaining $84$% of dense CE-loss recovered. Control experiments show that the improved storage--fidelity tradeoff is driven by sparse, diverse decoder support structure rather than by fewer learned decoder values, and that when sparse and dense decoders are compared at matched parameter count, part of the remaining gap comes from encoder amortisation. On the theoretical side, we show that expansion and column flatness are sufficient for identifiability of noiseless $k$-sparse codes, and we derive complementary sufficient conditions under which OMP recovers the support exactly.

AI.tldr: Expander SAEs replace the dense decoder of TopK sparse autoencoders with a sparse, expander-graph-structured decoder, dramatically reducing learned parameters (up to 293× fewer) while retaining ~84% of CE-loss recovery, and provide theoretical guarantees for sparse-code identifiability and OMP support recovery.
AI.motivation: Dense decoders in standard SAEs require O(mn) learned values, becoming prohibitively costly at large feature counts (n). The authors seek to reduce this parameter/storage cost while preserving the quality of sparse decomposition of neural network activations.
AI.method: The authors propose Expander SAEs, which constrain the decoder matrix W to a left-d-regular expander graph structure (d ≪ m), reducing learned values to O(dn). The encoder is tied to this sparse decoder. They also adapt Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP), turning the correlation step into an O(dn) gather-and-reduce operation. Experiments span Pythia-70M/160M, Qwen2.5-3B, and Llama-3.2-1B residual-stream activations, with control experiments isolating the effects of sparse structure vs. parameter count and encoder amortization. Theoretical results establish sufficient conditions (expansion and column flatness) for identifiability of k-sparse codes and for exact support recovery by OMP.
AI.result: Varying d traces a consistent storage–fidelity frontier across all tested models. At the most extreme setting (Qwen2.5-3B, d=7), Expander SAEs use 293× fewer decoder values than a dense decoder while recovering 84% of the dense model's CE-loss improvement. Control experiments reveal the fidelity gain is driven by sparse, diverse decoder support structure rather than merely fewer parameters, and that some residual gap vs. dense decoders stems from encoder amortization.
AI.conclusion: Expander SAEs offer a parameter-efficient, theoretically grounded alternative to dense SAEs, achieving a favorable storage–fidelity Pareto frontier. The approach highlights the importance of structured sparsity (expander graphs) over naive parameter reduction and opens directions for improving encoder design to close the remaining performance gap.

title: Visually Grounded Self-Reflection for Vision-Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Large vision-language models can reason over multimodal inputs by generating textual chains of thought (CoT). A key capability exhibited in CoT reasoning is self-reflection: revisiting earlier decisions and correcting previous errors. However, existing LVLMs often fail to properly attend to visual inputs during reflection, limiting their ability to translate feedback into grounded corrections, especially for out-of-distribution images. To address this issue, we propose a novel reinforcement learning training framework VRRL, with two components explicitly designed to elicit visually grounded self-reflection. First, we randomly mask trajectory prefixes during training to emphasize recovery from incorrect intermediate predictions rather than making early mistakes. Second, we introduce buffered roll-ins from an experience replay buffer to expose the model to diverse failure states that it must learn to correct. We evaluate our approach on visual grounding tasks involving tables and charts, as well as spatial navigation benchmarks. While off-the-shelf and conventionally fine-tuned models degrade substantially under distribution shift, our method substantially improves average out-of-distribution accuracy over standard RL and reflection-oriented fine-tuning baselines by using self-reflection effectively.

AI.tldr: VRRL is a reinforcement learning framework that improves visually-grounded self-reflection in LVLMs by masking trajectory prefixes and using buffered roll-ins from experience replay, yielding substantial out-of-distribution accuracy gains on visual grounding and spatial navigation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing large vision-language models (LVLMs) struggle to properly attend to visual inputs during chain-of-thought self-reflection, causing failures in translating feedback into grounded corrections—especially under distribution shift. The authors aim to explicitly elicit visually grounded self-reflection to improve robustness on out-of-distribution images.
AI.method: The VRRL (Visually-grounded Reflective Reinforcement Learning) framework introduces two components: (1) random masking of trajectory prefixes during training to force recovery from incorrect intermediate predictions rather than early mistakes, and (2) buffered roll-ins sampled from an experience replay buffer to expose the model to diverse failure states it must learn to correct.
AI.result: VRRL substantially improves average out-of-distribution accuracy over standard RL and reflection-oriented fine-tuning baselines on visual grounding tasks involving tables and charts, as well as spatial navigation benchmarks, where off-the-shelf and conventionally fine-tuned models degrade significantly.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly training LVLMs to perform visually grounded self-reflection via prefix masking and experience replay significantly enhances their ability to correct errors under distribution shift, outperforming both standard RL and existing reflection-oriented fine-tuning approaches.

title: OntoLearner: A Modular Python Library for Ontology Learning with Large Language Models
comment: 30 pages. Under review at Nature Communications. This version is reformatted with a different section structure; content is unchanged
summary: Ontology learning (OL) aims to automatically construct structured knowledge models from text, yet progress remains fragmented across methods, domains, and evaluation practices. Despite decades of research, OL lacks a shared infrastructure for systematic evaluation and ontology access. This absence has hindered progress and fragmented research, leaving the central challenges of OL largely unaddressed. We introduce OntoLearner, a modular, cross-domain, and first-of-its-kind framework that unifies ontology access, large language model (LLM)-driven learning pipelines, and standardized benchmarking. OntoLearner releases 180 machine-readable ontologies spanning 22 domains and provides pipeline-ready datasets with train/dev/test splits for three core OL tasks: term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relation extraction. Using this infrastructure, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of OL, evaluating 22 retrieval models and 12 LLMs across domains and tasks. The results converge on a finding that reframes the central challenge of OL: failure modes scale with ontological complexity rather than model size or architectural sophistication. The primary bottleneck is not model capability, but a structural mismatch between how models encode knowledge and how ontologies organize it. These findings establish that effective OL is reachable through the cross-domain, multi-task benchmarking enabled by OntoLearner. OntoLearner is open-source (MIT license) at https://github.com/sciknoworg/OntoLearner/.

AI.tldr: OntoLearner is an open-source framework unifying ontology access, LLM-driven learning pipelines, and standardized benchmarking for ontology learning. It releases 180 ontologies across 22 domains and evaluates 22 retrieval models and 12 LLMs, finding that the central challenge in OL is not model capability but a structural mismatch between how models encode knowledge and how ontologies organize it.
AI.motivation: Ontology learning research remains fragmented across methods, domains, and evaluation practices, lacking shared infrastructure for systematic evaluation and ontology access. This absence has hindered progress and left core challenges unaddressed.
AI.method: The authors introduce OntoLearner, a modular, cross-domain framework that provides: (1) 180 machine-readable ontologies across 22 domains, (2) pipeline-ready datasets with train/dev/test splits for term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relation extraction, and (3) a large-scale empirical evaluation of 22 retrieval models and 12 LLMs across these tasks and domains.
AI.result: The key finding reframes the central challenge of OL: failure modes scale with ontological complexity rather than model size or architectural sophistication. The primary bottleneck is a structural mismatch between how models encode knowledge and how ontologies organize it, not model capability per se.
AI.conclusion: Effective ontology learning is achievable through cross-domain, multi-task benchmarking enabled by OntoLearner. The framework establishes that addressing the structural mismatch between model knowledge encoding and ontological organization is the critical path forward for the field.

title: Do LLMs Truly Generalize in the Molecular Domain? A Perturbation-Based Analysis
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promise in molecular discovery, yet a gap remains between their probabilistic nature over discrete sequential tokens and the rigid topological constraints of chemical space. This raises the question of whether molecular LLMs can generalize beyond the local neighborhoods induced by their sequence-based representations. To systematically investigate this question, we introduce a Molecular Perturbation framework that generates syntax-valid structural variants of training molecules under controlled Graph Edit Distance (GED) to probe the manifold regularity of molecular LLMs. Our analysis shows that even a single edit can cause substantial performance drops on common molecular tasks, revealing a narrow local trust region and fragile sensitivity to structural changes. Since similar molecules tend to exhibit similar properties, In-Context Tuning (ICT), which anchors predictions on structurally similar molecules, offers a natural way to mitigate such fragility. Our experiments also examine whether ICT confers robustness under controlled structural perturbations, and the results suggest that it can partially expand the local trust region and offer a promising direction for stabilizing molecular LLMs against structural variation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether molecular LLMs can generalize beyond local sequence neighborhoods by introducing controlled structural perturbations via Graph Edit Distance (GED). Even single edits cause substantial performance drops, revealing fragile local trust regions. The authors propose In-Context Tuning (ICT) — anchoring predictions on structurally similar molecules — as a mitigation strategy that partially expands the local trust region.
AI.motivation: Molecular LLMs operate on discrete sequential token representations that may not respect the topological constraints of chemical space. There is an open question whether these models genuinely learn robust chemical structure-property relationships or merely memorize narrow local neighborhoods induced by their tokenization, motivating a systematic investigation of their manifold regularity under controlled structural perturbations.
AI.method: The authors introduce a Molecular Perturbation framework that generates syntax-valid structural variants of training molecules under controlled Graph Edit Distance (GED). This probes model manifold regularity by systematically varying structural similarity. For mitigation, they propose In-Context Tuning (ICT), which anchors predictions on structurally similar reference molecules to improve robustness against structural variation.
AI.result: Even a single graph edit causes substantial performance degradation on common molecular property prediction tasks, demonstrating a narrow local trust region and fragile sensitivity to structural changes. ICT partially expands this local trust region and offers improved stability against structural perturbations, though the robustness gains are not complete.
AI.conclusion: Molecular LLMs suffer from fragile local trust regions that collapse under minimal structural perturbation. ICT provides a promising direction for stabilizing predictions against structural variation by leveraging structurally similar molecules, but further work is needed to achieve broader generalization across chemical space.

title: Reasoning LLM Improves Speaker Recognition in Long-form TV Dramas
summary: Long-form TV dramas present a formidable challenge for comprehensive video understanding, where deciphering complex storyline often relies on \textbf{speaker recognition}, the task of accurately attributing each spoken utterance to its respective character. In this paper, we advance this field through two primary contributions. (1) We introduce \textbf{DramaSR-532K}, a large-scale benchmark comprising 532K annotated dialogue lines across more than 900 unique characters, necessitating the integration of auditory, linguistic, and visual cues for speaker recognition. (2) We propose \textbf{DramaSR-LRM}, a robust approach built upon a large reasoning model (LRM). DramaSR-LRM is designed to autonomously aggregate contextual evidence via multimodal tool-use, synthesizing diverse inputs to achieve high-fidelity attribution. Experimental results demonstrate that DramaSR-LRM significantly outperforms existing baselines, particularly on short utterances where acoustic biometrics are inherently unreliable. \textit{All the data and code will be made publicly available at the project page: https://www.github.com/198808xc/DramaSR-LRM.}

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DramaSR-532K, a large-scale benchmark for speaker recognition in TV dramas with 532K annotated dialogue lines, and DramaSR-LRM, a multimodal large reasoning model that aggregates auditory, linguistic, and visual cues to attribute utterances to characters, outperforming existing baselines especially on short utterances.
AI.motivation: Long-form TV dramas pose a significant challenge for video understanding because comprehending complex storylines requires accurate speaker recognition — attributing each spoken utterance to the correct character. Existing methods struggle particularly with short utterances where acoustic biometrics alone are unreliable, motivating the need for a multimodal approach that integrates auditory, linguistic, and visual evidence.
AI.method: The authors contribute two components: (1) DramaSR-532K, a benchmark dataset with 532K annotated dialogue lines spanning 900+ unique characters, designed to require multimodal integration; (2) DramaSR-LRM, a large reasoning model that autonomously aggregates contextual evidence through multimodal tool-use, synthesizing auditory, linguistic, and visual inputs to perform high-fidelity speaker attribution.
AI.result: DramaSR-LRM significantly outperforms existing baselines for speaker recognition, with particularly notable gains on short utterances where traditional acoustic-based biometric approaches are inherently unreliable.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DramaSR-LRM, leveraging multimodal tool-use within a large reasoning model framework, effectively addresses the speaker recognition challenge in long-form TV dramas. The DramaSR-532K benchmark provides a valuable resource for future research. All data and code will be publicly released.

title: Multimodal Knowledge Edit-Scoped Generalization for Online Recursive MLLM Editing
summary: Online multimodal knowledge editing requires injecting a continual stream of visual-textual corrections into multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with bounded overhead and minimal disruption to unrelated behaviors. Existing editors mainly emphasize edit reliability and long-horizon stability, but rarely control the semantic boundary of each edit. Our pilot analyses of post-edit behaviors and internal neuronal activities reveal a scope gap behind reliable edits: instance-level success neither guarantees transfer to valid cross-modal variants nor prevents leakage to unrelated inputs, while edit-related cross-modal responses concentrate in deeper semantic layers. Therefore, we formulate Edit-Scoped Generalization, reframing online MLLM editing from merely correcting an instance to controlling the propagation boundary of each edit. To this end, we propose ScopeEdit, a scope-aware online editor that decomposes each update into a modality-local absorption branch and an evidence-gated shared generalization branch. The local branch supports stable edit absorption, whereas the shared branch enables cross-modal propagation only when visual and textual evidence are sufficiently aligned. Both branches perform scope-separated write geometries in orthogonal low-rank spaces and maintain branch-wise preconditioners via Sherman--Morrison recursions, yielding constant per-edit overhead. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks, long-horizon edit streams, MLLM backbones, real-world VLKEB scenarios, and complex vision-language architectures show that ScopeEdit consistently improves the trade-off between in-scope cross-modal transfer and out-of-scope locality, while preserving edit reliability, stability and online efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/lab-klc/ScopeEdit.

AI.tldr: ScopeEdit proposes a scope-aware online knowledge editing method for MLLMs that decomposes each edit into a local absorption branch and an evidence-gated shared generalization branch, operating in orthogonal low-rank subspaces with constant per-edit overhead, to control the semantic propagation boundary of edits and improve the trade-off between cross-modal transfer and out-of-scope locality.
AI.motivation: Existing online multimodal knowledge editing methods focus on edit reliability and long-horizon stability but fail to control the semantic boundary of edits. A "scope gap" exists where instance-level editing success does not guarantee transfer to valid cross-modal variants (under-generalization) and causes leakage to unrelated inputs (over-generalization). Edit-related cross-modal responses concentrate in deeper semantic layers, motivating layer-specific scope control.
AI.method: ScopeEdit formulates Edit-Scoped Generalization and decomposes each update into: (1) a modality-local absorption branch for stable edit absorption, and (2) an evidence-gated shared generalization branch that enables cross-modal propagation only when visual and textual evidence are sufficiently aligned. Both branches use scope-separated write geometries in orthogonal low-rank spaces and maintain branch-wise preconditioners via Sherman-Morrison recursions, achieving constant per-edit overhead.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks, long-horizon edit streams, multiple MLLM backbones, real-world VLKEB scenarios, and complex vision-language architectures demonstrate that ScopeEdit consistently improves the trade-off between in-scope cross-modal transfer and out-of-scope locality, while preserving edit reliability, stability, and online efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Controlling the semantic propagation boundary is critical for online multimodal knowledge editing. By decomposing edits into local absorption and evidence-gated shared generalization with orthogonal low-rank geometries and efficient recursive preconditioning, ScopeEdit effectively bridges the scope gap and advances the state of online MLLM editing.

title: Gaming Consensus: Coordinated Manipulation in Crowdsourced Fact-Checking
summary: Crowdsourced fact-checking systems have been adopted by major social media companies such as X, Meta, TikTok and Google with the aim of combating misleading information at scale without relying on centralized editorial control. These systems have been developed around a common underlying concept: a bridging mechanism that identifies notes flagging misleading information when they receive support from people with different perspectives rather than simple majority support. To our knowledge the only publicly disclosed bridging algorithms deployed for fact-checking are based on matrix factorization, as deployed by both X and Meta, augmented with additional components addressing abuse, targeted manipulation, and contributor brigades. This work examines the core matrix factorization portion of these systems, presenting theoretical and empirical evaluations of the degree to which coordinated users could vote strategically by leveraging the latent representations to fabricate the appearance of synthetic consensus within the bridging mechanism. Using historic production data, we find that up to 10.7% of lower quality notes could be manipulated above consensus thresholds using less than 10 ratings. We complement these findings with a theoretical analysis, revealing counterintuitively that rating a note as "Not Helpful" can increase its helpfulness score, as well as a cost model quantifying manipulation effort. We have developed and deployed mitigations within X's Community Notes algorithm to address synthetic consensus.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the vulnerability of matrix factorization-based bridging algorithms (used by X and Meta for crowdsourced fact-checking) to strategic manipulation. The authors demonstrate that a small number of coordinated ratings (fewer than 10) can push up to 10.7% of low-quality notes above consensus thresholds, and reveal a counterintuitive property where "Not Helpful" ratings can increase helpfulness scores. Mitigations have been deployed in X's Community Notes.
AI.motivation: Major social media platforms (X, Meta, TikTok, Google) have adopted crowdsourced fact-checking with bridging algorithms to combat misinformation at scale without centralized editorial control. However, the only publicly disclosed bridging algorithms (matrix factorization-based, used by X and Meta) had not been rigorously analyzed for vulnerability to coordinated strategic manipulation. The authors aim to fill this gap by evaluating whether coordinated users can fabricate synthetic consensus by exploiting latent representations.
AI.method: The authors conduct both theoretical and empirical evaluations of the core matrix factorization component of deployed bridging algorithms. Using historic production data from X's Community Notes, they simulate coordinated voting strategies that exploit latent representations. They complement empirical findings with a theoretical analysis of the scoring mechanism, including a counterintuitive property demonstration and a cost model quantifying manipulation effort. Mitigations were subsequently developed and deployed within X's Community Notes algorithm.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Up to 10.7% of lower-quality notes can be manipulated above consensus thresholds using fewer than 10 coordinated ratings. (2) A counterintuitive theoretical result: rating a note as "Not Helpful" can paradoxically increase its helpfulness score due to the mechanics of the bridging algorithm. (3) A cost model is provided that quantifies the effort required for manipulation. (4) Mitigations addressing synthetic consensus were successfully developed and deployed in X's production system.
AI.conclusion: Matrix factorization-based bridging algorithms, while effective for identifying cross-perspective consensus, contain structural vulnerabilities that coordinated actors can exploit with relatively little effort. The authors' analysis directly informed real-world mitigations deployed in X's Community Notes, demonstrating the practical impact of adversarial evaluation of content moderation systems. The findings underscore the importance of robust mechanism design in crowdsourced fact-checking platforms.

title: LACUNA: A Testbed for Evaluating Localization Precision for LLM Unlearning
summary: LLMs memorize sensitive training data, including personally identifiable information (PII), creating a pressing need for reliable post hoc removal methods. Unlearning has emerged as a promising solution, with state-of-the-art(SOTA) methods often following a localize-first, unlearn-second paradigm that targets specific model parameters. However, existing benchmarks evaluate unlearning solely at the output level, leaving open the question of whether unlearning truly erases knowledge from a model's parameters or merely obfuscates it, a concern reinforced by the success of resurfacing attacks. To bridge this gap, we introduce LACUNA: the first unlearning testbed with ground-truth parameter-level localization. LACUNA injects PII of synthetic individuals into predefined parameters of 1B and 7B OLMo-based models via masked continual pretraining, enabling direct evaluation of whether unlearning targets the weights responsible for knowledge storage. We use LACUNA to benchmark current SOTA unlearning methods and find that, despite strong output-level performance, existing methods are highly imprecise and susceptible to resurfacing attacks. We further show that when localization is successful, even a simple gradient-based unlearning method achieves strong erasure and robustness to resurfacing attacks, highlighting the importance of precise unlearning. We release LACUNA to complement behavioral evaluations and drive further advances in robust, localization-based unlearning.

AI.tldr: LACUNA is a testbed that injects synthetic PII into known model parameters, enabling ground-truth evaluation of unlearning localization. Current SOTA methods achieve good output-level performance but suffer from imprecise parameter targeting and vulnerability to resurfacing attacks; when localization is precise, even simple gradient-based unlearning is robust.
AI.motivation: Existing unlearning benchmarks only evaluate at the output level, leaving uncertainty about whether knowledge is truly erased from parameters or merely obfuscated. The success of resurfacing attacks reinforces this concern, creating a need for parameter-level ground-truth evaluation.
AI.method: The authors introduce LACUNA, which injects PII of synthetic individuals into predefined parameters of 1B and 7B OLMo-based models via masked continual pretraining. This creates a controlled testbed where the exact weights responsible for storing target knowledge are known, enabling direct evaluation of unlearning precision.
AI.result: Current SOTA unlearning methods are highly imprecise at the parameter level despite strong output-level performance, and remain susceptible to resurfacing attacks. When localization is accurate, even simple gradient-based unlearning achieves strong erasure and attack robustness.
AI.conclusion: Precise parameter-level localization is critical for robust unlearning. LACUNA complements behavioral evaluations and serves as a benchmark to drive advances in localization-based unlearning.

title: Episodic-to-Semantic Consolidation Without Identity Drift
summary: Long-running adaptive intelligent agents face a structural tension between knowledge consolidation and information integrity. Memory consolidation is conventionally treated as an agent-changing operation: a model is fine-tuned, a prompt rewritten, a policy distilled, or a reflection appended to the context that governs future behaviour. In regulated autonomic deployment this is a liability because the agent operates under commitments and audit contracts that bind to a specific, cryptographically certified identity. We propose to treat consolidation not as a mutation of the planner or the identity manifest, but as a deterministic function f: M^ep -> M^sem over episodic memory whose output is a separately addressable semantic knowledge layer; the identity hash does not read M^sem, so consolidation updates knowledge without changing the agent's certified identity. We give a formal account of the agent representation, prove identity invariance through a structural lemma on the manifest's hash-input set, specify a deterministic aggregation algorithm whose outputs are auditable database rows with explicit confidence and supporting-event provenance, and validate the construction with synthetic experiments demonstrating per-field correctness, byte-equal identity across consolidation passes, and a mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%] across 10 seeds) against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline. The construction is a knowledge-update discipline for autonomic agents in which lessons accumulate as queryable facts while the agent's certified identity remains byte-equal across its operational lifetime, with an embodied service agent as the running case study.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel memory consolidation framework for autonomous agents that separates episodic memory from semantic knowledge, enabling knowledge updates without altering the agent's cryptographically certified identity. A deterministic aggregation function produces auditable semantic knowledge with provenance tracking, validated through synthetic experiments showing 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts while maintaining byte-equal identity hashes across consolidation passes.
AI.motivation: Long-running adaptive agents face a fundamental tension: conventional memory consolidation methods (fine-tuning, prompt rewriting, policy distillation, context augmentation) mutate the agent's internal state, which breaks cryptographic identity commitments required in regulated autonomic deployments. Agents operating under audit contracts cannot simultaneously learn from experience and maintain verifiable identity integrity under standard consolidation approaches.
AI.method: The authors formalize a two-layer agent architecture: an episodic memory layer M^ep and a semantic knowledge layer M^sem. Consolidation is defined as a deterministic function f: M^ep → M^sem whose output is a separately addressable knowledge base. Critically, the agent's identity hash is computed solely over a manifest that excludes M^sem, so semantic updates leave the certified identity byte-equal. The aggregation algorithm produces auditable database rows with explicit confidence scores and supporting-event provenance. Identity invariance is proven via a structural lemma on the manifest's hash-input set.
AI.result: Synthetic experiments demonstrate: (1) per-field correctness of consolidated knowledge, (2) byte-equal identity hashes across all consolidation passes, and (3) a mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%] across 10 seeds). An embodied service agent serves as the running case study.
AI.conclusion: The proposed construction establishes a knowledge-update discipline where lessons accumulate as queryable, provenance-tracked facts while the agent's certified identity remains invariant across its operational lifetime. This enables autonomic agents to learn continuously under regulatory audit constraints without sacrificing identity integrity.

title: Many Voices, One Reward: Multi-Role Rubric Generation for LLM Judging and Reward Modeling
summary: Reliable reward and preference signals are critical for evaluating and optimizing large language models on open-ended tasks. Rubric-based judges offer a transparent way to decompose such judgments into explicit evaluation criteria, but existing annotation-free rubric generators typically rely on a single generic evaluator. As a result, they may overlook important dimensions of human preference, a failure mode we term dimensional blind spots. To address this limitation, we propose Multi-Role Rubric Generation (MRRG), a training-free and reference-free framework that elicits evaluation criteria from multiple complementary roles and consolidates them into an auditable rubric-based scorer. This scorer can be used both to validate pairwise preferences and to provide rewards for GRPO-style Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). Experiments on preference validation benchmarks show that MRRG consistently outperforms single-role rubric generation baselines across multiple backbone models. Further RLVR experiments demonstrate that MRRG yields a stronger reward signal for improving open-ended generation.

AI.tldr: MRRG proposes a training-free framework that generates evaluation rubrics from multiple complementary roles to overcome "dimensional blind spots" in single-role rubric generators, improving both preference validation and RLVR reward signals.
AI.motivation: Existing annotation-free rubric generators rely on a single generic evaluator, which causes "dimensional blind spots"—the systematic omission of important human preference dimensions. This limits the reliability of automated evaluation and reward signals for LLM optimization.
AI.method: MRRG is a training-free, reference-free framework that elicits evaluation criteria from multiple complementary evaluator roles, then consolidates these into a unified auditable rubric-based scorer. The scorer serves dual purposes: validating pairwise preferences and providing rewards for GRPO-style RLVR training.
AI.result: On preference validation benchmarks, MRRG consistently outperforms single-role rubric generation baselines across multiple backbone models. RLVR experiments show MRRG yields stronger reward signals that improve open-ended generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Multi-role rubric generation effectively mitigates dimensional blind spots in LLM evaluation, offering a practical and performant path toward more reliable automated judging and reward modeling without requiring training or reference annotations.

title: Traceable Fault Diagnosis for Battery Energy Storage Systems via Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent O&M Assistant
summary: Large-scale battery energy storage systems (BESSs) require O&M decisions that combine alarms, cell-level measurements, device topology, diagnostic tables, historical cases, and maintenance documents. Monitoring platforms can flag threshold violations, but they often cannot explain whether voltage inconsistency, resistance drift, short-circuit risk, capacity divergence, or thermal abnormality needs intervention. This digest presents a traceable BESS fault-diagnosis assistant that uses retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning to connect operational data, domain knowledge, visual evidence, and report generation. Reliability is improved through BESS-specific task routing, schema-constrained natural-language database access, hybrid text-image retrieval, and evidence-based answer synthesis. Preliminary internal evaluation is reported for routing, database access, and diagnostic reasoning.

AI.tldr: A traceable BESS fault-diagnosis assistant leveraging retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning is presented, integrating operational data, domain knowledge, visual evidence, and automated report generation with reliability mechanisms including task routing, schema-constrained NL-to-DB access, hybrid text-image retrieval, and evidence-based synthesis.
AI.motivation: Existing BESS monitoring platforms can flag threshold violations but lack the explanatory capability to determine whether specific anomalies (voltage inconsistency, resistance drift, short-circuit risk, capacity divergence, thermal abnormality) genuinely require intervention. O&M decisions demand synthesis across heterogeneous sources — alarms, cell measurements, topology, diagnostic tables, historical cases, and maintenance documents — which current systems fail to integrate meaningfully.
AI.method: The proposed system employs retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning with four reliability-enhancing components: (1) BESS-specific task routing to direct queries to appropriate agents, (2) schema-constrained natural-language database access for structured operational data retrieval, (3) hybrid text-image retrieval to incorporate visual evidence alongside textual knowledge, and (4) evidence-based answer synthesis for traceable, report-ready diagnostic outputs.
AI.result: Preliminary internal evaluation is reported across three axes: task routing accuracy, database access performance, and diagnostic reasoning quality. The digest itself acknowledges the evaluation is preliminary and internal.
AI.conclusion: The digest outlines a system architecture that advances beyond threshold-based monitoring toward explainable, traceable fault diagnosis for large-scale BESS, though full experimental validation remains pending given the preliminary nature of the reported evaluation.

title: Adaptive Group-Based Counterfactual Explanations for Time-Series Rehabilitation Data
comment: To be published at IEEE CBMS 2026
summary: Counterfactual explanations (CEs) for multivariate time-series classifiers are often difficult to interpret in domains where experts reason in terms of semantic feature groups rather than individual channels. In rehabilitation movement analysis with multi-sensor inertial measurement units (IMUs), clinicians interpret motion through muscle-group and joint-segment abstractions; yet, most existing counterfactual methods operate at the channel level, producing scattered and biomechanically incoherent explanations. We propose a two-stage framework for group-based counterfactual generation in high-dimensional IMU data. We first show that Shapley-Adaptive (SA) group ranking preserves counterfactual validity but fails to enforce group-level sparsity, motivating the need for explicit group selection. We then introduce Learnable Gate (LG) methods, which incorporate trainable per-group relevance gates jointly optimized with perturbation masks. Experiments on the KneE-PAD rehabilitation dataset demonstrate that LG substantially improves modality-group sparsity compared to the channel-level M-CELS baseline while maintaining or improving validity, temporal smoothness, and generation efficiency. Exercise-specific analyses further show that group-structured counterfactuals yield concise, muscle-level corrective guidance aligned with clinical reasoning. Overall, the proposed framework enhances interpretability without sacrificing counterfactual quality, enabling more actionable explanations for rehabilitation movement analysis.

AI.tldr: A two-stage framework is proposed for generating group-based counterfactual explanations in multivariate IMU time-series data. Shapley-Adaptive ranking preserves validity but lacks group sparsity; Learnable Gate methods jointly optimize per-group relevance gates with perturbation masks, achieving superior modality-group sparsity, validity, and temporal smoothness on the KneE-PAD rehabilitation dataset, yielding clinically interpretable muscle-level corrective guidance.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual explanation methods for multivariate time-series classifiers operate at the individual channel level, producing scattered, biomechanically incoherent explanations. In rehabilitation movement analysis using multi-sensor IMUs, clinicians reason through semantic feature groups (muscle groups, joint segments) rather than individual sensor channels. There is a need for group-structured counterfactuals that align with clinical reasoning while maintaining explanation quality.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: (1) Shapley-Adaptive (SA) group ranking, which ranks feature groups by counterfactual importance but lacks explicit group-level sparsity control; (2) Learnable Gate (LG) methods, which introduce trainable per-group relevance gates that are jointly optimized with perturbation masks during counterfactual generation, explicitly enforcing group sparsity. Evaluated on the KneE-PAD rehabilitation dataset against the channel-level M-CELS baseline.
AI.result: LG methods substantially improve modality-group sparsity compared to M-CELS while maintaining or improving counterfactual validity, temporal smoothness, and generation efficiency. Exercise-specific analyses demonstrate that group-structured counterfactuals provide concise, muscle-level corrective guidance aligned with clinical reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed group-based framework enhances interpretability of counterfactual explanations for rehabilitation movement analysis without sacrificing counterfactual quality (validity, smoothness, efficiency), enabling more actionable, clinically coherent explanations that align with how domain experts reason about movement.

title: InduceKV: Fixed-Footprint Continual Adaptation of Multimodal LLMs via Inducing KV Memories
summary: Multimodal large language models must adapt to evolving tasks and domains, yet continual improvement under bounded deployment footprint remains difficult because repeated parameter updates or growing replay stores can accumulate adaptation state over time. We study fixed-footprint continual adaptation: the deployed adaptation state is kept under a fixed memory budget, while the backbone model is left unchanged and task-specific updates are externalized. We propose InduceKV, a retrieval-based method that stores each selected training prefix as an attention-ready memory entry, consisting of a frozen retrieval key and compact layerwise key--value (KV) payloads that can be appended to the model's self-attention cache. Under a strict memory budget, InduceKV constructs a compact inducing set through bilevel selection: a lightweight calibration is fit for retrieval, while the selected memory balances current-task likelihood, anchor-based retention, and coverage in the frozen retrieval space. Across task-incremental instruction tuning, continual VQA, domain-incremental adaptation, and lifelong multimodal instruction tuning, InduceKV consistently improves over PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines under matched memory budgets. We further report backbone-matched, stage-1 CoIN, compute-matched, and scalability diagnostics, showing that the gains are not due to a stronger backbone, replay alone, or an unbounded candidate pool.

AI.tldr: InduceKV is a retrieval-based method for fixed-footprint continual adaptation of multimodal LLMs. It stores selected training prefixes as attention-ready memory entries (frozen keys + compact KV payloads), constructed via bilevel selection that balances task likelihood, anchor-based retention, and coverage. The method outperforms PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines across multiple continual learning settings under matched memory budgets.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs face the challenge of adapting to evolving tasks/domains under bounded deployment footprints. Existing approaches suffer from accumulating adaptation state through repeated parameter updates or growing replay stores. The paper addresses the problem of fixed-footprint continual adaptation, where memory budget is strictly bounded, the backbone is frozen, and task-specific updates are externalized.
AI.method: InduceKV stores each selected training prefix as a memory entry comprising a frozen retrieval key and compact layerwise KV (key-value) payloads that can be appended to the model's self-attention cache. A bilevel selection algorithm constructs a compact inducing set: (1) a lightweight calibration model is fit for retrieval, and (2) selected memory entries balance current-task likelihood, anchor-based retention (preserving past knowledge), and coverage in the frozen retrieval space.
AI.result: InduceKV consistently improves over PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines under matched memory budgets across task-incremental instruction tuning, continual VQA, domain-incremental adaptation, and lifelong multimodal instruction tuning. Additional diagnostics (backbone-matched, stage-1 CoIN, compute-matched, scalability) confirm gains are not attributable to stronger backbones, replay alone, or unbounded candidate pools.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-footprint continual adaptation with retrieval-augmented KV memory is a viable and effective paradigm. InduceKV demonstrates that compact, attention-ready memory construction via bilevel selection can achieve strong continual adaptation performance without modifying the backbone or exceeding memory constraints.

title: Decomposer: Learning to Decompile Symbolic Music to Programs
summary: Musical performance involves executing a set of high-level musical instructions, yet recovering those instructions from the performance is a challenging inverse problem. We present Decomposer, a post-training framework for symbolic music decompilation: the task of recovering executable, editable music programs from symbolic music. We instantiate the task as MIDI-to-Strudel decompilation, where the model takes symbolic MIDI as input and produces a program in Strudel, a music programming language, that reconstructs the input when executed. The task poses two challenges: Strudel is a low-resource language with little naturally paired MIDI-code data, and optimizing faithful reconstruction of MIDI alone can collapse to unreadable note-by-note transliteration. We address these challenges in two stages. First, we construct Strudel-Synth, a synthetic corpus of paired Strudel programs and rendered MIDI, and use it for supervised fine-tuning. Second, we refine the model with reinforcement learning on unpaired MIDI, optimizing rewards for both MIDI reconstruction faithfulness and code readability. Our evaluation across synthetic and real-world MIDI benchmarks shows that Decomposer achieves substantially higher MIDI reconstruction faithfulness than closed-source LLMs while producing more readable and diverse code than the heuristic converter.

AI.tldr: Decomposer is a two-stage framework for decompiling symbolic MIDI into executable Strudel music programs, using synthetic data fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning to balance MIDI reconstruction faithfulness with code readability.
AI.motivation: Recovering high-level musical instructions from symbolic music performances is a challenging inverse problem. Strudel, as a low-resource music programming language, lacks naturally paired MIDI-code data, and optimizing solely for MIDI reconstruction can degenerate into unreadable note-by-note transliteration.
AI.method: Decomposer operates in two stages: (1) construct Strudel-Synth, a synthetic corpus of paired Strudel programs and rendered MIDI, for supervised fine-tuning; (2) refine the model via reinforcement learning on unpaired MIDI using dual rewards: MIDI reconstruction faithfulness and code readability.
