AI.result: Decomposer achieves substantially higher MIDI reconstruction faithfulness than closed-source LLMs on both synthetic and real-world MIDI benchmarks, while producing more readable and diverse code than heuristic converters.
AI.conclusion: A post-training framework combining synthetic supervised data with RL-based refinement can effectively decompile symbolic MIDI into readable, executable music programs, overcoming both data scarcity and the faithfulness-readability trade-off.

title: Hidden Forgetting in Continual Multimodal Learning: When Accuracy Survives but Grounding Fails
summary: Multimodal large language models must continually adapt to evolving tasks and domains, yet standard continual learning metrics mainly measure whether old answers remain correct, leaving the stability of multimodal grounding largely unexamined. We study this overlooked failure mode and ask whether a continually adapted MLLM can preserve not only what it answers, but also how it uses visual, textual, OCR, chart, and document evidence. We identify \emph{hidden evidence-use forgetting}, where answer accuracy is retained while the model silently shifts toward different or less grounded evidence channels, and propose \textsc{RCL}, a replay-free reliance-constrained continual learning framework. \textsc{RCL} freezes the previous checkpoint as a behavioral reference, estimates teacher and student evidence-reliance profiles through counterfactual channel interventions, and jointly optimizes task learning, prediction preservation, and reliance preservation without adding inference-time cost. Across CoIN, COAST, MCITlib, and an evidence-sensitive multimodal stream, \textsc{RCL} consistently improves final performance and reduces forgetting over replay-free, PEFT, routing, and memory-assisted baselines, while substantially lowering modality reliance drift, dominant evidence flips, and hidden forgetting rates. These results suggest that robust continual multimodal learning requires preserving the evidence path behind correct answers, not merely the answers themselves.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "hidden evidence-use forgetting" in continually adapted multimodal LLMs—where answer accuracy remains stable but the model silently shifts its reliance across visual, textual, OCR, chart, and document evidence channels. It proposes RCL, a replay-free framework that freezes the previous checkpoint as a behavioral reference, estimates reliance profiles via counterfactual channel interventions, and jointly optimizes task learning, prediction preservation, and reliance preservation, demonstrating consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard continual learning metrics for multimodal LLMs only assess whether old answers remain correct (output-level stability), but fail to capture whether the model continues to use the same grounding evidence (process-level stability). This gap leaves an underexamined failure mode: a model can retain correct answers while silently shifting toward different, weaker, or less appropriate evidence channels, undermining interpretability and robustness.
AI.method: RCL (Reliance-Constrained Continual Learning) is a replay-free framework with three components: (1) freezing the previous model checkpoint as a behavioral reference teacher; (2) estimating teacher and student evidence-reliance profiles through counterfactual interventions that ablate individual input channels (visual, textual, OCR, chart, document) and measure prediction divergence; (3) a joint optimization objective combining task loss, prediction preservation (KD on outputs), and reliance preservation (aligning the student's channel-reliance distribution to the teacher's), all without additional inference cost.
AI.result: Across CoIN, COAST, MCITlib, and a custom evidence-sensitive multimodal stream, RCL consistently outperforms replay-free, PEFT, routing, and memory-assisted baselines in final performance and forgetting reduction. It substantially lowers modality reliance drift, reduces dominant evidence flips, and decreases hidden forgetting rates, demonstrating that preserving the evidence path is critical for robust continual multimodal learning.
AI.conclusion: Robust continual multimodal learning requires preserving not just what the model answers but how it grounds those answers in evidence. RCL provides a practical, inference-cost-free solution by constraining evidence-reliance consistency, and the results suggest that future continual learning benchmarks should incorporate process-level evaluation metrics beyond output accuracy.

title: Learning the Supports for Categorical Critic in Reinforcement Learning
summary: Value functions are an essential component in actor-critic based deep reinforcement learning (RL). Conventionally, these functions are trained as a regression task by minimising the mean squared error (MSE) relative to bootstrapped target values. Meanwhile, in distributional RL, a distribution of returns is modelled based on the distributional Bellman operator. This work investigates the Gaussian Histogram Loss (HL-Gauss), a recent approach that reframes value estimation as classification by encoding each scalar Bellman target as a Gaussian-smoothed categorical target. Despite its potential, applying histogram-based losses to RL presents inherent challenges, most notably the requirement to pre-define a fixed support interval, which is often complicated by the non-stationary and stochastic nature of target values typically found in RL tasks. In this work, we propose an approach that dynamically learns the lower and upper bounds of the support instead of assigning them beforehand. We derive an objective that jointly learns these bounds whilst learning the categorical representation of the scalar values, and we show that this objective forms an upper bound on the mean-squared Bellman error. Our theoretical analysis further shows that this bound is tighter than that of non-learned supports of HL-Gauss. Empirically, the proposed objective enables stable adaptation of the support interval and matches HL-Gauss-based actor-critic algorithms on most continuous-control tasks whilst improving on a subset, without requiring a pre-specified support interval.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dynamic, learnable support interval for histogram-based value estimation in RL, replacing the fixed support required by HL-Gauss. The learned bounds form a tighter upper bound on the mean-squared Bellman error and match or improve upon fixed-support HL-Gauss in continuous control tasks.
AI.motivation: Histogram-based losses like HL-Gauss reframe value estimation as classification, but require pre-defining a fixed support interval — a significant practical limitation given the non-stationary, stochastic nature of RL targets.
AI.method: The authors derive a joint objective that simultaneously learns the lower and upper support bounds alongside the categorical value representation. They prove this objective constitutes an upper bound on the mean-squared Bellman error and demonstrate theoretically that this bound is tighter than that of HL-Gauss with a fixed, non-learned support.
AI.result: The proposed method matches HL-Gauss-based actor-critic algorithms on most continuous-control benchmarks and outperforms on a subset, all while eliminating the need to pre-specify a support interval and enabling stable, adaptive support adjustment.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic support learning resolves a key practical barrier to histogram-based value estimation in RL, delivering competitive empirical performance with greater autonomy and theoretical guarantees of tighter Bellman error bounds.

title: PACE: A Proxy for Agentic Capability Evaluation
summary: Evaluating LLM agents on benchmarks like SWE-Bench and GAIA can be expensive, time-consuming, and requires complex infrastructure. A single evaluation can cost thousands of dollars and take days to complete. In contrast, non-agentic LLM benchmarks that test individual capabilities (e.g., reasoning, code generation) are fast and cheap to run. In this paper, we investigate whether performance on expensive agentic benchmarks can be accurately predicted by the performance on a small, carefully selected subset of atomic evaluation instances. We introduce PACE, a framework that constructs proxy benchmarks by selecting instances from existing non-agentic evaluations whose aggregate scores most reliably predict model performances on agentic benchmarks. Given a pool of candidate instances spanning atomic capabilities, PACE fits a regression that maps a model's scores on a compact subset of source instances to its score on the target agentic benchmark. The subset itself is curated by combining two complementary instance-selection strategies, target-relevance local selection and globally informative global selection. We apply PACE to the 4 target agentic benchmarks in this paper, which yields PACE-Bench, the concrete proxy benchmark that we evaluate in the paper. Experiments across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks show that PACE-Bench predicts agentic scores with leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) mean absolute error (MAE) under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and pairwise model-ranking accuracy around 85%, all at much less than 1% of the full agentic evaluation cost. We further analyze the selected proxy instances, revealing which skills each agentic benchmark uniquely demands. PACE enables practitioners to obtain reliable estimates of agentic performance during model development, selection, and routing, without the overhead of full agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: PACE introduces a framework that selects a small subset of non-agentic benchmark instances to cheaply and accurately predict LLM performance on expensive agentic benchmarks, achieving under 4% MAE and >0.80 Spearman correlation at <1% of the cost.
AI.motivation: Evaluating LLM agents on benchmarks like SWE-Bench and GAIA is prohibitively expensive (thousands of dollars, days of compute) and requires complex infrastructure, while non-agentic benchmarks are fast and cheap. The authors seek a cost-effective proxy to estimate agentic performance without running full agent evaluations.
AI.method: PACE (Proxy Agent Capability Evaluation) constructs proxy benchmarks via a two-pronged instance selection strategy: (1) target-relevance local selection, which picks source instances most correlated with the target agentic benchmark, and (2) globally informative global selection, which ensures diversity and coverage. A regression model is then fitted to map a model's scores on the selected compact subset of non-agentic instances to its predicted score on the target agentic benchmark. The concrete instantiation across 4 agentic benchmarks is called PACE-Bench.
AI.result: Evaluated across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks, PACE-Bench achieves leave-one-out cross-validation mean absolute error under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and pairwise model-ranking accuracy around 85%, all while costing less than 1% of full agentic evaluation. Analysis of selected proxy instances reveals which specific skills each agentic benchmark uniquely demands.
AI.conclusion: PACE enables practitioners to obtain reliable estimates of agentic performance during model development, selection, and routing without incurring the overhead of full agent evaluation. The framework demonstrates that expensive agentic benchmark scores can be accurately predicted from cheap, atomic capability evaluations.

title: Regularized Variational and Spectral Log-Density-Ratio Estimation in the Gaussian Location Model
summary: We study ridge-regularized log-density-ratio estimation in the Gaussian location model with a common covariance matrix. By affine invariance, the model is written as q $\sim$ N(0, I), p $\sim$ N($Δ$, I), with linear features, where $Δ$ is a mean vector. The variational estimator is the empirical Kullback-Leibler (KL) log-normalized fit with a squared L2-penalty on its nonconstant coefficient, and the spectral estimator recently introduced in [1] replaces a single variational problem by a continuum of ridge-regularized least-squares problems. We derive high-dimensional deterministic asymptotic equivalents when the numbers of observations and dimension tend to infinity with fixed ratios. The regularized variational limit is characterized by a scalar entropy minimization problem derived from the convex-Gaussian-min-max theorem (CGMT), while the regularized spectral limit follows from deterministic equivalents for resolvents of weighted sums of two independent Gaussian sample covariance matrices. We use these formulas to compare population risks, with experiments focused on fixed-signal aspect-ratio sweeps and optimized regularization. Our conclusion is that with many observations, under the criteria and asymptotic regimes analyzed here, the well-specified variational estimator has the smaller risk, while with fewer observations, the spectral estimator is favored because its covariance-based construction has lower variance. We also study how a nuclear penalty can be used and partially analyzed to perform feature learning.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes two ridge-regularized log-density-ratio estimators in a high-dimensional Gaussian location model, deriving asymptotic behavior as both sample size and dimension grow proportionally. The variational (KL-based) estimator outperforms with more data, while the spectral estimator (based on a continuum of least-squares problems) is favored with fewer observations due to lower variance. A nuclear penalty extension for feature learning is also explored.
AI.motivation: To rigorously compare the population risk of two competing approaches to log-density-ratio estimation — the variational (empirical KL) estimator and the recently proposed spectral estimator — under high-dimensional asymptotics, and to identify regimes where each method is preferable.
AI.method: The authors analyze a Gaussian location model \(q \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\), \(p \sim \mathcal{N}(\Delta, I)\) with common covariance. The variational estimator is an L2-penalized empirical KL fit; the spectral estimator solves a continuum of ridge-regularized least-squares problems. High-dimensional deterministic equivalents are derived: the variational limit via the Convex-Gaussian Min-Max Theorem (CGMT), and the spectral limit via resolvent asymptotics for weighted sums of two independent Gaussian sample covariance matrices. Population risks are then compared analytically and through numerical sweeps over aspect ratios with optimized regularization. A nuclear-norm penalty is also partially analyzed for feature learning.
AI.result: Deterministic asymptotic equivalents are obtained for both estimators. The variational estimator has lower risk in the well-specified, many-observations regime. The spectral estimator is favored with fewer observations because its covariance-based construction exhibits lower variance. The nuclear penalty extension shows promise for feature learning but is only partially analyzed.
AI.conclusion: There is no uniformly superior estimator: the variational method excels when data are abundant, while the spectral method is preferable in low-data regimes due to its variance properties. The work also opens a direction for nuclear-penalized variants that may enable feature learning.

title: Algebraic Model Counting for Global Analysis of Optimal Decision Trees
comment: Proc. Joint European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (ECML-PKDD 2026), LNCS, Naples, Italy, 7-11 September 2026
summary: Ensuring model reliability in Explainable AI requires a global assessment of the hypothesis space. We propose a formal framework for the exhaustive analysis of optimal and near-optimal decision trees, called Algebraic Decision Tree Counting (ADTC). Inspired by Algebraic Model Counting (AMC) in knowledge representation, ADTC reformulates diverse analytical tasks, such as optimization, counting, and sampling, into a unified sum-of-products computation over a semiring $R$. While the hypothesis space of decision trees is doubly exponential with respect to the maximum depth $Δ$, our dynamic programming algorithm achieves $O^*(n^{O(Δ)})$ time complexity in the number of features $n$, where $O^*$ suppresses polynomial factors. To handle complex constraints consisting of multiple tree metrics, we introduce model behavior tensors that aggregate semiring values via convolution products over a tensor semiring. This algebraic approach efficiently constructs a model profile that captures the global landscape and trade-offs between criteria such as accuracy, size, and fairness. We demonstrate the utility of our software, emtrees, on real-world datasets, illustrating how ADTC facilitates evidence-based model selection in sensitive domains.

AI.tldr: ADTC reformulates optimal/near-optimal decision tree analysis as sum-of-products computation over a semiring, using dynamic programming (O*(n^O(Δ))) and tensor semirings with convolution products to construct model profiles capturing accuracy-size-fairness trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Ensuring model reliability in Explainable AI requires global assessment of the hypothesis space beyond finding a single optimal model. Existing methods lack a unified framework for exhaustively analyzing optimal and near-optimal decision trees across multiple criteria simultaneously.
AI.method: Algebraic Decision Tree Counting (ADTC) adapts Algebraic Model Counting from knowledge representation, casting optimization, counting, and sampling as sum-of-products over a semiring R. A dynamic programming algorithm achieves O*(n^O(Δ)) time for doubly exponential hypothesis spaces. Model behavior tensors with convolution products over a tensor semiring aggregate multiple tree metrics, constructing model profiles that capture global trade-off landscapes.
AI.result: The emtrees software demonstrates ADTC on real-world datasets, enabling evidence-based model selection by profiling global trade-offs between accuracy, size, and fairness in sensitive domains.
AI.conclusion: ADTC provides a principled, unified algebraic framework for exhaustive analysis of decision tree hypothesis spaces, facilitating reliable and transparent model selection through comprehensive model profiling.

title: Rank-Then-Act: Reward-Free Control from Frame-Order Progress
summary: We introduce Rank-Then-Act (RTA), a framework for learning control policies from expert video demonstrations without environment rewards. RTA trains a Vision-Language Model (VLM) offline as a progress-based ordinal scorer, using a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective over shuffled frame sequences, which forces the model to recover temporal ordering from visual semantics rather than trivial time cues. Importantly, instead of using the scorer directly as a scalar reward model, we propose a correlation-based reward function for reinforcement learning: at each interaction window, we compute the Spearman rank correlation between predicted progress rankings and true temporal indices, yielding a bounded, scale-invariant learning signal. This design decouples reward learning from absolute calibration and enables stable transfer across tasks and environments. We evaluate RTA on discrete control benchmarks (PyBoy: Catrap, Kirby) and continuous control tasks (PointMaze, MetaWorld). RTA consistently matches or outperforms prior video-based reward learning methods and rank-based baselines, while demonstrating strong cross-task reuse of a single pretrained progress scorer. Our results suggest that correlation-structured supervision over video-derived ordinal signals is sufficient for policy learning, offering a scalable alternative to explicit reward design.

AI.tldr: RTA learns control policies from expert videos by training a VLM as a progress scorer via ordinal frame ranking, then uses Spearman rank correlation between predicted rankings and temporal indices as a reinforcement learning reward, achieving stable, reward-free policy learning across diverse control benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Learning control policies from video demonstrations typically requires explicit environment rewards or well-calibrated scalar reward models, both of which are brittle and hard to scale. The authors aim to provide a scalable, decoupled alternative that leverages the ordinal structure inherent in expert video frame sequences without needing absolute reward calibration.
AI.method: The RTA framework has two stages: (1) Offline VLM training: A VLM is trained as a progress-based ordinal scorer using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on shuffled frame sequences, forcing recovery of temporal ordering from visual semantics. (2) Correlation-based RL reward: During policy learning, the Spearman rank correlation between the scorer's predicted progress rankings and true temporal indices over an interaction window is used as a bounded, scale-invariant reward signal, decoupling reward learning from absolute calibration.
AI.result: RTA matched or outperformed prior video-based reward learning methods and rank-based baselines on discrete control (PyBoy: Catrap, Kirby) and continuous control (PointMaze, MetaWorld) tasks. A single pretrained progress scorer transferred effectively across tasks.
AI.conclusion: Correlation-structured supervision over video-derived ordinal signals is sufficient for policy learning, offering a scalable alternative to explicit reward design. The decoupling of reward learning from absolute calibration enables stable cross-task and cross-environment transfer.

title: Evidence-State Rewards for Long-Context Reasoning
summary: Long-context reasoning requires models to locate, revise, and synthesize evidence distributed across lengthy inputs. Existing long-context RL methods usually reward final answers or static evidence extraction, offering little feedback on how intermediate actions change the model's evidence state. We propose Maven, a reinforcement learning framework with an editable evidence memory. Maven defines an answer-conditioned evidence-state value and rewards action-level state transitions: add actions are credited by marginal gain and hindsight contribution, link actions by evidence synergy, and drop actions by improved answer support after removing misleading evidence. These rewards are assigned to the corresponding action spans in GRPO. Across Llama and Qwen models on LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER, Maven outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines, producing more sufficient evidence sets and lower distractor retention. Our results show that long-context RL benefits from optimizing stateful evidence navigation rather than one-shot evidence extraction.

AI.tldr: Maven introduces a reinforcement learning framework for long-context reasoning that rewards action-level evidence-state transitions (add, link, drop) using an editable memory, outperforming outcome-only RL baselines on long-context benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing long-context RL methods only reward final answers or static evidence extraction, providing no feedback on how intermediate actions affect the model's evidence state. This limits the model's ability to learn effective evidence navigation — locating, revising, and synthesizing distributed evidence.
AI.method: Maven uses an editable evidence memory with an answer-conditioned evidence-state value function. It rewards three action types at the span level within GRPO: (1) Add actions — credited via marginal gain and hindsight contribution; (2) Link actions — rewarded by evidence synergy; (3) Drop actions — rewarded by improved answer support after removing misleading evidence. These fine-grained rewards guide stateful evidence navigation rather than one-shot extraction.
AI.result: Across Llama and Qwen models on LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER, Maven outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines, yielding more sufficient evidence sets and lower distractor retention.
AI.conclusion: Long-context RL benefits substantially from optimizing stateful evidence navigation with action-level feedback, rather than relying on one-shot evidence extraction or final-answer-only rewards.

title: SABER: A Semantic-Aligned Brain Network Analysis Framework via Multi-scale Hypergraphs
comment: Accepted to IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo (ICME) 2026;
summary: Effective brain disease diagnosis requires the synergy of brain connectivity patterns and high-level semantic knowledge. Existing methods, however, largely treat semantics from large language models (LLMs) as auxiliary features or supervision, limiting their direct role in decision-making and constraining classification stability and robustness. To overcome this, we propose a semantic-aligned brain network framework that actively integrates LLM-derived semantics into the prediction process. Specifically, ROI-level semantics are first incorporated via global self-attention to enrich node representations and provide whole-brain context. Multi-scale hypergraphs are then constructed to explicitly model functional subnetworks and multi-ROI interactions, addressing the locality limitations of traditional GNNs and capturing high-order dependencies. Finally, a decision-level semantic alignment mechanism selectively injects patient-specific textual embeddings into graph representations, enabling semantics to directly guide predictions without perturbing the underlying network structure. Experiments on public brain network datasets ABIDE and ADHD-200 demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, enhanced stability, and improved interpretability, particularly in small-sample settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a semantic-aligned brain network framework that integrates LLM-derived semantics into brain connectivity analysis via ROI-level attention, multi-scale hypergraphs, and decision-level semantic alignment, achieving SOTA on ABIDE and ADHD-200 datasets with improved stability and interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing brain disease diagnosis methods treat LLM semantics only as auxiliary features or weak supervision, limiting their direct role in decision-making and compromising classification stability and robustness. There is a need for deeper integration of semantic knowledge into the prediction pipeline.
AI.method: The framework operates in three stages: (1) ROI-level semantic incorporation via global self-attention to enrich node representations with whole-brain context; (2) multi-scale hypergraph construction to explicitly model functional subnetworks and multi-ROI interactions, overcoming locality limitations of traditional GNNs; (3) a decision-level semantic alignment mechanism that selectively injects patient-specific textual embeddings into graph representations, enabling semantics to directly guide predictions without perturbing network structure.
AI.result: Experiments on ABIDE and ADHD-200 public brain network datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art classification performance, enhanced stability, and improved interpretability, with particularly strong gains in small-sample settings.
AI.conclusion: Actively integrating LLM-derived semantics at multiple levels—node, subnetwork, and decision—yields a more robust and interpretable brain disease diagnosis framework, especially effective under data scarcity.

title: SUNTA: Hierarchical Video Prediction with Surprise-based Chunking
summary: Hierarchical state-space models (HSSMs) offer a promising approach to long-horizon prediction by segmenting sequences into temporal chunks. However, their performance hinges on how chunk boundaries are determined. While prior HSSMs typically rely on fixed-length chunking or similarity-based boundary detection, these methods often misalign with the intrinsic temporal structure of the data. We argue that chunking should instead be driven by prediction errors, which more directly indicate when longer-range context becomes necessary. Nevertheless, integrating surprise-based chunking into HSSMs introduces critical challenges, including hierarchical collapse during end-to-end training and the absence of surprise signals during open-loop prediction. To address these issues, we propose Surprise-based Nested Temporal Abstraction (SUNTA), a method that employs a decoupled training strategy to preserve surprise signals and uses internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric to determine chunk boundaries within imagined rollouts. Experiments on video prediction tasks in 2D and 3D environments demonstrate that SUNTA outperforms baselines, uniquely maintaining accurate predictions over 250 timesteps, whereas all baselines degrade within the first 10 timesteps.

AI.tldr: SUNTA is a hierarchical state-space model that uses prediction errors (surprise) to determine temporal chunk boundaries, overcoming limitations of fixed-length and similarity-based chunking. It employs decoupled training to prevent hierarchical collapse and internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric for open-loop predictions, achieving accurate long-horizon predictions over 250 timesteps where baselines fail within 10.
AI.motivation: Existing HSSMs rely on fixed-length chunking or similarity-based boundary detection, which often misalign with the data's intrinsic temporal structure. Prediction errors are a more direct signal for when longer-range context is needed, but integrating surprise-based chunking into HSSMs introduces two key challenges: (1) hierarchical collapse during end-to-end training and (2) the absence of surprise signals during open-loop generative prediction. The paper aims to resolve these.
AI.method: SUNTA (Surprise-based Nested Temporal Abstraction) uses a decoupled training strategy that separates the training of hierarchical levels to preserve informative surprise signals and avoid collapse. For open-loop prediction, where ground-truth surprise signals are unavailable, it introduces internal inconsistency — a top-down surprise metric computed from disagreements between hierarchical levels within imagined rollouts — to determine chunk boundaries autonomously.
AI.result: In video prediction tasks across 2D and 3D environments, SUNTA consistently outperforms all baselines. It uniquely maintains accurate predictions over 250 timesteps, while all baseline methods degrade within the first 10 timesteps.
AI.conclusion: Surprise-driven temporal abstraction is both viable and superior for long-horizon prediction, provided that the challenges of hierarchical collapse and missing surprise signals during generation are properly addressed via decoupled training and internal inconsistency metrics.

title: Population-Based Multi-Objective Training of Discriminators for Semi-Supervised GANs
comment: The 2nd International Conference on Federated Learning and Intelligent Computing Systems (FLICS2026)
summary: Semi-supervised generative adversarial networks (SSL-GANs) can exploit large unlabeled datasets while retaining a classifier in the discriminator, but their training is often unstable. This paper proposes a population-based evolutionary training strategy in which discriminator learning is formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem. Instead of aggregating the supervised and unsupervised components of the SSL objective into a single scalar loss, the method maintains a population of discriminators ranked by Pareto dominance, enabling the exploration of different trade-offs between classification accuracy and real/fake discrimination. This formulation aims to improve both roles of SSL-GANs: learning accurate classifiers and training generators capable of producing realistic samples. We analyze several variants, including an elitist strategy and a mono-objective ablation, to assess the role of multi-objective selection. Experiments on MNIST with limited labels show improved training robustness compared to SSL-GAN and CE-SSL-GAN state-of-the-art baselines, while the elitist variant consistently achieves the highest classification accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multi-objective evolutionary training strategy for semi-supervised GANs, where a population of discriminators is Pareto-ranked to balance classification accuracy and real/fake discrimination, improving training stability and classification performance on limited-label MNIST.
AI.motivation: Standard SSL-GAN training is unstable because it combines supervised and unsupervised objectives into a single scalar loss, forcing an often-conflicting trade-off between classification accuracy and adversarial discrimination. The authors seek to address this by explicitly treating the two objectives separately.
AI.method: A population-based evolutionary approach formulates discriminator learning as a multi-objective optimization problem. A population of discriminators is maintained and ranked via Pareto dominance over two objectives: (1) supervised classification accuracy and (2) unsupervised real/fake discrimination. Variants include an elitist strategy and a mono-objective ablation to isolate the effect of multi-objective selection.
AI.result: Experiments on MNIST with limited labeled data demonstrate improved training robustness compared to SSL-GAN and CE-SSL-GAN baselines. The elitist variant consistently achieves the highest classification accuracy among all tested configurations.
AI.conclusion: Multi-objective evolutionary optimization effectively decouples the competing objectives in SSL-GAN discriminators, leading to more stable training and better classifiers, with the elitist Pareto-based selection providing the strongest results.

title: ContextNest: Verifiable Context Governance for Autonomous AI Agent
summary:
Autonomous AI agents increasingly depend on external knowledge stores, yet most retrieval pipelines provide relevance without durable guarantees of provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, or point-in-time reconstruction. We formalize this as context governance and present ContextNext, an open specification and reference implementation for governed AI-consumable knowledge vaults. ContextNext does not replace Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG); it supplies the governance layer beneath retrieval, determining which artifacts are approved, current, attributable, and integrity-verified before retrieval systems operate over them.
  The specification combines typed Markdown documents with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URI references, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph-level checkpoints, source nodes for live data through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and audit traces of agent context consumption. These mechanisms let organizations reconstruct which knowledge versions informed an agent output and whether those versions were AI-eligible when consumed.
  We report first empirical results from two controlled experiments. In a stale-version attack isolating the governance-versus-retrieval failure mode, governed selection strictly Pareto-dominates BM25 sparse retrieval, with higher answer-quality pass rate (97% versus 93-90%) at about one-third the input-token cost. In a retrieval-determinism experiment over a 1,060-document corpus, deterministic selectors and BM25 return stable document sets across repeated identical queries (Jaccard 1.0), while a dense+HNSW baseline is non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210). These results suggest that context governance addresses failure modes retrieval quality alone is not designed to resolve. We release a core engine, CLI, and MCP server under open licenses.

AI.tldr: ContextNext is an open specification and reference implementation for governed AI-consumable knowledge vaults that adds provenance, versioning, integrity, and auditability beneath RAG pipelines. Experiments show governed selection outperforms BM25 on answer quality (97% vs 90-93%) at lower token cost, and deterministic selectors guarantee stable retrieval (Jaccard 1.0) versus non-deterministic dense+HNSW (mean Jaccard 0.611).
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI agents increasingly rely on external knowledge stores, but current retrieval pipelines lack durable guarantees of provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, and point-in-time reconstruction. The authors formalize this gap as "context governance" — the need to determine which artifacts are approved, current, attributable, and integrity-verified before retrieval systems operate.
AI.method: The ContextNext specification combines: (1) typed Markdown documents with metadata; (2) deterministic set-algebraic selectors; (3) contextnest:// URI references; (4) SHA-256 hash-chained version histories; (5) graph-level checkpoints; (6) source nodes for live data via Model Context Protocol (MCP); and (7) audit traces of agent context consumption. Two controlled experiments evaluate governance-versus-retrieval failure modes and retrieval determinism on a 1,060-document corpus.
AI.result: In the stale-version attack experiment, governed selection strictly Pareto-dominates BM25 sparse retrieval with higher answer-quality pass rate (97% vs 93-90%) at roughly one-third the input-token cost. In the determinism experiment, deterministic selectors and BM25 return stable document sets (Jaccard 1.0) across repeated identical queries, while dense+HNSW is non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210).
AI.conclusion: Context governance addresses failure modes that retrieval quality alone cannot resolve. The authors release a core engine, CLI, and MCP server under open licenses to support adoption.

title: Zeus: Towards Tuning-Free Foundation Model for Time Series Analysis
summary: We present Zeus, a unified tuning-free Time Series Foundation Model (TSFM) that delivers superior performance across diverse analysis tasks without any task-specific fine-tuning. Unlike prior studies that primarily focus on zero-shot forecasting but require task-specific tuning for other tasks, Zeus bridges this gap by addressing two fundamental challenges in multi-task generalization. First, to reconcile point-level granularity with long-sequence scalability, Zeus incorporates a multi-scale Transformer featuring point-wise tokenization and a U-shaped hierarchy, effectively balancing fine-grained fidelity with computational efficiency. Second, to accommodate varying inductive biases across different tasks, Zeus introduces Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM), a unified strategy that supports heterogeneous tasks (e.g., extrapolation, interpolation, and global abstraction) within a single framework. Extensive experiments across five representative tasks demonstrate that Zeus consistently achieves competitive results in tuning-free settings, underscoring its potential as a general-purpose TSFM.

AI.tldr: Zeus is a tuning-free Time Series Foundation Model that achieves competitive performance across five diverse time series tasks (forecasting, imputation, classification, anomaly detection, and representation learning) without any task-specific fine-tuning, enabled by a multi-scale U-shaped Transformer and Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM).
AI.motivation: Existing TSFMs focus primarily on zero-shot forecasting but still require task-specific tuning for other tasks. The authors aim to bridge this gap by building a truly unified, tuning-free model capable of multi-task generalization — handling heterogeneous tasks such as extrapolation (forecasting), interpolation (imputation), and global abstraction (classification, anomaly detection) within a single framework without any fine-tuning.
AI.method: Zeus employs two key innovations: (1) A multi-scale Transformer architecture with point-wise tokenization and a U-shaped hierarchy (encoder-decoder with skip connections) that balances fine-grained point-level fidelity with long-sequence computational scalability. (2) Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM), a unified pretraining strategy that generates diverse masking patterns corresponding to different task types — e.g., future masking for forecasting, random masking for imputation, and global masking for representation learning — allowing the model to learn varied inductive biases simultaneously during pretraining.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across five representative tasks show that Zeus achieves competitive results in fully tuning-free (zero-shot) settings, matching or approaching the performance of task-specific fine-tuned models, demonstrating its viability as a general-purpose TSFM.
AI.conclusion: Zeus demonstrates that a carefully designed architecture and a unified multi-objective pretraining strategy can enable a single TSFM to generalize across heterogeneous time series tasks without any fine-tuning, representing a step toward truly general-purpose foundation models for time series analysis.

title: Enhancing Fitness Intelligence through Domain-Specific LLM Post-Training
comment: 8 pages, 6 tables, 2 figures. Accepted by the 12th International Conference on Big Data Computing and Communications (BigCom 2026)
summary: Scientific Fitness Coaching (SFC) is typically delivered by human professionals, making it costly and inaccessible to many. While recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) show considerable promise for more inclusive fitness coaching, directly deploying prevailing general-purpose LLMs in SFC reveals critical limitations. These models often lack sufficient domain-specific knowledge integration, leading to weak performance on complex SFC scenarios. In this paper, we introduce FitOne, a series of fitness LLMs (with 8B and 32B parameters) designed to improve reliability and domain specialization for SFC applications. Built upon the Qwen3 foundation models, FitOne is developed through a three-stage post-training pipeline consisting of continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, using large-scale, high-quality datasets derived from rigorous knowledge engineering. We conduct comprehensive evaluations of FitOne on professional fitness certification exams, including ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS, as well as general capabilities such as knowledge reasoning and instruction following. Experimental results show that, while retaining strong general capabilities, FitOne-8B/32B achieves average improvements of up to 10.09%/9.29% and 12.73%/7.01% on the ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS exams, respectively, compared with the Qwen3 base models. Furthermore, in-depth ablation studies confirm the necessity of each training stage, highlighting the pipeline's effectiveness in balancing domain expertise enhancement with general ability retention. We believe this research advances LLM systems toward more reliable fitness intelligence and will inspire future research on developing domain-specific LLMs.

AI.tldr: FitOne is a family of domain-specific LLMs (8B/32B) for scientific fitness coaching, built on Qwen3 via a three-stage post-training pipeline (continual pre-training, SFT, RL). It achieves significant gains on professional fitness exams (ACSM-EP, NSCA-CSCS) while retaining general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Traditional scientific fitness coaching relies on costly human professionals, limiting accessibility. General-purpose LLMs lack the domain-specific knowledge integration needed for reliable performance in complex SFC scenarios, motivating the development of a specialized fitness LLM.
AI.method: FitOne is built on the Qwen3 foundation model using a three-stage post-training pipeline: (1) continual pre-training, (2) supervised fine-tuning, and (3) reinforcement learning. All stages leverage large-scale, high-quality datasets constructed through rigorous knowledge engineering.
AI.result: FitOne-8B/32B achieves average improvements of up to 10.09%/9.29% on ACSM-EP and 12.73%/7.01% on NSCA-CSCS over Qwen3 base models, while retaining strong general capabilities. Ablation studies confirm each training stage is necessary for balancing domain expertise and general ability retention.
AI.conclusion: The three-stage post-training pipeline effectively yields reliable, domain-specialized fitness LLMs without catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities. This work advances LLM systems toward more reliable fitness intelligence and may inspire future domain-specific LLM development.

title: Conditional Co-Ablation: Recovering Self-Repair Backups in Transformer Circuits
summary: Mechanistic interpretability often relies on component-level interventions to discover how a model produces a behavior. This guides attribution, capability knockout, and model pruning downstream to operate by scoring each unit by the effect of ablation in isolation. Such first-order scoring is natural when component importance is additive, but becomes misleading when a transformer self-repairs: after a primary component is removed, a dormant backup can take over, muting the primary's measured effect while the backup itself appears irrelevant on the intact model. We recast this failure as a recovery task, conditional circuit completion, and introduce Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a label-free, output-grounded score that asks how much each remaining unit's ablation effect grows once a primary set has been removed. This conditional growth exposes the second-order interaction that single-unit scores discard. On the GPT-2-small IOI circuit, CoAx raises backup-head recovery from 0.33 to 0.91 ROC-AUC, outperforming all baselines, including self-repair-aware gradient scores (best 0.82); counterfactual patching verifies that the recovered heads causally carry the repair. The same label-free procedure transfers to induction across eight models. Beyond discovery, the recovered backups correct self-repair-masked attribution, identify the components required for capability knockout, and yield repair-aware structured pruning scaling from 124M to 7B. Component importance is therefore not merely an isolated-unit property: in robust circuits, the components that matter can become visible only under the interventions that make them necessary.

AI.tldr: Standard first-order ablation scoring fails when transformer models self-repair via dormant backup components. The authors introduce Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a second-order metric that measures how much a component's ablation effect grows after a primary set is removed, revealing hidden backups. CoAx substantially improves backup detection (0.33→0.91 ROC-AUC) on GPT-2-small's IOI circuit and generalizes across eight models, with downstream applications in attribution correction, capability knockout, and structured pruning.
AI.motivation: First-order ablation scores assume component importance is additive, but transformers exhibit self-repair: removing a primary component can activate dormant backup components that compensate. This mutes the primary's measured importance and keeps the backup invisible in the intact model. The authors argue that component importance is conditional—some units only become visibly important under interventions that remove their primary counterparts—necessitating a second-order scoring approach.
AI.method: The paper introduces Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a label-free, output-grounded score. Given a primary set of components, CoAx measures how much each remaining unit's ablation effect grows once that primary set is removed. This captures the second-order interaction: a unit is a backup if its ablation causes little harm alone but substantial harm after the primary is knocked out. The method requires no labels and uses only model outputs. Experiments span the GPT-2-small IOI circuit and induction heads across eight models (124M–7B).
AI.result: On the GPT-2-small IOI circuit, CoAx raises backup-head recovery from 0.33 to 0.91 ROC-AUC, outperforming all baselines including self-repair-aware gradient-based scores (best 0.82). Counterfactual patching confirms the recovered heads causally carry the repair. The method transfers to induction across eight models. Downstream, CoAx-identified backups correct self-repair-masked attribution, identify components essential for capability knockout, and enable repair-aware structured pruning that scales from 124M to 7B parameters.
AI.conclusion: Component importance is not an isolated-unit property; in robust circuits, the components that matter only become visible under interventions that make them necessary. CoAx operationalizes this insight as a conditional second-order score, providing a principled way to discover backup mechanisms, correct attribution, and improve pruning in transformer models.

title: Coding-agents can replicate scientific machine learning papers
summary: Scientific machine learning papers typically make computational claims, e.g., that the relative mean square error is less than 5% or that the 95% predictive credible interval covers the test data. A coding agent can be prompted to replicate those claims from paper materials alone, but the prompt does not by itself reliably preserve progress or check whether generated evidence supports the paper's claims. We introduce Paper-replication, a workflow that makes each selected paper claim a target with recorded evidence, and implement it as a coding-agent skill. The workflow makes the agent record those targets, reconstruct the paper's method, run computational experiments, link generated outputs to provenance and comparisons with the paper's claims, record where matched evidence appears in the replication report, and pass validation checks before completion. We evaluate Paper-replication on twelve independent runs across four scientific machine learning papers. All twelve workspaces pass the completion gate, and all 158 recorded targets are matched with report coverage. Even in this completed workspace state, repeated runs differ in how papers are divided into targets, in numerical fidelity to the source papers, in elapsed replication time, in the number of intermediate executions replaced before final evidence is accepted, and in the rules used to accept evidence. Paper-replication makes completion depend on workspace evidence and validation checks rather than on the agent's final message.

AI.tldr: Paper-replication is a coding-agent workflow that formalizes the replication of scientific ML paper claims by converting them into verifiable targets with recorded evidence, provenance tracking, and automated validation gates, ensuring completion depends on workspace evidence rather than agent outputs.
AI.motivation: Scientific machine learning papers make quantitative computational claims, but prompting a coding agent to replicate them does not reliably track progress or verify whether generated evidence actually supports those claims. There is a need for structured, accountable replication workflows.
AI.method: The Paper-replication workflow converts each selected paper claim into a target with recorded evidence. The agent reconstructs the paper's method, runs computational experiments, links outputs to provenance and claim comparisons, records where matched evidence appears in the replication report, and must pass validation checks before completion. The workflow is implemented as a coding-agent skill and evaluated across 12 independent runs on four scientific ML papers.
AI.result: All 12 workspaces passed the completion gate, and all 158 recorded targets were matched with report coverage. However, repeated runs exhibited variation in how papers were divided into targets, numerical fidelity to source papers, elapsed replication time, number of intermediate executions replaced before final evidence acceptance, and the rules used to accept evidence.
AI.conclusion: Paper-replication successfully shifts the completion criterion from the agent's final message to objective workspace evidence and validation checks, enabling reliable, auditable replication of scientific ML claims while revealing inherent variability across replication runs.

title: Hybrid quantum-classical neural network for sentiment analysis
summary: Quantum machine learning has recently emerged as a promising paradigm that leverages the expressive power of quantum circuits to address complex learning tasks. In this work, we investigate the applicability of hybrid quantum-classical neural networks to sentiment analysis, a central problem in natural language processing. We focus on a dataset of tweets related to COVID-19, where the textual content is vectorized using TF-IDF and fed into both classical feedforward networks and hybrid architectures incorporating parameterized quantum circuits. Our results show that hybrid models can achieve accuracy comparable to the classical baseline, while exhibiting distinct learning dynamics, especially in terms of validation loss and accuracy, that suggest a richer representational capacity. Moreover, when applying transfer learning to an SMS spam classification task, the hybrid models consistently outperform the classical counterpart, achieving an accuracy increase of 15 percentage points (from 66% to 81%) on the spam class, demonstrating enhanced generalization. These findings highlight the feasibility of employing QML for natural language processing and point toward the potential advantages of hybrid models as quantum hardware continues to advance.

AI.tldr: Hybrid quantum-classical neural networks applied to sentiment analysis achieve accuracy comparable to classical models on COVID-19 tweets, while significantly outperforming them in transfer learning on SMS spam classification (81% vs 66%), suggesting richer representational capacity and better generalization.
AI.motivation: To explore whether hybrid quantum-classical neural networks can offer practical advantages over purely classical models for natural language processing tasks, specifically sentiment analysis and transfer learning, leveraging the expressive power of parameterized quantum circuits.
AI.method: TF-IDF vectorization of COVID-19 tweet text fed into both classical feedforward networks and hybrid architectures with parameterized quantum circuits. Models compared on sentiment analysis accuracy and validation loss/accuracy dynamics. Transfer learning evaluated by applying trained models to an SMS spam classification task.
AI.result: Hybrid models matched classical baseline accuracy on sentiment analysis with distinct learning dynamics indicating richer representational capacity. In transfer learning (SMS spam), hybrid models outperformed classical by 15 percentage points (81% vs 66% accuracy on the spam class), demonstrating superior generalization.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid quantum-classical models are feasible for NLP tasks and show promise for superior generalization in transfer learning settings, with potential advantages expected to grow as quantum hardware matures.

title: A$^{2}$utoLPBench: An Auto-Generated, Agent-Friendly LP Benchmark via Inverse-KKT Construction
summary: Most LP-from-text benchmarks are static datasets of word problems written and labeled by hand. Once such a dataset is released, its size is fixed, its difficulty is fixed, and every problem can leak into the training data of future LLMs. We present \textbf{A$^{2}$utoLPBench}, a benchmark for testing LLM-driven agents on linear programming problems written in plain text. We first pick a feasible point and dual, then write down a problem for which that point is optimal and the objective value is known. The answer is known by construction, with no solver call and no human annotator. The evaluation environment bundles a reference solver-critic baseline and a Docker image whose usage instructions are written for an LLM-driven agent to read. With these in place, any agent can run the benchmark and get a calibrated score with one command. Because the benchmark is a generator rather than a fixed dataset, it has properties no fixed dataset can match: an unlimited supply of fresh problems, a difficulty knob set by $(n,m)$, ground-truth answers correct by construction, low LLM-side cost per problem relative to human authoring, repeatable scores across independent batches, and resistance to training-data leakage when fresh post-cutoff seed ranges are used.

AI.tldr: A²utoLPBench is a generative benchmark for testing LLM agents on linear programming problems. Instead of a static dataset, it constructs problems from a known feasible point and dual, ensuring ground-truth answers by construction. This provides unlimited fresh problems, controllable difficulty via (n,m), resistance to data leakage, and repeatable scoring — all without human annotation or solver calls.
AI.motivation: Static LP-from-text benchmarks have fixed size, fixed difficulty, and risk training-data leakage into future LLMs. Human authoring is costly and doesn't scale. The authors aim to create a benchmark generator that is unlimited, difficulty-tunable, leakage-resistant, and free of human annotation bottlenecks.
AI.method: The benchmark works by reverse-engineering LP problems: first pick a feasible point and a dual solution, then synthesize a linear programming problem for which that point is provably optimal with a known objective value. No solver is needed to verify answers. The evaluation environment includes a reference solver-critic baseline and a Docker image with usage instructions tailored for LLM-driven agents. Difficulty is controlled by the number of variables (n) and constraints (m).
AI.result: The benchmark achieves: (1) unlimited supply of fresh problems, (2) difficulty controlled by (n,m), (3) ground-truth answers correct by construction, (4) low cost per problem vs. human authoring, (5) repeatable scores across independent batches, and (6) resistance to training-data leakage when using post-cutoff seed ranges.
AI.conclusion: A²utoLPBench demonstrates that generative benchmarks — where answers are known by construction rather than by human labeling or solver calls — can overcome fundamental limitations of static datasets, offering a scalable, leakage-resistant evaluation paradigm for LLM-driven agents on optimization tasks.

title: A More Accurate Algorithm Comparison through A/B Testing using Offline Evaluation Methods
summary: A/B testing is the gold standard for selecting the better algorithm in online services. While offline evaluation has attracted attention as a safer alternative due to the high experimental costs and the potential risk of degrading user experience and revenue in A/B testing, it is widely recognized that the estimation accuracy of offline evaluation is substantially lower. As a result, final selection decisions are typically made through A/B testing. Contrary to this conventional view, we reveal a counterintuitive phenomenon in which A/B testing can produce a higher algorithm selection error rate than offline evaluation. This occurs because the sample mean estimator used in A/B testing does not induce positive correlation, which is crucial for reducing critical selection errors, namely underestimating the truly superior algorithm and overestimating the truly inferior one. In contrast, offline evaluation methods unintentionally generate this beneficial correlation by relying on shared offline data when estimating and comparing the performance of multiple algorithms. Building on this insight, we propose an estimator that intentionally induces positive correlation to improve algorithm selection in A/B testing. The key idea is to introduce a hypothetical middle algorithm and to estimate the performance difference between algorithms A, M, and B in a stepwise manner using shared data at each step. This approach enables the application of offline evaluation techniques in each step, thereby inducing positive correlation and reducing critical selection errors. Furthermore, we derive the optimal middle algorithm regarding the resulting variance and analyze its advantages over existing methods through bias-variance analysis. Experiments on real-world data demonstrate that our estimator achieves the same selection error rate as existing approaches while using only one half of the A/B testing data.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that A/B testing can paradoxically yield higher algorithm selection error than offline evaluation due to lack of positive correlation in the sample mean estimator. The authors propose a novel estimator using a stepwise comparison via a hypothetical "middle" algorithm to intentionally induce positive correlation, reducing selection errors while requiring only half the A/B testing data.
AI.motivation: Conventional wisdom holds that A/B testing is superior to offline evaluation for algorithm selection, despite offline evaluation being safer and cheaper. The authors challenge this view by identifying a structural flaw in A/B testing: its sample mean estimator fails to induce positive correlation between performance estimates of competing algorithms, making it prone to critical selection errors (underestimating superior algorithms and overestimating inferior ones).
AI.method: The authors propose an A/B testing estimator that introduces a hypothetical "middle" algorithm M and estimates performance differences stepwise (A vs. M, M vs. B) using shared data at each step. This stepwise structure enables application of offline evaluation techniques that induce positive correlation. They also derive the optimal middle algorithm configuration to minimize variance and conduct bias-variance analysis comparing against existing methods.
AI.result: The counterintuitive finding is that A/B testing can underperform offline evaluation in algorithm selection accuracy due to the absence of positive correlation. The proposed stepwise estimator with the optimal middle algorithm achieves the same selection error rate as conventional A/B testing while requiring only 50% of the data. Real-world data experiments validate these findings.
AI.conclusion: Positive correlation in performance estimation is critical for reducing algorithm selection errors. The proposed estimator bridges the gap between offline evaluation's safety/efficiency and A/B testing's reliability by intentionally engineering beneficial correlation structures within the A/B testing framework, substantially reducing data requirements without sacrificing decision accuracy.

title: A rubric-based controlled comparison of frontier language models on expert-authored clinical reasoning tasks
summary: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are increasingly saturated, and recent rubric-based evaluations such as HealthBench have shown that open-ended clinical performance is far from solved - its "Hard" subset top score remains 32%. We present a small, deliberately difficult evaluation dataset of five clinician-authored clinical scenarios spanning four specialties (anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, and obstetrics), each accompanied by an atomic, weighted, MECE rubric (25-62 criteria per task; 184 criteria total) authored from a clinician-drafted golden answer. We evaluate three frontier models: GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Mean rubric pass rates were 0.47 (Claude), 0.39 (GPT), and 0.37 (Gemini). The central finding is an inversion of clinical priority: the highest-weighted (weight-5, critical) criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, while low-stakes weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%. 56 of 108 critical (weight-5) criteria (52%) were satisfied by no model. Three LLM autoraters reproduced expert met/not-met labels on 92.8-94.7% of 552 graded criteria. We position this as a methods-and-preliminary-findings contribution: the five tasks demonstrate a scalable, defensible pipeline ready to develop into a large-scale benchmark.

AI.tldr: A deliberately difficult, clinician-authored evaluation dataset of five open-ended medical scenarios (184 MECE rubric criteria) reveals that frontier LLMs (GPT, Claude, Gemini) achieve only 37-47% rubric pass rates, with a critical inversion: highest-weighted criteria pass far less often (32-42%) than low-stakes criteria (80-90%), and 52% of critical criteria were satisfied by no model. LLM autoraters show >92% agreement with expert labeling.
AI.motivation: Medical benchmarks are increasingly saturated, and open-ended clinical reasoning remains poorly measured. The authors aim to create a deliberately difficult, rubric-based evaluation to expose LLMs' clinical reasoning failures, particularly on high-stakes criteria.
AI.method: Five clinician-authored clinical scenarios across four specialties (anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, obstetrics), each with an atomic, weighted, MECE rubric (25-62 criteria per task; 184 total). Weights range from 1 (low-stakes) to 5 (critical). Three frontier models evaluated against gold-standard answers. Three LLM autoraters validated against expert labels on 552 graded criteria.
AI.result: Mean rubric pass rates: Claude 0.47, GPT 0.39, Gemini 0.37. Critical finding: weight-5 (critical) criteria passed at 32.4-41.7%, while weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%. 56 of 108 critical criteria (52%) were unmet by any model. LLM autoraters achieved 92.8-94.7% agreement with expert labels.
AI.conclusion: Current frontier models exhibit an inversion of clinical priorities — failing most on the highest-stakes criteria while succeeding on trivial ones — revealing a fundamental misalignment in clinical reasoning. The five-task pipeline is positioned as a scalable, defensible foundation for a full-scale benchmark.

title: Probabilistic Low-Voltage Peak Load Forecasting with Time Series Foundation Models Evaluated on Application-Oriented Metrics
comment: A poster abstract of this publication will be available at the 15th DACH+ Conference on Energy Informatics (2026 in Linz, Austria)
summary: Low-voltage load forecasting is an important component in current and future energy systems with a high degree of electrification and decentralized generation. However, current forecasting methods require significant manual effort, often lack uncertainty estimation and proper peak prediction, and they are often not adequately evaluated in terms of grid requirements. In the present study, we provide an extensive evaluation of short-term net load forecasts of 200 real-world low-voltage feeders with a focus on the rapidly evolving time series foundation models. Our study compares Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2 and TabPFN-TS to six baseline models and demonstrates superior performance, in particular for Chronos-2. An ablation study, in which weather covariates are omitted, shows that time series foundation models adapt to increased uncertainty, despite the importance of weather information. A novel application-oriented metric links the model's forecasting capabilities in peak prediction to the trade-off in grid asset planning and operation between cost reduction and minimizing the risk of failure.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates time series foundation models (Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TabPFN-TS) against six baselines for short-term net load forecasting on 200 real-world low-voltage feeders, finding Chronos-2 superior. It introduces a novel application-oriented metric linking peak prediction quality to grid asset planning trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Current low-voltage load forecasting methods demand substantial manual effort, rarely provide uncertainty estimation, fail at peak prediction, and lack evaluation against real grid operational requirements — gaps that become critical as electrification and decentralized generation increase.
AI.method: Extensive empirical evaluation of short-term net load forecasts across 200 real-world low-voltage feeders. Three time series foundation models (Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TabPFN-TS) are benchmarked against six baseline models. An ablation study removes weather covariates to test model robustness to increased uncertainty. A novel application-oriented metric is proposed that quantifies the trade-off between cost reduction and failure risk in grid asset planning and operation.
AI.result: Time series foundation models, particularly Chronos-2, demonstrate superior forecasting performance over all baselines. The ablation study reveals that foundation models adapt better to increased uncertainty when weather covariates are omitted, despite weather information being important. The proposed metric effectively links peak prediction accuracy to the cost-risk trade-off in grid planning.
AI.conclusion: Time series foundation models — especially Chronos-2 — offer a compelling, low-manual-effort solution for low-voltage net load forecasting, with strong peak prediction and inherent uncertainty handling. The application-oriented metric provides a practical bridge between forecast quality and real-world grid asset decision-making.

title: UA-ChatDev: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Reliable Software Development
summary: Software development is a complex task that demands cooperation among agents with diverse roles. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled autonomous multi-agent software development frameworks that leverage role-based collaboration to automate requirements analysis, coding, testing, and refinement. However, existing approaches typically assume that intermediate agent outputs are equally reliable, leaving them vulnerable to hallucination propagation, where incorrect decisions generated in early development phases are transferred to downstream agents and negatively impact final software quality. To address this challenge, we propose UA-ChatDev, an uncertainty-aware multi-agent software development framework that integrates uncertainty quantification into agent interactions. It introduces a lightweight uncertainty estimation mechanism based on token-level log probabilities to assess the confidence of agent responses and employs phase-aware threshold calibration to selectively trigger retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels. Extensive experiments on the SRDD benchmark demonstrate that UA-ChatDev consistently outperforms existing single-agent and multi-agent software development frameworks across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality metrics. Further ablation studies and communication analyses verify that uncertainty-aware interactions enhance code execution reliability.

AI.tldr: UA-ChatDev introduces uncertainty quantification into multi-agent software development, using token-level log probabilities to detect unreliable agent outputs and trigger verification, outperforming existing frameworks on the SRDD benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent software development frameworks treat all intermediate agent outputs as equally reliable, making them susceptible to hallucination propagation—where erroneous decisions from early phases cascade through downstream agents and degrade final software quality.
AI.method: UA-ChatDev integrates uncertainty quantification into agent interactions via: (1) a lightweight uncertainty estimation mechanism based on token-level log probabilities to assess agent response confidence, and (2) phase-aware threshold calibration that selectively triggers retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels.
AI.result: On the SRDD benchmark, UA-ChatDev consistently outperforms both single-agent and multi-agent baselines across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality metrics. Ablation studies and communication analyses confirm that uncertainty-aware interactions improve code execution reliability.
AI.conclusion: Integrating uncertainty awareness into multi-agent software development frameworks effectively mitigates hallucination propagation, leading to more reliable code generation and higher-quality software outputs.

title: Do Newer Lightweight CNNs Perform Better Under Resource Constraints? A Controlled Multigenerational Study of Architecture, Initialization, Training Budget, and Efficiency
summary: Newer lightweight convolutional neural networks are often presented as improving predictive performance and deployment efficiency, but such claims require controlled evaluation. This study compares nine lightweight CNN model packages across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under a shared downstream protocol. We report top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on an NVIDIA L4 and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA allocated tensor memory, and point estimate Pareto frontiers. EfficientNetV2-S achieves the highest observed top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 at 97.57% and 86.98%, while RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet at 79.87%. EfficientNet-B0 remains within 0.22, 0.85, and 1.79 percentage points of the best result on the three datasets while using approximately 79% fewer parameters and 86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S. It also appears on every evaluated accuracy and resource Pareto frontier, making it the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option. MobileNetV3-Small has the lowest GMAC count, is the fastest model under both CPU thread settings, and records higher observed accuracy than MobileNetV4-Conv-S on all three datasets. Under random initialization, it leads MobileNetV4-Conv-S by 2.55, 1.76, and 0.99 points, with paired test-set intervals excluding zero for the fixed trained models. EfficientNet-B0 remains 3.29, 10.10, and 17.54 points below its pretrained counterpart after 100 epochs of scratch training, despite requiring about five times the recorded training time. SqueezeNet1.1 has the fewest parameters and lowest peak CUDA allocation, but substantially weaker accuracy. Latency rankings differ sharply between the L4 and CPU environments, showing that GMACs alone do not predict measured inference performance. Overall, newer designs provide selective rather than universal gains

AI.tldr: A controlled comparison of nine lightweight CNN architectures across three image classification benchmarks reveals that newer designs offer selective rather than universal improvements. EfficientNetV2-S achieves top accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, RepViT-M1.0 leads on Tiny ImageNet, while EfficientNet-B0 emerges as the most consistently Pareto-optimal intermediate-budget choice. Latency rankings diverge sharply between GPU and CPU, and GMACs alone poorly predict measured inference speed.
AI.motivation: Newer lightweight CNNs are frequently claimed to improve both predictive performance and deployment efficiency, but such claims lack rigorous controlled evaluation under a shared protocol. The authors aim to provide a systematic, multi-metric comparison to determine whether gains are universal or selective.
AI.method: Nine lightweight CNN model packages (including EfficientNet variants, MobileNet variants, RepViT, and SqueezeNet) are evaluated on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under a unified downstream protocol. Metrics include top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on NVIDIA L4 GPU and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA allocated tensor memory, and point-estimate Pareto frontiers. Both pretrained and randomly initialized (scratch) training settings are examined.
AI.result: EfficientNetV2-S achieves highest top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 (97.57%) and CIFAR-100 (86.98%); RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet (79.87%). EfficientNet-B0 trails the best by only 0.22–1.79 points while using ~79% fewer parameters and ~86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S, appearing on every accuracy–resource Pareto frontier. MobileNetV3-Small has the lowest GMACs, is fastest on CPU, and outperforms MobileNetV4-Conv-S across all datasets. Scratch-trained EfficientNet-B0 lags its pretrained counterpart by 3.29–17.54 points. SqueezeNet1.1 uses fewest parameters and lowest CUDA memory but has weakest accuracy. Latency rankings differ sharply between L4 GPU and CPU, demonstrating GMACs do not reliably predict inference performance.
AI.conclusion: Newer lightweight CNN designs provide selective rather than universal gains across accuracy and efficiency metrics. EfficientNet-B0 offers the best balanced trade-off for intermediate budgets. Practitioners should not rely on GMACs alone for latency prediction and should benchmark on target deployment hardware.

title: Criticality-Based Guard Rail Validation for AI Agent Decisions in Autonomous Telecom Networks
summary: The evolution toward fully autonomous telecommunications networks (Autonomous Network Levels 4-5) requires AI/ML agents to make real-time network decisions without human intervention. However, no standardized runtime mechanism exists to intercept and validate individual inference outputs before they trigger live network state changes, creating risks of erroneous autonomous decisions. This paper proposes the Guard Rail Validation (GRV) framework, a standardizable runtime architecture for intercepting and validating AI-driven decisions before execution. The framework evaluates decisions across multiple weighted dimensions -- including action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, and temporal behavioural patterns -- to determine a criticality level. Based on this level, graduated validation mechanisms are applied: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. The framework additionally provides cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging for regulatory compliance (e.g., EU AI Act Article 14). We present the architecture, algorithmic procedures, O-RAN deployment model, and evaluate threat coverage against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications.

AI.tldr: Proposes GRV, a runtime framework to intercept and validate AI/ML decisions in autonomous telecom networks before execution, using multi-dimensional criticality scoring and graduated validation mechanisms, with O-RAN deployment and threat coverage analysis.
AI.motivation: Autonomous Networks (Levels 4–5) require AI/ML agents to make real-time decisions without human oversight, yet no standardized runtime mechanism exists to validate individual inference outputs before they alter live network state, posing risks of erroneous autonomous actions.
AI.method: The GRV framework intercepts AI-driven decisions at runtime and evaluates them across weighted dimensions (action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, temporal behavioural patterns) to compute a criticality level. Graduated validation is then applied: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. It also features cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging for regulatory compliance (e.g., EU AI Act Article 14).
AI.result: The paper presents the architecture, algorithmic procedures, and an O-RAN deployment model. It evaluates threat coverage against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications, demonstrating the framework's ability to mitigate risks from erroneous autonomous decisions.
AI.conclusion: The GRV framework offers a practical, standardizable approach to safeguarding autonomous network operations, enabling safe progression toward fully autonomous networks while meeting emerging regulatory requirements.

title: Liquid Latent State Dynamics for Interpretable Turbofan Degradation Modeling
summary: Multivariate time-series models for prognostics are often evaluated by point prediction accuracy, yet their internal states rarely expose a coherent degradation process. We study liquid neural networks as latent dynamics models for aircraft engine health monitoring on the C-MAPSS benchmark.
